item.title: [SCMP] Indonesian families of Lion Air crash victims suffer again, ‘predatory’ lawyer evades jail
item.description:
For Indonesian families who lost loved ones in the 2018 Lion Air crash that killed 189 people, the latest development in the US courts has deepened their pain that justice remains out of reach.

Keith Griffin, a Californian lawyer who worked with disgraced Hollywood celebrity lawyer Tom Girardi in compensation suits related to the crash, was sentenced by a federal court in Chicago last week to one day in prison with credit for time served, meaning he avoided any further time behind bars.

Girardi’s firm represented some of the Lion Air victims’ families in claims against Boeing, which agreed to pay undisclosed compensation after the crash of Lion Air flight JT610, one of two fatal disasters involving the US firm’s 737 Max planes.
item.content:encoded:
For Indonesian families who lost loved ones in the 2018 Lion Air crash that killed 189 people, the latest development in the US courts has deepened their pain that justice remains out of reach.

Keith Griffin, a Californian lawyer who worked with disgraced Hollywood celebrity lawyer Tom Girardi in compensation suits related to the crash, was sentenced by a federal court in Chicago last week to one day in prison with credit for time served, meaning he avoided any further time behind bars.

Girardi’s firm represented some of the Lion Air victims’ families in claims against Boeing, which agreed to pay undisclosed compensation after the crash of Lion Air flight JT610, one of two fatal disasters involving the US firm’s 737 Max planes.

Griffin had pleaded guilty to criminal contempt of court after admitting that he knew Girardi had failed to distribute settlement funds to families of the Lion Air victims, despite a court order requiring the money to be paid.

He was also sentenced to two years of supervised release, under which he must comply with conditions set by the court and report to probation officials.

His boss Girardi was convicted of illegally pocketing more than US$2 million in money meant for the victims’ families and US$15 million in other compensation and personal injury cases. Last year, he was sentenced to over seven years in prison. He has also declared bankruptcy and was disbarred.

For families who had already endured years of litigation after the fatal crash, the sentence marked another blow in their effort to hold to account the lawyers entrusted with the compensation.

Bias Ramadhan, whose mother Hasna was on the doomed Lion Air flight, told This Week in Asia that he was “disappointed” with the verdict against Griffin.

“But I had not been getting my hopes up, considering how long and complicated the legal process has been,” said Ramadhan, who attended Girardi’s sentencing in 2024.

Ramadhan said he had wanted to be in court to see Griffin sentenced but had not been able to travel to the US for the hearing.

“Unfortunately, the majority of Girardi-Keese’s clients will never receive the settlement money they are owed,” he said, referring to the name of Girardi’s law firm.

Prosecutors had sought a three-month jail sentence for Griffin after David Lira, another Girardi-Keese lawyer, received a four-month term as part of the same case last year.

In court, Griffin argued that he was “the least culpable participant in this offence”.

Anton Sahadi, whose wife lost her 24-year-old cousins, Riyan Aryandi and Ravi Andrian, in the crash, said Girardi-Keese had originally reached out to his family with an offer to act on their behalf when suing Boeing for compensation.

However, Sahadi said that he had felt uncomfortable with the firm and decided to seek legal representation elsewhere.

Following the news of Griffin’s sentencing, Sahadi said: “The court should not have shown leniency simply because Griffin claimed to have been ‘pressured by his superiors’. Being aware that the wrongdoing persisted while remaining silent makes Griffin complicit,” he said.

“The families of the plane crash victims were in a highly vulnerable position, both emotionally and financially. Withholding their financial entitlements further exploited the victims’ powerlessness.”

Lion Air flight JT610 was travelling from Jakarta to the Bangka-Belitung islands in October 2018 when it plunged into the Java Sea shortly after take-off, killing everyone on board.

Following the crash, Boeing initially insisted that its planes were safe and claimed that pilot error had been a factor.

In March 2019, Ethiopian Airlines Flight 302, which was also flying with the then-new Boeing 737 Max aircraft, crashed shortly after taking off from Addis Ababa, killing all 157 people on board.

An investigation later found that the flight manoeuvring systems on the two planes malfunctioned after take-off. In the case of the Lion Air crash, the pilots were not informed about the new system and had not been trained on its use.

Apart from the undisclosed compensation to the families, Boeing was also slapped with a US$200 million fine by the United States Securities and Exchange Commission after it found that the company misled investors about the safety of its planes.

The case against Girardi, Griffin and Lira only came to light when their firm engaged Chicago-based law firm Edelson to sue Boeing.

After a settlement deal was secured from Boeing, Edelson received word from the families in Indonesia that they had not received the money from Girardi-Keese.

Ramadhan and four other families were finally awarded a total of US$2 million in 2022 when Edelson compensated them and alerted the authorities, which led to dozens of victims in other cases filing complaints against Girardi-Keese about their missing funds.

Speaking about the latest verdict, a US lawyer involved in the Lion Air litigation, who requested anonymity because of his role, told This Week in Asia that Griffin had received a low sentence because of the sentences handed down to others involved in the case.

As Lira was only sentenced to four months in prison, it was determined that Griffin was less culpable in comparison and that he did not deserve to be in prison, the lawyer continued. The one-day sentence allowed the judge to impose a term of supervised release, the lawyer added.

“Federal judges in the United States have a great deal of autonomy with respect to sentencing. There are factors they are required to consider and a guideline sentencing range, but they get to decide which factors are more or less important.”

Alvin Lie, the head of the Indonesian Air Transportation Service User Association who assisted the affected families in 2018, said the Girardi debacle and Griffin’s sentencing should be viewed as separate from the wider issues surrounding the Lion Air crash. The cases against the two men were purely about “theft and embezzlement”, he added.

“I am disappointed as these kinds of predatory lawyers were quite active in contacting the families of the victims of the Lion Air crash at the time. They would come to the victims and offer that they would fight for compensation on a no-win, no-fee basis,” Lie said.

“I have the greatest sympathy for the families who became victims twice over, once when the crash happened and they lost their loved ones, and again when their right to compensation was violated by these predatory lawyers.”

item.title: [SCMP] UN atrocity report adds friction to Myanmar junta’s diplomatic push for legitimacy
item.description:
A UN investigative report accusing Myanmar’s military of carrying out a “sustained campaign of deliberate attacks on civilians” has muddied Min Aung Hlaing’s push for regional acceptance – but analysts say it is unlikely to derail his efforts to win recognition for his post-election government.

The report by the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), a body appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, documents a year-long investigation into alleged “war crimes and crimes against humanity” committed by Myanmar’s military and its linked militias, as well as by armed opposition groups.

It said the military campaign included air strikes on homes, schools and camps for displaced people, alongside arbitrary detention, torture and sexual violence.
item.content:encoded:
A UN investigative report accusing Myanmar’s military of carrying out a “sustained campaign of deliberate attacks on civilians” has muddied Min Aung Hlaing’s push for regional acceptance – but analysts say it is unlikely to derail his efforts to win recognition for his post-election government.

The report by the Independent Investigative Mechanism for Myanmar (IIMM), a body appointed by the UN Human Rights Council, documents a year-long investigation into alleged “war crimes and crimes against humanity” committed by Myanmar’s military and its linked militias, as well as by armed opposition groups.

It said the military campaign included air strikes on homes, schools and camps for displaced people, alongside arbitrary detention, torture and sexual violence.

Investigators said the military had increased its use of low-cost aircraft, such as motorised paragliders and gyrocopters, in strikes against anti-government groups. “Double-tap” aerial attacks, in which a second strike follows the first, harming first responders, those helping the wounded and fleeing residents, are also on the rise.

According to the report, there was an escalation of abuses in December and January, around the time the country was conducting junta-led elections that saw Min Aung Hlaing elected as president and its military-backed party winning seats in the absence of any viable opposition.

Min Aung Hlaing, now a retired general, led the 2021 coup that overthrew Myanmar’s elected leader Aung San Suu Kyi, who has remained under military custody.

The military government did not immediately respond to the UN report or separate claims by the Arakan Army, a major ethnic armed group in Rakhine state, alleging that 20 civilians had been killed in military-led strikes this month. It has previously said it attacks only legitimate military targets and has accused resistance forces of terrorism.

Legitimacy push

The report comes amid a series of efforts by Min Aung Hlaing to seek legitimacy for his government, years after facing sanctions from the West and a ban from Asean meetings until the country complies with the bloc’s five-point consensus.

The president visited two Association of Southeast Asian Nations members recently: Thailand last week and Laos in July. He has previously visited India and China.

But he has refused to deal with Asean as a whole – rejecting the five-point consensus this month as well as a request for its special envoy, Philippine Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, to meet Suu Kyi.

“Min Aung Hlaing and his military administration are clearly not willing to engage Asean’s terms,” said Mai Van Tran, an assistant professor at the Department of Political Science and faculty associate with the Centre for Southeast Asian Studies at Northern Illinois University.

“Further support for the Min Aung Hlaing-led administration is unlikely to benefit these Asean states and might even facilitate humanitarian consequences that go against these countries’ values.”

But while the report might cloud the junta government’s optics, it was unlikely to affect its president’s push for legitimacy, other analysts say.

“It does not derail Min Aung Hlaing’s plans; however, it does puncture the narrative,” said Dipannita Maria Bagh, chief editor at Spring University Myanmar’s Institute of Human Rights and Democratic Governance.

One report could not stop the momentum, said Joanne Lin, a senior fellow at the ISEAS-Yusof Ishak Institute. “Countries that were already prepared to engage Myanmar, especially immediate neighbours with border, trade and security concerns, are unlikely to reverse course just because of this IIMM’s report.”

Min Aung Hlaing’s political objective “is likely to keep separating the external legitimacy track from the accountability track”, she said. “He might continue seeking meetings, photo opportunities, business forums and security cooperation with countries willing to engage him, while presenting Myanmar as a government dealing with internal conflict and restoring stability.”

Countries looking to re-engage Myanmar are likely looking at pragmatic considerations.

“Thailand’s priorities, for example, have been to deal with practical problems such as border security, transnational crime, online scams, drugs and humanitarian issues,” Lim said. “The report is unlikely to change neighbouring countries’ priorities but might make them more cautious about presenting engagements as normal diplomacy.”

Countries willing to engage bilaterally, such as Thailand, had “shown they will compartmentalise the atrocity documentation from the diplomacy”, Bagh said. “But it raises the cost of that compartmentalisation.”

Awkward position

The report could, however, reinforce the perception that Myanmar is not ready for bigger overtures.

“The rejection of the special envoy and [consensus] in general will complicate the case of recalibrating ties with Myanmar,” Lin said. “For more cautious Asean members, the report could reinforce the argument that fuller re-engagement should remain conditional.”

Bagh said that Myanmar’s rejection of Asean oversight mechanisms was the latest among multiple methods of controlling the narrative and painting a picture of stability.

“The junta is likely to emphasise the election and the formation of a post-election government to argue that Myanmar has entered a new political phase,” Lin said.

Thailand’s re-engagement with Myanmar would put it in an awkward position with the bloc but it had little option as it was directly affected by concerns such as refugee flows, migrant labour, border trade, online scam centres, drugs, haze, pollution and security conditions along the joint border, Lin said.

“From Bangkok’s perspective, some form of working relationship with Naypyidaw is necessary, regardless of Asean’s broader political discomfort,” she said. “The risk is that Myanmar may read Thailand’s position as evidence that it can regain regional acceptance through bilateral channels without making sufficient concessions on violence reduction.”

Thailand’s own foreign minister had to publicly insist the country was not abandoning the five-point consensus, “right as Naypyidaw was rejecting the bloc’s envoy and Myanmar’s parliament was calling the peace plan interference”, Bagh said.

“That’s a junta showing Asean that engagement doesn’t buy compliance. For Asean states more cautious about Myanmar, the lack of compliance from Naypyidaw and the lack of need for an envoy give them a clean, evidence-based argument against full re-engagement. It doesn’t stop the diplomacy, but it makes the case for it much harder to make in public.”

item.title: [SCMP] China urged to avoid ‘us or them’ split with US over AI governance
item.description:
China should try to make sure that its new international artificial intelligence body is not seen as “naturally opposed” to the United States and its allies in case it puts off prospective members, analysts have warned.

They said the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico) was not designed as an alternative to the US Pax Silica partnership, which was established last December with the aim of reducing “coercive dependencies”.

Waico was established at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai last month, with an initial 29 members, mainly from the Global South. It has since gained another nine members.
item.content:encoded:
China should try to make sure that its new international artificial intelligence body is not seen as “naturally opposed” to the United States and its allies in case it puts off prospective members, analysts have warned.

They said the World Artificial Intelligence Cooperation Organisation (Waico) was not designed as an alternative to the US Pax Silica partnership, which was established last December with the aim of reducing “coercive dependencies”.

Waico was established at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference in Shanghai last month, with an initial 29 members, mainly from the Global South. It has since gained another nine members.

Although China has repeatedly insisted that Waico was designed to advance “AI for good and for all”, it came under intense international scrutiny amid claims it was a strategic move by Beijing to rally friendly capitals against Washington in the race for global AI leadership.

Pax Silica, which has 24 members and core objectives that include building “supply chain security”, is widely perceived as being, at least in part, an effort to build a tech bloc that is walled off from China.

The emergence of the two blocs has also raised concerns that the global AI landscape will become polarised between two rival camps.

But Sun Chenghao, a senior fellow of the Centre for International Security and Strategy at Tsinghua University, said the two organisations were focused on different areas and were “not naturally opposed”.

But he said the “competitive” dynamic between the two frameworks could become increasingly prominent as AI governance, industrial policy and national security became intertwined, warning this could prompt the US-led bloc to impose “external constraints” on Waico members.

Sun added: “Whether Waico can build influence will ultimately depend on whether it can offer open cooperation, capacity building and tangible opportunities for development, rather than simply engaging in bloc-based confrontation with US mechanisms.”

Huang Ping, assistant dean of the Chinese University of Hong Kong (Shenzhen)’s school of public policy, said the short-term relationship between the two blocs appeared competitive, but “from China’s perspective, what we have always wanted is not a bloc to counter Pax Silica but an inclusive international AI organisation under the UN system”.

He added: “As long as the US does not exclude us, we have always been willing to welcome the US.”

At present, only Kazakhstan is a member of both Waico and Pax Silica, which suggested some countries do have strategic concerns, Sun said. But he added that “what warrants greater attention is the caution of European countries”.

The European Commission formally signed the Pax Silica initiative in June on behalf of the 27 EU member states.

Italy also sent an official representative to the AI summit in Shanghai last month but did not join Waico. Instead, it signed up to Pax Silica two weeks later.

Sun said it highlighted how US allies were constrained by “alliance relationships, technology supply chains and domestic politics”, adding that the greatest risk to Waico’s future expansion lay in it being labelled as a “China bloc” by the outside world.

“Once this impression takes hold, many middle countries will worry that joining [Waico] would entail geopolitical costs, even if they agree with the development orientation,” Sun said.

Huang, who is also a deputy director of the Shenzhen-based think tank Institute of International Affairs, Qianhai, said Waico might be little more than a “circle of friends” at present but bringing in the next Pax Silica member could be the key to turning it into a genuine international organisation.

He argued that China could minimise the political cost of joining Waico by not setting any exclusionary clauses to ensure countries do not have to pick sides and invite Pax Silica members to participate as observers.

“The bar should be low enough [to make] joining Waico become something countries do not need to explain to the US,” he said.

Huang also said that while Waico’s formation was driven by state diplomacy, concrete action should be left to businesses, adding: “Governments set up the stage, enterprises put in the show.”

He said: “Once it is perceived externally as state behaviour rather than market action, the cost of participation for middle countries and Pax Silica members will spike immediately.”

He said Waico should let open-source, cost-effective AI models and products “speak for themselves” and draw in more members, including Pax Silica members.

While the White House, Silicon Valley and Wall Street are debating whether Chinese open-source models should be banned, Huang said China should allow US firms such as Nvidia and Tesla to share in the dividends from its AI development to “break down prejudices”.

Last month, Huang wrote on social media that Waico could avoid being positioned as an “anti-Pax Silica” camp by following the example of the Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, whose 57 founding members included many US allies.

Some critics have argued that Waico’s influence could be very limited due to the lack of technologically advanced countries or Group of 7 members.

But Sun argued that signing up more Pax Silica members would not be the key to success because changing the bloc’s open and development-oriented approach to attract Western countries could undermine its distinct features.

Sun argued Waico’s membership was more inclusive than that of many “values-based clubs”.

“The challenge is that the members’ needs are highly diverse,” he said.

“If the agenda is too broad, it can easily result in an organisation with many members but few projects.

“At the current stage, the most important thing for Waico is not rapid expansion but proving that it can deliver.”

Sun said Waico could prioritise building AI capacity for the Global South, including computing support, talent training, open-source models and public data platforms.

He also suggested it should build a cross-border AI safety testing network and cooperate on evaluating models, incident reporting and safety standards.

He further proposed developing pilot projects in areas such as healthcare, agriculture, education and climate and disaster warnings.

“If Waico can show members that joining genuinely brings access to computing power, talent, technology, governance experience and concrete projects, its appeal will be more sustainable than simply expanding the membership list,” Sun said.

item.title: [SCMP] Could China’s new transport-tanker capability boost PLA power beyond first island chain?
item.description:
China has confirmed that its new Y-20B heavy transport aircraft can be converted into an aerial refuelling tanker, potentially boosting PLA Air Force capacities deeper into the western Pacific.

A documentary aired by state broadcaster CCTV on August 5 said the Y-20B, an improved variant of China’s Y-20 strategic transport powered by domestically developed WS-20 turbofan engines, could switch between transport and aerial refuelling missions using pallet-ready fuel tanks and removable refuelling equipment.

The official confirmation aligns with long-standing open-source intelligence.
item.content:encoded:
China has confirmed that its new Y-20B heavy transport aircraft can be converted into an aerial refuelling tanker, potentially boosting PLA Air Force capacities deeper into the western Pacific.

A documentary aired by state broadcaster CCTV on August 5 said the Y-20B, an improved variant of China’s Y-20 strategic transport powered by domestically developed WS-20 turbofan engines, could switch between transport and aerial refuelling missions using pallet-ready fuel tanks and removable refuelling equipment.

The official confirmation aligns with long-standing open-source intelligence.

Andreas Rupprecht, an aviation analyst who specialises in the Chinese military, said observers had tracked the capability since the third Y-20B prototype was spotted with in-flight refuelling pods in January 2022.

Further evidence emerged in April 2023, when the first Y-20B in standard military grey appeared at Kaifeng airbase bearing characteristic refuelling alignment markings.

The significance lies in what the capability could mean operationally.

“What matters most now is the potential impact on the PLA Air Force’s tanker and fighter fleet,” Rupprecht said.

The convertible Y-20B offered “a tremendous boost” in capacity and flexibility because individual aircraft could be assigned to transport or refuelling missions, he noted.

Rupprecht said a common configuration could also simplify maintenance compared with separate Y-20A transports and YY-20A tankers. The YY-20A is the dedicated aerial-refuelling variant of the Y-20.

The concept itself is not unique to China. Europe’s A400M military transport aircraft can also be reconfigured for aerial refuelling by fitting underwing refuelling pods while retaining its airlift role.

For China, the potential impact comes from the scale of its expanding heavy-transport fleet.

By allowing commanders to draw on part of that fleet during a contingency, the Y-20B could help sustain fighter sorties and other air operations beyond the first island chain and deeper into the western Pacific, as well as across the vast area covered by the PLA Western Theatre Command and over the South China Sea.

The CCTV programme highlighted the greater thrust and fuel efficiency of the Y-20B’s WS-20 high-bypass turbofan engines. This could reduce the aircraft’s own fuel consumption, potentially leaving more fuel available for transfer or allowing it to operate farther from base, although actual fuel-offload performance has not been made public.

Before the Y-20-derived tanker, the PLA Air Force relied primarily on a small fleet of H-6-based tankers and three imported Il-78s, limiting the scale of long-range operations it could support.

The Pentagon’s 2024 China Military Power Report estimated that the People’s Liberation Army operated 16 Y-20U tankers – known in China as the YY-20A – as of March that year, and said the tanker variant “significantly expands” China’s ability to conduct long-range offensive air operations.

The fleet has expanded substantially since that assessment: Rupprecht said open-source tracking had identified at least 35 individual YY-20A tankers, alongside more than 24 Y-20Bs capable of serving as multi-role tanker transports.

The same Pentagon report said PLA aviation missions were evolving from territorial defence towards offensive operations beyond the first island chain, while air force leaders had repeatedly called for a “strategic” air force capable of projecting power over long distances.

Rupprecht said the Y-20B development showed how seriously the PLA Air Force was taking aerial refuelling after years of relatively limited capacity. He pointed to China’s large numbers of J-10, J-16 and J-20 fighters capable of receiving fuel in flight, saying greater tanker availability would allow refuelling to be practised “more frequently and intensively than before”, while supporting longer and more persistent operations.

Another military expert, speaking on condition of anonymity, said additional tankers could be particularly useful closer to China for maintaining combat air patrols, allowing fighters to remain on station longer.

The implications could also extend to China’s long-range strike forces. Recent official footage showed an H-6N strategic bomber carrying the JL-1 air-launched nuclear-capable ballistic missile, while separate footage released in June showed an H-6N receiving fuel from a Y-20-family tanker.

China has been developing the operational foundations for such missions for years. Rand research found PLA Air Force aircraft practising aerial refuelling during “distant sea” training beyond the first island chain and assessed that greater tanker capacity could extend bomber reach and enable fighter escorts over greater distances.

More recent evidence suggests refuelling is becoming increasingly integrated into routine training. A December 2025 report by the US Air Force’s China Aerospace Studies Institute found that aerial refuelling was being incorporated into flight-academy transition and combat-training programmes.

CCTV also presented the tanker capability as part of a broader effort to use the Y-20 airframe for different missions. Pang Rongqi, an officer with a PLA Air Force unit, said the boundaries between transports, bombers, early-warning and electronic-warfare aircraft were “becoming increasingly blurred”.

“In the future, it is entirely possible that our transport aircraft platform could be used to perform all of these missions,” he said.

Both experts cautioned that Pang’s comments did not mean individual Y-20Bs could switch between all of those roles. Rupprecht said they more likely referred to using the Y-20B airframe as the basis for specialised variants, such as China’s new airborne early-warning and control aircraft.

Unlike the modular tanker conversion, the early-warning variant requires extensive airframe modifications, including a radar dome, the anonymous expert said.

Questions remain over how long the conversion between transport and tanker configurations takes, how frequently aircraft switch between the roles and how much fuel a converted Y-20B can transfer.

The anonymous expert said fuel-offload capacity would determine how many and what types of aircraft each tanker could support – whether, for example, it could refuel one bomber or several fighters.

Rupprecht said conversion times and how frequently the aircraft switched roles were not publicly known, but argued that aircraft availability was unlikely to be a major constraint.

He estimated that China now had “a good 150 Y-20s of all versions”, compared with a transport fleet that for years relied on little more than 30 Il-76s and three Il-78 tankers.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Prabowo’s softened tone might not signal a change in Indonesia’s economic course
item.description:
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto acknowledged on Friday that his government had yet to fulfil all its promises, an unusual note of self-criticism as he sought to reassure Indonesians and investors while pressing ahead with his ambitious economic agenda.

Analysts said the shift in tone was notable but saw little evidence that Prabowo was changing course on his more state-directed economic policies.

In his annual state address ahead of Independence Day and a later budget speech, Prabowo said the country’s problems were being addressed, predicted economic growth could reach 6 per cent this year and defended greater state oversight of strategic industries.
item.content:encoded:
Indonesian President Prabowo Subianto acknowledged on Friday that his government had yet to fulfil all its promises, an unusual note of self-criticism as he sought to reassure Indonesians and investors while pressing ahead with his ambitious economic agenda.

Analysts said the shift in tone was notable but saw little evidence that Prabowo was changing course on his more state-directed economic policies.

In his annual state address ahead of Independence Day and a later budget speech, Prabowo said the country’s problems were being addressed, predicted economic growth could reach 6 per cent this year and defended greater state oversight of strategic industries.

“I cannot yet say that all the nation’s problems have been resolved, or that every promise I made has been fulfilled. Not yet,” he told parliament.

Wasisto Raharjo Jati, a political sociologist at Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency, described the acknowledgement as “very surprising”, saying Prabowo had rarely publicly conceded that his policies had fallen short.

He said the change in tone appeared partly aimed at responding to public criticism that had begun to damage the president’s reputation.

Prabowo’s approval rating fell to 51.1 per cent in July from 81.2 per cent last November, according to a survey by Saiful Mujani Research and Consulting, with dissatisfaction over the economy a major factor behind the decline.

Nicky Fahrizal, a researcher at Jakarta’s Centre for Strategic and International Studies, also described Prabowo’s acknowledgement of unmet targets as “an act of statesmanship”.

But he said it would need to be followed by measurable improvements in bureaucracy and governance.

“Without real improvements, public dissatisfaction will continue to build and risks undermining the president’s position in the near term,” Fahrizal said.

The former special forces commander took office in October 2024 after a sweeping election victory built on promises to root out corruption, lift economic growth ‌from 5 per cent to 8 per cent and give free meals to millions of children.

But his administration ⁠has struggled this ⁠year with a depreciating rupiah and a poorly performing stock market, as well as concerns over government overspending and central ‌bank independence, while his flagship free meals programme has been hit by budget cuts and allegations of mismanagement.

Prabowo nevertheless said investment in Indonesia would continue to grow and create jobs, arguing that gross domestic product growth could reach 6 per cent by the end of the year.

He also presented food and energy self-sufficiency as crucial protections against global instability, saying Indonesia could not remain dependent on outside supply if international conditions worsened.

Prabowo has made food self-sufficiency a main priority of his administration, framing lower reliance on imports as essential to national security.

He said on Friday that Indonesia had so far achieved self-sufficiency in eight food commodities and that supplies remained secure despite the threat of the El Nino dry weather pattern.

One closely watched part of the speech was Prabowo’s clarification of a controversial plan to exert greater state control over commodity exports.

When he last addressed parliament in May, Prabowo announced plans to centralise exports of strategic natural resources under a new state-run entity, Danantara Sumberdaya Indonesia (DSI), prompting concern among investors and exporters about how the system would work.

On Friday, Prabowo stressed that DSI would monitor and process commodity exports rather than take over the trading itself, although its role would continue to expand.

“We do not want the Indonesian people to be cheated any more. Indonesia’s wealth must not enrich a select few while leaving our people to live in hardship,” he said.

Prabowo said DSI had monitored more than 6,500 transactions involving three key commodities during its first two months, covering US$14 billion in exports, and had identified a potential US$5 billion in export proceeds from differences between reported and actual prices.

The system would soon expand to 50 ports and eventually cover all strategic commodity exports, Prabowo said.

But Prabowo also used his later budget speech to announce a new exchange for strategic minerals and commodities that is expected to begin operating by January 1, 2027, part of an effort to give Indonesia greater influence over the prices of its key exports.

Made Supriatma, a visiting fellow in the Indonesia Studies Programme at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute, said the new approach differed from Prabowo’s original proposal to route exports through DSI, but questioned how much power Indonesia could wield over prices set in international markets.

“The issue then arises: given the nature of trade, does Indonesia possess the leverage to dictate prices?” Made said.

“If international prices are low but Indonesia sets a high price, the country will fail to generate revenue.”

In a report after the speech, Bank Danamon analyst Irman Faiz said it would be important “to ensure that tighter oversight does not increase transaction costs for exporters or discourage private investment”.

Prabowo’s 2027 budget proposal, meanwhile, set out plans to spend 4,097.2 trillion rupiah (US$229.73 billion), up 3.9 per cent from the projected spending level for this year.

Revenues are expected to reach 3,426 trillion rupiah next year, up 6.8 per cent from this year’s estimate.

The proposed fiscal deficit of 2.4 per cent of GDP would be the smallest since 2024 and down from the 2.85 per cent deficit projected for 2026. Indonesian law limits the government’s annual budget deficit to 3 per cent of GDP.

Prabowo said the budget would remain expansive while focusing on eight key programmes, including food and energy self-sufficiency, development of domestic industries and education.

The figures assume GDP growth of 6 per cent in 2027, inflation of 2.5 per cent, an average rupiah exchange rate of 17,500 to the US dollar and an average 10-year bond yield of 6.9 per cent.

Nailul Huda, director of economy at the Centre of Economic and Law Studies (CELIOS), was considerably more sceptical, calling the 6 per cent growth target “too optimistic” given weakening global conditions and pressures on household purchasing power and employment.

CELIOS expects growth of no more than 4.7 per cent in 2027, Nailul said, arguing that the boost from government spending in 2025 and 2026 would be difficult to repeat next year.

By contrast, Maybank economist Brian Lee said that, aside from the growth target, the budget assumptions were “rather conservative” compared with those in the 2026 proposal.

The government’s official GDP growth target for this year is 5.4 per cent, although Prabowo said on Friday that he believed growth could reach 6 per cent.

He has set a target of lifting growth to 8 per cent by 2029. The economy expanded 5.3 per cent in the second quarter of this year.

Inflation in July stood at 2.88 per cent, comfortably within the central bank’s target range, helped by government fuel subsidies.

Prabowo also used his state address to highlight tighter control over other parts of the economy, including a crackdown on illegal tin mining and a sweeping reorganisation of state-owned enterprises.

He said the government had identified 1,074 state-owned entities and subsidiaries, of which 290 had already been closed. His administration aims to reduce the total to no more than 300 by the end of this year, retaining businesses that are productive and create value.

Made said the restructuring illustrated the increasingly central role Prabowo envisaged for Danantara in directing development and investment.

“Danantara is clearly no ordinary sovereign wealth fund; it serves as both an economic and a political arm,” he said, adding that it was “set to become the driving force behind development”.

Nicky said the change in how the DSI policy was presented did not, in his view, signal a broader shift in Prabowo’s approach to government.

“A centralised command model will remain a hallmark of the Prabowo era,” he said. “If there is an adjustment in the narrative, it is most likely tactical, aimed at satisfying markets and investors in the short term.”

Indonesia also plans to revise its citizenship law to allow some citizens to hold dual nationality for the first time, Prabowo said, in an effort to allow “millions” in the Indonesian diaspora to contribute to the country’s development.

Prabowo said the dual citizenship policy would be “limited” and designed in a measured way, with national interests fully protected.

Indonesian law does not currently recognise dual citizenship for adults, and minors with two passports must choose their nationality when they turn 18.

item.title: [SCMP] US accuses 9 Latin American countries of helping China avoid Trump’s tariffs
item.description:
Three Latin American governments that moved against Chinese commercial interests over the past year were named in a White House report on Thursday, which accused Chinese exporters of routing goods through third countries to evade US tariffs.

Mexico, Panama and Colombia now join Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic among more than 40 countries the report says carry elevated risk of illegal transshipment, the practice of moving goods through an intermediate country so they enter the US under a different origin and a lower duty.

Previously, the three Latin American countries appeared to support the Trump administration during the relentless US-China trade war.
item.content:encoded:
Three Latin American governments that moved against Chinese commercial interests over the past year were named in a White House report on Thursday, which accused Chinese exporters of routing goods through third countries to evade US tariffs.

Mexico, Panama and Colombia now join Brazil, Argentina, Chile, Peru, Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic among more than 40 countries the report says carry elevated risk of illegal transshipment, the practice of moving goods through an intermediate country so they enter the US under a different origin and a lower duty.

Previously, the three Latin American countries appeared to support the Trump administration during the relentless US-China trade war.

Mexico imposed tariffs of up to 50 per cent on Chinese cars in December, ahead of the review of the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement (USMCA).

Panama’s Supreme Court annulled the concessions held by Hong Kong’s CK Hutchison at both ends of the canal in January, drawing an arbitration claim of more than US$2 billion and a freeze on Chinese state investment.

Colombia applied a 35 per cent duty in March on steel and metalworking imports from countries without a trade agreement, the ceiling permitted under World Trade Organization (WTO) rules and aimed principally at its largest supplier, China.

Countries identified as engaging in illegal transshipment face concrete costs at the US border.

Washington has included anti-transshipment clauses in its recent trade agreements. Executive Order 14326, signed in July, 2025, applies a 40 per cent penalty duty to goods that US Customs and Border Protection determines were diverted to evade tariffs, in place of the reciprocal rate that would otherwise apply.

The order also requires the US Commerce and Homeland Security departments to publish a list every six months that names countries, entities and facilities involved in transshipment.

Chinese exporters accused of moving shipments through third countries

The Office of Trade and Manufacturing Policy, the White House unit run by Peter Navarro, produced the 25-page document titled “The Great Transshipment Scam”. It argues that Chinese exporters responded to the 2018 tariffs by shifting shipments through third countries, where light assembly, relabelling, or changes in paperwork could disguise the goods’ origin.

That the rerouting is happening is not what specialists on regional trade dispute. Diego Marroquin Bitar, a fellow with the Americas Programme at the Centre for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) and on the USMCA initiative, said the practice does real damage.

“Transshipment is a genuine threat to US industrial capacity, to American jobs, and to revenue collection. That case does not need to be argued,” he said.

But his disagreement begins at the next step, where the report treats the size of a country’s trade as grounds for calling it an accomplice.

It places Mexico and Canada in a tier of large trading partners, where it says the risk is embedded within broad, legitimate trade flows, a classification Marroquin Bitar said describes scale rather than conduct.

What separates the two countries from others on the list, he said, is the rule book they already trade under.

“Mexico and Canada operate inside a framework with the United States that carries strict regional content thresholds, labour provisions, and wage requirements,” he said, adding that Central American partners work under comparable terms in their own agreements.

No comparable set of content and labour rules covers the South American countries on the list, whose trade has tilted the other way over the same period.

China took 28.7 per cent of Brazil’s exports last year, worth US$100 billion and more than two and a half-times what Brazil shipped to the US, according to trade ministry figures. It is also the leading buyer from Chile and Peru.

Chinese capital has also moved with the trade, from the US$1.3 billion of Chinese investment in the deep water port at Chancay in Peru to the plants Chinese carmakers are building across the region.

The report was released six weeks before US President Donald Trump is due to host Chinese President Xi Jinping in Washington next month.

The USMCA review is under way after Washington declined an automatic extension, and Brazil filed for consultations at the WTO last month over US tariffs that its trade ministry says amount to 23.1 per cent of Brazilian exports to the American market.

The report sorts the countries it names into three tiers of risk, and the region is spread across all of them.

Mexico ranks at the top, alongside Canada, the European Union, India, Israel, Japan, South Korea and Taiwan. Brazil sits in the middle tier with countries like Turkey and Vietnam. The other seven fall into a lower tier of what the report calls “opportunistic targets” defined by free zones, port access, bonded warehousing, or limited customs enforcement capacity.

Only three of the nine are tied to particular goods anywhere in the document. Mexico’s Guanajuato-Queretaro corridor is matched to electric motors, generators, transformers and static converters under tariff headings HS 8501 to 8504, set against Detroit, Grand Rapids and Indianapolis.

Costa Rica’s Limon-Moin corridor appears under heading HS 850300, covering electric motor and generator parts, opposite Dallas-Fort Worth and Oklahoma City.

And the Dominican Republic’s Caucedo-Haina corridor covers insulated conductors and cable assemblies, weighed against Portland, Seattle and Spokane.

Report claims US loses whenever the foreign hub wins

The report calls these pairings the ugly sisters of a zero-sum trading system and argues that the US loses whenever the foreign hub wins. Marroquin Bitar said the arithmetic rests on an assumption that does not hold.

“That only holds if you assume every motor built in Queretaro would otherwise have been built in Michigan, and it would not have been. The realistic alternative is Asia, not Detroit,” he said.

Roughly three-quarters of every dollar of Mexican manufactured exports to the US originates in North America, he said, describing US labour and US value returning home inside goods that are counted as imports.

“The job in Michigan depends on the one in Queretaro,” he said.

The report applies the same reasoning to Central America, counting permissive free-zone rules among the weak-link advantages that draw Chinese rerouting.

In Costa Rica, those zones are the core of its export economy. The regime accounts for about 15 per cent of national output, three-quarters of foreign direct investment and more than 265,000 jobs, according to 2024 figures from the state trade agency Procomer.

San Jose concluded talks in May to join the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, part of a push to widen its export markets.

Panama is named without any product line, grouped with Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic in a category of maritime gateways alongside Malaysia, Oman and the United Arab Emirates.

The report said only that Panama and Costa Rica offer maritime access, free-zone logistics, and re-export platforms, and did not identify any Panamanian facilities, products, or volumes.

The five South American countries named are placed in a category the report calls Latin American Corridors, its function given as Pacific and Atlantic re-routing, bonded warehousing and regional assembly.

Brazil singled out in document as US ramps up pressure

The largest economy in the group, Brazil, appears four times in the document, three of which are in lists that name it and nothing more. The single descriptive sentence says it serves, with Turkey, as a larger regional platform capable of supporting re-routing or transformation claims in selected product categories. Which categories, the report does not say.

Mexico is the only economy in the region carrying a dollar figure. The report ranks it among three leading hubs worldwide, with India and Vietnam, through which the US Commerce Department traced about US$67 billion in Chinese goods into the American market last year.

The report qualifies its own figures in several places in the text. It said the shift in US import sourcing after 2018 does not prove that all displaced Chinese trade was illegally diverted.

It also puts the annual value of the trade anywhere between US$40 billion and US$303 billion across five analyses it says are not directly comparable; and presents its estimates of 450,000 American jobs and up to US$150 billion in output as model-based illustrations.

Navarro said on a call with reporters that anti-transshipment terms would form part of the administration’s trade negotiations and that countries found to be rerouting goods would face penalties.

Those qualifications point to where Marroquin Bitar said the document is on firmer ground: the difficulty of knowing what is actually inside a shipment.

“What needs closing is the visibility gap,” he said, describing the distance between what customs authorities can assume about a good crossing a border and what they can verify.

“Closing that gap is a technical problem with a technical answer, and the partners best positioned to solve it alongside Washington are the ones already building things with US firms.”

item.title: [SCMP] How AI is helping to open a new chapter for ancient Chinese literature
item.description:
For generations, working with ancient Chinese texts has been a painstaking task. Specialists would spend years deciphering unfamiliar characters, copying manuscripts by hand, adding punctuation to texts written without it, comparing different editions and tracing references scattered across thousands of years of records.

But artificial intelligence is now changing that process, not only by helping to preserve fragile manuscripts but also by transforming how ancient texts are recovered, studied and shared.

As China accelerates its efforts to digitise a vast collection of ancient works, universities, technology companies and volunteers are taking part in a nationwide effort to turn the country’s rich literary heritage – once largely the preserve of specialists – into an open digital resource.
item.content:encoded:
For generations, working with ancient Chinese texts has been a painstaking task. Specialists would spend years deciphering unfamiliar characters, copying manuscripts by hand, adding punctuation to texts written without it, comparing different editions and tracing references scattered across thousands of years of records.

But artificial intelligence is now changing that process, not only by helping to preserve fragile manuscripts but also by transforming how ancient texts are recovered, studied and shared.

As China accelerates its efforts to digitise a vast collection of ancient works, universities, technology companies and volunteers are taking part in a nationwide effort to turn the country’s rich literary heritage – once largely the preserve of specialists – into an open digital resource.

An example of how this works in practice is Shidian Guji, an online database of more than 70,000 ancient works, all of them freely available to the public, that was launched in 2022 and jointly developed by ByteDance and Peking University.

The database provides tools for organising, searching and reading classical works, including modern language versions of classical texts and chatbot-based interactions that help users to explore them.

Last month, it published a collection of almost 2,000 traditional scientific works covering fields such as astronomy, mathematics, agriculture and engineering.

Sun Xianbin, a researcher at the Institute for the History of Natural Sciences at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, told Shangguan News the digital archive contained centuries of accumulated knowledge and formed part of China’s “indigenous knowledge system”.

This concept has gained increasing prominence in recent years, as Beijing tries to promote ideas rooted in China’s own history and intellectual traditions rather than imported Western ideas.

The platform forms part of China’s broader push to preserve and paIT’ss on its literary heritage, a policy included in the latest five-year plan for national development.

Such a push has particular significance in China, where ancient texts are closely tied to concepts of cultural confidence and civilisational continuity stretching across thousands of years.

Ancient texts are regarded by Beijing as a cornerstone of this civilisational history, with an estimated 200,000 works surviving in various editions, according to state news agency Xinhua.

President Xi Jinping has thrown his full weight behind such efforts, saying technology could help promote the “philosophical ideas, humanistic spirit, values and moral principles” embedded in classical texts and “promote the creative transformation and innovative development” of traditional culture.

Last month the National Cultural Heritage Administration published its latest five-year plan. This included a drive to recover cultural relics from overseas and calls to explore how AI could assist in these efforts.

For China, AI-driven digitisation offers a way to facilitate the “digital return” of ancient manuscripts from overseas.

Millions of volumes are now kept in collections in neighbouring countries such as Japan and South Korea, while others are kept in North America – partly as a consequence of war and social upheaval.

A number of projects have been set up to make these works available to the general public, including a partnership between the University of California, Berkeley and Sichuan University to digitise nearly 10,000 rare pre-1912 titles from the American university’s C. V. Starr East Asian Library.

The project, set up in 2021, was funded by the Alibaba Foundation, a non-profit founded by the company that owns the South China Morning Post.

Berkeley said the texts were being given a “new digital life” that marked “the next phase in a great journey through time and space” by providing a trove of easily searchable treasures to scholars, enthusiasts, and amateurs alike.

“The project is also notable for uniting institutions that are half a world apart for a common cause,” it said.

Another such project is run by the Harvard-Yenching Library, which has made digital copies of more than 6,000 rare Chinese books in its collection online.

These include some works that are particularly valuable because no surviving copies exist in mainland China.

Many digitised texts already exist online, but they are difficult for non-specialists to read.

Tsui Lik-hang, an associate professor from the Department of Chinese and History at City University of Hong Kong, said AI was helping to remove “genuine barriers” for modern readers by adding punctuation, providing glossaries and translating ancient texts.

“Much premodern Chinese material is inaccessible not because it is locked away but because it is unreadable to most people,” he said.

Researchers and museums have also begun experimenting with avatars that visitors can question and interact with directly, based either on real historical figures or fictional characters designed to represent a certain time and place.

Tsui said the main value of this approach was that it helped stimulate people’s curiosity and imagination, but warned users should be clear about which elements were supported by historical sources and which were “reconstruction or conjecture”.

For Tsui, the value of AI lies beyond simply preserving ancient texts.

“Preservation often gives you a digital image of a text, but actual scholarly research requires a text you can work with,” he said.

The more difficult stage comes after digitisation, he said, because “interpretive operations” were needed to create usable research materials. These operations can include punctuating the text, identifying persons, offices, places and dates, as well as annotating allusions and quotations.

Such tasks were “until recently mostly done by hand”, but machine learning has become increasingly useful in assisting with them. Handwritten text recognition was also improving rapidly with AI models, he said.

For historians, the use of AI changes “the speed at which familiar questions are answered and the range of questions worth asking”, he said.

Tsui said historians had always sensed there were connections between certain authors, texts and different historical periods – but proving them often needed a course of reading and note-taking beyond the ability of even the most dedicated scholar.

He said AI tools could help him shift from studying a single written letter to finding patterns across “hundreds of documents by various different authors”.

He gave the example of letters written by members of the Song dynasty literary class, saying AI could help researchers trace the hidden links between people and ideas, and identify stylistic similarities across texts and images.

But the technology can only help so far in revealing patterns, and Tsui said historians must still do much of the hard work.

He also warned that AI-generated historical interactions carried risks. Large language models sometimes made up names, dates or citations, and their “confidence” could make it hard for non-specialists to spot the problems.

More importantly, Tsui warned: “Interpretation in the humanities is multiple and contested by nature. An AI model returning one confident reading could flatten that.

“Classical Chinese is especially exposed: unpunctuated, unreferenced, deliberately subtle, often obscure and vast in the amounts of texts. Meaning frequently depends on recognising what is being quoted and why.”

Tsui also said that AI should not become a substitute for directly engaging with historical sources.

“Historical research is … a trade in which scholars find pleasure in reading, interpreting, explaining,” he said. “If we always let a predictive machine sit between ourselves and the sources, we lose that.”

Historians, he added, should also play a role in shaping these AI systems, adding that it was wrong to ask whether they could replace historians.

“Historians and humanities scholars are trained critics and readers of all kinds of sources. We weigh evidence, argue over meaning and context, and go deep,” he said. “This is precisely what we need in the age of AI models.”

item.title: [SCMP] Zhu Rongji’s legacy: how the late premier reshaped state firms, Pudong and China’s economy
item.description:
Turn-of-the-century images of Zhu Rongji alongside former US president Bill Clinton have largely accompanied coverage following the former Chinese premier’s death on Wednesday.

The moment in April 1999 was more than a diplomatic milestone. It underpinned some of China’s most consequential reforms that defined Zhu’s tenure, from its drive to join the World Trade Organization to an overhaul of the state sector and opening its markets to the world.

And in recent years, Zhu’s historic trip to Washington has also become a subject of reflection among American lawmakers, think tanks and officials, as a strategic rivalry with China has emerged across nearly every economic and business front.
item.content:encoded:
Turn-of-the-century images of Zhu Rongji alongside former US president Bill Clinton have largely accompanied coverage following the former Chinese premier’s death on Wednesday.

The moment in April 1999 was more than a diplomatic milestone. It underpinned some of China’s most consequential reforms that defined Zhu’s tenure, from its drive to join the World Trade Organization to an overhaul of the state sector and opening its markets to the world.

And in recent years, Zhu’s historic trip to Washington has also become a subject of reflection among American lawmakers, think tanks and officials, as a strategic rivalry with China has emerged across nearly every economic and business front.

Zhu, who died on Wednesday at the age of 97, was also remembered for promoting entrepreneurship, introducing foreign management expertise, and reviving Chinese enterprises, according to four people who knew him for decades.

“Intelligent, insightful, outspoken and decisive,” said Zhang Chongqing, honorary president of China Group Companies Association, recalling his first impression of Zhu and their early work together on economic reform, dating back to 1980 when they were both at China’s top economic planner.

Zhang, who pioneered enterprise reform as deputy director general of the government-backed China Enterprise Management Association – now known as the China Enterprise Confederation – in the 1980s and ’90s, recalled the eagerness of the late premier to learn foreign management expertise and find a way forward for state-owned enterprises, which were a core part of China’s centrally managed economy for decades.

When Beijing was forging ties with the Switzerland-based European Management Forum in the 1980s, before it became known as the World Economic Forum in 1987, Zhu was an active participant in their joint meetings.

Zhang recalled how Zhu did not simply give a prepared speech at these meetings; he also dared to speak candidly and engage directly with participants.

“On one occasion in Beijing, he shared his office phone number” with foreign guests, Zhang said. “He was a bold, free-spirited sort of person – daring, open, and uninhibited in his speech.”

Domestically, Zhu placed great value on home-grown entrepreneurs.

Zhang recalled a particular moment in 1996, about two years before the retirement of Zhao Zhongyu from Pangang Group – the southwestern Chinese steelmaker that Zhao had spent decades building into a leading producer.

Zhao had asked Zhu, who was then vice-premier, to conduct a field inspection of Pangang. Zhu was said to have replied quickly, and he went on to help advance the company’s technological innovation and preparations for a stock market listing.

When it came to supporting entrepreneurs, “he was very generous”, Zhang recalled.

After all, what would have happened if state-owned enterprises hadn’t been reformed?

Zhang Chongqing, China Group Companies Association

As premier, Zhu launched China’s biggest reform campaign involving state-owned enterprises (SOEs), bankrupting tens of thousands of inefficient “zombies” and laying off millions of workers. The controversial measures helped revitalise the economy and create room for more efficient private and foreign-owned firms.

Despite the lay-offs becoming a source of generational pain in regions heavily reliant on SOEs, Zhang said it was a price that had to be paid.

“He was surely a leader who made outstanding contributions to driving China’s economic revitalisation,” Zhang said of the late premier. “That deserves full recognition.

“After all, what would have happened if state-owned enterprises hadn’t been reformed?”

Zhu Tian, a chair professor and co-dean of the Shanghai-based China Europe International Business School (CEIBS), said he had long been impressed by the “immense personal charisma” of Zhu Rongji, dating back to the early days of Tsinghua University’s School of Economics and Management, which the former leader helped establish in 1984.

Although trained as an engineer – a common background among leaders of his generation – Zhu Rongji recognised the importance of economic management. In addition to helping set up the business school, he advocated for the broad adoption of advanced foreign management textbooks to align teaching and research with international standards.

The CEIBS professor, who graduated with a degree in management information systems from the business school in 1986, recalled how the founding dean would write personal yearbook messages to graduates, and had made a point of noting to him the importance of “combining economics, management and technology”.

“[Zhu Rongji] was the premier with the deepest understanding of the economy; he possessed exceptional leadership and execution capabilities,” professor Zhu Tian added. “Pragmatic, witty and wise, he eschewed empty rhetoric in favour of plain speaking.”

[Zhu Rongji] was always curious and investigative, and had the urgency to bring change to China

Joerg Wuttke, former president of EU Chamber of Commerce in China

The late leader also introduced a powerful advisory board of world-class entrepreneurs and scholars in 2000. The current cohort includes SpaceX founder Elon Musk, Meta Platforms founder Mark Zuckerberg, Apple CEO Tim Cook, Bridgewater founder Ray Dalio, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon, Blackstone chairman Stephen Schwarzman and former United States Treasury secretary Henry Paulson.

Up until about 2018, the former premier was still regularly meeting with visiting foreign entrepreneurs. He remained the board’s “honorary chairman” until 2024, when the title was passed to former vice-president Wang Qishan. Zhu Rongji was then designated the “founding honorary chairman”.

For Joerg Wuttke, who worked in China for decades, Zhu Rongji was always keen to sit down with foreign investors, listen to their concerns and present a friendly face – in sharp contrast with his impatience towards Chinese officials who delivered long, unproductive reports.

When the late leader was tackling economic work as vice-premier in the early 1990s, Beijing faced deep scepticism overseas and was making extensive efforts to attract foreign investment.

“[He has been] my hero since … he was still vice-premier,” said Wuttke, former president of the European Union Chamber of Commerce in China, who had frequent contact with Zhu Rongji.

On one occasion, Wuttke recalled, when the former leader was asked what kind of economic data he valued the most, he answered simply: “Tax.” During his tenure as vice-premier, Zhu coordinated the overhaul of China’s central-local tax-sharing and fiscal reform.

“He was never shy of pointing out problems,” Wuttke recalled from their meetings. “He was always curious and investigative, and had the urgency to bring change to China.”

For many people from Shanghai, the late premier, who was once the city’s mayor, is remembered as one of the most important architects of the Pudong New Area, now a booming district in one of the mainland’s most developed metropolises, and home to the Shanghai Stock Exchange and a Disney resort.

Zhou Hanmin, now a standing committee member of the Chinese People’s Political Consultative Conference, and once a prominent think tank researcher who advised in the 1980s and ’90s on Pudong’s development, said Zhu Rongji’s resolve and reformist outlook helped drive the district’s rise.

At the end of April 1990, the Shanghai government unveiled 10 preferential policies to encourage foreign investment and participation in the region’s business activities. Months later, Zhou accompanied Zhu Rongji on an official visit to the US. Their first stop was New York, where they were confronted with a pointed question from an American reporter on how to persuade foreigners to invest capital in the city.

Zhou recalled how Zhu Rongji quickly replied off the cuff, vowing: “We will enforce relevant legislation to ensure the success of the development and opening-up, as well as safeguard the legitimate rights and interests of foreign investors.”

Zhou recalled being impressed with the rapid answer.

“Upon our return to China, we plunged straight into research work,” Zhou told the South China Morning Post on Wednesday. “Within two months … nine sets of regulations governing Pudong’s development and opening-up were released to the world simultaneously in Chinese, English and Japanese.”

Turning an ambitious vision into action, Zhu Rongji helped “draw people and enterprises from near and far”, added Zhou, who was a deputy governor of Pudong from 2000 to 2008.

And today, despite 36 years passing since the former leader helped set Pudong’s transformation in motion, “images of that time remain vividly etched in my memory”, Zhou said.

Additional reporting by Emma Ma

item.title: [SCMP] ‘India’s biggest corporate decision’: Tata Group chair’s exit raises hard succession questions
item.description:
The sudden announcement that N Chandrasekaran will not seek another term as chairman of Tata Sons has raised a pressing question for India: who can steer one of the country’s most powerful and influential conglomerates through its next phase?

The answer matters well beyond the group’s boardroom. Tata’s businesses span salt, software, cars, steel, airlines and hi-tech manufacturing, with annual revenue equivalent to about 5 per cent of India’s gross domestic product and more than a million employees, giving the trust-controlled empire an outsize role in the country’s economic ambitions.

Chandrasekaran, 63, said on Wednesday that he had informed the board he would not seek reappointment once his tenure ended in February next year, after directors failed to reach a decision on his future role.
item.content:encoded:
The sudden announcement that N Chandrasekaran will not seek another term as chairman of Tata Sons has raised a pressing question for India: who can steer one of the country’s most powerful and influential conglomerates through its next phase?

The answer matters well beyond the group’s boardroom. Tata’s businesses span salt, software, cars, steel, airlines and hi-tech manufacturing, with annual revenue equivalent to about 5 per cent of India’s gross domestic product and more than a million employees, giving the trust-controlled empire an outsize role in the country’s economic ambitions.

Chandrasekaran, 63, said on Wednesday that he had informed the board he would not seek reappointment once his tenure ended in February next year, after directors failed to reach a decision on his future role.

His announcement sparked a rout in the shares of Tata Group companies on Wednesday, eroding billions of dollars in a single day amid investor concerns about a leadership crisis at the iconic group.

Tata Sons is the principal holding company of the Tata Group, whose foundations date back to before India’s independence from British rule and whose controlling shareholder, Tata Trusts, gives the charitable trusts unusual influence over one of Asia’s most prominent business empires.

The Tata Group comprises 31 key mainstream companies operating across 10 distinct business verticals, though the broader ecosystem includes over 100 operating and subsidiary companies globally.

Chandrasekaran’s move reportedly followed disagreement among board members over issues including losses at some group companies.

The dispute leaves Noel Tata, head of the influential Tata Trusts and half-brother of late chairman Ratan Tata, to manage the transition after he pushed back against a Chandrasekaran-led spending spree amounting to US$120 billion over the next five years.

Suresh Prabhu, a former Indian minister and a chartered accountant, articulated investor concerns in a social media post, pointing out that the group had become “India’s flag bearer with substantial global presence”.

“I sincerely hope (that) the resignation of N Chandrasekaran, a seasoned professional, will lead to a smooth leadership transition,” he said.

Chandrasekaran, who was chief executive of the group’s flagship information technology company Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) before being appointed as chairman of Tata Sons in 2017, currently oversees the management of dozens of major companies, including Tata Motors and Air India.

Under Chandrasekaran, the Tata Group saw its revenue nearly triple, while its net profit and listed market capitalisation grew roughly fivefold and threefold, respectively, over his tenure from 2017 to 2026.

The group also pushed into hi-tech manufacturing such as semiconductors, digital enterprises including online grocery app BigBasket, and aerospace and defence equipment manufacturing, embellishing his reputation that he once described in an interview as a “man in a hurry”.

Chandrasekaran’s exit could mean that many of the conglomerate’s current and planned projects could slow down, according to a Bloomberg report.

Lloyd Mathias, a leading New Delhi-based angel investor and business strategist, said Chandrasekaran’s resignation was not “all that surprising” given reports about concerns over lack of profitability in some of the group’s ventures.

Tata Group “virtually has its leg in every aspect of the Indian economy” and the “immediate priority will be to find a successor,” Mathias said, but noted that finding a new chairman before February could prove difficult.

“It is easily India’s biggest corporate decision to be made in the next six months. There are challenges ahead.”

The development comes as TCS, the group’s largest profit generator, is under pressure from a slowdown in global technology spending. The company is also grappling with threats from generative AI software and its shares have fallen more than 20 per cent in the past year.

The Tata Group’s efforts to revive the loss-making Air India have suffered setbacks following the crash of a London-bound flight last June and reports last week that a pilot of a flight to Phuket, which experienced severe turbulence, had smoked marijuana.

Vijay Govindarajan, distinguished professor of management at the Tuck School of Business at Dartmouth, said on social media that Chandrasekaran’s successor “will inherit a paradox”.

TCS, the cash machine that funds the empire, including Air India’s planned turnaround, is “staring down the most disruptive force it has ever faced” because its legacy IT services model catering to Fortune 500 companies is being threatened by generative AI, according to Govindarajan.

Vaibhav Kakkar, senior partner at law firm Saraf and Partners, said the end of Chandrasekaran’s tenure “should primarily be understood as a leadership transition at Tata Sons, rather than a sign of potential operational instability across the Tata Group’s diversified businesses”.

“He has been instrumental in shaping the group’s growth trajectory over the past decade, but one must bear in mind that institutions such as Tata are built over decades on governance, professional management and continuity – and those foundations do not change overnight,” Kakkar said.

The institutional depth of the group companies was often underappreciated during times of transition, he added.

Looming uncertainty

Amritraj Kaushal, a lawyer at the Supreme Court of India, said the priority “should be a swift and transparent succession process”.

An extended period of uncertainty could slow down distribution of finance, group initiatives and coordination, which are particularly important for businesses like Air India that are still in transformation, according to Kaushal.

He pointed out that Chandrasekaran was closely involved in Air India’s integration and turnaround after Tata reacquired it in 2022 from the government, 69 years since it was brought under state control from its founder, the Tata Group.

“So continuity of vision matters here more than most group companies,” Kaushal said.

The implications for Air India’s business go beyond India because Singapore Airlines has faced direct shareholder questions regarding its 25.1 per cent equity stake in the carrier.

Mayur Patel, regional commercial and industry affairs leader for Asia-Pacific, Middle East and Africa at OAG, a travel data and aviation analytics firm, said Singapore Airlines had consistently viewed its investment as a long-term strategic play to participate in India’s significant domestic market and international growth.

“While Air India is undergoing a significant transformation and faces near-term challenges, Singapore Airlines has continued to emphasise the strategic rationale behind the investment,” he said.

Chandrasekaran’s departure was unlikely to make much of a difference to Air India, Patel noted.

Earlier this month, Air India appointed aviation veteran Tewolde Gebremariam, former group head of Ethiopian Airlines, as its new CEO and managing director. He succeeds Campbell Wilson, who previously led Scoot, Singapore Airlines’ low-cost subsidiary.

item.title: [SCMP] The 11 key achievements of China’s ‘iron premier’ Zhu Rongji – in his own words
item.description:
Known for his sharp intellect, no-nonsense demeanour and relentless drive for reform, China’s former premier Zhu Rongji was the primary architect of the country’s transition from an isolated, rigidly planned economy to a market-driven titan connected to the rest of the world. During his tenure from 1998 to 2003, he engineered an economic “soft landing”, steered the nation through the Asian Financial Crisis and secured entry into the WTO, laying the groundwork for the country’s historic transformation.

Here is a look back at his key contributions, remembered through his most memorable and hard-hitting quotes.

1. Spearheading Shanghai’s revival
item.content:encoded:
Known for his sharp intellect, no-nonsense demeanour and relentless drive for reform, China’s former premier Zhu Rongji was the primary architect of the country’s transition from an isolated, rigidly planned economy to a market-driven titan connected to the rest of the world. During his tenure from 1998 to 2003, he engineered an economic “soft landing”, steered the nation through the Asian Financial Crisis and secured entry into the WTO, laying the groundwork for the country’s historic transformation.

Here is a look back at his key contributions, remembered through his most memorable and hard-hitting quotes.

1. Spearheading Shanghai’s revival

During his time as Shanghai’s mayor from 1988 to 1991, Zhu restructured the city’s industrial base, focused on exports and kick-started the construction of the Pudong New Area, an economic development zone. Early on, he recognised that foreign direct investment was key to the city’s future growth.

“If there’s one thing about me, my guiding principle, it’s independent thought. I feel that whatever’s on my mind is what I should say out loud. … What Shanghai needs most right now is grounded, practical follow-through.” – Giving a speech as a candidate for Shanghai mayor in 1987.

2. Defusing “triangular debt”

When Zhu was appointed governor of the People’s Bank of China in 1993, the country’s financial and payments system faced immense challenges with banks and state-owned enterprises (SOEs) hopelessly enmeshed in “triangular debt”.

Put simply, the phrase describes a chain of debts – Company A owing money to Company B, Company B owing money to Company C and Company C owing money to Company A – which can paralyse the economy.

Zhu tackled this issue by injecting targeted funds, establishing the responsibility of borrowers and allowing those unable to pay their debts to go bankrupt.

“The main source of triangular debt is that government departments, localities and enterprises blindly carry out construction projects in pursuit of rapid growth, resulting in a large fixed asset investment gap.” – Speaking at a national conference on clearing up triangular debt on September 3, 1991.

3. Engineering a “soft landing” for the Chinese economy

In the early 1990s, China’s breakneck economic expansion led to surging inflation and speculation, prompting fears that the boom would spin completely out of control. As head of the central bank, Zhu imposed strict macroeconomic tightening, controlled the money supply and clamped down on loose credit and speculative fixed-asset investments. Such tough measures successfully steered China towards a “soft landing” without triggering a devastating crash.
