Political veterans said Beijing had assessed the political climate as finally ripe for “institutionalising” long-term planning in Hong Kong. The city was now more stable following the implementation of the national security law and an electoral overhaul after the 2019 anti-government protests, which were aimed at ensuring that only “patriots” govern Hong Kong.

Sonny Lo Shiu-hing, a veteran political commentator specialising in Beijing’s relations with Hong Kong and Macau, explained that the shift in political discourse had allowed Beijing to address Hong Kong’s persistent failure to align itself with national planning cycles.

Political discussions in the city had long focused primarily on maintaining “two systems”. But the paradigm had now shifted towards greater integration with the mainland while making use of the advantages offered by “two systems”, he said.

“More importantly, there’s a strong executive-led system, meaning that the political system should be aligned with the central government’s vision, both economically and politically.”

Will planning dilute the city’s free-market edge?

The impending shift towards a more planned approach has raised a soul-searching question: will Hong Kong’s reputation as a free-market economy suffer? American economist Milton Friedman once called it his “favourite economy”.

In 1978, Nobel laureate Friedman chose Hong Kong as the backdrop for his exploration of free-market economics. He praised the city’s low taxes and lack of state intervention as engines of prosperity, describing its approach as “positive non-interventionism”.

In a recent commentary, former Morgan Stanley Asia chairman Stephen Roach cautioned that “Chinese-style central planning” could often “over-promise and under-deliver”.

His remarks prompted a rebuttal from Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun, who wrote in a separate commentary that the critic, whom he did not name, appeared to be driven by anti-China bias and that his views were “neither backed by evidence nor aligned with facts”.

The conflation of planning with a command economy is an issue the government has had to address. During the launch of the consultation exercise in mid-June, Secretary for Constitutional and Mainland Affairs Janice Tse Siu-wa stressed that Hong Kong was not pivoting towards a command economy.

The government “steadfastly adheres to a free-market economy that is market-led and government-facilitated”, she said.

Economists have also pointed out that many countries with different economic models incorporate some form of long-term planning.

Moreover, the idea of a command economy could itself be a relic of the past if viewed through the lens of pre-reform mainland China or the Soviet bloc, where the state strictly controlled production quotas and prices.

This was vastly different from the indicative planning adopted by capitalist economies such as post-war Japan, South Korea and Singapore, where governments provided strategic direction while leaving the allocation of resources to market forces.

During his 1992 tour of southern China, the late paramount leader Deng Xiaoping said that both planning and the market were tools for allocating resources.

“A planned economy is not the same as socialism, as capitalism also involves planning. A market economy is not the same as capitalism, as socialism also involves a market,” Deng said in Zhuhai. His remarks helped accelerate the pace of China’s reform and opening up.

For Hong Kong, some critics have argued that the city was paying the price for its supposed laissez-faire principles. The resulting lack of a comprehensive industrial policy and the absence of strategic coordination, as demonstrated by the early efforts to develop Cyberport and the Science Park, had hobbled the city, they said.

They argued that the “small government, big market” policy that Hong Kong once treated as sacred was outdated, particularly as competing economies had already moved in this direction.

Can strategic planning and free markets coexist?

Lau Siu-kai, a consultant for semi-official think tank the Chinese Association of Hong Kong and Macau Studies, maintained that Hong Kong’s inaugural five-year plan would not alter the essence of its capitalist system.

The government was not attempting to replace private enterprise, commercial capital and professionals as the bedrock of the city’s long-term growth, he stressed.

Politically, he said, the framework would bring numerous benefits to Hong Kong.

For example, it would set a higher benchmark for the city’s leadership by requiring officials to grasp global macroeconomic shifts and national priorities, and to identify precisely where Hong Kong could leverage its unique advantages to drive growth.

“The bureaucratic culture has been focusing on short-term execution instead of visionary foresight,” he said.

“Formulating and executing this first five-year plan offers a steep learning curve, as well as a challenging test, for officials to cultivate a macro-level mindset and elevate strategic thinking, which is key to Hong Kong’s development.”

HKU economist Tang pointed to Asian powerhouses such as Singapore, South Korea and Japan as proof that strategic state guidance and free-market dynamism were not mutually exclusive.

He said these countries had flourished under “very strong governments” with top-down industrial policies while maintaining “open, free and capitalist” economies.

He said the five-year plan was also a crucial step towards helping Hong Kong diversify its economy, generate fresh growth momentum and navigate geopolitical shocks.

“Given the geopolitical turmoil … [we shouldn’t] allow just the global free market to drive us in any direction. And Hong Kong needs to be more resilient and continue to be open. And at the same time, we need to think more strategically about our position in the global economy.”

After all, he said, whether the inaugural plan could achieve its goals would hinge on the rigour of its execution.

“We need specific action plans, clear KPIs across the design, implementation and review stages, and accountability for government officials if targets are missed,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] Too high, too fast? China’s rocket failure prompts questions about intense launch schedule
item.description:
The rare failure of China’s Long March-7A rocket on Monday – which resulted in the loss of a communications satellite – has prompted questions over whether it was an isolated operational setback or a systemic problem.

While space experts caution against immediately linking the incident to China’s rapidly increasing launch cadence, the ongoing investigation will determine if the event was caused by a localised technical anomaly or deeper systemic vulnerabilities within the Long March rocket family.

With attention turning to coming missions – particularly for the lunar-bound Chang’e-7, which shares engine technology with the failed booster – China’s ability to balance its ambitious launch schedule with the rigorous scrutiny required to secure its track record will be under the spotlight.
item.content:encoded:
The rare failure of China’s Long March-7A rocket on Monday – which resulted in the loss of a communications satellite – has prompted questions over whether it was an isolated operational setback or a systemic problem.

While space experts caution against immediately linking the incident to China’s rapidly increasing launch cadence, the ongoing investigation will determine if the event was caused by a localised technical anomaly or deeper systemic vulnerabilities within the Long March rocket family.

With attention turning to coming missions – particularly for the lunar-bound Chang’e-7, which shares engine technology with the failed booster – China’s ability to balance its ambitious launch schedule with the rigorous scrutiny required to secure its track record will be under the spotlight.

Around 8pm on Monday, the 60-metre (197-foot) Long March-7A blasted off from the Wenchang Space Launch Site on the southern island of Hainan, piercing the night sky as it carried the ChinaSat-4B satellite towards high-Earth orbit.

But less than 90 seconds into the flight, the rocket erupted into a fireball engulfed in thick black smoke, according to videos posted on social media by spectators near the launch site.

Space observers suggested a major anomaly might have triggered the rocket’s flight termination system, destroying the vehicle. Both the rocket and satellite were lost over the South China Sea.

State news agency Xinhua confirmed the failure and said the cause was being investigated.

Reacting to the incident on social media, American space flight company SpaceX founder Elon Musk said: “Rockets are insanely hard. There is a reason for the idiomatic expression. I hope they have a speedy recovery.”

Images circulating online, apparently taken from long-wave infrared tracking footage of the launch, appeared to show the rocket snapping near its upper section moments before it was destroyed.

The apparent snap happened around Max-Q, the point in a launch when a rocket comes under the greatest aerodynamic pressure as it accelerates through the atmosphere, according to space observers.

Some speculated that the rocket experienced a structural failure, likely triggered by a sudden surge in wind force at high altitudes shortly after launch, leading it to bend and break.

One military blogger wrote on social media: “A single setback does not mean a retreat. The key is whether the cause can be found and eliminated. For China’s space programme, what deserves real vigilance may not be any one failure, but rather how to maintain uncompromised quality control across every flight within an intensive launch schedule.”

This launch marks the fourth launch failure in China this year, following the state-owned Long March-3B and private company Galactic Energy’s Ceres-2 launches in January, as well as Beijing-based start-up Space Pioneer’s Tianlong-3 attempt in April.

China has conducted 56 launches this year, before Monday’s failure, which would have been the 18th launch of a Long March-7A vehicle.

Astrophysicist Richard de Grijs, the immediate former executive director of the International Space Science Institute-Beijing, said while the incident was a significant failure, it was not evidence of a systemic problem in China’s space programme.

“Rocket failures do occur, even in mature programmes, and the more frequently you launch, the more often you will eventually encounter one,” said de Grijs, who is a professor at the school of mathematical and physical sciences at Macquarie University in Australia.

He cautioned against connecting the incident with China’s rapidly increasing launch cadence, noting that while a high operational tempo put pressure on manufacturing, quality control and operations, one failure did not prove there was a systemic link.

“What matters now is whether investigators identify an isolated component failure or something with implications across a wider family of launch vehicles.”

The ChinaSat-4B satellite was expected to provide radio, television and other communications services to users around the world. Low-numbered ChinaSat satellites are also believed to be used for military communications.

No official details have been released about the satellite, but it is reportedly one of the most expensive of its kind China has built, with a price tag exceeding 1 billion yuan (US$148.20 million).

Its sister satellite ChinaSat-4A, launched in 2024 and now operating about 36,000km above Earth, had an estimated launch mass of about 5 tonnes at launch, according to space-flight tracker Jonathan McDowell.

The Long March-7A is one of China’s new-generation rockets and has become a workhorse for sending large satellites to high orbits. It burns mainly kerosene and liquid oxygen.

The rocket failed on its maiden flight in March 2020 but successfully returned to flight a year later. It has since completed a string of successful missions, most recently sending the Tianlian-3 (01) satellite towards geostationary orbit on July 29.

Those consecutive successful flights carried a wide range of communications, remote-sensing and data-relay satellites, mostly to high orbits, giving the Long March-7A a well-established track record for high-orbit missions.

Monday’s launch had been expected to set a speed record of a different kind. Chinese media reported before lift-off that the roughly 12-day gap since the previous Long March-7A mission would be the shortest turnaround yet for the rocket – and for any of China’s new-generation Long March launchers.

The loss of ChinaSat-4B means the communications capacity it was intended to provide will now be delayed. Geostationary communications satellites can play important roles in both civilian and military communications, and the broader impact will depend in part on how quickly China can launch a replacement.

The failure could have knock-on effects for coming launches. LandSpace’s Zhuque-3, which had been due to launch from Jiuquan early on Tuesday, has been postponed ahead of what would be the company’s second attempt to achieve China’s first orbital-class rocket recovery.

It is not clear if the incident will affect Chang’e-7, China’s robotic mission to the lunar south pole, which is scheduled to lift off from Wenchang on August 24 aboard a Long March-5.

The Long March-5’s boosters use engines from the same YF-100 family as the Long March-7A, meaning an engine-related problem could potentially have implications for its schedule. If the failure proves to be structural and specific to the Long March-7A, however, the impact may be more limited.

De Grijs said that given they shared some technologies, “because Monday’s accident occurred early in flight, before we know its cause I would not say categorically that Chang’e-7 is unaffected”.

He said that because Chang’e-7 was a critical scientific and strategic lunar mission, Chinese authorities remained highly motivated not to take unnecessary risks. Delaying the launch by several days or weeks was considered far less damaging than launching before the underlying cause of this failure was properly understood.

“If the investigation quickly identifies an issue specific to the Long March-7A, I would expect the broader programme, including Chang’e-7, to proceed largely as planned,” he said.

“If it points to a shared engine, component or quality-control issue, the consequences could be considerably wider.”

Meanwhile, de Grijs said the Zhuque-3, whose launch planned for Tuesday was postponed, was a commercial rocket that was developed independently and used distinct technology, meaning that a Long March-7A failure was unlikely to have a direct technical impact on it.

“At this stage I would interpret that primarily as sensible caution rather than evidence of a shared problem,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] China is building nuclear reactors faster than the West. Can it keep up the pace?
item.description:
When Francois Morin, China director at the World Nuclear Association – a leading international industry body – took a group of foreign nuclear engineers to a Shanghai Electric plant last year, the scale of production caught them off guard.

Heavy machinery, from steam generators to reactor cores, was already assembled and ready for shipment to sites where construction had not even begun. The equipment towered over the delegates, many of whom were accustomed to supply chains back home that produce such components one at a time, if at all.

“It was in this place that they understood how China’s construction capability compared to Western ones,” Morin said.
item.content:encoded:
When Francois Morin, China director at the World Nuclear Association – a leading international industry body – took a group of foreign nuclear engineers to a Shanghai Electric plant last year, the scale of production caught them off guard.

Heavy machinery, from steam generators to reactor cores, was already assembled and ready for shipment to sites where construction had not even begun. The equipment towered over the delegates, many of whom were accustomed to supply chains back home that produce such components one at a time, if at all.

“It was in this place that they understood how China’s construction capability compared to Western ones,” Morin said.

Despite connecting its first nuclear power plant to the grid in 1991, decades after Western pioneers, China today is building reactors faster and at lower cost than its peers. Since the end of 2016, it has added 27 operational nuclear units, nearly doubling installed capacity, according to calculations based on official data.

By contrast, the United States – still the global leader in nuclear capacity – added just two new units over the same period, hampered by lengthy delays and financing challenges.

“In terms of continuity in construction experience, China is now the only country in the world that has that,” said Victor Nian, founding co-chairman of the Centre for Strategic Energy and Resources think tank based in Singapore.

Yet, even as nuclear power remains central to Beijing’s green transition, sustaining that breakneck pace over the long term presents new challenges. As prime space for sites grows scarce, the industry is racing to develop next-generation alternatives – and potentially look inland.

The economics behind China’s nuclear edge

While scientists broadly consider modern nuclear energy one of the safest forms of electricity generation, a handful of high-profile historical disasters has slowed global adoption over the decades.

China is so efficient ... because the builders have access to loans at low interest rates

Francois Morin, World Nuclear Association

In the US, expansion ground to a halt following the Three Mile Island accident in Pennsylvania in 1979, as protests and lawsuits drove up regulatory hurdles and damaged public support. European construction similarly froze after the Chernobyl disaster in Ukraine in 1986.

Decades later, the 2011 Fukushima Daiichi meltdown in Japan triggered another global retreat. Even China temporarily paused new project approvals to conduct nationwide safety audits, but by late 2012 it lifted the suspension as much of the world remained hesitant.

This continuous buildout allowed Chinese companies to gain experience, reduce construction timelines and lower costs, Nian explained, while standardisation pushed prices down further.

Today, China’s nuclear deployment centres on two primary pressurised water reactor designs: the domestic Hualong One, co-developed by state enterprises China National Nuclear Corporation (CNNC) and the China General Nuclear Power Group, and the CAP1000, a localised adaptation of American manufacturer Westinghouse’s AP1000.

“The supply chain is all built around this standardisation,” Nian said, noting that domestic suppliers now manufacture nearly every component required for new reactors. With equipment produced locally and project schedules coordinated by state planning, China’s ability to complete reactors in five years was “not a surprise”, Nian added.

By contrast, the latest commercial nuclear additions in the US – Units 3 and 4 at Plant Vogtle in Georgia – each took more than a decade to complete, suffering severe cost and schedule overruns before entering service in 2023 and 2024 respectively.

Morin of the World Nuclear Association argued that financing costs were the main obstacle to Western build times, contrasting with China’s model. “That is the true brake on speed,” Morin said. “China is so efficient ... because the builders have access to loans at low interest rates.”

Backed by state-directed capital, domestic heavy equipment makers secure funding to build major components long before site assembly begins. This, in turn, enables suppliers to deliver finished parts ahead of construction schedules, as Morin’s delegation saw at Shanghai Electric.

Standardised designs and a steady pace of approvals by the State Council, China’s cabinet – which has greenlit at least 10 reactor units annually since 2022 – also reassured manufacturers that they would continue to receive future orders, he added.

The result of the model, Morin said, was shorter construction timelines and a lower levelised cost of electricity (LCOE) – a metric used to measure the average cost of power generation over a plant’s lifespan, calculated at 60 years for nuclear plants.

According to Morin’s estimates, the LCOE for a 1 gigawatt (GW) reactor financed at a 5 per cent interest rate was about US$83 per megawatt-hour (MWh). Under China’s state-backed model, where borrowing rates can fall to just 1.5 per cent, that cost drops by nearly half to US$42 per MWh.

With speed and cost under control, China’s nuclear ambitions are rapidly gaining pace as it targets 110GW of installed capacity by 2030, bolstering fixed-asset investment amid a broader soft domestic economy.

The country currently operates 62 nuclear units with a combined capacity of 66.1GW, while another 58 units totalling 69.5GW were under construction, according to National Energy Administration data reported by state-run People’s Daily on August 3.

By comparison, the US had about 98.4GW of capacity currently in operation, according to the US Energy Information Administration, albeit with no major commercial reactors under construction. This puts China on track to surpass America within the next few years.

Modest share, big ambitions

Despite this rapid growth, Chinese nuclear power has accounted for only about 5 per cent of the national electricity mix in recent years – a share Morin expected to rise only marginally even as absolute capacity expands. Coal continued to generate about half of the country’s total electricity, while renewables like wind and solar accounted for 41.2 per cent in the first half of 2026, according to the National Energy Administration.

That remained far below the world’s other two top nuclear operators, the US and France, where nuclear provided about one-fifth and 70 per cent of electricity respectively, according to official data.

Even so, industry analysts warned against dismissing nuclear energy based solely on its relatively modest share.

China’s overall power consumption is expanding rapidly as it moves towards its climate targets – peaking carbon emissions by 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality by 2060 – prompting Beijing to deploy every available low-carbon energy source.

“We’re in this incredible race to add enough power generation capacity in China to meet what is adding one extra Germany of new electricity consumption every year,” said David Fishman, a principal at energy consultancy The Lantau Group.

“Nuclear in China is cost-competitive enough to actually be part of the equation, and it is low carbon.”

National power consumption rose 5 per cent to surpass 10 trillion kilowatt-hours for the first time in 2025, driven by surging demand from advanced manufacturing and artificial intelligence, and is only expected to continue rising.

However, Fishman noted that maintaining stability on a grid with such a high share of renewables would create distinct challenges.

Solar and wind generation fluctuate with the weather and require costly utility-scale battery storage to help keep the grid stable. They also need substantial investment in ultra-high-voltage transmission lines to move power from western regions – home to most of the country’s solar and wind farms – to coastal demand centres.

Nuclear power provides reliable, continuous baseload output and would help relieve some of the structural pressures on the grid, Fishman said.

The coastal expansion conundrum

While nationally modest, nuclear power’s role shifts drastically at the provincial level, Morin pointed out.

In the southeastern province of Fujian – which has a population of 42 million, comparable with Canada – nuclear power accounted for 28.1 per cent of electricity generation last year, according to a report published by a nuclear centre under the National Energy Administration last month.

In Liaoning province, an industrial base in the northeast, it supplied more than one-fifth of total electricity generation last year and about 18.5 per cent and 16.9 per cent in the southern provinces of Hainan and Guangdong respectively.

In those provinces, nuclear power plays a crucial role in the grid instead of merely acting as a supplement. “Once you have it, you cannot switch it off,” Morin said.

At the same time, all operational and under-construction commercial reactors are currently restricted to coastal regions, after Beijing suspended approvals for inland nuclear plants following the 2011 Fukushima meltdown.

Unlike coastal plants that draw on open ocean water, inland reactors often rely on rivers for cooling. This exposes them to drought, which could hinder cooling capacity, while accidents risk contaminating vital downstream drinking supplies.

Industry analysts warned, however, that the country would eventually hit an expansion ceiling.

“China will physically run out of suitable sites at some point,” Fishman said, adding that inland reactors would help provide stable, dispatchable power to central and western regions.

Morin agreed, noting that China’s 31 identified coastal sites could accommodate about 163 reactors, representing about 192GW of total capacity.

In May, a representative for CNNC said national operational capacity was projected to reach 170GW by 2035, before rising to between 400 and 500GW by 2060 – more than double the capacity that existing coastal sites can support.

If China lifted the inland moratorium, Morin said, the development pipeline would expand to 77 total sites nationwide, providing capacity for 345 reactors and about 419GW. This could reach 500GW should China develop more CAP1400 reactors, the enlarged version of the CAP1000 design, he added.

Embracing next-generation technology

Beijing is pushing next-generation reactor designs that require less water and enhance safety, making them better suited to inland deployment. Among these are fast-neutron reactors, which typically use liquid sodium or lead rather than water as a coolant, Morin said.

China already operates two 600-megawatt (MW) demonstration fast-neutron reactors in Xiapu, Fujian province, designed to recycle spent fuel and generate more fissile material than they consume.

Nian of the Centre for Strategic Energy and Resources noted that thorium molten-salt reactors could present another option. These use liquid salt instead of water and operate close to ordinary atmospheric pressure.

While early tests at a 2MW experimental reactor in Gansu province had progressed as planned, Nian cautioned that commercial scaling faced major technical hurdles because of the high corrosiveness of molten salt and the lack of a commercial supply chain for thorium fuel processing.

Still, these experimental reactors could one day reduce China’s reliance on uranium – a crucial step for a nation almost entirely reliant on imports.

According to Damien Ma, director and chair of the Carnegie China research centre, the country accounted for about a quarter of global uranium demand but was dependent on imports for 80 to 90 per cent of its supply.

The next four to five years are going to be a very telling period, because a lot of things are supposed to come online around then

Damien Ma, Carnegie China

To hedge against supply risks, state-owned nuclear companies have bought controlling stakes in Namibian uranium mines and acquired mining assets in Kazakhstan, two countries with some of the richest uranium reserves in the world, Ma noted.

Morin also pointed to estimates that China had likely maintained several years of strategic uranium stockpiles to buffer against potential supply disruptions.

Additionally, Beijing announced major uranium discoveries in two of the country’s autonomous regions last year: Ordos Basin in Inner Mongolia and the Tarim Basin in Xinjiang, in the country’s north and west, respectively. Authorities have not disclosed the ore grades or commercial viability of the finds.

Beyond conventional nuclear power, China has also joined the global race to develop nuclear fusion. Unlike fission, which generates power by splitting heavy atoms, fusion combines light atomic nuclei and promises abundant energy without long-lived radioactive waste or meltdown risks.

However, analysts remain divided on its near-term commercial viability. “I don’t think it will be a relevant energy play for the global decarbonisation timeline, which is carbon neutrality by 2050 or 2060,” Fishman said.

Nian echoed these concerns, noting that while scientific progress had been exciting, widespread deployment was likely decades away because of technical, supply chain and regulatory constraints.

In contrast, Ma offered a more optimistic outlook, highlighting a surge of investment and private sector activity in recent years – particularly in the US, which could hold an edge over China’s predominantly state-directed initiatives.

“I’ve just not seen this amount of private sector energy and entrepreneurialism put behind fusion in my lifetime,” he said. “The next four to five years are going to be a very telling period, because a lot of things are supposed to come online around then.”

item.title: [SCMP] Historian Wang Gungwu on US credibility and why Xi thinks ‘only the party can save China’
item.description:
Professor Wang Gungwu is regarded internationally as an authority on Chinese history. The 95-year-old is best known for his explorations of Chinese history in the long view, and for his writings on the Chinese diaspora. He has been a professor at the National University of Singapore since 2007 and emeritus professor at the Australian National University since 1988. He was vice-chancellor of the University of Hong Kong from 1986 to 1995.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The US-China rivalry is now quite prominent on the world stage. Do you think these two countries are facing the Thucydides Trap? How do you see their rivalry unfolding?
item.content:encoded:
Professor Wang Gungwu is regarded internationally as an authority on Chinese history. The 95-year-old is best known for his explorations of Chinese history in the long view, and for his writings on the Chinese diaspora. He has been a professor at the National University of Singapore since 2007 and emeritus professor at the Australian National University since 1988. He was vice-chancellor of the University of Hong Kong from 1986 to 1995.

This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The US-China rivalry is now quite prominent on the world stage. Do you think these two countries are facing the Thucydides Trap? How do you see their rivalry unfolding?

At one level, it is really similar to the United States and Soviet Union Cold War because both have nuclear weapons.

The question of having to fight one another and the possibility of using nuclear weapons makes it unlikely that they will fight each other. Fighting through proxies would be the same as during the Cold War.

I think military strategists would think that the way to deal with the situation when there’s US and China rivalry is to have another Cold War, and for the US to use the same methods that they used to destroy the Soviet Union.

They would destroy the China threat in the sense of undermining its power. If they can do that without fighting, that would be ideal because fighting is dangerous.

I think the strategists ever since the fall of the Soviet Union have decided that there’s no power out there that can threaten the United States. The only possible one was China in the long run.

They have been preparing for this for quite some time and have had arguments within the United States as to how to deal with China.

There are those who say that if you give China the chance to join the World Trade Organization, the Chinese economy will develop more like a capitalist economy. Then one day China will have a large middle class, no ideology to divide us. We can coexist and there’s no need to fight.

That view took precedence, and China was allowed to join the World Trade Organization. And the Chinese developed economically at a fantastic rate.

Some US analysts said that was the wrong decision because China is now strong enough to challenge the United States. How do you see the future US-China relationship?

What they discovered was that China was not like the Soviet Union. The Soviet Union had military power but was economically weak. One key reason was that they had no access to the oceans. The Baltic was blocked. So was the Black Sea. They never managed to develop an economy like that of western Europe.

The Chinese people were not only entrepreneurial but also had easy access to maritime trade. That has given them the capacity to fund military expansion. When the Russians tried to match the United States in their arms race, their economy collapsed. China can manage an arms race to defend itself if its economy continues to do well.

But I think the Chinese believe that they will never benefit from fighting the Americans. They just want to be secure from any aggression from the oceans.

In the past, China’s enemies had come only from the continent. But in the 19th century, the British and the French attacked from Southeast Asia where they had their naval bases.

The Americans joined in when they took the Philippines. When the whole of Southeast Asia was in the hands of foreign powers, the Chinese coasts were vulnerable.

That forced China to accept all those unequal treaties. But it taught the Chinese a lesson. They will never neglect maritime power again. They are now prepared for any threats by land, sea or air.

They are very concerned about attacks by sea. You can see how, in the South China Sea, their focus is on missiles that can deter powerful naval forces like aircraft carriers from getting near China. You can make a long list of what the Chinese have done. It is basically defensive to make sure that the Americans can never attack China from nearby.

As the US marks the 250th anniversary of its independence, some are asking if America’s golden days are over, especially after what has happened in Iran and the Strait of Hormuz. What’s your take on this?

They have certainly lost their credibility. In other words, in the past when they said they would do something, they succeeded because they had the power to do so.

In the Iraq-Afghanistan conflicts after 20 years of fighting, spending billions of dollars and achieving absolutely nothing, they lost credibility. The Iran thing looks a bit like that. They want to control and destroy the regime in Iran, but they find they can’t do so.

The only way they can do so is to invade Iran, but the Iraq-Afghanistan affair taught them a lesson. Don’t attack on land.

They are trying to destroy everything that Iran has, hoping Iranians will give up and just surrender. That has turned out to be much more difficult than they expected. The only way they can win is to land troops.

I think [Donald] Trump knows that he has made a mistake to have gone this far and is trying to end the war by persuading the Iranians to do a deal. But the Iranians are making it difficult for him to say that he has won.

Their main weapon is to control the Strait of Hormuz. It’s not a legal problem any more. It’s a question of whether they have the capacity to control the strait. In the meantime, the allies of the United States are also having a hard time, shipping is almost completely blocked, and the whole world is being badly affected.

So we cannot conclude that the US is in decline yet – we can only say it lost the Iranian war?

The word “decline” is not the right word because it is still the most powerful military force in the world. The US spends far more on their military than most of the major powers added together.

I have lost count of how many military bases they have in all continents. They have aircraft carriers in every ocean, and they have tremendous air power. And nuclear weapons which only a few other countries have.

I would say that in military terms and in terms of the economy, the Americans are not doing badly despite all these problems. They are still in charge of so many economic levers, imposing tariffs on everybody.

They’re probably not doing as well as they want, but there is no doubt that the military and the arms industry are doing extremely well. It is obvious that the richest people in America are getting richer every day.

Also, the capacity to be inventive and make technological advances is still very great. I think that the Chinese know that they’re catching up but they’re still behind. The Chinese are still learning from the people they sent to America to learn.

Furthermore, the US has one advantage that China and others don’t have. It is totally safe in its hemisphere. No country in the Americas can threaten the United States. Therefore, they are free to send their aircraft carriers anywhere around the world to exercise their hegemonic power.

In comparison, China has problems in its neighbourhood. On land, China tries hard to keep good relations with Russia and North Korea. At sea, they have to make friends with the countries in Southeast Asia and are trying very hard to make sure that their borders are safe.

China is working closely with Russia to promote a multipolar world order, which the US probably doesn’t like. Do you think this multipolar world order will happen and the US will have to face it?

The Chinese say that they want a multipolar order and believe that that’s safer for them.

The Americans believe that a multipolar order would be a very difficult one to control and the disorder would be distracting. If they can’t have universal hegemony, they would prefer a bipolar order.

With bipolarity, they could concentrate on China. They have learned lessons from the way they destroyed the Soviet Union and would focus on undermining China’s economic growth.

They can limit China’s rich markets in North America and western Europe. They could allow the Belt and Road Initiative to help China reach the markets and resources of the underdeveloped world, but those countries cannot buy much from China.

The Chinese could go on producing manufactured goods cheaper and faster, but if the West can limit the Chinese sales, China’s economy would slow down significantly.

In one interview you talked about continuity in Chinese history – how the rulers highlighted the importance of a centralised bureaucracy and the people believed it and this was the case for hundreds of years. Do you think the way modern China is governed continues this pattern, and is there anything unique about the governance of modern China?

I think China is unique in its sense of continuity from the Shang-Zhou dynasty down to the present. And although it had dynastic changes, many foreign invaders, and was even under total foreign rule, it has always been China. Even the Mongols and the Manchus had to rule China primarily in the Chinese way – what the Chinese literati believed was the best way to rule China.

In historical records, they kept a picture of China as having had one history as a centralised bureaucratic state.

It was the Qin-Han empires that produced the mix of Legalist and Confucian ideas by which everything had to be decided from the centre. Officials were appointed to ensure total control.

The Qin dynasty did not last long. The people couldn’t stand its harsh Legalist system and revolted against it after Qin Shi Huang’s death.

The Han dynasty was wiser. Its founder led the rebellion against the Qin. He and his successors developed a softer regime. They retained the Legalist central bureaucratic state but brought in Confucian officials to reform the structure.

The new officials placed emphasis upon the emperor being a good man, being moral and caring, serving and looking after the people, making sure there is social harmony, and so on. That way, you have security within the country and the people won’t rebel.

Confucius advised that rulers must be good. They must make their people feel that they care for their livelihood. For example, they should worry about them and make sure, for example, that their taxes are very low. They should on the whole leave people alone to live their lives with minimum government interference.

They appointed officials from the centre, but these officials were not asked to do much. Don’t do much more than just collect the taxes and make sure that there were no rebellions. Those were the two main jobs they had to do well so the people were left very much alone to do whatever they wanted for their families.

Every part of the country could develop in its own way. The idea was that in this way everyone looked to the centre for a caring ruler who would always have the mandate of heaven. Although the mandate of heaven was normally won on the battlefield, heaven was on the side of the people, and the mandate was given to the person whom the people believed would be a good ruler.

If you were a good ruler, you would have the mandate. If you were a bad one, the people had the right to rebel against you. That was the mechanism of dynastic change whereby the people could determine who should head the new dynasty.

Another test was whether the ruler could defend the country against the enemy. Rulers who could always do so would retain the people’s respect. Their dynasties would then survive for longer with the people’s loyal support.

The Confucians described the various ways the rulers could best care for their people. That was the most important contribution to the good governance that was so valued throughout all Chinese history. In short, performance record was the key.

In modern times, the 1911 revolution threw out the emperors of the dynastic system and became a republican state modelled on France and the United States. Sun Yat-sen’s Republic of China became a nation state – that is, the state of all the citizens of China.

It didn’t work because the Chinese simply didn’t understand what a republic was, what was a citizen, what were his/her constitutional rights, freedom, liberty, democracy because all these ideas were new. It took a couple of decades to teach people about modern politics.

In the meantime, the country was pressured by the Japanese and there were unequal treaties that hampered economic development. Also, the country was falling apart because of the civil war among the warlords and the ideological struggles between the Nationalists and the Communists. In the end, the Nationalist Party were ousted in 1949 by Mao Zedong’s Communist Party.

Now the Communists brought in something new. They brought in the idea of a very disciplined party dedicated to revolution to make sure that you don’t depend on the past. They set out on a new path to progress. As you know, the Marxist idea of historical progress was a European idea.

Karl Marx showed that in history, stages of change meant that there was progress. His example of progress was to prove that socialism was the stage after capitalism. Before that, there had been slavery and feudalism followed by capitalism.

By the 19th century, capitalism was all-powerful. But capitalism will eventually become socialist. This was what Marx predicted. The progress to socialism meant there would then be a state that was more caring.

In China, this was taken up by the Communists who set out to revolutionise society so that there would be no poverty, better distribution of wealth, with nobody too rich, nobody too poor and where social harmony prevailed.

In recent years, some leaders in the People’s Republic have revived the idea of a caring state organised to produce a fairer distribution of wealth. There are thinkers who have compared that to some Confucian references to rulers being committed to the well-being of their people.

The terminology used by the Communists is quite different but the sentiments behind the words can be compared favourably with some moral goals that would find favour with Confucian philosophers.

The caring is not by one man as a good and moral emperor, but a political party consisting of highly disciplined members. In the Chinese tradition, the emperor was above the law because he made the law. The Communist Party, like the emperor, is not subject to the law courts because it made the law.

When the Communist Party discovers that somebody in the party has done something wrong and party discipline has found him guilty, the person is sacked from the party. He would then be charged in a court of law because, as a party member, he is above the law. That would be very strange in most countries, but it is more like the way Chinese emperors were above the law.

As a result, serious problems can be created. With the country ruled in that way, it is understandable that people have little confidence that the legal system can be just.

When the economy was doing very well under Jiang Zemin and Hu Jintao, corruption was pervasive throughout the country. Xi Jinping saw it when he was in Fujian and Zhejiang. He didn’t have the power to do much, but he must have observed it with deep concern.

When he was given the power to act as secretary general of the party, the first thing he did was to tell the Communist Party to study what happened to the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.

The CCP was modelled on that, so look how quickly that party collapsed. There was corruption and factionalism and the leaders could not agree as to what they could do. They had lost their revolutionary ideals and the party did not have the sense of purpose to discipline its members.

Xi Jinping talked to the party about every member being subject to the law of corruptibility. In that sense, his legalistic intervention was to try and save the party. I think he genuinely believes that only the party can save China and make China strong so that it can recover its position in the world today.

He believes that, to save the party, the party must be clean and disciplined. Only then will the people love the party and believe that only the party can save China.

I think this is what he is determined to do and why he wants better control of everything in the country. It’s not easy because corruption is so pervasive.

He has been in power for about 14 years now and he is still finding corrupt people in high office. He is still catching thousands of party leaders every year, sending them to the law courts and putting them in jail, including having some of his most senior PLA generals sentenced to death.

That’s how serious it is after 14 years. This shows that fighting corruption is not enough. There are important institutions that need to be totally reviewed and restructured.

In the meantime, the system could be locked up so that few dare to take initiative with original projects. Officials would feel safer by continuing with projects that have worked in the past.

Everyone is wary of being caught in the anti-corruption campaign. If you were a bureaucrat or a party secretary, you would have to be brave to start a new project. If you start a project with other officials, how can you be sure that none of them are corrupt?

The net result is that less is being done and only safe decisions are being made.

Of course, not everything depends on the centre. It is in the Chinese tradition that the centre did not expect every part of the country to wait for the centre to tell them what to do.

There had always been decentralisation of power to provinces, cities, counties where officials were encouraged to familiarise themselves with local conditions and find the best way to make their respective areas successful.

Today, when GDP rises, everybody is happy, and if protests occur, they are resolved effectively and not allowed to spread. If the official manages these well, he can expect to be promoted.

If an official initiates something new, there are always risks. To be ever careful, it is probably wiser to do as little as possible.

In general, the industrial economy looks as if it is stagnating. Unemployment has become serious. The number of graduates looking for jobs is huge. As a result, the sense of security is not as good as the party leaders had hoped for.

And because of this lack of social security, there has been the trend to extend control over anything foreign – for example, restrictions on reading materials published outside. Professors refrain from teaching from textbooks that are not published and approved by the party. A picture emerges that such controls are actually making people less confident in their daily lives.

There are tensions in China, especially among the young generation, that the party has not been able to lighten.

My view is that China’s problems are more domestic. Outside, its leaders know how to handle the United States, like the way they managed the visits of Presidents Trump, [Vladimir] Putin and Kim [Jong-un].

In external affairs, the Chinese are managing alright. The domestic problems look much more serious. It is not a matter of having enough fresh talent. The people are very talented, but they need to be given more freedom and opportunity to be creative and make things even better.

What’s your view on Taiwan? How can it be resolved? Or do you think the tension will only worsen?

Taiwan reminds me of the “one country, two systems” issue that Hong Kong is familiar with. Taiwan was always part of China. After the war ended in 1945, everything taken by Japan had to be returned to China. That was internationally recognised.

When Chiang Kai-shek went to Taiwan in 1949, the issue was still clear and open.

A few months afterwards, however, North Korea invaded the South and United Nations forces were sent to war. China’s volunteers supported North Korea and drove the UN troops back to the 38th Parallel.

With China fighting the UN armies, conditions rapidly changed for the PRC’s [People’s Republic of China’s] chances to replace the ROC [Republic of China, Taiwan’s official name] in the UN.

As a result, the Republic of China in Taiwan was recognised as China for another 22 years.

The PRC was the enemy of the US in the Cold War and any question of the United States and China talking about diplomatic relations and admission into the UN was completely lost. The US could use its veto power to stop the PRC from taking over the ROC’s position in the Security Council.

It was not until the United Nations General Assembly voted with a two-thirds majority in favour that China was admitted.

At that point, America was prepared to recognise the ROC in Taiwan as an independent state and support its membership in the United Nations.

I believe that Chiang Kai-shek refused on the grounds that there was only one China and it was wrong to allow the PRC to take over from the ROC.

Once the PRC was in the UN Security Council, it would have used its veto against the ROC’s admission anyway.

What was significant at the time was that Mao Zedong would have agreed with Chiang that there was only one China.

Later, the local Taiwanese people found that the constitution of the Republic of China allowed for democracy. After Chiang Ching-kuo passed the presidency to Lee Teng-hui, the elections that followed could for the first time vote in a pro-independence party to form the government.

The new Taiwanese leaders were then able to claim that the Taiwan people had voted to say that they wanted to be independent. They now had a government that was of the people, by the people and for the people.

The PRC leaders did not accept that and made it quite clear that if the new leaders declared independence, they would have to take the island by force.

This led the Americans to intervene to tell the Taiwanese not to count on their support if they declared independence. They recognised that a declaration of independence would have crossed China’s red line.

For now, it is a balanced situation with the status quo acceptable for both sides. It allows the Taiwanese to say that they don’t need to declare independence as the Republic of China has been there since 1912. And the US Congress continues to vote for military equipment to be sold for Taiwan’s defence as long as it does not declare independence.

Taiwan continues to make friends with other countries that are anti-communist. Japan for one seems ready to help. This angers the Chinese.

But I believe that the Chinese do not want to fight over Taiwan because that would mean killing other Chinese and it would involve interventions by countries coming to Taiwan’s defence. No one would gain out of that war.

I think both Americans and the PRC would agree not to fight a war over Taiwan.

What Beijing wants to be sure of is that Taiwan is not used by its enemies in any attack on China.

If Taiwan remains friendly to Beijing or at least stays neutral or in sympathy with Beijing and recognise themselves as Chinese people with the same culture and civilisation, I think the status quo could remain for quite a while.

In any case, the Chinese can take a long view. There’s no immediate hurry.

With the long view, such divisions within China have happened many times in Chinese history. During those periods of division, the view was that China would always become one again.

How do you see your own legacy?

I don’t know that I have any legacy. I would like to believe that I have convinced some people that history is very important.

Everybody has history and everybody’s history is useful to know so that you have some idea of what it was like in the past. What mistakes were made, what would be the right things to do. What made for good governance, for example, would be very important in modern affairs in any kind of world order.

Good governance is extremely important and history tells us about that in the way that is part of the Chinese tradition.

History is not about the truth. Finding out what exactly happened is important. But it is not why knowing the past is often crucial.

History is what is known about the past that could help you understand the present and give you a clearer idea of what is likely and what can and cannot happen.

To make history meaningful to your own thinking about anything in the world could be very interesting and valuable anyway.

It would be very satisfying if I could convince people that everything has a past and every past has some usefulness. If they learn to use the past to get a better understanding of what is happening, they would find that enlightening.

I believe that knowing the past also helps good governance. History changes all the time and is often rewritten. Therefore, governments who pay no attention to history are likely to make mistakes.

Think of the number of times history has been rewritten in the last few decades. How many are written by the Europeans, by the Americans, by the Chinese Nationalists, by the Japanese, by the Communists? Every one of their histories can be changed over time.

During the early decades of the PRC, people wrote history using Marxist arguments about everything, but today nobody writes like that any more.

People don’t write Chinese history following Marx’s stages of change. What Marx did teach them was about the idea of progress. He showed that human beings have been progressing; they produced more and better goods, became better than slaves and feudal peasants.

In today’s terms, he could be interpreted to argue that capitalist wealth could lead to a better socialist redistribution of that wealth.

The idea of progress shows that the past helps you to understand where we came from and might be going to. This can be seen in the way the Chinese say, look at China today. Can you imagine the kind of science and technology that is happening in China today a hundred years ago? Unimaginable. Therefore, progress is possible and progress will continue to be possible.

I think this is what the Chinese learned by looking at their past. The past has taught them not only that China can survive but can also fall and rise yet again.

But whatever they did, if they put their heart into it, worked hard at it, learned from the past and provided good governance, there would be more progress. And to believe in that idea of progress would depend on their understanding of the past.

item.title: [SCMP] Vietnam pays the price at home for sending workers abroad
item.description:
Vietnam’s seafood and garment sectors are facing a labour shortfall even with raised wages, as Hanoi expands a drive to send more workers overseas for higher-paying jobs.

The contradiction reflects a broader challenge for the Southeast Asian country as it pushes to move up the value chain while banking on labour migration to generate remittance revenue, analysts say.

According to the home ministry, between 130,000 and 150,000 Vietnamese go abroad to work annually. The overseas labour market totalled nearly 900,000 by the end of last year.
item.content:encoded:
Vietnam’s seafood and garment sectors are facing a labour shortfall even with raised wages, as Hanoi expands a drive to send more workers overseas for higher-paying jobs.

The contradiction reflects a broader challenge for the Southeast Asian country as it pushes to move up the value chain while banking on labour migration to generate remittance revenue, analysts say.

According to the home ministry, between 130,000 and 150,000 Vietnamese go abroad to work annually. The overseas labour market totalled nearly 900,000 by the end of last year.

This May alone, 1,948 Vietnamese went abroad to work in places such as China, Japan, South Korea, Singapore and Europe, according to a Department of Overseas Labour report on June 3.

Vietnamese abroad remit between US$6 billion and US$7 billion a year, contributing significantly to the national economy.

This exodus has led to a labour shortage at home.

A report submitted in late June by the Vietnam Association of Seafood Exporters and Producers to the Ministry of Finance highlighted worker shortages as a major shortcoming the industry is facing in key hubs such as the Mekong Delta and Ho Chi Minh City. Even salary increases of 25 to 30 per cent did not help with recruitment and retaining labour.

Similarly, the Vietnam Textile and Apparel Association issued a report after a meeting with Deputy Prime Minister Pham Gia Tuc in May saying that competition for labour was “increasingly fierce”.

The industry was contending not just with overseas rivals but also higher-paying electronics and machinery producers, said Hoang Lan Anh, a labour migration researcher at the University of Melbourne.

Association chairman Do Ngoc Tai said in an industrial conference on July 30 that many garment factories lacked “sufficient manpower to ensure order deadlines or secure new contracts” and had to compete for workers with “electronics and many other manufacturing sectors”.

Forced migration

However, the picture is more complicated than factory workers simply leaving for overseas jobs.

For many people from poorer central provinces, the choice was between overseas or domestic migration, and low-paid work in industrial hubs – rather than a local job versus emigration, Anh said.

“Labour exports have been treated by the government primarily as a poverty-reduction strategy because migrant workers mainly come from the disaster-prone and resource-poor central Vietnam, where food processing and manufacturing roles offer very low wages,” she said. Salaries in the area usually range from US$200 to US$250.

Hoang said most central Vietnamese she interviewed told her they would need to migrate to earn a living, as there were no viable local opportunities. So it was more worthwhile to go overseas and earn more money than what would be offered in north or south Vietnam.

“If someone migrates from Nghe An province [in central Vietnam] to Binh Duong [a major industrial hub just north of Ho Chi Minh City] to work, their capacity to visit the family and perform care duties is not much different from that of someone in Japan or South Korea,” Anh said.

Moreover, central Vietnam migrants were “socially disadvantaged when competing for the higher-paying electronics or industrial manufacturing jobs in the north and south, where social networking was important for entry and mobility in the labour market”, she added.

Though there were plenty of vacancies in the seafood export and garment sectors, workers usually earn between US$250 and US$350 a month – barely sufficient for household expenses.

“By comparison, Vietnamese workers in destinations such as Japan and South Korea can earn three to five times more. Overseas employment offers rural migrant workers the only avenue for ensuring the family’s economic security,” Anh said.

Workers’ protection

This is a familiar calculation for Jiho Yoshimizu, the representative director of the Japan-Vietnam Tomoiki/Mutual Support Association.

The association has provided consultation and support to about 50,000 Vietnamese – from students and technical trainees to skilled workers – in Japan since it was registered as a non-profit organisation in 2014.

“Many Vietnamese workers hoped to earn and save more than they can at home, send money to family, pay their recruitment debts, build a house and support their families, or start a business when they return,” Yoshimizu said.

However, the high earnings expected do not always reflect the final savings, with deductions such as tax, social insurance, housing, utilities and other costs taking a chunk out of the worker’s salaries.

Recruitment and training debts could also leave some Vietnamese workers vulnerable to exploitation and unable to leave workplaces, even when they encountered harassment, unpaid wages, overworking or a totally different job than what had been promised.

“The main issue is not simply whether wages in Japan are higher than those in Vietnam,” Yoshimizu said. “It is whether workers receive accurate information before departure, whether recruitment costs are reasonable, and whether they can work in a safe environment where their rights are protected.”

Nguyen Thi Bich Ngoc, from the central Ha Tinh province, moved to Japan first as an international student, then found a full-time job through an online recruitment platform and obtained a work visa.

“In Vietnam, I worked as a customer support agent for an international online learning platform. Here, I work for a company that provides support services for foreign residents, helping them set up essential utility services,” Ngoc said.

She would return to Vietnam, she said, if she could find a job that would pay her a competitive salary and give her the opportunity to use her English and Japanese skills. “Being close to my family and friends is something I value very much,” Ngoc added.

Ngoc has the luxury of being able to wait for the right opportunity. Most of her fellow Vietnamese in Japan tended to be rural residents with limited formal education or recognised skills – who would likely have ended up in similarly low-skilled or manual jobs had they remained in Vietnam.

“Most migrant workers aim only to earn a fair wage and save enough money to provide for their families. They may pick up new skills along the way but there is a high chance those skills are irrelevant to their future livelihoods back home,” Anh said.

Rather than assuming overseas work would automatically provide a route into higher-skilled employment on return, Anh said the more immediate task was to protect workers’ rights abroad.

“What seems to be more realistic is to make sure that workers’ rights are protected, they receive the same wages and benefits offered to local workers doing the same jobs, and intermediaries’ involvement, exploitation, and abuse are done away with,” she said.

Nguyen Van Duan, an automotive technician from the central Quang Nam province, said he went to Japan after learning of the opportunity through a recruitment agency. The higher salary was a draw, but so was the chance to learn technical skills, improve his Japanese and work in a more disciplined professional environment.

Like Ngoc, if he could earn a stable income back home, save money and continue his career growth, he would have seriously considered staying.

Duan hopes to use his experience and knowledge gained in Japan to build a career in Vietnam’s automotive repair industry upon his return.

“A workplace that offers opportunities to learn, fair treatment, job stability, and a clear career path is just as important,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] As mainland China tightens its tax rules, can Hong Kong remain a magnet for billionaires?
item.description:
For decades, Hong Kong has been a magnet for the rich.

From wealthy Chinese setting up family trusts to millionaires migrating from across Southeast Asia, all of them have been sucked in by the city’s promise of free capital flows, a trustworthy legal system and extensive financial expertise.

It is a winning combination that helped Hong Kong leapfrog Switzerland as the world’s biggest cross-border wealth hub last year, as the city rode a wave of blockbuster listings by Chinese technology companies.
item.content:encoded:
For decades, Hong Kong has been a magnet for the rich.

From wealthy Chinese setting up family trusts to millionaires migrating from across Southeast Asia, all of them have been sucked in by the city’s promise of free capital flows, a trustworthy legal system and extensive financial expertise.

It is a winning combination that helped Hong Kong leapfrog Switzerland as the world’s biggest cross-border wealth hub last year, as the city rode a wave of blockbuster listings by Chinese technology companies.

But some worry this model could now come under threat. Over the past few months, Beijing has launched a slew of measures to tighten controls over cross-border financial flows, seeking to prevent tax avoidance and capital flight.

Major brokerages have been punished for helping mainland investors illicitly buy overseas stocks, while banks have tightened checks for mainland customers applying to set up Hong Kong accounts.

Perhaps the most significant news came in late July, when Beijing announced that offshore trusts would now be subject to China’s personal income tax – closing a loophole that had allowed wealthy Chinese families to shield massive amounts of income from taxation.

In Hong Kong, some fear the new rules could disrupt – or even divert – capital flows into the city’s vast wealth management industry. But analysts said the city could benefit over the long term.

“In the short run, the new tax rules may push some mainland investors to adopt a wait-and-see approach,” said Tian Xuan, dean of Peking University’s Guanghua School of Management.

However, “Hong Kong’s future competitiveness lies in compliance capabilities and the depth of its professional services, rather than simply the tax haven effect”.

Hong Kong’s Private Wealth Management Association (PWMA) – which counts 44 financial institutions in Hong Kong as full members – said Beijing’s new offshore trust tax rules provided “regulatory clarity and certainty for global wealth management” and that the city’s unique role as a “super-value adding connector” for global capital remained unchanged.

This move towards compliance will enhance the long-term credibility of Hong Kong’s trust industry

Tian Xuan, Peking University

A hub for Chinese wealth

In May, Hong Kong received a boost when a report by Boston Consulting Group (BCG) found the city had surpassed Switzerland last year to become the world’s largest centre for cross-border wealth.

The amount of cross-border wealth parked in Hong Kong grew by more than 10 per cent to US$2.95 trillion last year, driven by an initial public offering (IPO) bonanza and an influx of capital from mainland China, according to the report.

Hong Kong’s success was built on “cementing its role as China’s gateway to global markets”, with “mainland flows representing over 60 per cent of assets under management” in the city, BCG said.

But that same concentration also “ties its trajectory tightly to economic and regulatory developments on the mainland”, the report cautioned.

As of 2025, Hong Kong was home to 76 billionaires with combined wealth of US$328 billion, while mainland China housed 470 with a combined worth of some US$1.77 trillion, according to a report by UBS in December.

What’s more, the city’s wealth management industry is likely to benefit as an entire generation of Chinese entrepreneurs ages and prepares to transfer their wealth to their younger relatives.

Over the next 15 years, more than US$300 billion of wealth in mainland China and Hong Kong will be handed over to the next generation, according to UBS.

Behind Beijing’s clampdown

But the new tax rules, announced by China’s Ministry of Finance last month, could complicate that process.

The policy – which took effect immediately – will levy a 20 per cent tax on the gains from offshore trusts with mainland Chinese beneficiaries or whose underlying assets are from the mainland.

The levy will apply to each major part of a trust’s lifespan, from set-up to termination, as well as the distribution of any income. It will also affect any gains dating back to as early as January 1, 2023.

To encourage voluntary reporting, Beijing offered a 90-day grace period for individuals who put their domestic assets – ranging from corporate equities to properties – into offshore trusts between 2023 and 2025 to declare them.

The rules raised concerns in Hong Kong, which has long been a destination of choice for affluent – and often high-profile – Chinese investors to set up offshore trusts, drawn by its low tax rate and strong privacy protections.

The issue became a hot topic in China recently, when children of the late Zong Qinghou – the billionaire founder of drinks company Wahaha Group – launched a legal battle for control over offshore trusts containing assets worth about US$2 billion.

For Beijing, such offshore trusts are a serious issue, as they have allowed the country’s wealthiest families to avoid paying tax on vast amounts of assets.

With Chinese government revenues under pressure amid a prolonged property market downturn, Beijing urgently needs to raise more money from taxes – and clamping down on tax avoidance is a key part of that effort.

Last year, Chinese authorities collected 1.62 trillion yuan (US$240 billion) of income-tax revenues – a steep 11.5 per cent increase over 2024 – as officials stepped up enforcement and closed tax loopholes.

The new rules on offshore trusts are the latest step in that drive. “Not only existing loopholes in tax administration will be plugged, but also a comprehensive cross-border personal income tax system will be established,” lawyers at multinational law firm King & Wood said in a report released on July 26.

For China’s billionaires, the campaign could be painful. As the report noted, a significant proportion of high-net-worth individuals’ overseas income is linked to offshore trusts.

What the rules mean for Hong Kong

The offshore trust tax marks a sharp escalation in China’s tax clampdown, but analysts stressed that the policy was in line with international practices.

“[It] will only eliminate non-compliant ‘grey-area’ practices, without undermining Hong Kong’s status as a global wealth centre,” said Tian of Peking University.

“Indeed, this move towards compliance will enhance the long-term credibility of Hong Kong’s trust industry.”

China is far from alone in fighting tax avoidance. In 2021, members of the G20 agreed to introduce a global corporate minimum tax rate of 15 per cent as part of an effort to prevent large companies from shifting profits to low-tax jurisdictions.

Key Chinese policies such as the country’s tax residency rules – which define anyone living in China for more than 183 days a year as tax resident – are closely modelled on overseas systems such as the US Internal Revenue Service.

To prosper under the new regime, Hong Kong needs to proactively drive the transition of the local offshore trust business towards greater compliance and allay mainland clients’ compliance concerns, according to Tian, who also serves as a Chinese government adviser and a deputy to the National People’s Congress.

Meanwhile, the city should further optimise its tax rules on share-based incentive schemes and trust isolation services to reduce cross-border tax costs for executives at artificial intelligence (AI) firms, Tian added.

That would help attract start-ups to set up related funds in Hong Kong, allowing the city to continue riding China’s tech boom.

Tapping China’s new tech elite

Hong Kong’s ability to serve China’s growing class of billionaire tech entrepreneurs will be key for the future of the city’s wealth management industry, analysts said.

Since early 2025, when the emergence of AI start-up DeepSeek reignited global investor interest in the Chinese tech sector, more than 200 companies have gone public in Hong Kong, raising nearly HK$500 billion between them, according to data from Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing.

The wave of blockbuster listings is being driven primarily by mainland start-ups, which are increasingly choosing to go public in Hong Kong rather than Western markets such as New York amid rising US-China geopolitical frictions.

These IPOs, in turn, are minting an entire new generation of super-rich tech founders, who have their own asset-allocation needs.

For example, Liu Debing, chairman of Chinese AI firm Knowledge Atlas Technology – also known as Zhipu AI – saw his net worth skyrocket after his firm’s Hong Kong IPO at the start of the year.

Liu’s wealth swelled from about US$1 billion in mid-January to US$16.2 billion as of early August, after Zhipu AI’s stock price rose more than sixfold, data from Hurun Group and Forbes showed.

Zhu Yiming, chairman of Chinese chipmakers ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) and GigaDevice Semiconductor, has also seen his net worth inflate from US$2 billion in mid-January to US$15.4 billion as of early August.

As cross-border tax reporting becomes inevitable, compliance might help Hong Kong gain more support from Beijing

Liu Jing, Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business

Hong Kong is well-placed to continue benefiting from the Chinese AI boom – bringing more talent and capital to the city – even as Beijing presses ahead with tighter offshore tax rules, according to Liu Jing, director of the investment research department at the Cheung Kong Graduate School of Business.

“As cross-border tax reporting has become inevitable, compliance might help Hong Kong gain more support from Beijing,” Liu said.

Hong Kong’s proximity to the mainland should help it maintain its competitiveness as an offshore wealth management hub for affluent Chinese investors, he added. After all, rival hubs such as Singapore will also need to deal with the stricter tax rules.

If it can do so, the rewards will be lucrative. With optimism rising regarding China’s ability to overcome US tech sanctions, Chinese AI start-ups have surged in value this year, propelling at least 20 domestic entrepreneurs onto the Hurun Global Rich List 2026.

Though US tech billionaires still dominate the list, Hurun Group’s CEO and co-founder, Sinclair Lyu, said the wave of AI-driven wealth creation had just begun, and China was primed to become a major driver of it.

“With the exciting Hong Kong IPO market and China’s reserves of young talent, we would definitely see more Chinese AI entrepreneurs stand at the top of the future global billionaire rankings,” Lyu said.

Deepening central support

Meanwhile, Beijing is backing Hong Kong to strengthen its role as an international asset and wealth management centre, with a related target included in China’s latest five-year plan.

Wu Qing, chairman of the China Securities Regulatory Commission (CSRC), reaffirmed that support in early August.

“Hong Kong has become the world’s largest cross-border wealth management centre,” Wu said at an event to mark the launch of China’s first offshore government bond futures in the city.

“We will deepen cooperation with Hong Kong counterparts across the board – spanning markets, institutions and products – and spare no effort in injecting new vitality and momentum into the development of the capital market.”

Financial institutions are also expanding their operations in Hong Kong.

HSBC, the city’s top lender, said in May that it would continue to expand the front desk of its wealth management team, with a goal of becoming Asia’s largest wealth manager.

Last month, Sun Life joined the race by launching an integrated wealth management platform to meet rising cross-border demand from high-net-worth individuals.

The PWMA – Hong Kong’s wealth management association – said the enhanced cross-border policies, coupled with accelerating wealth creation driven by the AI boom, would “inject fresh energy and momentum into cross-boundary wealth management, reinforcing Hong Kong’s position as a leading global wealth management hub”.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia’s monarchy charts a new course amid political flux
item.description:
When Malaysian artist Darwisy Mustafani received a commission to paint the country’s king and queen, he did not reach for an ordinary canvas.

Instead, the 25-year-old from the northeastern city of Kota Bharu transformed songket – the lustrous handwoven fabric once reserved for Malay courts and ceremonial dress – into a portrait of the sultan and his wife before a golden-domed palace.

The portrait, commissioned in 2024 by Malaysia’s police force as a gift for Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar and Queen Raja Zarith Sofiah, opened a door Darwisy had never expected. Further royal commissions followed, including work linked to other Malaysian palaces and Brunei’s royal household.
item.content:encoded:
When Malaysian artist Darwisy Mustafani received a commission to paint the country’s king and queen, he did not reach for an ordinary canvas.

Instead, the 25-year-old from the northeastern city of Kota Bharu transformed songket – the lustrous handwoven fabric once reserved for Malay courts and ceremonial dress – into a portrait of the sultan and his wife before a golden-domed palace.

The portrait, commissioned in 2024 by Malaysia’s police force as a gift for Sultan Ibrahim Iskandar and Queen Raja Zarith Sofiah, opened a door Darwisy had never expected. Further royal commissions followed, including work linked to other Malaysian palaces and Brunei’s royal household.

“My focus has never been about painting royal figures simply because they are royal,” he told This Week in Asia. “I never planned for my work to become closely associated with royalty, but I’m grateful that it has opened the door for me to share Malaysian culture with a wider audience.”

On TikTok, viewers watch Darwisy layer paint over woven gold thread, gradually revealing royal faces against patterns that carry centuries of courtly history. Many of those following the process are young Malaysians encountering the monarchy not through a constitutional textbook or palace ceremony, but through an algorithm.

“They first discover my work because they enjoy watching the creative process,” he said. “Then they become curious about the story behind the artwork and the cultural meaning of the materials.”

That curiosity is growing at a moment when Malaysia’s royal institutions have become increasingly visible far beyond ceremonial life.
