Since the country’s first transfer of federal power in 2018 shattered six decades of rule by one coalition, Malaysia has endured collapsing alliances, three prime ministers in less than three years, shifting parliamentary majorities and its first hung federal parliament.

Those ruptures repeatedly placed decisions about government formation before the king, drawing greater public attention to powers that had long existed in the constitution but were rarely exercised under the stable, dominant-party politics of an earlier era.

The result is not an absolute monarchy supplanting parliamentary democracy, constitutional experts say, but an old institution operating under new political conditions.

“The rulers tend always to have been influential players,” Anthony Crothers Milner, an Australian historian of Southeast Asia who has written extensively on Malay political culture, told This Week in Asia. “From time to time one reads that the rulers have suddenly gained power, but, in fact, they tend always to have been influential players.”

What has changed is the political landscape around them, according to Milner.

Broken majorities

Malaysia has one of the world’s most unusual constitutional arrangements. Nine of its 13 states are headed by hereditary Malay rulers, who elect one among themselves as the Yang di-Pertuan Agong, or king, for a five-year term through a secret ballot conducted by the Conference of Rulers.

The other four states, Penang, Melaka, Sabah and Sarawak, have appointed governors and do not take part in choosing the federal monarch.

Executive authority is exercised by the elected government, while the king generally acts on ministerial advice. The constitution nevertheless grants the monarch limited discretionary authority, most notably in appointing as prime minister the lawmaker whom he believes commands the confidence of parliament’s majority and in withholding consent to a request to dissolve parliament.

For decades, those reserve powers attracted little public attention because the governing coalition normally arrived at the palace with a clear majority.

That changed in February 2020, when Mahathir Mohamad’s resignation brought down the Pakatan Harapan (PH) government and sparked a sequence of royal consultations with lawmakers and party leaders to determine who commanded sufficient parliamentary support.

The constitutional machinery was tested again after the November 2022 general election produced no outright winner. Then king Sultan Abdullah Sultan Ahmad Shah interviewed political leaders and urged rival coalitions to consider a unity government before appointing Anwar Ibrahim as prime minister.

Azmi Hassan, a senior fellow at the Nusantara Academy for Strategic Research, said the monarchy’s role was not new, but had become more conspicuous. “Previously, much of it was done behind closed doors and in a very discreet manner,” he said.

Without a resolution, Malaysia might have returned to another election and produced another inconclusive result, Azmi said. “In that sense, the nation has looked to the monarchy as a stabilising institution.”

Constitutional lawyer Lim Wei Jiet said weaker parties and unstable coalitions had created greater room for royal institutions to influence the course of government formation.

“When political parties are not as strong as they used to be, the monarchs invariably fill that power vacuum and play a much more influential role in governance, at least compared to pre-2018,” he said.

The monarchy’s higher profile has continued under Sultan Ibrahim, the Johor ruler who began his five-year federal reign in January 2024.

In April, the king said he would determine the best candidate to lead the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission after the incumbent’s term ended, while warning that the appointment should not be politicised. Under the constitution, the commission’s chief is appointed by the king on the prime minister’s advice.

Such episodes have prompted renewed debate over how convention, written law and royal influence intersect, particularly when the constitution vests formal authority in the monarch but requires most decisions to follow government advice.

Wan Ahmad Fauzi Wan Husain, a Malaysian constitutional scholar specialising in the monarchy, said the institution should not be interpreted solely through the conventions of Britain’s Westminster system, which shaped Malaya’s colonial administration before independence in 1957.

“Our monarchy does not mirror Westminster,” he said. “It is rooted in the Great Malay Melaka Sultanate.”

He argued that the rulers retained constitutional prerogatives inherited from the pre-colonial Malay states and were obliged to safeguard Islam, constitutional supremacy, the rule of law and public peace.

“The growing presence of the monarchy in the political sphere is not unconstitutional, but rather consistent with the constitutional order,” he said.

Other constitutional lawyers take a narrower reading, emphasising that royal authority is largely exercised on advice and that personal discretion is confined to specified circumstances.

The Malaysian Bar, the professional body representing lawyers in Peninsular Malaysia, has described the monarch as possessing extensive formal authority but limited personal power, except during exceptional situations in which discretion comes into play.

The state vs the crown

The palace’s growing prominence has not come without friction.

“Dr [Mahathir] came quite close to abolishing the monarchies in 1983 and 1993,” Andrew Harding, a leading scholar in Malaysian constitutional law, told This Week in Asia.

In 1983, Mahathir confronted the Malay rulers, triggering a constitutional crisis when he introduced amendments aimed at limiting the king’s authority to withhold or remove the palace’s power of assent to legislation while shifting emergency powers away from the monarch.

Mahathir faced strong opposition as the rulers resisted, leading to a months-long constitutional stand-off before a compromise was reached.

The outcome was a subsequent constitutional amendment in 1984 – limiting royal assent: if the king does not assent to a bill within 30 days, it automatically becomes law. The king was also granted 30 to 60 days, depending on the approved bill, to return it to parliament for further debate if it was not assented to.

The palace’s constitutional role regarding emergency remained intact, as Mahathir backed down from his initial proposal to transfer that power to the prime minister, and state-level powers also remained intact.

This was the first modern-day battle between state-elected leaders and the monarchy in Malaysia’s history. But it was not the last.

Mahathir has had a sticky relationship with Johor’s royal family dating back to the early 1990s, when his government revoked immunities from the Malay rulers following alleged assaults by the Johorean royalty.

Between 2018 and 2020, when Mahathir returned to power as prime minister, he again opposed the Johor palace. He went as far as calling the Johor crown prince, Tunku Ismail Sultan Ibrahim, a “little boy” during a public argument over whether the federal government or the royal family had the ultimate right to administer the state government and appoint top officials.

The latest row in June involved the crown prince criticising Member of Parliament Syed Saddiq over his political stance and governance.

Syed responded that politics was “not a Hollywood movie”, sparking a heated public exchange between him and the Johor royal.

Harding said political fragmentation since 2018 had created greater room for the monarchy to exercise and extend its established constitutional functions, including in the appointment of governments and decisions over whether to dissolve legislatures.

“It is true that politics abhors a vacuum,” he said.

Nine crowns

The public clashes only showcase one dimension of Malaysia’s constitutional monarchy.

The debate is complicated by the fact that Malaysia does not have a single uniform monarchy.

Each royal state has its own constitution, succession rules and historical relationship between palace, government and traditional authorities. Johor’s royal house has long maintained a highly visible place in the state’s public life, while Negeri Sembilan follows a distinctive system drawn from Minangkabau custom.

There, the Yang di-Pertuan Besar is selected from eligible princes by four territorial chieftains known as the undang. The system amounts to an elective state monarchy nested within Malaysia’s elective federal monarchy.

Its complexity burst into national view this year when a succession dispute involving Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, several chieftains and a rival claimant spilled into public declarations, court proceedings and competing interpretations of the state constitution.

The palace consolidated its position following the Negeri Sembilan polls on August 1, with Tuanku Muhriz dismissing the undang of Jelebu and revoking the royal titles of several figures linked to the succession dispute, clearing the way for the swearing-in of the new state government and Barisan Nasional’s Ismail Lasim as the new menteri besar the following day.

BN secured a win in the state polls, taking 18 of the 36 seats, defeating PH’s 11 and ultimately forming the state government with a supermajority of 25 through electoral cooperation with opposition Perikatan Nasional.

Tuanku Muhriz urged freshly elected assemblymen to ensure the interests of the state and its people are put above political or personal considerations.

“To the candidates who were unsuccessful in this election, I hope that all of you will continue to serve the people with dedication and contribute to the well-being of society and the progress of Negeri Sembilan,” the ruler said during the swearing-in ceremony at Istana Besar Seri Menanti.

His remarks followed months of political and royal uncertainty that strained Negeri Sembilan’s unique constitutional system, underscoring that the state constitution remains intertwined with state governance even as the broader royal dispute continues through the courts.

A rare postponement of the Conference of Rulers’ meeting set for June 23-25 had pushed the Negeri Sembilan succession dispute into politics. The next meeting is yet to be determined.

In June, Prime Minister Anwar said the federal government continued to recognise Tuanku Muhriz, after Tunku Nadzaruddin Tuanku Ja’afar was proclaimed as the new ruler at a hotel in neighbouring Melaka.

The dispute remained entangled in litigation and arguments over the authority of the undang and the state’s royal council.

Wan Ahmad Fauzi said the controversy exposed a widespread misunderstanding of Negeri Sembilan’s royal structure.

“The ruler of Negeri Sembilan is not the Yang di-Pertuan Besar alone,” he said, arguing that the constitutional duties of the ruling chieftains should not be dismissed as merely customary positions.

The episode differed sharply from the 2022 federal deadlock, but both forced Malaysians to confront the architecture beneath their monarchy, including powers and traditions that usually remain distant from everyday political debate.

Historian Milner said the central question was whether the monarchy could continue supplying stability when elected institutions faltered.

“Monarchy, on the face of it, is an outdated institution,” he said. “In recent times, however, it may be gaining new support, especially as people look at other types of constitution.”

Constitutionally, Malaysia’s political upheavals stemming from its democratic process have shown that the monarch has played a decisive role, exercising some level of discretion on who leads the nation based on parliamentary majority and support.

Lim, the constitutional lawyer, said decisions made by the palace had gone beyond what was widely deemed as a ceremonial role previously.

“So when political parties are not as strong as they used to be, the monarchs invariably fill that power vacuum and play a much more influential role in governance, at least compared to pre-2018,” he told This Week in Asia.

According to Lim, rulers’ constitutional powers are enumerated in the federal constitution and have the force of law which is not open to question while the constitutional convention acts as a long-standing practice derived from the UK which Malaysia’s system is largely based on.

From legal observations, Lim said monarchs were not overstepping their constitutional powers. “I think the constitution is working as intended for now.”

However, he said constitutional convention might evolve, stemming from any instability of political coalitions.

“For example, it may now be a constitutional convention for the king to be consulted on the annual budget or on major public policies before they are rolled out, which I definitely see happening unlike before,” Lim said. “The monarchs will no doubt be playing a larger role in governance due to the instability of political coalitions.”

New normal

Awang Azman Awang Pawi, a political analyst at the University of Malaya, said Malaysia appeared to be entering a form of conditional new normal as long as politics remained fragmented.

He said the monarchy was likely to remain more visible in matters involving government formation, legislation dissolution and determination of majority support.

“The healthiest constitutional model is one in which the monarchy remains influential but firmly bound by the constitution; respected but not politicised; and committed to safeguarding the democratic process rather than competing with the elected government.”

That prominence carries advantages and risks. Royal intervention can help break a deadlock when no political leader commands a majority, but sustained dependence on the palace may allow political parties to avoid the harder task of rebuilding durable coalitions and settling disputes through parliament.

The institution’s legitimacy also rests partly on remaining above partisan combat, even as political actors increasingly appeal to rulers, invoke palace relationships or portray royal approval as a source of authority.

For Darwisy, those arguments remain beyond the purpose of his portraits. His focus is the cultural language surrounding the institution and how it can reach a generation more familiar with short videos than royal archives.

“Not everyone reads history books, but today many people connect with art on social media,” he said. “My hope is that people don’t just see a royal portrait, but also discover and appreciate the beauty of Malaysian culture through the artwork.”

item.title: [SCMP] Thai teen kills at least 5 in school, after shooting grandparents at home
item.description:
At least five people were killed at a school near Thailand’s capital Bangkok on Friday morning after a student went on a gun rampage, with the tragedy shocking the nation and reopening questions over access to firearms.

The 14-year-old suspect had killed his grandparents before opening fire at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, about an hour outside the capital, and then took his own life, officials said.

Those killed at the school were all teachers and staff, and police said the shooter fired at least 26 bullets using a gun that ‌belonged to his grandfather. An additional 34 rounds were found.
item.content:encoded:
At least five people were killed at a school near Thailand’s capital Bangkok on Friday morning after a student went on a gun rampage, with the tragedy shocking the nation and reopening questions over access to firearms.

The 14-year-old suspect had killed his grandparents before opening fire at the Debsirin Nonthaburi School, about an hour outside the capital, and then took his own life, officials said.

Those killed at the school were all teachers and staff, and police said the shooter fired at least 26 bullets using a gun that ‌belonged to his grandfather. An additional 34 rounds were found.

Police said 23 people were wounded in the incident.

The boy appeared to have shot his grandparents first before attending school as normal, said Royal Thai Police spokesman Police Lieutenant General Trairong Phiwphan. After class started, the boy opened fire inside his classroom before walking out and continuing to shoot.

Trairong said the teen fired more than 20 shots and over 30 rounds were found on him after he shot himself.

Several family members of the alleged shooter told police the boy usually kept to himself and was a good student. They said they were unaware of any troubles he faced at home or school.

Harrowing video footage shared on social media, apparently filmed by a pupil during the shooting, shows children in blue uniforms cowering under wooden desks, as five shots ring out while the school’s automatic public address system announces the time is 10am.

One pupil in the clip extends an arm out to comfort another who is crying as the shots are fired in what appears to be a methodical manner.

“It’s really awful, this shouldn’t have happened,” Thai Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul told reporters. “I’m not just sad about the people who died, I’m sad that something like this could happen in our country at all.

“This is exactly what I’ve been saying – the reason the government doesn’t allow people to carry guns, doesn’t allow ownership, doesn’t allow licence renewals, is because of exactly this kind of thing.”

Anutin confirmed reports that the shooter was 14 years old and killed himself, according to Associated Press. He said the boy, who lived with his grandparents, had shown signs of stress related to school.

The gun, described by police as small and compact, was legally registered to the boy’s grandfather, Anutin said.

The prime minister on Friday also vowed to introduce a new firearms control law.

Anutin, who previously tightened gun ‌laws when he was interior minister, will now propose a law to restrict the carrying of firearms by the public.

“The new law will only allow government officials on duty to carry guns,” he told reporters on Friday, but did not provide any specifics for the envisaged legislation, including whether it would tighten gun ownership requirements.

Images shared by police showed what appeared to be the gunman’s weapon, a semi-automatic pistol with multiple rounds packed in a pouch, as questions emerged over his mental health and the motive behind the attack. Several pupils suggested the shooter had been bullied.

“Our school doesn’t check our bags when entering school,” Kittipat Choolert, 16, told This Week in Asia. “He fired several shots, I was two buildings away from him and I heard the gunshots, the entire school heard it and we were in shock.”

Tearful students in school uniforms held each other outside the school.

“I’m still in shock,” 16-year-old Thatchai Jaiyen told Agence France-Presse, expressing disbelief that a kind former teacher of his had been killed.

“She was such a good person. I thought that if she had encountered the shooter, she might have been able to reason with him. I never expected that the child would actually shoot her,” he said, his voice trailing away.

Student Purin Khumchoo said he felt depressed and bad for the people who were killed.

“The two teachers who were killed were lovely, and many students became better people because of them,” he said.

Emergency worker Kiatikhun Verapongpradith, 47, described arriving during the shooting and his team treating students with injuries to the back, ‌chest and arms. They found a teacher dead on an upper floor of the school, and in another room a female teacher with chest and arm wounds.

Kiatikhun said he was called to treat the teenage shooter after hearing a final shot. “We rushed up ‌and found ‌that the perpetrator had shot himself in the right side of the head and collapsed. When we got up there, we checked his pulse, he still had one, so we started CPR.”

The school suspended all classes for next week and instructed staff to work from home during that time.

It is the latest shooting to stun a nation where millions of firearms are in circulation, many unlicensed and unregistered and where shootings are commonplace, but mass killings involving children are rare.

Last weekend, Anutin was at the scene of the killing of five people in Chonburi, including Russian siblings, one shot by an alleged robber.

In February, a teacher ‌died and a ‌student was injured in southern Thailand’s Hat Yai district after a gunman opened fire at a school.

In 2023, a shooting by a 14-year-old boy killed two – a Chinese and a Myanmar citizen – at Siam Paragon, one of Thailand’s most famous downtown malls.

It was a tragedy that spurred calls for stricter gun controls, yet killings have continued, with regular police raids unearthing large caches of heavy weapons and pistols.

Thailand has one of the highest rates of gun ownership in Asia, second only to Pakistan but far surpassing its Southeast Asian neighbours.

Data collected in 2017 by the groups Small Arms Survey and GunPolicy.org in their last extensive international study found civilian gun ownership in Thailand was about 15.1 guns per 100 people, compared with fewer than one per 100 in neighbouring Malaysia.

Thailand had 3.49 deaths by firearms per 100,000 people, according to 2023 statistics published by World Population Review.

“I think we need to [look at] why we still haven’t learned from everything that’s happened,” Krisanaphong Poothakool, a leading criminologist and adviser to the Royal Thai Police on police reform, told Channel One News.

“Why do firearms in Thailand seem so easy to access? The fact that children and youth have access to guns and gun sets is really not something normal in Thai society.”

In the worst episode of its kind in living memory, Panya Khamrab, a 34-year-old former policeman with a history of drug abuse, massacred 37 people – 24 of them children – in a shooting and stabbing rampage at a day care centre in the northeastern province of Nong Bua Lam Phu in 2022.

Additional reporting by Associated Press, Reuters and Agence France-Presse

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong aims to be a global tech hub, but can it hold on to its young talent?
item.description:
At just 18, Hong Kong tech enthusiasts Rexan Wong Chak-chi and Ken Mochizuki are both rushing to deliver their business ideas.

However, their choices of launch pad could not be further apart. While Wong is eyeing Silicon Valley in the United States for better support, Mochizuki is keen to stay in the city and contribute to the local community.

Their contrasting approaches highlight Hong Kong’s advantages and challenges as it strives to become a global innovation and talent hub under China’s strategic blueprint, with artificial intelligence (AI) and research transformation listed among the priorities of the city’s first five-year plan, to be released by the government later this year.
item.content:encoded:
At just 18, Hong Kong tech enthusiasts Rexan Wong Chak-chi and Ken Mochizuki are both rushing to deliver their business ideas.

However, their choices of launch pad could not be further apart. While Wong is eyeing Silicon Valley in the United States for better support, Mochizuki is keen to stay in the city and contribute to the local community.

Their contrasting approaches highlight Hong Kong’s advantages and challenges as it strives to become a global innovation and talent hub under China’s strategic blueprint, with artificial intelligence (AI) and research transformation listed among the priorities of the city’s first five-year plan, to be released by the government later this year.

While the city boasts cutting-edge university research, critics have warned that an increasingly risk-averse culture and a lack of early-stage support may push young tech talent towards overseas ecosystems.

California dreaming

Wong developed an interest in AI when he was 15 after joining a class on building mobile applications.

He later connected with many leading tech entrepreneurs through X, formerly known as Twitter, and built an AI-powered app called Text Behind Image in 2024. He said the app allowed its 500,000 users to design images with text behind featured objects.

Despite launching his first product in Hong Kong, Wong is looking to San Francisco and nearby Silicon Valley as the future launch pad for his AI business, believing the US tech hub can offer him better support.

“The main reason was really the access to support for early-stage founders. In Hong Kong, I think there is really a lack of support,” said Wong, a computer science undergraduate at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

“In San Francisco, there are a lot of incubators that help young founders go from zero to one.”

In January, he joined a two-month incubation programme with Founders Inc, a major San Francisco-based start-up community, making connections and receiving guidance from those with experience.

The “beauty” of the programme was having founders at different stages under the same roof, allowing them to discuss problems they faced, he said.

Intending to run an AI-powered market analytics company in the future, Wong is busy reaching out to tech start-ups in San Francisco and observing their operations.

Wong also pointed to the United States’ early adoption of advanced AI tools, such as models developed by Anthropic and OpenAI, as an advantage, while most Hongkongers used AI “at a very basic level” and some tools were not even available in the city.

“So it is really a lack of talent density, a lack of support and a lack of accessibility to these tools and knowledge on how to use frontier technology that holds Hong Kong back, which is why I picked San Francisco over Hong Kong,” he said.

Silicon Valley has been ranked the top start-up ecosystem in the world, while Hong Kong has come 29th, according to this year’s Global Startup Ecosystem Report, released by consultancy firm Startup Genome.

On a scale of one to 10, Hong Kong scored only two to four for its start-up performance, funding, talent, market reach and the degree to which it encourages AI start-ups. In contrast, Silicon Valley received full marks for each of these indicators.

Hong Kong only scored one for its research and development capacity, compared with Silicon Valley’s score of five.

Other Asian markets, such as Singapore and Seoul, and some major mainland Chinese cities, including Beijing, Shanghai, Shenzhen and Hangzhou, also outperformed Hong Kong.

Kenny Shui Chi-wai, vice-president of think tank Our Hong Kong Foundation, said Beijing’s strength lay in its strong research capabilities, supported by top universities and close collaboration among the industrial, education and research sectors.

South Korea excelled because major enterprises devoted resources to research in key sectors such as semiconductors and biotechnology, while Singapore had outperformed Hong Kong because of its high density of venture capital firms and incubators – all of which Hong Kong could learn from, Shui added.

“If we cannot have our own major [tech] companies now, we should think about how to attract some of the largest institutions from other places to operate in Hong Kong,” he said.

According to the government’s investment arm, InvestHK, Hong Kong was home to 5,221 start-ups as of 2025, with 186 of them focusing on core or applied AI.

The San Francisco Bay Area, which includes Silicon Valley, has nearly 200,000 funded start-ups, with 80 per cent of funding going into AI, according to start-up data tracking platform dealroom.co.

‘A-Eye’ funding

But as Mochizuki sees it, Hong Kong’s young tech entrepreneurs are blessed with abundant support, and the only problem is that they are not told about available resources, so more publicity was needed.

Mochizuki, who is studying electrical engineering at City University (CityU), learned coding on his own in 2022, when he was still in secondary school and the Covid-19 pandemic forced pupils to study at home.

Within two years, he built “A-Eye”, an AI shopping assistant designed to help visually impaired people identify products and compare prices.

The project recently received HK$200,000 (US$25,500) in funding from CityU and the Hong Kong Science and Technology Parks Corporation (HKSTP) through the university’s HK Tech 300 project.

CityU’s law school also offered free legal consultation under the programme, he added.

“My goal is to stay in Hong Kong and try to use my skills to contribute to this place and serve people,” Mochizuki said.

“Although other countries like the US or the United Kingdom may have better resources or a better culture for start-ups, the competition is much [fiercer] than in Hong Kong.”

Apart from university-based projects, Hong Kong authorities have made multiple start-up programmes available through the government-backed HKSTP and Cyberport.

HKSTP offers a range of start-up support programmes covering different stages, including ideation, incubation, acceleration and global expansion.

According to its latest annual report, 570 start-ups graduated from its support programme in 2024-25, and it spent more than HK$415 million on incubation and tenant support during the period.

Cyberport had more than 200 start-ups graduate from its entrepreneurship schemes in 2025-26, including an incubation programme offering grants of up to HK$500,000 and rental subsidies of up to HK$200,000, as well as the Creative Micro Fund, which helps early-stage start-ups move towards incubation.

The Home and Youth Affairs Bureau has also launched a funding scheme for young entrepreneurs to start their businesses in Hong Kong, Macau and the nine Guangdong cities under Beijing’s Greater Bay Area blueprint.

Shui said funding for early-stage start-ups remained insufficient as local investors preferred “easier and more certain” options, and investment activity tended to be cautious amid a turbulent economic environment.

“Tech start-ups have a higher chance of failure, but when they succeed, they can bring high returns,” he said, urging the government to step up support for early-stage founders.

A start-up usually goes through multiple rounds of financing, including the pre-seed stage, when founders develop an idea and work towards a minimum viable product (MVP); the seed stage, when they refine the MVP for market fit; and the series A to C stages, when they scale the business, before exiting through an initial public offering or an acquisition.

According to a recent Our Hong Kong Foundation report, only 10 per cent of founders in the city received support from venture capital or angel investors, 30 per cent got funding from the government, and 85 per cent had to tap personal savings.

But the report highlighted a stark imbalance in the government’s funding allocation.

As of 2024, funding was concentrated heavily at the pre-seed stage, at HK$49.5 billion, and in late-stage investment beyond series C, at HK$62 billion, leaving those in between – often described as the “valley of death” – largely underserved, with only HK$3.4 billion in capital support.

Apart from a lack of funding and support, Hong Kong founders have complained on online forums about high office rents, talent costs and the city’s small market size, with some pointing to places such as Bangkok and Shenzhen as better choices.

Headwinds

Alberto Moel, a professor of practice in finance at the University of Hong Kong, said it would be harder for young entrepreneurs such as Wong and Mochizuki to grow businesses built from their own ideas in the city, as the government and universities dominated the local start-up ecosystem.

“We are in a stage in Hong Kong where university research projects are the ones driving the pool of innovation,” he said.

“If your idea is outside that pool, then you are basically up against the usual headwinds in venture capital that have been around for a long time, namely that it is difficult to get capital and difficult to put together a team.”

Moel added that Hong Kong’s risk-averse culture was also reflected in the investment behaviour of venture capitalists, resulting in limited capital for very early stage start-ups or those taking on more risk.

In contrast, funding for such companies in the US was much broader because the culture there was more inclined to “try things and see what happens”, while there was much more capital in the country, he said.

Hong Kong’s young entrepreneurs would stand a better chance of success if they looked at opportunities arising from university research projects, Moel said.

“If the policy is not focused on [independent ideas], you are more likely to fail, and it is going to discourage you,” he said.

“I would recommend young entrepreneurs look at the existing platforms and work within them because you will find much better chances and opportunities to monetise [ideas] into a company.”

The government should do more to publicise and create opportunities for building businesses from research projects by linking tech-minded businesspeople with innovative ideas, he added.

Derek Chim, HKSTP’s head of start-up ecosystem and development, agreed that access to early-stage capital remained important in helping innovative ventures scale up, and said the park had teamed up with the private sector to catalyse start-up growth.

“While different investors naturally have different risk appetites and return expectations, we are seeing growing interest in deep-tech and innovation-driven companies that require longer development horizons,” he said.

The Innovation, Technology and Industry Bureau said the government attached importance to encouraging and cultivating a thriving I&T ecosystem for start-ups, and acknowledged that its sustainability relied heavily on private sector participation.

It said the government would launch an HK$10 billion Innovation and Technology Industry-Oriented Fund this year to channel more social capital into “emerging and future industries of strategic importance”, benefiting companies at different stages of development.

Despite the growing range of start-up funding options in Hong Kong, Mochizuki and Wong agreed the city’s cautious culture still made it hard for young entrepreneurs to strike out on their own.

“In Hong Kong, the culture drives most people down a very traditional path – primary school, high school, graduating from college, working in a full-time job – and it is very hard to pivot if you want to change your profession based on your interests,” Wong said.

“Everything is laid out for you, and this sense of security is embedded into young Hong Kong people growing up.”

item.title: [SCMP] Vintage charm is blended with modern elegance in a timeless Hong Kong flat
item.description:
Needing a designer to renovate his newly purchased, 38-year-old apartment in Central, businessman Harry Sun found the perfect fit in an unexpected place. He and interior designer Dominic Cheung, co-founder of Crimson Company, were both regulars at the same tailor’s shop – and when their paths crossed, the introduction sparked an instant connection. The two shared sensibilities that extended beyond sartorial savoir faire to a mutual appreciation for classicism with a youthful touch.

Thus began a harmonious collaboration to make over the 620 sq ft mid-rise apartment in quintessentially “old” Hong Kong, with its views of historic St Paul’s Church ringed by mature trees.

Sating his penchant for vintage and antique European designs, Sun already had an assemblage of finds he’d been collecting from markets since his university days in Britain. These would inform the interiors, as Cheung revised the floor plan from two bedrooms to one, enabling a bigger dining room and a slightly enlarged bathroom.
item.content:encoded:
Needing a designer to renovate his newly purchased, 38-year-old apartment in Central, businessman Harry Sun found the perfect fit in an unexpected place. He and interior designer Dominic Cheung, co-founder of Crimson Company, were both regulars at the same tailor’s shop – and when their paths crossed, the introduction sparked an instant connection. The two shared sensibilities that extended beyond sartorial savoir faire to a mutual appreciation for classicism with a youthful touch.

Thus began a harmonious collaboration to make over the 620 sq ft mid-rise apartment in quintessentially “old” Hong Kong, with its views of historic St Paul’s Church ringed by mature trees.

Sating his penchant for vintage and antique European designs, Sun already had an assemblage of finds he’d been collecting from markets since his university days in Britain. These would inform the interiors, as Cheung revised the floor plan from two bedrooms to one, enabling a bigger dining room and a slightly enlarged bathroom.

“Our goal was to create a space with a strong, yet quiet, architectural identity that feels both intentional and deeply personal,” says Cheung. “By integrating classic European details within a modern, clean envelope, we created a backdrop designed not to dominate, but to age gracefully over the years.”

His client’s brief for “cosiness” – a space that could tastefully house his furniture and objets d’art – excited Cheung, himself a lover of things vintage.

“Vintage pieces big and small can introduce a storytelling element, adding more depth to the space. Our shared vision was to juxtapose old and new, without making it look like an antique shop.”

An 18th century Louis XVI commode and a 19th century Louis Philippe gilded mirror set the tone for the dining room, where, additionally, mid-century modern Wishbone chairs are paired with a custom-made Calacatta marble table. Resisting the temptation to install ornate chandeliers, lighting designer and Crimson Company co-founder Rosana Asencios opted instead for two simple brass pendants. “Their patina will change with age,” she says, “responding very well to the antique pieces and the history in the room. It’s about having a sleek accent, without being too overwhelming.”

French-inspired wall mouldings and herringbone oak flooring lend subtle sophistication.

In the separate living room, twin bay windows frame neighbourhood views, and a mahogany library wall houses Sun’s collections of books – history and literature among his favourites – and vinyl records.

A green velvet sofa adds a youthful, mid-century modernist touch beside a vintage handmade rug. Sun’s prized analogue turntable sits atop a minimalist, Scandinavian-inspired coffee table; all other audiovisual equipment is concealed behind slatted joinery inlaid within the wall panelling.

With his client needing to work from home only occasionally, Cheng tucked a study nook into a walkway, behind two pocket doors inlaid with antique glass panels.

Cheung’s intent to “frame different moments in the home” is evident in the simply furnished bedroom, where two elegant oak and glass pendants, a custom bed and an oak-finish wardrobe take centre stage. The only hung artwork is a small framed print picked up on a trip to Italy during his school days.

Proving that even a compact kitchen can have style as well as substance, handmade Moroccan splashback tiles pair gracefully with natural stone benchtops, brass knobs and pulls punctuating the light-grey, powder-finished cabinetry.

The same quiet refinement carries through to the bathroom. Neither space is merely entered – one arrives from the dining room via a dramatic Nero Marquina marble arched portal and floor threshold.

Every corner and every wall holds a focal point, yet nothing feels forced or crowded.

“In this not-so-big apartment, a lot is happening, but you don’t feel like a lot is happening. The flow is easy,” Cheung says.

The result is a harmonious dialogue between modernism and classicism, where all details are intentional but never laboured.

A delighted Sun says the refurbishment, completed in December 2024, never ceases to amaze him. “It’s one of those places that’s well built, well designed and feels very comfortable when you live there.”

Living room

Mahogany bookcase, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life. Sofa, from B&B Italia. Coffee table, from Norr11. Record turntable, from Cambridge Audio. Side table, from Mater. Wall lamp, from Santa & Cole. Vintage handmade rug, from Blanc Marine Boutique. Artwork is a Liu Peng landscape, from Asian Art Platform Singapore

Dining room

Calacatta Viola dining marble, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life. Wishbone chairs, from Carl Hansen & Søn. Candela di Vals pendant lamps in natural brass, from Viabizzuno. Sun found the small oil painting of a fig years ago. In the alcove, a Louis XVI mahogany commode with Carrara marble top, from Inessa Stewart’s Antiques. Above it, a Louis Philippe gilt mirror with crown, from 1stDibs. Behind the mirror, Ianthe Mono wallpaper in Lapis from Liberty Fabrics

Dining room detail

Nero Marquina marble arched portal defines the threshold leading to the bathroom and kitchen. Wall mouldings and wall finish, in St Leo plaster paint (stleointeriors.com). Polished brass dimmer switches and sockets, from Varilight (varilight.co.uk). Wall-hung printed abstract, from The Poster Club (theposterclub.com)

Study nook

Pocket doors in the study nook feature antique glass inlay panels. Vintage brass handles from Etsy. Desk joinery in burl wood veneer, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life, who also installed the herringbone-pattern engineered timber floor

Bathroom

Brass-framed mirror and cabinetry with custom Calacatta Viola marble vanity top, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life. Basin and French gold-finish tapware, from Kohler. Small lamp, from Audo Copenhagen. Overhead light, from Visual Comfort

Bedroom

Bed with upholstered headboard, custom-designed by Crimson Company and built by Sankon Interiors. Pair of hanging lamps, from Santa & Cole. Bedside tables, from Ikea. Wardrobe in oak timber finish, designed by Crimson Company and built by Design for Life

Kitchen

Kitchen cabinetry with natural quartz stone tops, by Crimson Company and Design for Life. Handmade Zellige tiles, from Zia Tile. Brass knobs and pulls, from Willow & Stone. Artwork on benchtop, by Molly Supplee

item.title: [SCMP] Wok with Yan’s return: Hong Kong-Canadian TV chef Stephen Yan resurfaces decades after disappearing
item.description:
“When Marco Polo went to China, you know what he did? We showed him how to make chow mein noodles, we showed him how to make wontons.”

An energetic Chinese man with a high forehead and gregarious smile is standing in a studio kitchen, dishing out as many puns as he is plates of wok-fried rice for a studio audience at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), in Vancouver.

From 1978 to 1995, Stephen Yan garnered legions of fans in Canada, the United States and beyond, largely thanks to half-hour episodes of Wok with Yan, each seeing a dish prepared from start to finish in real time. The chef would cook up Cantonese classics such as beef and broccoli, garlic spare ribs and stir-fried prawns while dressed in aprons emblazoned with witticisms such as “Wok’s New, Pussycat?”, “Wok up a Storm” or, in this early episode, “Wok-a-Doodle-Doo”.
item.content:encoded:
“When Marco Polo went to China, you know what he did? We showed him how to make chow mein noodles, we showed him how to make wontons.”

An energetic Chinese man with a high forehead and gregarious smile is standing in a studio kitchen, dishing out as many puns as he is plates of wok-fried rice for a studio audience at the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC), in Vancouver.

From 1978 to 1995, Stephen Yan garnered legions of fans in Canada, the United States and beyond, largely thanks to half-hour episodes of Wok with Yan, each seeing a dish prepared from start to finish in real time. The chef would cook up Cantonese classics such as beef and broccoli, garlic spare ribs and stir-fried prawns while dressed in aprons emblazoned with witticisms such as “Wok’s New, Pussycat?”, “Wok up a Storm” or, in this early episode, “Wok-a-Doodle-Doo”.

“When [Polo] went back to Italy, he learned how to make it all right,” says Yan to the camera, in his Cantonese-inflected English, “but he changed the name chow mein to spaghetti and changed wonton to ravioli. Wok the heck, I’m going to make one thing perfectly clear: I want to make this thing right and correct. I don’t want to make it the wrong way. I want to make it the Yan way.”

Once Yan had plated a dish, he’d invite someone from the audience to dine with him, and, this being Canada in the 1980s, they would not all be proficient with chopsticks. Yan would open a fortune cookie, translate the Chinese message inside and then, as the credits rolled, the rest of the studio audience would make sure no food went to waste.

With the coast-to-coast-to-coast reach of the CBC, Yan became a national figure and arguably the first Asian celebrity television chef in the West.

“I watched [Yan] with my grandparents because, back then, your house had one TV,” says Karon Liu, who was only a few months old when his family moved to Toronto in 1987, one of more than 355,600 Hongkongers who moved to Canada in the late 80s, according to the Canadian International Council. “So, what they watched, you had to watch,” says Liu, who is now a food reporter with the Toronto Star newspaper. He remembers his grandmother hollowing out a cucumber and filling it with stir-fried beef, making it look like a boat, because that’s what Stephen Yan did in one episode.

“He was the Chinese Julia Child. He wasn’t some snooty Michelin French chef; he cooked the way my grandmother would cook at home,” says Liu. “He explained a lot of ingredients that weren’t as well known outside of a Chinese audience at that time.”

While Chinese-Canadians delighted in Yan’s familiarity, other Canadians were learning that Chinese food was not just egg foo yung or sweet and sour chicken balls, a step towards the multiculturalism the country would more fully embrace. But then one day in 1995, after more than 500 episodes, Wok with Yan ended, and the chef was not seen on television or in other media again – well, until he briefly surfaced the year before last.

Born and raised in the Toronto, Ontario suburb of Scarborough in the 80s, one of Yan’s biggest fans was Steve Gaskin. Before he was old enough to go to school, Gaskin’s Guyanese father and Chinese mother would drop him off at his grandparents’ home at 7am before going to work, and pick him up 12 hours later.

“I found it very hard to connect with my gung-gung [maternal grandfather] because my parents never spoke Cantonese, and he didn’t speak much English. I took Cantonese lessons, but I didn’t retain any of it,” says Gaskin. His grandfather, who ran a laundromat business in his adopted home, brought his family from Hong Kong to Canada via Guyana more than 50 years ago.

“My gung-gung only communicated in Chinese,” says Gaskin, “but just from grunts and facial cues, I knew what he was saying.”

The pair managed to bond over Wok with Yan. “I would sit next to him on the La-Z-Boy and just without even talking, we would laugh at the jokes and he would just kind of nudge me when something funny came on, or he wanted me to watch the technique.

“In the 80s, Stephen Yan was probably the only Chinese-Canadian celebrity. I was probably six years old, and the only Asian person on the big screen was Bruce Lee or Jackie Chan, so to see somebody like Stephen Yan, who’s in Canada, who was so approachable, was really important.”

In 2018, Gaskin and a friend launched Retrokid, a company that, through T-shirts and accessories, recalls childhood memories for Gen Xers who grew up watching Canadian television shows such as Mr Dressup, Polka Dot Door and Degrassi. Gaskin was determined to track down his hero.

After years of dead ends, in 2022, he finally got a response. But it wasn’t until a year later that Yan agreed to meet him.

Gaskin is coy about how he finally got in contact with Yan, divulging only that the former chef wanted “to work with a company that understands everything he’s done”. And with the success of Retrokid and the wider appetites for online nostalgia spun into products, Yan the savvy businessman must have seen that the time was ripe for a revival.

“Stephen Yan always said that he appreciated that there was this personal connection I had with my gung-gung as to why he wanted to do this with us.”

Together, they turned out “Wok with Yan” T-shirts, hoodies, tote bags, badges and fridge magnets, bearing the chef’s likeness from his television days. And, of course, a range of aprons with witty Yan-isms has proved to be the bestseller.

To help launch the collection, Yan agreed to fly from Vancouver to Toronto in August 2024 for a meet-and-greet with fans.

“It was pretty shocking to see him just come out of the arrivals gate,” says Gaskin, who picked Yan up at the airport. “Like, oh my God, it’s Stephen Yan. I didn’t know if he was going to come off a plane in a wheelchair or on crutches, right? But no, he’s super strong and mentally healthy for 85.”

While Yan was in Toronto, Retrokid gave Liu a chance to interview the chef for the Star, and, like Gaskin, the reporter was transported back to his childhood.

“It was really surreal,” says Liu. “He was still making jokes, he was just like a grandpa, where you ask one question and then his answer is, like, 10 minutes long because he’s lived such a full life.”

According to what he said in the interview, it was Yan who decided to pull the plug on his show in 1995.

“One day, I asked my accountant how much money I needed to survive,” Yan told Liu. “He said I already had a house and I didn’t need a dollar more. I wanted to contribute my time to those less fortunate, so I helped out with orphanages and schools in places like Thailand and China. I had enough earthly belongings.

“Back then, I had three restaurants [in Vancouver] and I had three disciples, including Martin Yan [no relation; a Hong Kong-American who worked with Yan in the 70s],” he explained. His protégé’s own television show, Yan Can Cook, also first aired on Canadian television in 1978 (initially as Yan Can), before having a highly successful run in the US, on PBS.

Stephen Yan also told Liu that, after quitting the show, he spent more time with his family and became much more active. “I ran 11 marathons, four times at the Boston Marathon and won the masters division. I also climbed Mount Everest.”

For someone so beloved, there isn’t a lot of biographical information available online about Yan, and he guards his private life closely. His birth date, for example, is not widely known, only that he was born in Hong Kong in 1939.

Not long after, in December 1941, the Japanese occupation of the city began and basic ingredients such as rice, flour and oil were rationed.

“[As a child,] I was poor and went to people’s stores where they would give me leftover food,” Yan told Liu.

“I was spending my time on the streets next to a theatre that was starring a Chinese actor, who was Bruce Lee’s father. Bruce and I became friends, and we used to play in a nearby warehouse, but I needed a job.”

When Yan was nine years old, a restaurant cook gave him work in exchange for food. One of his most laborious tasks was to take thousands of lotus seeds from a pot of boiling water, without gloves, and use a toothpick to push out their bitter cores. After three months, Yan was allowed into the kitchen, to learn from the cook, who taught him how to kill and pluck chickens, and use every part of the bird, as well as shop for the best ingredients.

Yan claimed to have been the fastest dishwasher at the restaurant. “Humans are adaptable and can do anything if they have the opportunity,” he told Liu.

He became a fully-fledged cook, and when he was around 15 years old, the chief cook of the restaurant arranged for him to go to school. Later, Yan said, he was one of two students chosen by an American senator to study business administration in the US, to which he sailed on an 18-day voyage to San Francisco.

Fearing being called up to the military as the US fought in Vietnam, Yan crossed the border to Canada in the late 50s or early 60s, he told Liu, one of 20,000 to 30,000 draft dodgers to have done so, according to Canadian immigration statistics.

By the late 70s, Yan was already managing his own restaurants when he was noticed by a television talent scout while leading cooking demonstrations in a shopping mall in the run-up to Chinese New Year.

The weekly Yan’s Woking debuted on Vancouver station BCTV in 1978. Two years later, national broadcaster CBC bought the show, rebranded it as Wok with Yan and shifted formats to present a daily afternoon cooking series.

Gaskin says some 230 people showed up at Toronto’s storied Royal Theatre for 2024’s meet-and-greet.

“It was great to give [Yan] a platform where he could just say thank you to all of his fans and the fans showed up,” says Gaskin. “Obviously, we could have packed that theatre to 500 people, but we also wanted to give the fans a chance to meet him, to actually go up and take a photo, and they loved it.”

Since then, Yan has remained elusive. All attempts to contact him by this author have been fruitless. The Retrokid team has been sworn to secrecy; Liu says he never got direct contact. And even now, almost two years after Yan’s rarest of public appearances, he shows no signs of emerging into the spotlight again, even to contribute to this article, to connect with his hometown, Hong Kong.

Vancouverite Billy Snaychuk wasn’t at the meet-up but considers himself a fan. “My most favourite part about Stephen Yan would have to be his aprons, and the way he always made the audience laugh,” he says. “He just captured the audience right away from the get-go. He definitely caught me as a kid, because I just loved watching him.”

Snaychuk’s father, a fisherman and entrepreneur, got to know Yan through Chinese friends who caught fish for the chef, delivering them to his restaurant, Yan’s Garden. From the age of six, Snaychuk watched Wok with Yan with his mother every day after school.

“My parents had the largest collection of Stephen Yan books, and I remember sneaking out of my room in the middle of the night and grabbing his books on the bookshelf and bringing them back. And I would just look at all the pictures and read the recipes,” he recalls, with a chuckle.

Once a month, his parents invited friends over and cooked dishes from Yan’s cookbooks, including Snaychuk’s favourite, gold coin beef.

“The flavour profile in it is just next level. And the texture of the beef, you can almost chew it with the roof of your mouth and your tongue, it’s just that tender,” says Snaychuk, who would follow in his hero’s footsteps and become a chef himself. He was promoted to executive chef at the age of 28 and went into restaurant consulting and even competed in the Food Network Canada cooking reality TV show Wall of Chefs.

As he got older, Snaychuk paid attention to Yan’s technique, particularly how he created flavour profiles by adding ingredients to the wok at different times.

“A lot of people, when they cook, they just kind of throw everything in there. If you do that, the whole dish is basically going to taste the same. But if you add things at different times and take them out and put them back in, you layer the flavours. And that’s something I really noticed – he layered his flavours with his cooking.”

While watching Yan was a joy for so many, working for him was not always so pleasurable, says former assistant Brenda Gonneville, who also has no idea where Yan lives now. “He’s not the face you see on TV.”

In 1981, Yan hired a 26-year-old Gonneville to help him in his office, which was above Yan’s Chinese restaurant, in Port Coquitlam, British Columbia. She had worked as an assistant to high-powered executives in the steel industry, says Gonneville, so was “well versed in dealing with high-powered, difficult people”.

Her job, as a native English speaker, was to look after Yan’s public relations, devise witty lines for the aprons and procure props and have them shipped to Ottawa, where his show was taped for two seasons before moving back to Vancouver. She recalls being the only Caucasian in an office full of Cantonese-speaking people but says she got on well with all the other staff. Gonneville was aiming to forge a career in entertainment, so worked for a low wage. After paying rent, she says, she was left with enough money only for a diet of white rice and boiled eggs.

“After three months, I’d had enough,” she says, “because he is a perfectionist, and nothing pleases him. He’s a hard worker. He expects more than 100 per cent from his employees.”

One day, she says, he was dictating content for a show and Gonneville was struggling to write it all down in shorthand, because he was speaking quickly.

“He had me read it back and I said, ‘I’m sorry, I didn’t get most of that.’ I decided then and there, and so did he, that we’d come to the end of the road.”

Fortunately, her brief stint with Yan led to a 20-year career in film and television.

When she returned to pack up her things, the office manager “took my hand and said, ‘Don’t you worry, you lasted longer than anybody’”, she recalls with a laugh.

“[Yan’s] an A-type personality, he’s driven. He expected everybody to put in the same effort as him, and if you failed, he wouldn’t put up with it.”

Difficult he may have been for those he employed, but, given the delight he’s brought to television viewers, one cannot begrudge his telling the hosts of Toronto daytime talk show The Social, in August 2024, that, “I was hiding; I want a simple life.

“I […] cannot believe that people remember me after 30 years,” he said on The Social. “And they want to know, am I alive? I am! I’m alive!”

And maybe that’s enough, to know that he’s alive. With Yan now well into his 80s, a quiet, simple life is perhaps just wok he needs.

item.title: [SCMP] Shaoxing wine goes upmarket: Dongqu’s luxury touch elevates the Chinese pantry staple
item.description:
For a small city of three million people, Shaoxing stands as a giant in the global Chinese collective consciousness. After all, the name of the eastern Chinese city is emblazoned on the quintessential bottles of cooking wine that are found in Asian households and restaurants the world over, with which numerous Chinese regional cuisines – from the complex braises of Shanghai and Zhejiang (the province where Shaoxing is found) to the spicy marinades of Sichuan province and the subtle steamed seafood of Cantonese fare – would be nigh on impossible to cook without.

Shaoxing wine is one of China’s oldest grain ferments, evolving from ancient rice ales into a polished yellow wine poured at rites and family banquets for more than two millennia. First linked to early ritual offerings in the Spring and Autumn period (770BC to 476BC) and Han era (206BC to AD220), it later soaked the verses of Tang and Song dynasty poets, becoming a favoured pour at riverside feasts and scholarly gatherings. By the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), it had settled into its role as a symbol of longevity and good fortune, especially around autumn and winter festivals.

The character of Shaoxing wine is defined by three markers of terroir: the base grain of glutinous rice, Jianhu lake water fed by the Kuaiji Mountains and the qu (a wheat-based starter) that seeds fermentation with a complex microbiome. Today, Shaoxing is protected as a geographical indication, so any bottle bearing the name must be born of this landscape.
item.content:encoded:
For a small city of three million people, Shaoxing stands as a giant in the global Chinese collective consciousness. After all, the name of the eastern Chinese city is emblazoned on the quintessential bottles of cooking wine that are found in Asian households and restaurants the world over, with which numerous Chinese regional cuisines – from the complex braises of Shanghai and Zhejiang (the province where Shaoxing is found) to the spicy marinades of Sichuan province and the subtle steamed seafood of Cantonese fare – would be nigh on impossible to cook without.

Shaoxing wine is one of China’s oldest grain ferments, evolving from ancient rice ales into a polished yellow wine poured at rites and family banquets for more than two millennia. First linked to early ritual offerings in the Spring and Autumn period (770BC to 476BC) and Han era (206BC to AD220), it later soaked the verses of Tang and Song dynasty poets, becoming a favoured pour at riverside feasts and scholarly gatherings. By the Qing dynasty (1644-1911), it had settled into its role as a symbol of longevity and good fortune, especially around autumn and winter festivals.

The character of Shaoxing wine is defined by three markers of terroir: the base grain of glutinous rice, Jianhu lake water fed by the Kuaiji Mountains and the qu (a wheat-based starter) that seeds fermentation with a complex microbiome. Today, Shaoxing is protected as a geographical indication, so any bottle bearing the name must be born of this landscape.

Yet, for an industry that produces more than 600,000 tonnes annually, only a fraction of Shaoxing wine is intended for table-drinking, and just a hair’s sliver of that is produced by boutique wineries at the luxury end of the market.

Chen Zhi is looking to change that. In his late 30s, the boisterous, bespectacled businessman is a rare presence in a slow-moving, tradition-bound industry that is closely tied to the state, where the cultural concept of guanxi (connections) still reigns supreme.

In 2017, suffering from spontaneous nerve spasms that paralysed one side of his face, Chen was on his way to an acupuncture appointment when he chanced upon a fair organised by the China Alcoholic Drinks Association, where he was roped into a tasting of Shaoxing wine from the historic Pagoda Brand, leading him down a rabbit hole into which he has “been sinking deeper and deeper ever since, right up to this day”, he says.

Chen went on to launch Dongqu in 2019, defying many of the norms associated with Shaoxing wine.

First, there’s the price: at a starting price of HK$600 (US$77), even its most affordable bottling, the 2009 vintage, is almost triple the price of other high-quality sipping Shaoxing wines, such as the 10-year-aged bottling from the famed Nu’er Hong brand. This is largely a result of Dongqu’s laborious production processes, which depart from the industry practice of blending different wines for a consistent flavour. Instead, Dongqu opts for single-year vintages drawn directly from the earthenware jars they’re aged in – all the better to bring out the unique growing and fermentation conditions of each particular season.

Then there’s the move-fast-and-break-things approach that Chen has cultivated at Dongqu that, despite falling under the umbrella of the vast Pagoda Brand Winery, functions like a start-up.

“The mission of state-owned enterprises is not to make mistakes,” Chen tells me over a sumptuous dinner at the one-Michelin-star, Taizhou fine-dining restaurant Wild Yeast in Hangzhou. “There’s a slang term – mo yu [to stroke a fish] – which means to slack off and do nothing. Doing well isn’t necessarily a good thing, and doing badly also doesn’t really matter – you just have to guarantee a tiny bit of growth every year.”

In contrast, Dongqu has done everything but rest on its laurels. In just seven years, the boutique brand has expanded to more than 200 Michelin- and Black Pearl-awarded establishments across China, which have found it to be a perfect food pairing.

Like sake production, the brewing process for high-end Shaoxing wine takes place over the colder winter months, to prevent spoilage and allow for careful control of fermentation. On an overcast day in early November, the brewing halls at the Pagoda Brand Winery, on the shores of the Jianhu, are in full swing, pumping billowing, rice-scented columns of steam onto osmanthus-lined roads of the compound. There are 15 shifu (brewmasters) in charge of the process, each responsible for the operations of a brewing hall. Despite the sheer physicality of the job, experience is crucial here, with the youngest shifu already well into their 50s.

Mao-capped brewmaster Ni Xingjun is already working up a sweat despite the chill in the air, as he rakes a mixture of yeast, glutinous rice and Jianhu lake water in a large earthen jar – a labour-intensive task that must be repeated every four to five hours around the clock over four days for the hundreds of jars on the main brewing floor.

The winemaking is highly technical: the rice must be soaked and steamed to kick-start the brewing process, and the temperature of the grains meticulously controlled throughout by calibrating the steaming time to the temperature of the water as well as the ambient environment to ensure proper fermentation later. The shifu combines his intuition and years of experience with hard data to tease out the best qualities of the rice grains, a varietal from Anqing, Anhui province, that is allowed a longer growth cycle to increase its stores of starch, resulting in a wine with bolder flavours.

“If you’d like, lean in and take a deep breath of this aroma,” says Ni, pulling me towards a freshly raked vat. I breathe in, filling my nostrils with a milky, malty scent that is both gentle and all-encompassing, comforting and intoxicating all at once; a scent that is instantly nostalgic to anyone for whom a freshly steamed bowl of rice was a fixture at the dinner table.

Today, Dongqu is spearheading a return to dinner tables not just in homes, but across some of the most in-demand restaurant tables across the country. In Hong Kong, the brand’s layered, umami-forward pours have been featured in traditional-leaning pairings, such as with braised vermicelli with hairy crab at neo-Cantonese restaurant Jee and spritzed atop a crispy stuffed sea cucumber at Vea, to more left-field match-ups as with the signature king crab arroz caldoso at one-Michelin-star Ando, and even transformed into a Shaoxing wine ice cream to cap off an Edomae omakase meal at Sushi Kumogaku.

“Compared to sake, Dongqu offers a richer and more complex flavour profile, which is fully released when heated, making it particularly suited to grilling and simmering,” says Kumogaku’s head chef, Chan Wing-kin. He believes that it adds a deeper aroma to seafood that is difficult to find in Japanese cuisine.

This boundary-crossing milieu is all part of Chen’s mission to refashion the image of Shaoxing wine as a marker of Chinese haute gastronomy, rather than a cheap pantry staple relegated to the status of a mere condiment. He likens the winemaking process – tending to the yeast, keeping watch around the clock – and growing the brand as being akin to the process of raising his first daughter.

“As everyone knows, newborn babies need constant care, and what I saw at the brewing site was the same,” Chen recalls. “It’s like watching a child grow up. You don’t know what they’ll become; you can only wait patiently from the sidelines.”

item.title: [SCMP] Ready player 3: India offers Asean a US-China alternative
item.description:
At a food fair in New Delhi, a vegetable exporter from the Philippines set out its wares: bags of dried moringa and lemongrass, bundles of taro leaves and a bowl of laing, the creamy coconut-milk stew made from them.

The question Dry Tech Manufacturing wanted to answer was simple: could the simple Filipino food it sells under its Sheentaro brand tantalise the taste buds of the world’s most populous country?

India has hundreds of millions of vegetarians, more than any other country on Earth, making it the ideal market for Sheentaro’s plant-based and ready-to-cook products, Dry Tech vice-president Corinne Anne Cordero told This Week in Asia.
item.content:encoded:
At a food fair in New Delhi, a vegetable exporter from the Philippines set out its wares: bags of dried moringa and lemongrass, bundles of taro leaves and a bowl of laing, the creamy coconut-milk stew made from them.

The question Dry Tech Manufacturing wanted to answer was simple: could the simple Filipino food it sells under its Sheentaro brand tantalise the taste buds of the world’s most populous country?

India has hundreds of millions of vegetarians, more than any other country on Earth, making it the ideal market for Sheentaro’s plant-based and ready-to-cook products, Dry Tech vice-president Corinne Anne Cordero told This Week in Asia.

“That’s the main reason why we decided to sign up on short notice,” she said of the Indusfood expo, held in Greater Noida at the start of this year.

“With India having a bigger population than China … and a lot of them are vegetarian, we thought they’d be more open to those types of food ingredients.”

Sheentaro’s products were previously showcased at the China-Asean Expo in Nanning and Cordero said the reception was so positive that “when this opportunity in India came about, we said ‘let’s try it again’”.

Southeast Asian nations are increasingly looking to India as an alternative market, arms supplier and technology partner as China and the US vie for regional influence.

India is more than happy to oblige, observers say – though it also knows its limits. It cannot out-trade China, nor can it supplant America’s security umbrella. What is offers instead is room to manoeuvre, free of the demand to choose sides.

That message travelled to Manila last month, where India’s foreign minister, S. Jaishankar, used Asean-led meetings to press the case for deeper cooperation, calling it the only way to “de-risk and diversify”.

He spoke of energy security and food security, and how precarious both had become. Neither these nor public health could be taken for granted in this new “era of volatility and disruption”, Jaishankar said, identifying maritime trade as a further source of anxiety.

A more stable and secure future was in reach, he said, but only by working together: an animating theme of India’s Act East Policy, launched 12 years ago to forge stronger economic, strategic, and cultural ties with Southeast Asia and the broader region.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi were also in the Philippine capital last month for talks with the Association of Southeast Asian Nations on the South China Sea, supply chains and security – a reminder of how much great-power rivalry still shapes regional diplomacy.

The economic dimension of India’s engagement push was on full display earlier in July, when Delhi hosted talks on upgrading the Asean-India Trade in Goods Agreement, a decade-old free-trade pact that officials say no longer reflects current realities.

Two-way trade came in at US$128 billion in the 2025-26 financial year, according to India’s Commerce and Industry Ministry – respectable, but only a fraction of the US$1 trillion and change that China did with the bloc.

Analysts say India’s strategy appears to be centred around pairing diplomacy with trade, defence exports and maritime cooperation, offering Southeast Asia a third option beyond the US-China binary.

It is best described as “a search for mutual wins”, according to Arvind Raj, a geopolitical analyst and associate research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies’ Centre for Multilateralism Studies in Singapore.

A more multipolar neighbourhood would give Southeast Asian nations more choices and more room to hedge, he said – as India, in turn, secured a larger foothold in a region that it had long courted from the margins.

Summitry to substance

For years, India’s Asean diplomacy has been heavy on the ceremony, but light on the delivery.

“Asean sits at the centre of India’s Act East Policy on paper, but for most of the past decade the relationship ran on summitry rather than substance,” said Oorja Tapan, a doctoral researcher of international politics at Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi.

Analysts say the clearest evidence of how that dynamic is beginning to change can be seen in the region’s expanding arsenals.

During a three-day state visit last month, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi sealed a deal for Jakarta to buy BrahMos supersonic cruise missiles – jointly developed by India and Russia – making Indonesia the third Southeast Asian buyer after Vietnam and the Philippines.

A separate deal for Jakarta to acquire India’s Astra air-to-air missiles was also signed.

Pooja Bhatt, an associate professor of international relations at India’s O.P. Jindal Global University, calls such defence cooperation “not only part of increasing trade with Asean but also a form of strategic signalling” – proof that Delhi can deliver hardware, not just handshakes.

India wanted to become Southeast Asia’s “resident partner”, Tapan said, offering “capability without a formal alliance demand attached” and without asking the region to choose sides.

Pairing defence exports with renewed free-trade negotiations showed that Delhi wanted to be seen as “a dependable partner offering security cooperation, technology-sharing and balanced regional influence”, said Shristi Pukhrem, a visiting fellow at the India Foundation think tank and director of its Act East Centre.

Foreign policy researcher Joanne Lin concurred that weapons sales alone would not be enough to anchor the relationship.

India’s relevance depended on it delivering across “trade, maritime security, connectivity, tech and supply chains”, said Lin, a senior fellow at the ISEAS – Yusof Ishak Institute and visiting scholar at the MIT Centre for International Studies.

“This is why India is trying to address concerns over trade imbalance, rules of origin and possible re-routing of Chinese goods through Asean, while Asean looks forward to market access with fewer barriers.”

Beyond US-China?

Ultimately, India’s pitch boils down to optionality.

Delhi is not seeking “supremacy in Asean”, according to Abhishek Sharma of the Observer Research Foundation think tank in the Indian capital, but rather is trying to advance its own trade interests while pushing for a stronger, more secure – and more multipolar – Indo-Pacific region.

This framing allowed the South Asian nation to cast itself as an independent pole, distinct from both Beijing and Washington and without the associated baggage, said Sharma, a junior fellow with the foundation’s strategic studies programme.

Lin agreed that India functioned as an additional option for Asean rather than a direct replacement for either the US or China.

India’s appeal is more as a balancing and diversification partner

Joanne Lin, foreign policy researcher

“They are looking for partners that can widen their strategic space without forcing them into rigid alignments,” she said of Southeast Asian nations. “India’s strategic autonomy, multi-alignment and Global South positioning resonate with Asean’s own instinct to diversify partnerships and preserve room for manoeuvre.”

In Tapan’s telling, India “lowers the cost of hedging” for the region, due to it being “aligned enough with the West to be useful, [but] non-aligned enough that buying Indian missiles doesn’t read in Beijing as joining a containment bloc”.

Still, Lin was careful not to overstate Delhi’s diplomatic standing within the region.

India “is not yet in the same league as China or the US” in terms of Southeast Asia’s “perceptions of influence”, she said.

“China remains deeply embedded economically, while the US remains central to security calculations. India’s appeal is more as a balancing and diversification partner, useful, non-coercive and increasingly visible, but still needing stronger economic delivery.”

‘Some way to go’

India still had “some way to go” to match the scale of Chinese capital, trade volume and state-driven speed, said Bhatt, the international-relations professor.

China’s trade with Asean was about eight times higher than India’s last year – a gulf that does not look likely to close any time soon.

But Delhi’s diplomacy need not be based on countering China alone.

India and Asean spoke “a common language of non-alignment” and shared “a common belief in the Global South”, Bhatt said.

Soft-power advantages bolster India’s appeal, according to Pukhrem, pointing to Delhi-funded restoration work at heritage sites such as Cambodia’s Angkor Wat and Vietnam’s My Son temples as evidence of outreach that “builds soft power rooted in shared civilisational ties rather than transactional influence”.

Tapan agreed that it was not a case of “India vs China’s clout, but India raising the price of Chinese dominance”.

The recent BrahMos sales had demonstrated regional appetite for Indian weapons systems, she said, further pointing to demand for naval hardware, generic pharmaceuticals and digital public infrastructure “that no Chinese product can substitute”.

Tapan also identified India’s growing appeal as a “China plus one” destination for companies looking to diversify supply chains.

“None of this beats a trillion dollars of trade. But Asean’s operating logic is hedging,” she said. “The realistic question is whether India can be indispensable in the places where China is either unwelcome or absent.”

Lin cautioned against India defining its Asean engagement purely in oppositional terms.

“Asean does not want to be treated as a theatre for India-China rivalry,” she said, adding that Delhi could make the most impact by helping the bloc diversify supply chains, build maritime capacity and strengthen digital and health cooperation.

“India’s broader influence will depend on whether it can also deliver in areas that matter to Asean’s economic and development priorities,” Lin added.

item.title: [SCMP] Hong Kong’s 1,000-year-old tea heritage is being rediscovered and rehabilitated
item.description:
Ask a Hongkonger where the city’s tea story begins, and they will probably point to the British – the colonial traders who funnelled Chinese leaves through Victoria Harbour to the world.

Only, they would be off by about eight centuries.

Most Hongkongers today don’t know the city ever had its own tea plantations, let alone that tea had been growing here long before the British arrived in the mid-19th century. Li In, a co-founder of the Hong Kong Tea Production Institute (HKTPI) who has practised the art of tea-making for more than a decade, found out in 2017 – in a London classroom, at the UK Tea Academy.
item.content:encoded:
Ask a Hongkonger where the city’s tea story begins, and they will probably point to the British – the colonial traders who funnelled Chinese leaves through Victoria Harbour to the world.

Only, they would be off by about eight centuries.

Most Hongkongers today don’t know the city ever had its own tea plantations, let alone that tea had been growing here long before the British arrived in the mid-19th century. Li In, a co-founder of the Hong Kong Tea Production Institute (HKTPI) who has practised the art of tea-making for more than a decade, found out in 2017 – in a London classroom, at the UK Tea Academy.

“I was born and raised in Hong Kong and it took a British instructor, Jane Pettigrew, mentioning tea gardens in Lantau for me to first hear about [Hong Kong’s tea heritage],” she says.

Ngong Ping Tea Garden, the plantation in question, on Lantau Island, was founded in 1948 by Brook Bernacchi, a British lawyer and politician who arrived in Hong Kong as a marine with the World War II liberation forces in 1945. He built a life on the plateau near the Po Lin Monastery. His Lotus Brand was marketed as “the only Hong Kong tea”.

By the early 1980s, unable to compete with mass production, the tea plantation area was downsized.
