On July 21, a young man was gunned down by a masked gunman on a motorbike in Pak Kret. A week later, a former bank manager killed two relatives and injured four others in a bullet-strewn dispute over land.

But most of the lives were taken by a 14-year-old student who allegedly shot his grandparents before going on a killing spree at Debsirin school on Friday morning. By the next day, the death toll was nine and included the shooter, who apparently took his own life.

Over 20 people were shot dead nationwide in that period, according to an estimate from local media reports. But that is not a definitive tally in a country where conflict, gang disputes, robberies, debts, broken hearts and mental health breakdowns are often resolved in a hail of bullets.

No control

It is a gun violence problem everyone knows exists, but no one seems able to control.

“I’ve lost count of how many times I’ve repeated this, but let me say it again: no one has the right to carry a firearm around in public, especially not in public places,” Prime Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said on Monday.

He vowed to drive through new law to get on top of the illegal guns in circulation and make sure that only active personnel were allowed to carry weapons in public. There would be searches, roadblocks and harsh punishments for anyone who breached the law, he added.

“The last public-carry permit was issued three years ago. These carry permits are valid for only one year. Therefore, [right now] no one can carry a gun unless they are an official actively on duty.”

On Tuesday, Anutin suspended the issuance ⁠of permits to buy firearms and said existing licences would be reviewed, Reuters reported.

In the fallout from the school killings, gun control arguments have split along predictable lines: those calling for further tightening of laws and those who say it is not legal guns to blame but the individual who pulls the trigger.

It is already a complex process to obtain a gun legally in Thailand, according to Pat Hakimi, vice-president of the Firearms Traders Association of Thailand.

“Before you can buy a gun from a shop, there has to be a background check … the government does the checking. There’s fingerprinting, it gets sent to the district officer for review, and then another signature for approval,” he said.

“My family has been selling guns for 90 years, since my grandmother’s time. As far as I know, not a single one of our guns has ever been used to commit a crime.”

Instead, he said the overwhelming majority of gun crimes are committed with unlicensed, black market weapons – over one million of which may be in circulation.

Those include blank guns illegally altered to fire real bullets or so-called welfare weapons – bought via a cut-price quota scheme allowing civil servants to buy subsidised guns – that slip onto the black market. “Prevention starts by controlling guns in the wrong hands – they’re sold openly all over online marketplaces,” Pat said.

Sporadic Thai police raids on criminal gangs often uncover alarming evidence of the firepower on the streets: caches of military-grade weapons including automatic rifles and machine guns.

‘Flawed society’

Thailand is often cited as having the highest rate of gun ownership in Southeast Asia with the last data point, compiled in 2017 by the Small Arms Survey, reporting over 10.3 million firearms were in civilian hands, or around 15 guns per 100 people.

Experts say that abundance is partly to do with Thailand’s militarised culture as well as its location as a smuggling route between two active war zones: in the south, where insurgents battle authorities, and in civil war-torn Myanmar.

The school shooting has highlighted the complexity of gun control, as the weapon used was licensed to the shooter’s grandfather.

Kisanaphong Poothakool, a police lieutenant-colonel and leading criminologist, said firearms laws should be updated to require “periodic renewal and reassessment” for licensed gun holders.

He also called for tougher illegal firearm control, better databases and tracing for risk assessment and mandatory safe-storage requirements “especially in homes where children or other vulnerable persons are present”.

“Every society has conflict. The issue is why a firearm is available at the moment the conflict escalates,” he said. “If we can reduce the intersection between conflict, anger and access to firearms, we can reduce the number of disputes that end in death.”

In the absence of comprehensive data or government findings, those who regularly see the outcomes of violence are left to make their own diagnosis of the ills plaguing Thailand.

Ekkapop Luangprasert, founder of the Sai Mai Tong Rod, a leading volunteer group that members of the public often contact before the police, receives complaints of violence, including shootings, “almost daily”.

“I think what we’re seeing overall stems from a flawed belief embedded in Thai society – a culture that glorifies violence,” he said. “Whenever something goes wrong, Thai society has taught us that the answer is punishment.”

Old-school parenting and wider power values leave children ill-equipped to deal with anger and frustration, he said. “By the time they grow up and enter society, they end up defaulting to violence as the way to solve problems.”

“We need to take a hard look at what’s actually happening in Thai society today. Thai society is built on authoritarianism: you must listen to your teachers, you must listen to your elders. That era is over now. It doesn’t work any more in this day and age.”

item.title: [SCMP] Newcastle University Medicine Malaysia graduates in limbo after UK rule change
item.description:
When S* enrolled at Newcastle University Medicine Malaysia (NUMed Malaysia) in the Southeast Asian nation, the British-born Pakistani student believed the five-year medical degree would give him a realistic route into Britain’s National Health Service (NHS).

The pathway was never formally guaranteed, but S said NUMed had highlighted a decade-long record in which students who applied for the UK Foundation Programme (UKFP) – the supervised training route for medical graduates – had secured posts.

For international students such as S, who spent about US$134,500 on a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) degree, the UK route was crucial because alternatives were limited.
item.content:encoded:
When S* enrolled at Newcastle University Medicine Malaysia (NUMed Malaysia) in the Southeast Asian nation, the British-born Pakistani student believed the five-year medical degree would give him a realistic route into Britain’s National Health Service (NHS).

The pathway was never formally guaranteed, but S said NUMed had highlighted a decade-long record in which students who applied for the UK Foundation Programme (UKFP) – the supervised training route for medical graduates – had secured posts.

For international students such as S, who spent about US$134,500 on a Bachelor of Medicine and Bachelor of Surgery (MBBS) degree, the UK route was crucial because alternatives were limited.

Malaysian NUMed graduates could opt for housemanship locally, while NUMed says international graduates are not eligible for the pre-registration internship required to practise medicine in Malaysia.

Then, during S’s final year, the UK parliament changed the rules.

The Medical Training (Prioritisation) Act, which became law in March, gave priority for UKFP places to medical graduates who had completed most of their training in Britain.

The British government has said the policy aims to protect taxpayer investment in medical training, give domestically trained doctors a clearer route into the NHS and reduce reliance on overseas recruitment.

The law does not bar other applicants from applying, but changes the order in which posts are allocated.

Although S holds an MBBS awarded by Newcastle University and recognised by the General Medical Council (GMC) as a UK primary medical qualification, his five years of training in Malaysia mean he is allocated after priority applicants trained in Britain.

For students who had built their futures around the NUMed degree’s British status, the rule change has upended expectations about where it could take them after graduation.

As of July 30, Newcastle University told This Week in Asia that 68 of NUMed’s 102 eligible graduates had secured UKFP posts, leaving 34 without confirmed placements.

S remains among those without a post.

Across Britain, the UK Foundation Programme Office initially placed 738 non-priority applicants on a reserve list after allocating 10,810 priority-group individuals in March.

Reserve-list applicants are offered posts only as vacancies emerge after the priority group has been allocated, using a computer-generated rank and applicants’ preferences.

By the end of July, 204 remained on the reserve list, and a fifth and final allocation round from the reserve applicant list is slated for Wednesday.

Not guaranteed

“It [the UK pathway] was not something that was guaranteed, but this was one of the selling points which the university used. Everyone who applied from Newcastle University to UK foundation training got a UKFP position,” S said.

He acknowledged that prospective students had been told placement ultimately rested with British authorities, but said the experience of previous NUMed cohorts shaped how he and his classmates planned their careers.

“We saw four batches of our seniors, they all got it [training posts].”

Newcastle University said access to postgraduate training was never guaranteed and its published information always stated that routes including UKFP were subject to change.

The university added that the UKFP became a mainstream route for NUMed graduates from 2017, with over 600 graduates entering its training pipeline. Previously, most had undergone housemanship training in Malaysia or used overseas routes.

“The trend since 2017 has moved sharply towards UKFP: 31 per cent in 2019, 64 per cent in 2020, 75 per cent in 2021, and 83 per cent by 2025, with the rest going into Malaysian housemanship or other pathways each year,” the university said.

“That rise tracked NHS workforce pressure and a relaxing of UK immigration rules for overseas medical graduates from 2020. This is also the first cohort to graduate under the new prioritisation rules.”

The university said it wrote to students within two days of the bill’s introduction to parliament in January, tracked its progress and held briefings and town halls.

After the bill became law in March, the university confirmed to students that their eligibility to apply for the UKFP had not changed and individual support was available.

S said the change nevertheless came too late for final-year students to seek alternatives.

“They changed it mid-cycle, leaving us completely stranded,” S said.

Few alternatives

For international graduates, the alternatives are limited.

S’s family lives in a third country where he spent most of his life before medical school, but practising there would require accreditation and a medical licensing examination in a language in which he did not study medicine.

He estimated that the Australian Medical Council pathway would cost another US$7,000 to US$8,000.

Instead, he is pursuing the United States Medical Licensing Examination after completing a two-month elective at a US university while also considering research and a PhD.

“Whatever I had planned for five years has been pretty much down the drain because of whatever changes have taken place,” he said.

In a written reply to This Week in Asia, the GMC said NUMed’s MBBS remained recognised as a UK primary medical qualification despite the policy change.

“Newcastle University’s Medicine Malaysia campus is an overseas campus of a UK medical school. Its medical degree is recognised by the GMC as a UK primary medical qualification, and there have been no changes to that recognition,” it said.

The regulator has stressed, however, that deciding who receives a UKFP post is the remit of the programme office.

The UK Foundation Programme Office and Department of Health and Social Care did not respond to This Week In Asia’s requests for comment.

The change has forced current students to rethink their future plans.

Unaizah Ahmed, a fourth-year NUMed student from Pakistan living in the United Arab Emirates, said that earlier cohorts had reinforced students’ expectations that NUMed graduates could progress to UK training. Since the rule change, she and her classmates have been looking more seriously at alternatives including Australia and the US.

“I’d be lying if I said I am not concerned about my future with all these changes,” she said. “So far, my main goal is to complete my studies first, and I shall look at my options during or after I’m almost done with my final year.”

Newcastle University said it recognised that “this is a particularly stressful time” for students who could not secure UKFP posts, and was determined to support them.

Professor Geoffrey Williams, a higher education analyst and visiting fellow at Universiti Malaya, said the rule change exposed a distinction between the regulatory status of a degree awarded by an overseas British campus and its practical value for graduates seeking UK training.

NUMed’s qualification had not lost regulatory recognition, he said, but the difference lay in its practical value for graduates seeking priority access to the NHS training system.

“The loss of value is the difference between immediate priority access versus stand-in-line certificates,” he said.

“A Malaysian student who studied in the UK has immediate priority access to the UK training programme. A British student who studied in the Malaysian franchise campus as a foreign student here would stand in line too when she went home.”

*Name changed to protect interviewee’s identity

item.title: [SCMP] For China’s aspiring foreign workers, getting a job is only half the battle
item.description:
Even as an undergraduate in his native Barcelona, Aitor knew he wanted to work in China.

The young finance major reckoned an economy of such scale and speed had more to offer someone with his skill set than the market waiting for him closer to home.

After moving to Shanghai to complete a master’s degree, he had what he came for: a supply-chain job in the bustling financial centre. What Aitor – a nickname, requested to protect the identity of his employer – did not expect was that getting a job would be the easy part.
item.content:encoded:
Even as an undergraduate in his native Barcelona, Aitor knew he wanted to work in China.

The young finance major reckoned an economy of such scale and speed had more to offer someone with his skill set than the market waiting for him closer to home.

After moving to Shanghai to complete a master’s degree, he had what he came for: a supply-chain job in the bustling financial centre. What Aitor – a nickname, requested to protect the identity of his employer – did not expect was that getting a job would be the easy part.

Being hired at firms in China is already difficult for foreign graduates: employers barely give applications a look, given the number of qualified local candidates.

But Aitor’s Chinese language proficiency provided a way around this hurdle. He could search on Boss Zhipin, one of the country’s largest recruitment apps, which Aitor said was “not very friendly for foreigners” and not known to most expats.

Then came the real challenge: the visa. A points-based system for qualification, the overlapping categories and the volume of documentation involved have made obtaining a work permit a longer-running problem than the job search ever was.

“Visa applications are complicated, especially working visas, and I’m still in the process six months after my application,” Aitor said. “The amount of papers needed makes it very complicated.”

Yet as a degree holder from a Chinese university, he said he considered himself lucky, noting that others had it worse.

“I know many valuable and well-educated individuals are struggling to find ways to formalise their work in China, since family reunion visas are not flexible at all and working visas are very hard to get and [it is] hard to be sponsored by local companies; they are caught in between,” he said.

As China’s economy has grown in scale and its influence across global supply chains has expanded, more international graduates and professionals are eyeing opportunities in the world’s second-largest economy.

However, unlike traditional immigration destinations such as the United States and Canada, China has historically relied less on foreign workers to fill labour shortages, leaving the country to build a foreign talent system relatively slowly.

Many foreign workers in China are transferred there by multinational companies, with visa processing, housing and relocation costs typically covered by their employers. This provides a markedly different experience from younger candidates attempting to enter China’s job market independently.

At the same time, the country has been facing rising employment pressure, particularly among young workers, adding another layer of complexity to efforts to attract overseas talent. Its youth unemployment reached 21.3 per cent in June 2023, before the National Bureau of Statistics revised its calculation method. The rate stood at 14.9 per cent in June.

Last year, China introduced the “K visa”, targeting young science and technology professionals as it competes globally for engineers, researchers and innovators.

For most foreign workers, however, the standard “Z visa” remains the main route, requiring employer sponsorship, qualifications, work experience and extensive administrative procedures.

“In reality, we have not yet handled any K visa applications. The visa is still very new and at least from my experience, I have not heard of any successful cases so far,” said Anna Chen, a visa consultant based in Shenzhen.

Chen said the K visa, which attracted significant attention overseas when it was introduced, mainly targets young foreign scientists, engineers and other highly skilled technology professionals.

“The target group is quite narrow. Most foreigners coming to China for work do not meet that threshold,” she said. “And those who do often choose the United States instead, since salaries there are generally more attractive, based on my conversations with clients.”

Meanwhile, the Z visa is divided into three categories: A, which targets high-level talent such as leading researchers, executives and recognised experts; B, which covers most skilled professionals who must meet requirements related to education, work experience and salary; and C, a less common category reserved for seasonal or temporary employees.

“Most of the foreign workers I deal with are still applying for Category B work permits,” Chen said.

The visa agent said that compared with the US, China’s work visa system was generally less competitive for high-skilled applicants, as it did not have a lottery system like the H-1B programme in the US.

“But the process can still be complicated, since China requires employers to sponsor visas and most Chinese companies do not lack workforce domestically anyway, making them less likely to look overseas for talent,” she added.

Unlike China, countries such as the United Kingdom and US offer post-study work routes for international graduates.

In the UK, new degree holders can apply for a graduate visa, allowing them to work without employer sponsorship, usually for two years before switching to a skilled worker visa with an approved employer.

In the US, graduates can seek Optional Practical Training – temporary employment related to their field of study – before seeking employer-sponsored visas such as the H-1B.

China, by contrast, generally does not offer a similar transition route. Foreign graduates typically need to secure a job offer and employer sponsorship before applying for a work visa, even after studying at a Chinese university.

China has not released updated nationwide figures on foreign employment, but data showed that authorities issued 711,000 residence permits to foreign nationals in 2023, about 15 per cent below pre-pandemic levels.

Around 237,000 of these were work-related residence permits, according to Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development data.

Chen said China had tightened scrutiny of work visa applications in recent years, following cases in some cities where foreigners obtained permits through fake employment arrangements or shell companies.

“The process now takes longer, employers also face stricter documentation requirements and applicants are asked to provide more financial records. Overall, work visa approvals have slowed,” she added.

Marshall Ma, a former recruiter based in Shanghai, said demand for foreign professionals in the city – widely regarded as China’s largest market for overseas talent – has declined sharply in recent years.

“The last time I heard a company specifically asking to hire foreigners was in 2021,” Ma said. “After the pandemic, competition in Shanghai’s job market intensified.

“Foreign candidates [are] often seen as having higher expectations, not only in terms of salaries but also benefits such as annual leave.”

Ma said demand for foreign workers remained relatively strong mainly in English teaching roles, while many other white-collar positions could now be filled by younger Chinese jobseekers at lower cost and with native language proficiency.

Another factor discouraging companies from hiring foreigners, he said, was the additional administrative burden, including visa applications and social insurance requirements.

“Many that traditionally hired large numbers of foreigners were Asia-Pacific regional headquartered firms, but lots of them began scaling back their China operations since 2023. Naturally, demand for foreign workers declined as well,” Ma added.

China has taken steps to make everyday digital services more accessible for foreigners, initially targeting overseas visitors but also benefiting foreign residents living and working in the country.

Since 2023, authorities have expanded mobile payment options by allowing more international bank cards to link with platforms such as Alipay and WeChat Pay, while simplifying registration and identity verification procedures.

However, challenges remain for some foreigners navigating China’s digital ecosystem.

“Digital and internet services work very well for the most part, but as foreigners, we often encounter small issues with many apps because we need to use our passports or provide other information that can sometimes cause problems,” Aitor said.

“Since I came to China three years ago, I think things have been moving in a positive direction, but there is still work to be done in some internet services so that foreigners can have a smoother experience.”

The reason why I decided to stay in China is because I knew my skill set would be more valuable here

Marcos Sabio, British-Spanish dual citizen

Yet not all foreigners encounter the same visa hurdles. For British-Spanish dual citizen Marcos Sabio, the transition into China’s workforce was relatively smooth. He found his software industry role in Beijing through the career-oriented social media platform LinkedIn, where his employer handled the work permit application.

“Luckily, for the visa applications and all the administration and bureaucracy, everything was handled by the HR team in the company,” he said.

“The reason why I decided to stay in China is because I knew my skill set would be more valuable here. Being able to speak Chinese, English, Spanish and some Russian is a real asset,” said Sabio, who has lived in China for 12 years.

Despite the hurdles, China’s appeal among foreign professionals appears to be recovering. According to a 2025 survey from InterNations – an online platform for people living and working abroad – China ranked sixth out of 46 destinations, with respondents expressing relatively high satisfaction with career opportunities, personal finances and daily convenience.

However, the survey also highlighted persistent challenges, including language barriers, administrative procedures and adaptation to the domestic digital ecosystem.

For Malaysian citizen Jens Lee, his China career journey involved less adaptation than others. His ethnic background and previous study experience in the country meant that adjusting to daily life and workplace culture came relatively naturally. After completing his master’s degree, he moved smoothly into a full-time role at a European-backed consultancy.

But familiarity with China did not necessarily make the bureaucracy easier.

Lee turned to a visa agency to handle the process, but found the experience less than smooth. The agency was relatively inexperienced, partly because he chose a cheaper provider that charged 6,000 yuan (US$886).

He said the intermediary handled most of the application, leaving him with limited understanding of the points-based system and other requirements.

Despite the administrative obstacles, Lee said, “China’s scale, economic dynamism and fast-paced working environment offer significant opportunities for professional learning and personal growth, which is something I value tremendously at the current stage of my career.”

item.title: [SCMP] Why was a US Yale graduate hounded out of his job promoting Chinese culture?
item.description:
In just two months, Yale graduate Edward Kuperman went from being praised by Chinese state media to being bombarded by public accusations that he was a spy.

It began with a June 18 article from state news agency Xinhua, in which he was described as an eager 24-year-old sinophile who made the unconventional choice of spurning China’s eastern metropolises to live in Dunhuang, an oasis in the country’s northwestern Gansu province.

His interest in China started with a Chinese language class in junior high school, as well as books and films about China, Xinhua reported. At 17, he was an exchange student in Suzhou, Jiangsu province. After returning to the United States, his parents hired a Chinese tutor for him, it said.
item.content:encoded:
In just two months, Yale graduate Edward Kuperman went from being praised by Chinese state media to being bombarded by public accusations that he was a spy.

It began with a June 18 article from state news agency Xinhua, in which he was described as an eager 24-year-old sinophile who made the unconventional choice of spurning China’s eastern metropolises to live in Dunhuang, an oasis in the country’s northwestern Gansu province.

His interest in China started with a Chinese language class in junior high school, as well as books and films about China, Xinhua reported. At 17, he was an exchange student in Suzhou, Jiangsu province. After returning to the United States, his parents hired a Chinese tutor for him, it said.

Kuperman, who also goes by the Chinese name Gu Aihua – “Loving China” – started his first job as an intern live-streamer at the Dunhuang Culture International Communication Centre (DCICC) in April, the article said, adding that he believed the city was a “unique entryway to observing China, understanding China and telling China’s stories”.

Dunhuang was for centuries a stop along the Silk Road and in the article Kuperman’s life there is presented as typically rosy. One anecdote describes how he spent three hours helping a Dutch tourist find their lost backpack. “Kuperman told the relieved tourist, ‘In China, nothing gets lost.’ The tourist nodded in agreement,” the article said.

The DCICC’s Instagram account featured Kuperman in three videos in May and June, interviewing participants at the Third World Conference of Sinologists and introducing the city’s Crescent Lake, one of its main attractions.

Dressed in a buttoned-up waistcoat and trousers, he walked in the sand around the lake, introducing it as a place lovers flocked to. “I don’t know about romance for me, but I will say that I love this place,” he said.

But Kuperman’s problems began in July, when he was hired by the Dunhuang Convergence Media Centre, an outlet run by the local government.

The hiring notice, which was picked up by Chinese media, showed that Kuperman was the only foreigner among three new hires. The other two women, both Chinese, had studied translation and communications at British universities.

Posts questioning Kuperman’s qualifications soon emerged on Chinese social media. Some claimed that he received an annual salary of 900,000 yuan (US$133,000), and questioned the pay. “Aren’t they using taxpayers’ money to pamper foreigners?”

That salary would far exceed what a Western graduate would usually expect to be paid in China. For a fresh Chinese graduate, that wage would be astronomical. According to the Hong Kong-based MyCOS Research Institute, the average starting salary for Chinese bachelor’s graduates in the class of 2025 was 77,220 yuan a year.

Online rage and suspicion were further inflamed by the discovery that Kuperman had studied Chinese at National Taiwan University and had interned at the conservative American Enterprise Institute’s Coalition Defence of Taiwan programme.

Hu Xijin, the former editor-in-chief of state-run tabloid Global Times, which has an English edition, waded into the controversy.

He wrote in a now-deleted online post that most foreigners employed by Chinese organisations had “complex experiences”, such as previously working in American media or think tanks, where they may have written reports viewed as unfavourable by the Chinese.

Hu said netizens wanted to “spoil his job” using spy accusations, because they were unhappy Kuperman was paid so much.

Kuperman has said that his interest in East Asia is cultural, not political. He previously wrote on Yale’s website that he studied the region “because of its unique combination of ancient tradition and dialogue with the West”.

Regardless of netizens’ intentions, their furious posting got results.

By Friday, Kuperman had decided not to take the job, state broadcaster CCTV reported. The local authorities clarified that he was only offered an annual salary of about 330,000 yuan – not 900,000 yuan – with various allowances on top. An investigation had been launched to see if there were any problems with the hiring, it said.

A salary of 330,000 yuan is within the normal range for Western graduates working in China.

Kuperman could not be contacted for comment, while the DCICC and local media centre did not respond to interview requests.

Einar Tangen, senior fellow at the Centre for International Governance Innovation and chairman of Asia Narratives, said that while Dunhuang was a city of just 200,000 people, it had more than 20 million visitors annually, with its Mogao Caves representing shared heritage spanning Buddhist, Persian, Greek, Indian and Chinese civilisations.

Dunhuang has been using this identity to try to tell its story to global audiences through what it calls the “innovative Dunhuang model”. A 2025 article from the city’s propaganda department said the DCICC was an important part of that effort, with 28 global social media accounts, 800,000 fans, 5,100 posts and more than 65 million cumulative views.

“We will make Dunhuang an important window for the world to understand China and feel Chinese civilisation,” it said.

The Chinese authorities are keen to win foreigners’ praise for the country’s heritage and modern technology. In 2025, when American influencer IShowSpeed visited Beijing and Shanghai, the Chinese embassy in the US said he was “bridging cultural gaps” and multiple state media outlets ran glowing pieces praising the trip.

Governments often actively invite foreign influencers to China. In June last year, the Hainan provincial tourism board invited 19 influencers from 12 countries to explore the southern island and produce content.

Despite this, a political scientist who wished to stay anonymous acknowledged that in recent years Chinese public opinion had become increasingly sensitive when it came to any issue involving foreigners. He said the resolution of any controversy depended on the style of the decision-maker.

“If you have an open mind or do not think [such backlash] matters, then this will boost cross-cultural exchanges,” he said.

Tangen added that he was worried by the instinct to build walls rather than bridges.

“Dunhuang’s entire model is built on openness. It processes visa-on-arrival for international tourists, has established sister-city ties with cities abroad and hosted over 600 global events in 2025,” he said.

“China is extending visas and inviting the world to see the country as it is, not as hostile or ignorant media portray it. If Kuperman had genuine issues in his background, then they should be addressed – through proper channels.”

item.title: [SCMP] CJ Hendry brings Juju World to Hong Kong with exclusive collectibles
item.description:
The Australian artist Catherine Jenna Hendry, best known to the world as CJ Hendry, first entered the public consciousness through social media, by sharing her hyperrealistic interpretations of luxury items on Instagram. The ink drawings gained Hendry a following of almost a million, and celebrity collectors of her works include Kanye West, Vera Wang, Floyd Mayweather and Pharrell Williams – an impressive feat for someone without formal training or gallery representation.

The New York-based artist has expanded her drawing practice from black and white to colour. But not one to stay confined to a single medium, Hendry has also made waves with her viral plush “flower markets”.

She has also created Juju, a kawaii collectible with floppy ears and a flower for an eye. Running until August 16, Pacific Place is hosting “Juju World”, a fluffy and fun exhibition inspired by the character. Giant Jujus, swings and a chamber filled with 400 plushies await.
item.content:encoded:
The Australian artist Catherine Jenna Hendry, best known to the world as CJ Hendry, first entered the public consciousness through social media, by sharing her hyperrealistic interpretations of luxury items on Instagram. The ink drawings gained Hendry a following of almost a million, and celebrity collectors of her works include Kanye West, Vera Wang, Floyd Mayweather and Pharrell Williams – an impressive feat for someone without formal training or gallery representation.

The New York-based artist has expanded her drawing practice from black and white to colour. But not one to stay confined to a single medium, Hendry has also made waves with her viral plush “flower markets”.

She has also created Juju, a kawaii collectible with floppy ears and a flower for an eye. Running until August 16, Pacific Place is hosting “Juju World”, a fluffy and fun exhibition inspired by the character. Giant Jujus, swings and a chamber filled with 400 plushies await.

There’s also a pop-up store selling iridescent Jujus, created exclusively for Pacific Place. In this line, there are nine standard versions and five additional “secret” versions, which come in limited-edition blind boxes. Visitors can also unlock surprise accessories at the Capsule Toy Station and customise their Juju with interchangeable flower eyes, outfits and more.

At the launch of “Juju World”, we meet an energetic Hendry for a conversation about art, artificial intelligence and what it takes to make it in the industry today.

Describe your routine.

I have studios in Hong Kong and New York, so we’re here every other month. In the studio, every day is different. With three children aged between one and five, it’s mostly chaos. We are just piecing it together and there’s a lot we want to create and achieve, and that comes a little bit chaotically sometimes.

How has that influenced your art?

A lot of my artistic concepts are childlike and have a lot of whimsy. I’m not sure if that’s because I have children and I’m surrounded by childlike wonder, but creating ideas that appeal to both adults and kids is what I want to do. Sometimes, there’s no rhyme or reason to it.

You’ve tackled various mediums. Is there a thread that ties them all together?

Over the past three years, I have started to use this very feminine flower shape. Because I had so many unusual, different concepts, the flower shape allowed me to connect them all together. That has become a branding moment for everything. Even with the Juju logo, there’s a flower on top of the letter J.

Why the pivot from ink drawings to the kawaii collectibles realm?

My drawing practice is very labour-intensive, focused and intimate. I was finding it frustrating because those works are only available to a few people, as they are expensive and hard to come by. I was uncomfortable with that. I still draw, but maybe one-tenth of the time I used to. It has allowed me to spend time creating these other, kooky concepts, such as Juju and the flower markets.

I’ve created these concepts so that more people can appreciate and experience them. You don’t need money to appreciate the flower market: people can access it for free and even their first flower is free. Juju is not necessarily the same, but this fun, friendly character is appealing to many.

How would you explain Juju?

Juju is a fun character with a flower over their eye and no mouth, so they can’t talk back. They are a character that can take you through the happiest of times and the darkest of times, one who is with you no matter what.

How did Juju come about?

Juju’s name comes from my mother. Her name is Judy and my kids call her Juju. My mum is a very elegant lady who wears all white. So the rarest Jujus are always white.

I used AI to help design Juju in early 2025. AI is interesting because everyone kind of belittles it. But as an artist, it’s important to use different tools. I used AI for a very small portion of the design process.

AI is controversial, especially in art because it draws from existing works. Tell us more about your position on it

AI can be used very cleverly, and it can be used very poorly. It depends on what you want to do and the story you want to tell. Anyone can design anything in AI in seconds, but designing something and then making it a reality is a totally different skill set. My artistic process is more in bringing it to life and rolling it out.

I’ve been an artist for 15 years and I’ve been plagiarised for much of that time. So, I’ve become confident enough in my practice to know that no ideas are original, even before AI. Everyone’s referencing everyone else. AI is just speeding that up.

Art is all about collaboration and moving forward. If your entire practice is based on AI, I don’t think you’ll get very far. Mine is based pretty much entirely on design and creativity and using AI only for very small parts.

So, in the age of AI, do you see the role of an artist as more of a curator of sorts?

Yes, absolutely. It’s important to have your own voice. You can use AI to perhaps start a concept, but to build and develop that takes a lot of energy and thought.

Because I’ve been doing this for so long, I feel very comfortable talking about AI. People want to pretend it’s not there. But I’m like, “It’s here, you’ve got to go with it.” I’ve used AI and I will continue to use AI.

Building real-life experiences is so important to me. Like with “Juju World” in Pacific Place, for example, you can only buy these Jujus in person. I’ve purposely taken this offline. Also, we haven’t made many of them. So, when they sell out, they sell out. They’ll never be made again. We never revisit it and we never will.

Like Takashi Murakami, Kaws and others, you seem instinctively aware of how social media, branding and merchandising works. How important is that for an artist today?

It’s hard to be an artist nowadays. Everyone pines over the old days, but they are not coming back. Technology is a beautiful tool, if you can use it in a clever way. But because everyone has social media, it has become oversaturated. I’m interested in in-person experiences. When I build concepts and installations, it’s important to create something unique for people to experience.

That said, I also think there are so many ways to be an artist. I see my job as creating and starting discussions. I’m a commercially successful artist, but that’s not for everyone. Not everyone wants to have merch at their art exhibition. Some people just want to have one extraordinary painting that they’ve taken two years to make. That’s special and important. It depends on the artist you want to be. I’m just one type of artist. Art comes in so many ways, in so many voices.

Who inspires you?

I don’t think, for me, there are people who are inspirations. Like I said before, nothing is original any more. Everything’s being built on something else.

I’ve always interpreted my concepts off other things, blended them, meshed them, reinterpreted them in my own voice, in my own way. Actually, a lot of my ideas come from runway shows, which are extraordinarily inspiring in the way they bring together worlds to showcase concepts and clothing.

When we launched Juju at Phillips West Kowloon (in late 2025), a lot of that inspiration came from the Chanel runway show at the Grand Palais, in Paris, where they did it like a Chanel supermarket.

What do you want people to take away from this particular exhibition?

I’ve always been pretty open with the fact that when I build ideas and exhibitions, I don’t expect anything from anyone. That’s not my job. I believe, as an artist, you’re meant to build something and what people experience is none of my business. A lot of artists might put a plaque on the wall explaining the idea, but I’ve never done that and I never will. I build the idea and people can come and experience it however they want.

What’s next for you?

Gosh, I genuinely don’t know. It’s too hard to predict the future. My art could crash and burn, or I could reach the stars. You never know.

What I do know is that I’m relatively creative. I have a lot of energy, a lot of excitement and a lot of really kooky ideas. I love executing, building and creating. There’s no shortage of ideas. I just love working with my team to come up with stupid stuff all the time.

This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity

item.title: [SCMP] Daughter of ‘Chinese Schindler’ protests use of father’s WWII legacy to sell homes
item.description:
When Manli Ho saw her father’s name being used to advertise US$40,000 houses in his hometown in China, she was outraged.

“He Saved 18,000 Jewish Lives in WWII. His Hometown Has Homes for $40,000,” one headline on the now-removed English-language webpage read.

Manli Ho, 75, is the daughter of Ho Feng-shan, the Chinese diplomat widely known in the West as the “Chinese Schindler” for issuing thousands of visas to Jews fleeing Nazi persecution while serving as China’s consul-general in Vienna, Austria, from 1938 to 1940.
item.content:encoded:
When Manli Ho saw her father’s name being used to advertise US$40,000 houses in his hometown in China, she was outraged.

“He Saved 18,000 Jewish Lives in WWII. His Hometown Has Homes for $40,000,” one headline on the now-removed English-language webpage read.

Manli Ho, 75, is the daughter of Ho Feng-shan, the Chinese diplomat widely known in the West as the “Chinese Schindler” for issuing thousands of visas to Jews fleeing Nazi persecution while serving as China’s consul-general in Vienna, Austria, from 1938 to 1940.

The “Schindler” comparison refers to German businessman Oskar Schindler, who saved about 1,200 Jews by employing them in his factories in occupied Poland during the Holocaust. His story inspired the Academy Award-winning 1993 film Schindler’s List.

But now, a real estate website is using Ho Feng-shan’s legacy to sell homes in his hometown, drawing backlash from local authorities in Yiyang and his daughter in the United States.

The website, YiyangFangchan – “fangchan” means real estate in Chinese – markets property in Yiyang, a city in Hunan province with 4 million residents where Ho Feng-shan was born in 1901.

The website appears to have two distinct sections in Simplified Chinese and English. Its Simplified Chinese pages function as a conventional local property portal, featuring home listings and rental information.

Its English-language site, however, is linked to an American company and targets overseas buyers, promoting Yiyang as an affordable place to buy property or relocate while highlighting its connection to Ho Feng-shan.

The website also operates a pared-down Traditional Chinese-language page aimed at buyers in Hong Kong.

“This crass exploitation of the name and legacy of a humanitarian and the tragedy of the Holocaust to sell houses is not only horrifying but unconscionable,” Manli Ho said.

Manli Ho said she had contacted local officials in Yiyang, who told her they had referred the matter to authorities in the city’s Heshan district and that a preliminary investigation had confirmed the situation she reported.

The district’s market regulation bureau was handling the matter, officials told Ho. They also told her they would “not tolerate the improper use of Ho Feng-shan’s humanitarian legacy” for advertising or publicity.

It remains unclear what action Yiyang authorities can take against the website, which is operated by a US-registered company. The Yiyang local government did not respond to an inquiry.

She has also sent a cease-and-desist letter to the US-based operators of the website, demanding they remove references to her father, his likeness and his humanitarian legacy from what she describes as commercial marketing materials.

“Utilising a deceased humanitarian’s identity to drive commercial web traffic to private property sales crosses clear boundaries regarding postmortem publicity rights,” Manli Ho wrote.

The letter also alleged that using Ho Feng-shan’s story to market real estate, relocation services and investment opportunities in Yiyang is creating the impression that his legacy endorses the business.

Manli Ho, who lives in San Francisco, is a former journalist for the Boston Globe and China Daily.

She learned of her father’s wartime actions only after his death and has since dedicated herself to preserving and promoting his legacy.

She also claimed portions of the website’s narrative were copied from her own writings about her father.

Who’s behind the website?

According to publicly available domain registration records, the website was registered on May 12, 2026, with a partially redacted Hunan Province address and a US phone number. Other information about its ownership is limited.

The Chinese-language webpage lists a local address in Yiyang and Chinese telephone numbers on its “about” page, where prospective buyers can consult with property agents.

A representative of the website, reached through a US telephone number listed on the website, told the South China Morning Post that the company was in discussions with lawyers and declined to comment further.

“We take this matter seriously and are currently reviewing it with legal counsel,” the text statement said.

“We are not in a position to provide further comment at this time, but we will follow up as soon as we are able to.”

The English-language website identifies itself as “A Brand of SortLease LLC” and lists an address in Sheridan, Wyoming. SortLease describes itself on its website as a company specialising in “AI-powered parcel sorting equipment rental and sales”.

According to Wyoming business records, SortLease LLC is registered through Registered Agents Inc., a commercial registered agent.

In a statement, Registered Agents Inc. said it is not involved in clients’ business operations and will not share client information or comment on clients’ businesses.

‘Most offensive ad’

Since the legal letter served, some references to Ho Feng-shan appear to have been removed, but at least one stand-alone page featuring his story remained online as of Wednesday.

The page shows an article titled “He Feng Shan’s Last Visa”, which misspells his last name and compares Ho’s efforts to save Jews during the Holocaust with Yiyang offering refuge to Silicon Valley workers displaced by artificial intelligence.

“We invoke him not to be maudlin about it,” the page says.

“We invoke him because the structure of the moment rhymes: a particular group of people is being discarded by a system that no longer has use for them.”

The website continues: “Ho Feng-Shan offered a visa. Yiyang offers something slower but equally concrete: low cost of living, political stability, high-speed fibre, cheap power, and enough distance from Silicon Valley’s anxiety economy to think clearly again.”

Manli Ho blasted the comparison as “the most offensive ad”, arguing that it equated her father’s rescue of Jewish refugees during World War II with Yiyang’s effort to attract Silicon Valley workers seeking an alternative to the US tech industry.

If the company fails to comply, Manli Ho said she intends to pursue the matter through US authorities.

Her cease-and-desist letter states that she will file complaints with the Wyoming Secretary of State and the US Federal Trade Commission.

After leaving Vienna, Ho Feng-shan continued his diplomatic career in several overseas postings for the Republic of China government, which retreated to Taiwan in 1949 after losing the Chinese Civil War.

In 1972, he was accused of embezzling about US$300 in government expenses in Colombia and was later impeached on corruption allegations and denied a pension. He settled in San Francisco, where he died in 1997 at the age of 96.

Ho maintained that he had been unfairly persecuted by the Kuomintang government in Taiwan. Despite years of efforts by his family to clear his name, he has never been formally exonerated.

In 2015, then-Taiwanese leader Ma Ying-jeou commended Ho for saving Jews during the Holocaust and apologised to the Ho family for the government’s delayed recognition. SCMP has covered his story since 2000.

As the controversy continues, Manli Ho said she found it ironic that, after years of helping the local city preserve and promote her father’s legacy, a real estate website was now using his story to sell homes. She is also preparing to travel to Yiyang next month.

“Never a dull moment as I prepare to go to Yiyang in September to mark my father’s 125th birthday,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Beyond the numbers: why China’s carrier force won’t copy the US model
item.description:
Having marked its 99th anniversary on August 1, the People’s Liberation Army is now just a year away from its centenary goals, with its evolution highlighting the past, present and future of China’s military strategy. In the sixth part of a series, Gabriel Dominguez looks at Beijing’s evolving aircraft carrier doctrine.

Debate over China’s aircraft carrier ambitions has long centred on how many carriers it will build, with the Pentagon last year estimating that Beijing planned to expand its fleet to nine by 2035.

Yet behind the high-profile ship launches, experts say quieter changes in pilot recruitment, command structures and fleet integration point to a carrier doctrine distinct from the American model.
item.content:encoded:
Having marked its 99th anniversary on August 1, the People’s Liberation Army is now just a year away from its centenary goals, with its evolution highlighting the past, present and future of China’s military strategy. In the sixth part of a series, Gabriel Dominguez looks at Beijing’s evolving aircraft carrier doctrine.

Debate over China’s aircraft carrier ambitions has long centred on how many carriers it will build, with the Pentagon last year estimating that Beijing planned to expand its fleet to nine by 2035.

Yet behind the high-profile ship launches, experts say quieter changes in pilot recruitment, command structures and fleet integration point to a carrier doctrine distinct from the American model.

“The biggest misconception among Western analysts is the tendency to evaluate the [Chinese navy] through the doctrinal mirror of the US Navy,” said Brendan Mulvaney, director of the China Aerospace Studies Institute.

“Just because they have the same kinds of equipment doesn’t mean they will use it in the same way as the US. Their goals, missions and challenges are different than ours; they will come up with Chinese solutions to Chinese problems.”

China’s carrier force is evolving under strategic conditions unlike those that shaped the American naval doctrine of using carriers to project power thousands of kilometres from home.

Instead, China’s carriers appear intended to complement its land-based air power, long-range anti-ship missiles, integrated air-defence systems and rocket forces along its coastline, and to extend the People’s Liberation Army’s reach farther into the western Pacific and beyond.

The strike capacity of China’s aircraft carrier groups also seems to be more evenly distributed across the fleet than that of the US, which could help the PLA’s resilience in war.

From command to force distribution

A recent report by the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) argues that rather than judging Chinese carriers against American standards, analysts should focus on how they fit into the PLA’s broader operational architecture.

One of the clearest indicators is command.

The IISS report notes that all known Chinese navy carrier commanders have come from the surface warfare branch, unlike the US Navy, where carriers are traditionally led by naval aviators. Although China established a “pilot-captain class” programme to qualify naval aviators for carrier command, none of its nine known graduates have gone on to command a carrier, underscoring the continued dominance of the surface warfare career track.

The [Chinese navy] views its shipborne fighters as coequal assets that coordinate with the heavy missile arsenals of its surface escorts, rather than serving as the singular offensive arm of the fleet

Brendan Mulvaney, China Aerospace Studies Institute

Mulvaney said Beijing’s continued experimentation with pilot-commanders suggested this remained an unresolved organisational question rather than a settled doctrinal choice. But he cautioned there was also the opposite risk: commanders shaped primarily by ship-handling may underestimate the specialised demands of flight-deck operations.

“A carrier cannot be fought simply as a very large guided-missile warship,” he said.

Mulvaney pointed to another often-overlooked difference: how much authority a Chinese navy commander actually exercises.

American naval operations generally assume commanders have broad latitude once assigned a mission. In the PLA, by contrast, a ship’s commanding officer shares authority with a political commissar, whose role is to ensure the division toes the Communist Party’s ideological line. That arrangement does not eliminate battlefield initiative, but it is likely to shape how commanders weigh risk, signal intent and manage escalation, according to Mulvaney.

But command is only one aspect of the Chinese navy’s evolving approach.

Mulvaney said the navy increasingly treated carrier fighters, Type 055 and Type 052D destroyers, submarines, airborne early warning aircraft and long-range missile forces as complementary rather than hierarchical.

“The [Chinese navy] views its shipborne fighters as coequal assets that coordinate with the heavy missile arsenals of its surface escorts, rather than serving as the singular offensive arm of the fleet,” Mulvaney said.

This division of strike responsibilities between the air wing and surface combatants probably originated as much from necessity as doctrine. Early Chinese carrier air wings were constrained by shorter aircraft range, limited aerial refuelling and immature command-and-control networks, forcing accompanying warships to shoulder a larger share of the offensive burden.

That contrasts with the traditional American model, in which the carrier air wing has long served as the strike group’s principal offensive arm while escorts primarily defend the carrier and contribute secondary missile firepower.

Experts point to another aspect that could be a key difference from the US. Unlike an American carrier operating far from home, a Chinese carrier group would probably fight alongside land-based fighters, bombers and long-range missile forces contributing to the same campaign. Judging the carrier group in isolation therefore understates the combined combat power Beijing can bring to bear from the mainland.

Different tactics, new vulnerabilities

The US Navy has spent the past decade developing Distributed Maritime Operations (DMO), integrating aircraft, ships, submarines and space-based assets into a more networked force.

According to IISS analysts, while the Chinese navy is testing the GJ-21 carrier-capable drone, the US Navy has been developing the MQ-25 Stingray as part of this broader transition. Over time, such systems could reduce the carrier air wing’s role as a strike group’s principal offensive element.

Whereas the US Navy has traditionally concentrated most of its striking power in the carrier’s air wing, China appears to spread combat power more evenly across the fleet.

But spreading combat power also creates new vulnerabilities.

Asked whether such an approach made carrier strike groups more survivable, Mulvaney said it “mitigates vulnerability, but it does not abolish it”.

He said the danger was that even a more distributed force could still depend on a small number of highly visible ships and support vessels that remained attractive targets.

“The correct comparison is therefore not ‘a vulnerable carrier versus an invulnerable distributed force’,” he said.

“It is between a force whose combat power collapses when the carrier is neutralised and a force that can absorb the carrier’s loss but may still be degraded through attacks on its wider reconnaissance, command and logistics architecture.”

Extending the PLA’s reach

Experts also expect that China’s carrier groups are designed to fight alongside shore-based air and missile forces, instead of replicating US-style independent power projection.

The IISS experts noted that reforms encompassed cross-academy training, joint exercises and increasingly sophisticated air wings incorporating airborne early warning, electronic warfare and, eventually, unmanned aircraft. They said the emphasis was on building the institutional foundations needed to sustain multiple carrier strike groups over the long term, not simply producing more pilots.

Taken together, those reforms suggest Beijing is investing not just in warships, but in the personnel, doctrine, logistics and organisational structures needed to sustain a credible blue-water force. It is building the habits, command culture and institutional experience needed to fight with carriers – and that process is still under way.

Although China’s carrier force would matter in a regional conflict, Mulvaney argues its greatest value lies farther from the mainland, supporting sustained operations across the western Pacific, the Indian Ocean and other regions tied to China’s expanding interests.

“The PLA has a clear goal to have a world-class navy by mid-century,” he said. “Carriers are very much a functional capability but also a prestige capability.”

Recent deployments reinforce that trajectory. In mid-2025 the Liaoning and Shandong conducted coordinated dual-carrier operations beyond the second island chain, underscoring China’s growing ability to sustain increasingly complex far-seas deployments.

Christopher Sharman, director of the China Maritime Studies Institute (CMSI) at the US Naval War College, said those deployments were about more than showing naval power. They provided opportunities for the Chinese navy to test and refine the concepts that will shape its future carrier force.

“The [navy] will soon enter what Chinese media often refers to as the ‘three-carrier era’ – the point at which three operational aircraft carriers will be capable of sustained power projection,” Sharman said.

“As this capability matures, the [Chinese navy] will likely deploy carrier battle groups more frequently into the western Pacific and, over time, the Indian Ocean.”

He said those deployments would also serve as operational experiments, allowing the Chinese navy to refine tactics, logistics, command and control, and long-range power projection through experience rather than theory.

Unlike the US Navy, whose doctrine has been refined through decades of global operations and combat, China’s modern carrier force remains comparatively young, and many of its emerging concepts are still being tested and adapted.

Role in a Taiwan conflict

That raises a question closer to home: what role, if any, would these carriers play in a Taiwan contingency?

Neither Mulvaney nor Sharman saw them as central to such an operation.

“I do not regard carriers as the PLAN’s primary Taiwan weapons,” Mulvaney said, referring to the PLA Navy. He noted that Beijing already had ample land-based aircraft, missiles, surface ships and submarines for operations close to the mainland. Sending a carrier near Taiwan itself “could duplicate capabilities already available from shore while exposing a politically and militarily valuable platform”, he said.

Instead, he said he expected carriers to operate on the theatre’s outer flanks, supporting reinforcement-denial, air defence and counter-intervention missions deeper into the western Pacific rather than spearheading an assault close to Taiwan.

Sharman’s assessment, offered in a personal capacity, points in the same direction. Mainland Chinese military publications describe a layered defensive architecture around the carrier, with submarines and aircraft screening ahead of the formation, missile-armed destroyers forming the next ring, and point-defence systems providing the final layer of protection.

“This layered defensive architecture described in Chinese media suggests that, in wartime, the PLAN would seek to preserve the combat effectiveness of its carriers rather than expose them unnecessarily in the most heavily contested portions of the battlespace,” Sharman said.

Both assessments suggest Beijing sees its carriers less as the spearhead of a Taiwan assault than as high-value assets better employed on the conflict’s periphery while supporting broader campaigns against outside intervention.

item.title: [SCMP] Why are South Korean football fans choosing European clubs over the K League?
item.description:
Yoon Jin-woo had never gone to Seoul World Cup Stadium to watch FC Seoul, the city’s team and the club that calls South Korean football’s symbolic home its own.

But on Sunday night, he made the pilgrimage from the suburbs of Gimpo to see Manchester City and Atletico Madrid, two European clubs whose pull in South Korea rivals, and often overwhelms, interest in the domestic game.

The 21-year-old and his friends were among 50,000 fans who filled the stadium with City’s light blue and Atletico’s red-and-blue shirts, turning a pre-season friendly into a vivid display of where much of South Korean football passion now flows.
item.content:encoded:
Yoon Jin-woo had never gone to Seoul World Cup Stadium to watch FC Seoul, the city’s team and the club that calls South Korean football’s symbolic home its own.

But on Sunday night, he made the pilgrimage from the suburbs of Gimpo to see Manchester City and Atletico Madrid, two European clubs whose pull in South Korea rivals, and often overwhelms, interest in the domestic game.

The 21-year-old and his friends were among 50,000 fans who filled the stadium with City’s light blue and Atletico’s red-and-blue shirts, turning a pre-season friendly into a vivid display of where much of South Korean football passion now flows.

Yoon and his friends sounded like broadcast announcers, calling out every player’s name and reacting excitedly to every dribble and shot.

“I first became a fan in 2022 to cheer on Kevin De Bruyne. I’m his biggest fan,” he said, pointing to the former City midfielder whose jersey he was wearing.

Many fans had arrived hours early to buy merchandise, take photos and catch a glimpse of players they usually watched on screens after midnight.

The match, organised by Coupang Play, the streaming service of South Korean e-commerce giant Coupang, also marked South Korean star Lee Kang-in’s debut for Atletico, giving the occasion an added emotional pull for local fans.

City beat Atletico 3-1, but the broader winner was European football itself.

The night captured a deeper problem for South Korea’s domestic game: the K League struggles to convert the country’s love of football into regular support, while European clubs increasingly set the standard for quality, spectacle and emotional connection.

Against the backdrop of South Korea’s disappointing World Cup exit and mounting scrutiny of the Korea Football Association, the country’s so-called national sport is facing one of its deepest periods of unease in years.

Need for greener grass

The K League, South Korea’s top professional football league, briefly enjoyed a renaissance in 2024 when former England midfielder and Premier League star Jesse Lingard signed with FC Seoul.

His arrival brought record crowds and rare international attention, but the surge did not resolve the deeper problems facing the domestic game.

Since Lingard’s departure in December, attention around South Korean football has again been dominated by controversy, including the fallout from national team head coach Hong Myung-bo’s failed World Cup campaign and mounting scrutiny of the Korea Football Association.

Average K League attendance per match, which had remained above 10,000 since 2023 and previously hit a peak of 11,003 in 2024, has dipped to 9,008 so far this season, according to data from the league. Meanwhile, professional baseball continues to draw record crowds and dominate the country’s sporting conversation.

The contrast has been difficult to miss: the Korea Baseball Organisation League now averages about 18,000 fans per game, while the K League remains far behind in total attendance and media attention.

During Lingard’s final press conference with FC Seoul in December, the former captain highlighted pitch conditions, club infrastructure and refereeing as three areas for improvement.

Lee Jong-sung, a professor of sports management at Hanyang University, said Lingard’s comments reflected the “deeply rooted perception that the K League is simply too backward or underdeveloped compared with European football”.

“When you watch professional football in European leagues, the flow of passing and even the pitch itself gives you this overwhelming impression,” he told This Week in Asia. “K League stadiums simply haven’t been able to create that same feeling.”

The former football journalist said part of the gap stemmed from how South Korean stadiums were run.

“European club stadiums are often operated by the clubs themselves or by third parties affiliated with them. In Korea, by contrast, very few K League clubs actually own or operate their stadiums,” Lee Jong-sung said.

“Local governments have traditionally managed football stadiums in Korea, and that has meant there hasn’t been much investment or serious consideration given to professionally managing the pitches, whether in terms of personnel or financial resources.”

That also limited the commercial ecosystem around clubs, he said, as football offered far fewer home games than baseball, resulting in fewer opportunities to turn stadiums into year-round destinations.

“In legacy media and major media outlets, the K League has rarely been treated as a major news topic. Almost all of the headlines among professional sports are effectively dominated by professional baseball.”

Aftermath of 2002 World Cup

The 2002 World Cup was one of the most transformative moments in modern South Korean society that helped change the country’s sporting gaze.

South Korea’s historic run to the semi-finals as co-hosts turned players including Park Ji-sung, Lee Young-pyo and Ahn Jung-hwan into national heroes and global names as they were recruited by top European clubs.

“The world view of Korean sports fans shifted from the United States towards Europe, and people often refer to this as the era of overseas football,” Lee Jong-sung said.

“Fans call it haechuk for short, and this culture has become so big today that among peer groups, particularly among boys, not being familiar with European football could make it somewhat difficult to be part of conversations.”

The rise of European football was reinforced by a new generation of Korean stars whose careers unfolded on the continent.

Son Heung-min became one of the Premier League’s most popular players, while Lee Kang-in’s move to Paris Saint-Germain, before his latest transfer to Atletico, gave South Korean fans another reason to follow the European game.

“When young Koreans travel to Europe, it’s almost become a ritual for them to attend at least one or two football matches, whether that’s a Premier League game or a match in Spain,” Lee Jong-sung said.

“Even if they travel during the off season when there are no matches, they’ll often make a point of visiting a big club’s museum or stadium tour and spending money on souvenirs.”

Kim Se-hoon, content executive for Wolverhampton Wanderers, said European clubs were also far more conscious of keeping overseas fans engaged beyond matchdays.

The English Football League Championship club is best known in South Korea as the home of forward Hwang Hee-chan.

“Football leagues in the UK set global standards not only in terms of players’ performances, but also in content creation and distribution”, such as footage from training sessions and interviews, he told This Week in Asia.

Clubs there put “considerable thought” into maintaining relationships with fans and keeping them engaged through informal channels such as fan groups and online communities, he added.

“For us, we offer fans the opportunity to directly meet club officials to voice their concerns about the club’s activities.”

In the K League, by contrast, fan frustration has often taken more confrontational forms, with supporters sending protest trucks to club offices or stadiums and, in some cases, blocking team buses after unpopular decisions over managers, players or club management.

Lee Jong-sung said South Korean football needed to rethink what kind of sporting culture it wanted to build.

“Football in our country shouldn’t only be concentrated on World Cup results. We need to set goals for what we want to achieve in other areas as well, and have a broader discussion about those ambitions,” he said.

“Only then can Korean football become a team and a footballing nation that can continue to grow and remain competitive over the long term, rather than simply having a one-off successful World Cup.”

item.title: [SCMP] Bangkok branches out: secret to Thai capital’s green revival
item.description:
In recent years, Thailand’s capital has discovered a surprising new attraction to add to its temples, shopping malls and street food: urban greenery. Unlike the others, which took decades to develop, Bangkok’s green credentials are a more recent phenomenon, emerging only during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Despite their novelty, the city’s greening efforts are already bearing fruit. Visitors returning to Bangkok after the pandemic are often surprised by how green and walkable the city has become. It comes as a nice surprise given the city’s long-standing reputation as a concrete jungle with chronic traffic jams and accompanying air pollution.

It is even more unusual considering how Thai politics, in the last two decades, has been highly polarised. Bangkok’s early success in urban greening shows that it is possible, despite contentious politics and a divided and highly unequal society, to build a societal consensus around making the city greener.
item.content:encoded:
In recent years, Thailand’s capital has discovered a surprising new attraction to add to its temples, shopping malls and street food: urban greenery. Unlike the others, which took decades to develop, Bangkok’s green credentials are a more recent phenomenon, emerging only during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Despite their novelty, the city’s greening efforts are already bearing fruit. Visitors returning to Bangkok after the pandemic are often surprised by how green and walkable the city has become. It comes as a nice surprise given the city’s long-standing reputation as a concrete jungle with chronic traffic jams and accompanying air pollution.

It is even more unusual considering how Thai politics, in the last two decades, has been highly polarised. Bangkok’s early success in urban greening shows that it is possible, despite contentious politics and a divided and highly unequal society, to build a societal consensus around making the city greener.

There are three lessons from Bangkok’s urban greenery playbook that other cities, including Hong Kong, should pay heed to.

Clear goals

This first is to set clear, measurable goals. In December 2019, the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration (BMA) launched the Green Bangkok 2030 initiative that set three ambitious targets:

Increase green spaces in the city to 10 square metres (110 square feet) per person from 7.6–7.8 square metres per person;

Increase the green spaces that people can access within 400 metres – or five minutes’ walk – to at least 50 per cent of Bangkok’s total area; and

Increase the urban tree canopy to 30 per cent of Bangkok’s total area.

In mid-2022, the BMA initiated the Bangkok Million Tree Planting Project to increase urban green spaces, reduce air and dust pollution, and cool the city. Initially, the project sought to plant 1 million trees in the city by 2025. But after that goal was surpassed by mid-2024, it was increased by another 1 million. To date, nearly 1.2 million trees have been planted.

Pocket parks have also been built under transit lines and expressways as well as on under-utilised public or private lands such as abandoned piers, neglected canal paths and even garbage dumps.

The main benefit of setting such goals is to demonstrate the government’s seriousness of intent and its willingness to be held accountable. Governments are seldom short of visions but without committing to measurable goals and coming up with specific implementation plans such as the Million Tree Project, these will just be cheap talk.

A second benefit is to define exactly what is being measured and targeted. For example, much of Bangkok’s urban green spaces is not easily accessible. Actively accessible urban green spaces in Bangkok stand at a low 1.5-1.7 square metres per capita, well below the World Health Organization’s guideline of at least 9 square metres per capita for a healthy city. This is why the second target under the Green Bangkok 2030 blueprint is necessary: to highlight the importance of increasing green spaces that can be easily accessed by residents.

In a similar vein, BMA’s tree-planting initiative has not been sufficient to offset the city’s loss of urban tree canopy due to deforestation. This is why the third Green Bangkok 2030 target matters: to emphasise the protection of existing, mature trees even as new ones are planted.

Public support

The second lesson is to build public support and momentum with politically salient early successes. For Bangkok, this came in the form of the Benjakitti Forest Park, which opened in early 2022.

Situated between the two main commercial areas – Sukhumvit Road and Sathorn Road – the park has already become a popular destination that attracts tens of thousands of users daily. It also connects to the older Lumpini Park via a 1.6km-long treetop bridge that is reminiscent of New York’s High Line.

Sitting on 720,000 square metres of what used to be brownfield land that previously housed tobacco factories and warehouses, Benjakitti has become the city’s main green lung. Equally impressive is the fact that the forest park was planned to be a low-cost, low-maintenance operation through a self-sustaining, “messy nature” design and reliance on native plants to regenerate organically.

Since its opening, Benjakitti has served various environmental and social objectives. For example, its woodlands and constructed wetlands act as sponges to mitigate flooding in the city. It is home to diverse wildlife – including 91 species of birds – and its numerous boardwalks over the wetlands and a canopy skywalk provide visitors with an immersive urban nature experience. The sports centre and museum, both converted from old warehouses, provide residents with much-needed space for leisure activities, while an open-air amphitheatre can host events for 15,000 people.

Besides being aesthetically pleasing, the various functions of the forest park have helped endear it to the public. That it was built for under US$20 per square metre and was completed in about 18 months during the pandemic – a time when everyone could see the need for open public spaces – shows the BMA’s ability to deliver sustainability projects on time and on budget.

It is hardly surprising, therefore, that just four years after it opened, the park is already celebrated as the most vivid showcase of how Green Bangkok 2030 is transforming the city.

Good connections

Urban greening initiatives are also more likely to succeed if they are combined with efforts to make the city more walkable and public transit more accessible. To support the former, the BMA has upgraded more than 1,100km of pavements in recent years, including some along canals in the historic Hua Lamphong district.

While public transit in Bangkok has improved in recent years, the system is still inadequate for a sprawling city of more than 10 million. The sprawl makes public transit less viable financially, as more and longer lines are needed to serve a dispersed population. Reducing it, in turn, requires significant changes to urban and land-use planning.

Harnessing the energies of the private sector and the community is also key to the long-term success of greening efforts. Encouragingly, new commercial developments in Bangkok seem to have embraced the city’s greening push. For instance, Bangkok’s highest office building at the new One City Centre development in Ploenchit incorporates a large and verdant green space, including a rooftop garden.

Bangkok residents can also join tree-growing campaigns and support local groups to monitor and protect urban forests. The BMA engages local networks to come up with better rules for tree trimming and public space management.

Bangkok’s transformation into a green, walkable and sustainable city is far from complete. But already, its achievements in the last few years are a clear demonstration of what setting measurable goals, taking implementation seriously, having highly visible early success stories and synergising with the rest of society can do.

Donald Low is Senior Lecturer and Professor of Practice of Public Policy at the Hong Kong University of Science and Technology.

item.title: [SCMP] Chinese luxury brands rise from challengers to market shapers as global houses lose lustre
item.description:
After months of declining gold prices, Li Yue recently spent nearly 28,000 yuan (US$4,148) on a 10-gram (0.35-ounce) pure gold necklace – more than double the prevailing market rate for the metal.
