The piece in question: a gourd-shaped pendant from Laopu Gold, a Chinese heritage jewellery brand that has captured significant attention in recent years.

But for Li, a software engineer in Shanghai, the purchase had little to do with bullion value. She cared more about the necklace’s design – the gourd is a traditional symbol of fortune and prosperity – and the care with which it was crafted.
item.content:encoded:
After months of declining gold prices, Li Yue recently spent nearly 28,000 yuan (US$4,148) on a 10-gram (0.35-ounce) pure gold necklace – more than double the prevailing market rate for the metal.

The piece in question: a gourd-shaped pendant from Laopu Gold, a Chinese heritage jewellery brand that has captured significant attention in recent years.

But for Li, a software engineer in Shanghai, the purchase had little to do with bullion value. She cared more about the necklace’s design – the gourd is a traditional symbol of fortune and prosperity – and the care with which it was crafted.

“No one asks how much the fabric of their Louis Vuitton bag costs, right?” she said.

Li is precisely the kind of customer Laopu Gold is courting. Having cultivated a sophisticated customer base through its choice of retail locations and emphasis on craftsmanship and aesthetic expression, the brand has earned a place in the luxury echelon, becoming one of the bestselling labels in China’s high-end malls – even as overall luxury spending continued to decline, analysts said.

Like Laopu, a growing number of local brands are now appealing to premium consumers. As international luxury brands such as Cartier, Tiffany & Co, and Gucci close their doors on Huaihai Middle Road – one of Shanghai’s premier shopping thoroughfares – a wave of home-grown names has taken their place, from handbag label Songmont and shoe brand Pane to perfume house To Summer.

If top-tier Western luxury labels were status symbols that newly affluent Chinese consumers clamoured for in past decades, today’s shoppers were more discerning and rational – and they were increasingly turning to domestic brands that offered a “high-value sense of luxury”, according to Zhou Ting, a veteran researcher with decades of experience in the luxury goods industry.

The next decade will be [Chinese luxury brands’] golden era, with the entire segment growing into a market worth tens of trillions of yuan

Zhou Ting, Yaok Institute

Compared with global luxury houses, domestic brands had a superior grasp of Chinese consumers’ aesthetic sensibilities and contextual needs while offering a pricing framework that provided more compelling value, said Zhou, founder of the Shanghai-based Yaok Institute, which provides research and consulting services related to high-end goods.

“After the first wave of global expansion by European and American luxury houses, China is now emerging as the world’s second core incubator for luxury brands,” she said.

By 2035, Chinese luxury brands would match the China market share of their international counterparts in terms of sales, Zhou said.

The success of brands such as Laopu Gold and collectible toys creator Pop Mart extends beyond their financial performance. They had shown the viability of premium branding for Chinese labels, and provided a replicable framework for emerging domestic brands, she said.

Though no longer drawing the massive queues it saw during the recent surge in gold prices, Laopu Gold, with dozens of stores across China and one store in Singapore, “outperforms every other luxury brand in terms of sales revenue”, a source close to the firm told the South China Morning Post.

The company had 610,000 registered members as of the end of last year – more than 80 per cent of whom overlapped with those of major luxury brands such as Louis Vuitton and Cartier – and was now in talks with shopping malls in Japan and South Korea to open new stores, said the source, who declined to be named as they were not authorised to talk to the media.

Citing Frost & Sullivan data, the Hong Kong-listed company said in its 2025 financial report that it ranked second by revenue among global luxury brands in mainland China, and first in sales per store and per square metre within a single mall. Laopu issued a positive profit forecast for the first half of this year last week, estimating total revenue of about 20 billion yuan (US$2.96 billion), up about 60 to 65 per cent year on year.

“One major reason behind the brand’s rise is that it has created entirely new demand; before this, there was no gold-focused brand among top-tier luxury jewellery houses,” the source said.

“For established luxury players, gold is not a test of their technical mastery, but rather of cultural resonance and aesthetic sensibility.”

Global luxury leaders remain in the depths of a protracted downturn. Last week, Louis Vuitton parent LVMH reported a 3 per cent year-on-year decline in total revenue and a 4 per cent fall in profits for the first half of the year. The first-half results for Kering Group – manager of luxury brands Gucci, Balenciaga and Bottega Veneta, among others – showed revenue down 3 per cent and net income plunging 60 per cent from a year earlier.

China’s total retail sales of consumer goods grew just 1.3 per cent year on year in the first half of 2026, with the gold, silver and jewellery category contracting by 3.4 per cent in June alone, data from the National Bureau of Statistics showed.

Meanwhile, China’s high-end consumption market stood at 1.56 trillion yuan in 2025 – a 5 per cent decline from the previous year, according to a Hurun Research Institute report released in January.

More than half of the 470 high-net-worth Chinese consumers surveyed by Hurun said they planned to cut expenses on daily luxury goods this year, underscoring a widespread move towards more value-conscious consumption.

While the slowdown of the overall economy has played a role, this came after a gradual shift in consumer mentality – from obsession with logos and brand heritage to greater emphasis on product quality, craftsmanship, innovation and the overall brand experience, said Zhou, the Shanghai researcher.

It is within this evolving environment that Icicle, a premier Chinese fashion brand using natural materials with a focus on comfort and durability, has stood out.

When it first emerged in the late 1990s, luxury consumption in China was closely tied to status and external recognition. But today, consumers were increasingly looking for products that reflected their personal taste, lifestyle and values, which had contributed to the brand’s double-digit compound annual growth in China in recent years, it said in a statement to the SCMP.

“There has been a broader shift away from conspicuous consumption towards what might be called ‘quiet luxury’ – quality that speaks for itself, rather than through logos or status signalling,” it said, adding that this played directly to the brand’s strengths.

With more than 200 stores globally, including five in Europe, the brand is pushing for further international expansion through a partnership with Kering, which in April acquired a minority stake in ICCF, the brand’s owner.

As international luxury houses become demystified for mainstream consumers and stripped of social distinction for high-net-worth shoppers, local high-end brands are now capturing market share and redefining luxury.

Despite a strong recovery in overseas tourism, 65 per cent of Chinese luxury spending occurred within mainland China last year, while domestic brands captured more share by appealing to cultural connections and local preferences, according to a Bain & Co report in January.

“Chinese luxury brands have evolved from challengers to market shapers,” it said. “They are transforming the China luxury landscape with their distinctive fusion of global appeal and authentic Chinese identity and redefining what luxury means for modern Chinese consumers.”

Buying local luxury is not a compromise – it’s a statement of cultural identity and pride in Chinese heritage

Li Yue, Shanghai

And this was by no means a short-term phenomenon as consumers tightened their belts amid the current economic downturn, but a “long-term, irreversible shift” supported by multiple factors, Zhou said.

Those factors included a growing cultural affinity for home-grown brands, the maturation of China’s domestic supply chain, and the democratisation of information, she added.

“Chinese luxury brands are at the starting point of rapid growth. The next decade will be their golden era, with the entire segment growing into a market worth tens of trillions of yuan,” Zhou said.

On quality and service, Chinese brands were on par with – or even ahead of – top-tier luxury houses, thanks to China’s unrivalled supply chain and manufacturing expertise, she said. The real gap lay in brand legacy and global reputation, which required years of history and international exposure to cultivate.

Li, the Laopu Gold customer, said she would continue chasing traditional luxury brands while at the same time embracing new ones from local companies.

“To me, buying local luxury is not a compromise – it’s a statement of cultural identity and pride in Chinese heritage,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Masters of Hong Kong’s ‘kung fu’ cuisine on the struggle to save Cantonese classics
item.description:
For centuries, Chinese cuisine was a gatekept world where old masters hoarded knowledge, passing down recipes only to those deemed worthy – or taking them to the grave. Celebrated Cantonese dishes, such as Mythical Crane and Magical Needle, stuffed crab shell and Gold Coin Chicken, were among them.

Known as heritage “kung fu” dishes, these labour-intensive classics once defined Hong Kong’s kitchens. Now, the ageing masters are retiring, machines are replacing the apprentices who never got trained and there is no one left to continue the craft.

Well, almost no one. A handful of Hong Kong chefs have made it their mission to pass down their knowledge of traditional recipes, holding nothing back. Silas Li Mung-sheung, of Hong Kong Cuisine 1983, in Happy Valley, is one of them. “No secrets,” he insists. Having trained in both Western and Chinese cuisine and worked as a private chef for Hong Kong tycoon Dickson Poon for more than two decades, Li – who has 30-plus years of experience – describes gatekeeping culture as the main problem affecting the quality of Chinese restaurants.
item.content:encoded:
For centuries, Chinese cuisine was a gatekept world where old masters hoarded knowledge, passing down recipes only to those deemed worthy – or taking them to the grave. Celebrated Cantonese dishes, such as Mythical Crane and Magical Needle, stuffed crab shell and Gold Coin Chicken, were among them.

Known as heritage “kung fu” dishes, these labour-intensive classics once defined Hong Kong’s kitchens. Now, the ageing masters are retiring, machines are replacing the apprentices who never got trained and there is no one left to continue the craft.

Well, almost no one. A handful of Hong Kong chefs have made it their mission to pass down their knowledge of traditional recipes, holding nothing back. Silas Li Mung-sheung, of Hong Kong Cuisine 1983, in Happy Valley, is one of them. “No secrets,” he insists. Having trained in both Western and Chinese cuisine and worked as a private chef for Hong Kong tycoon Dickson Poon for more than two decades, Li – who has 30-plus years of experience – describes gatekeeping culture as the main problem affecting the quality of Chinese restaurants.

“Chinese cuisine is a lot less about following a recipe compared with Western cuisine. Apprenticeship is key to learning the ‘sixth sense’ of cooking – that’s why I always pass down all my tips and tricks, with no reservations,” he says.

Li is true to his word. When he taught his head chef, Cho Heung-man, the classic Fujian dish Buddha Jumps Over the Wall, he recalled his apprentice’s surprise at the addition of Shaoxing wine as a key ingredient. Other masters Cho had followed simply never told him.

Originating in Fuzhou during the Qing dynasty, Buddha Jumps Over the Wall is a famously difficult dish to master. Legend has it that a travelling scholar preserved his provisions for a long journey inside a clay wine jar. When the aroma of his food wafted to a nearby Buddhist monastery, a vegetarian monk was so tempted by the rich, meaty scent that he climbed over the wall to find its source. When he discovered the scholar and the jar, he declared the dish so delicious that even Buddha would jump over the wall for it.

Buddha Jumps Over the Wall entered the lexicon of Cantonese cuisine between the 1920s and 30s, when wealthy Fujian merchants and displaced chefs migrated to Guangzhou and Hong Kong, thus introducing the luxurious stew to local banquet restaurants.

Contrary to popular belief, it is not “just expensive ingredients stewed in a pot” – the real work is in preparing each ingredient, sourcing premium dried seafood such as abalone, fish maw and sea cucumber and rehydrating each one to its optimal state before it can be cooked. Li says there is a reason this dish is dubbed the “Avengers of dried seafood”.

“[Buddha Jumps Over the Wall] is a dish with no ceiling; it can be as expensive as you want it to be” because the true cost lies in the labour and intuition that machines cannot detect and recipes cannot convey. “It’s true that anyone can cook,” he says. “But the ‘sixth sense’ that a trained chef has cannot be input into a machine. No two abalones are the same; a great chef can tell the weight, density and texture just by looking at one, or with a quick touch.”

As times change, many dishes considered “legendary” have fallen out of fashion. Mythical Crane and Magical Needle, a dish Li is known for, traditionally sees shark fin stuffed into a deboned pigeon. During the 80s and 90s, it became a sought-after delicacy, a barometer of a restaurant’s prestige and a chef’s technical expertise. So demanding is its execution that it was once feared by chefs, apprentices and gourmands alike to be a vanishing craft.

Li’s version stuffs the pigeon with Buddha Jumps Over the Wall ingredients instead of shark fin. Stuffing poultry, once seen as old-fashioned, is now making a comeback. “Just like in fashion, with every revival, different chefs and generations add their own flavour, but there’s a reason it endures: it stands the test of time.” Each generation brings its own touch to the dish without changing the core: a labour-intensive, time-consuming true test of craftsmanship.

If Buddha Jumps Over the Wall and Mythical Crane and Magical Needle represent the ceiling of “kung fu” abilities, then Gold Coin Chicken shows that these heritage dishes are not defined solely by the price of ingredients.

For executive chef Li Chi-wai, of one-Michelin-star Legacy House, at Rosewood Hong Kong, in Tsim Sha Tsui, Gold Coin Chicken embodies the Cantonese spirit of making the most of the humblest components. Born from the frugality of the Republican era (1912-1949), when nothing was wasted, the resourceful dish, created in Shunde, Guangdong province, in the 20s by chefs of Cantonese roast-meat shops, is a testament to respect for ingredients. Despite being demeaned as “poor people food” for its use of trimmings, the name carries auspicious weight: a coin, round on the outside and square within, echoes the ancient belief that heaven is round and the Earth is square.

On the skewer sits chicken liver, fatback cured for 24 hours in rose wine until translucent and crystalline, water chestnut for a crisp, clean snap that cuts through the richness and char siu, ideally the caramelised offcuts. Gold Coin Chicken is made from siu mei leftovers and traditionally paired with inexpensive yuk bing siu, a rice liquor perfumed with pork fat.

But the simplicity of the ingredients belies the labour involved. For one, the fatback must be cured for a full day, massaged with sugar and rose wine until it becomes as transparent as ice. Each part must be cut to its own precise thickness – liver thin enough to cook through, fatback thick enough to hold its shape. Finally, they are skewered tightly, basted in sauce and roasted for 40 minutes, turned and watched. The sauce ratio is never written down; every chef must feel how the flavours marry over the fire. It is a dish that takes months to learn and years to master, built on nothing more expensive than offcuts – and nothing more demanding than patience.

Li Chi-wai entered the trade in the 80s. Back then, dishes such as Gold Coin Chicken were found only in jau ga – modest restaurants serving small plates and seafood – not grand jau lau that host banquets. As a child, he never ordered it. But he couldn’t stop looking at it.

“I would see these labour-intensive dishes emerge from the kitchen and wonder: what is that smell?” As an apprentice, he would sneak bites, known in the industry as da maau – stealing food like a cat. But curiosity didn’t kill this beast – it just gave him nine lives’ worth of determination. “Back then, apprentices in the kitchen competed to learn, fought for time at the stove in the dead hours between lunch and dinner. Late at night, we would pool our money to buy supper for our master just for a chance to practise,” Li Chi-wai recalls. But the old masters would never disclose the sauce ratio of Gold Coin Chicken, let alone the full recipe.

“This gatekeeping culture lasted partly because of the long-held fear that once you teach the apprentice, the master becomes disposable,” he says. “But the truth is the opposite – if the student never surpasses the master, the craft simply disappears. And so, eventually, does the master.” It is this narrowness of mind that has cost the industry dearly.

By the late 90s, Li Chi-wai had spent almost four years mastering Gold Coin Chicken. He also refined it for modern palates: king oyster mushrooms replaced water chestnut, absorbing the oils while lending their own fragrance and a gentler bite. Later, when he moved to Rosewood, he swapped chicken liver for goose liver – a more elegant but more temperamental ingredient that demands even greater control. More recently, he added his own signature: aged tangerine peel in place of fatback, for health-conscious diners who want to feel virtuous while surrendering to a guilty pleasure. He is happy to adapt. He is not, however, willing to outsource his hands.

“Machines have their place in the kitchen, of course; the new generation of chefs has taught me how to apply sous-vide machines in a Cantonese setting to unlock new techniques and reduce the overall physical burden. But they cannot detect scorching nor jup saang [improvise as you go]. Why paint if you have a printer? Because the machine won’t be able to sense when the foie gras has softened, nor skewer the ingredients without breaking them.”

Technology, then, cannot replace the hand. But if the gatekeeping culture that holds the hand back were to dissolve, would it change anything about the fate of “kung fu” cuisine?

Chui Wai-kwan, the seventh son of renowned Cantonese master chef Chui Fook-chuen, says perhaps not. His father founded Fook Lam Moon, often called the “tycoons’ canteen” for its high-profile clientele. Chui Snr became famous in the post-World War II era as the premier private-catering chef for Hong Kong’s elite. Fook Kee, his catering business, was founded in 1948 and renamed Fook Lam Moon in 1953. His flagship restaurant, opened in Wan Chai in 1972, achieved legendary status by treating traditional dishes with the precision of haute cuisine, pioneering painstaking techniques such as the oil-ladling method for its crispy chicken.

At Fook Lam Moon, blood relation meant there was no gatekeeping. “My father wanted me to go into other professions, but my grades were terrible,” Chui recalls. “I left school at 14 to become an apprentice under him. If anything, he was even harsher with me, because I was his son.”

Strict as his father was, keeping secrets was not an option. “Our private-catering business was booming. Every chef had to carry their weight and learn all the recipes just to keep up. Gatekeeping simply didn’t exist here; that’s why people call Fook Lam Moon the ‘Shaolin Temple of Cantonese cuisine’.”

In 1968, a 20-year-old Chui inherited the business. “His feng shui master told him to retire by 60, so he did,” says Chui. At first, the business nearly collapsed. Most of his father’s trusted apprentices broke away to open their own establishments, often adding their own twist to Fook Lam Moon dishes, such as the crispy chicken and roasted suckling pig. But that exodus lit a fire in him to preserve the restaurant and its original recipes.

One of his father’s most renowned creations is the deep-fried stuffed crab shell. Adapted from mid-century colonial influences, it is a masterclass in texture, but extremely difficult to execute. Fresh red flower crabs must be steamed daily and the meat must be hand-picked. It is a brutal, hours-long task where a single stray fragment of shell can ruin a diner’s experience. The delicate meat is bound with sweet, drained onion and a light Hong Kong-style roux before being stuffed back into the shell, where it is topped with breadcrumbs and deep-fried to a golden crisp. Oil control is the challenge; the chef must flash-fry it perfectly so the crust shatters instantly, without letting the hot oil breach the shell and split the cream sauce inside.

Equally demanding – though far less conspicuous – is the steamed chicken with Jinhua ham and bamboo shoots. It sounds simple, but the skill lies in meticulous knife-work and split-second timing; the chicken must be deboned while keeping the shape intact, then neatly layered, alternating slices of savoury Jinhua ham and earthy bamboo shoots.

Finishing the dish with lau lei him – a crystal-clear “glass glaze” – is the hardest part to master. If the cornflour slurry is off by a second or a gram, the glaze becomes cloudy or gloopy, and risks sullying Fook Lam Moon’s reputation for pristine elegance. Dishes like these are not inherited in a will – they live in the hands, or they don’t live at all.

Fook Lam Moon’s lineage of hands-on mastery faced its ultimate test when Chui split from the restaurant in December 2012, following a family dispute. Refusing to let five decades of culinary expertise fade, he opened Seventh Son in 2013.

While Seventh Son remains in the family, what has passed down is the business, not the muscle memory of executing “kung fu” dishes. His son, Daniel Chui Tak-yiu, is a doctor, specialising in pathology, though he still helps to manage the restaurant as executive director.

Chui Wai-kwan worries about the future of the “Fook” culinary lineage but speaks proudly of his children’s professional paths. “It’s understandable that there are fewer apprentices in Cantonese kitchens now. As a parent, of course I don’t want to see my son endure such hardships if he has a choice.”

At 78, Chui Wai-kwan still walks the kitchen daily to inspect his apprentices. He began thinking about passing down his recipes when Fook Lam Moon expanded to Japan in 1989. After decades of reflection, his perspective is clear. “We need to educate our diners. People have to learn to appreciate [the craftsmanship behind each dish]. Without that, ‘kung fu’ dishes won’t survive, and no one will be willing to learn.”

Silas Li adds, “If there were more masters willing to teach, there would be more apprentices in Chinese cuisine.” And not just head chefs who can pass on their knowledge, he notes: “There’s always at least one skill that you can learn from someone – whether it’s the owner of a dried seafood shop, or the dai pai dong uncle who cooks with kerosene.”

Without skilled chefs, there is nothing for diners to appreciate; without appreciative diners, there is no reason for chefs to keep cooking. Both sides are nearing their last orders. And so they wait – each for the other to revive a craft that needs them both.

item.title: [SCMP] As China’s tech firms adapt to AI era, workers worry they’ll be ‘optimised’ out of a job
item.description:
When a friend checked in on a Meituan employee late last month to see if he had survived the latest round of corporate culling at the food delivery giant, he responded drily: “I don’t know whether it will be me next.”

Anxieties were running high at the company then, after chat screenshots circulated on Chinese social media claiming Meituan planned to slash up to half of its product roles by the end of June, coupled with deep cuts to other departments.

While Meituan quickly denied the rumours, the viral speculation struck a sensitive nerve across China’s tech industry. Behind the online claims, employees whisper that a quieter, more insidious form of retrenchment has been under way for months.
item.content:encoded:
When a friend checked in on a Meituan employee late last month to see if he had survived the latest round of corporate culling at the food delivery giant, he responded drily: “I don’t know whether it will be me next.”

Anxieties were running high at the company then, after chat screenshots circulated on Chinese social media claiming Meituan planned to slash up to half of its product roles by the end of June, coupled with deep cuts to other departments.

While Meituan quickly denied the rumours, the viral speculation struck a sensitive nerve across China’s tech industry. Behind the online claims, employees whisper that a quieter, more insidious form of retrenchment has been under way for months.

For years, tech workers in China have harboured a deep-seated dread of the word youhua – “optimisation”. The term serves as corporate shorthand for painful lay-offs, often masked by euphemisms like “organisational restructuring”.

This year, however, the term carries a chilling new undertone. The increasingly urgent question echoing through office corridors is no longer whether a worker is performing, but whether their job can be done by artificial intelligence.

Meituan is far from an isolated case. From Baidu to Xiaomi, China’s technology giants have been trimming their teams, according to internal sources and tech recruiters.

The agents arrive

The shift follows prophetic warnings from global tech leaders. Last year, Dario Amodei, CEO of US generative AI pioneer Anthropic, cautioned that the technology’s rapid evolution could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within five years.

Today, the tools driving that shift are capable of far more than conversations and data retrieval. The industry has rapidly pivoted from basic chatbots to autonomous “AI agents” – systems capable of writing code, conducting market research, analysing legal documents and executing multi-step business tasks.

Anthropic said that as of last month, more than 80 per cent of the code merged into its codebase had been written by its Claude AI model.

Software engineers, long viewed as possessing one of the most secure and sophisticated white-collar skill sets, have found themselves on the front lines of this automation wave. Coding, it turns out, is a task where AI models excel.

We now require engineers to be full-stack ... even if they are doing it side-by-side with AI

Rose Cao, talent acquisition specialist

“I have barely written a line of code by hand for almost a year,” said a veteran AI developer known to the public as Tuxi, who has worked for several of China’s major technology companies.

At a live-streamed industry event this month, senior Tencent Holdings executive Dowson Tong said most of the tech giant’s code written this year was generated by AI systems.

Tong said human engineers were becoming supervisors, spending more time focused on architecture and system design. They delegated the coding work to AI and only stepped in periodically to guide and correct its output.

Such changes have significantly raised the baseline requirements for landing or keeping a tech job.

“We now require engineers to be full-stack,” said Rose Cao, a talent acquisition specialist at a Chinese AI firm, adding that “even if they are doing it side-by-side with AI”, programmers were now expected to handle everything from front-end to back-end tasks.

The automation contagion

AI automation is expanding beyond the engineering department. Specialised tools originally built for programmers – such as OpenAI’s Codex or Anthropic’s Claude Code – are evolving to support broader corporate workflows.

A parallel ecosystem of enterprise AI assistants has sprung up across China: Moonshot AI has pushed out Kimi Work; Tencent has rolled out WorkBuddy; ByteDance has launched Coze; and Alibaba Group Holding has introduced QoderWork CN. Alibaba is the owner of the South China Morning Post.

By embedding such tools into daily operations, businesses are eroding some of the traditional boundaries between various corporate functions, allowing a single employee to fulfil tasks that previously required a team of specialised workers.

Rather than being an optional résumé highlight, a headhunter who specialises in tech talent said that “AI fluency has become a requirement for many employers”, creating a hostile environment for fresh university graduates and inexperienced workers.

“It is hard to persuade an employer to hire a newcomer and spend more time and money training them when AI agents can already do a good job – and won’t quit,” she said.

It is a development that has prompted expressions of deep concern from some of the country’s leading economic minds. Cai Fang, a prominent labour economist and member of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, has warned that the initial shock wave of the AI boom will disproportionately hit “the young and the old”.

Cai’s research shows that traditional employment rates by age form an inverted U-shaped curve, where middle-aged workers experience the highest job stability, while younger and older cohorts face greater vulnerability.

He said AI was reinforcing that divide by eroding the economic value of entry-level skills for younger workers and also widening the digital capability gap for older employees who struggled to adapt to rapid technological advancement.

The economic data underlines the stakes.

China’s youth unemployment rate for 16- to 24-year-olds, excluding students, fell to 15.6 per cent in May but remained much higher than that of the whole urban population, according to data released by the National Bureau of Statistics on Monday. The Ministry of Education has estimated a record 12.7 million university graduates are preparing to enter the labour market.

A convenient scapegoat?

But some insiders argued that blaming AI for the wave of lay-offs misdiagnosed a conventional corporate malaise.

“To say that companies are laying people off just because AI has improved workflows is basically a lie,” said Tuxi, the veteran developer, who argued that many of China’s largest tech conglomerates spent years inflating their headcount. AI had simply provided executives with a convenient justification to trim the fat, he said.

Global tech leaders have also pushed back against the narrative that AI is the primary engine of global job cuts. In an interview last month with Singaporean broadcaster CNA, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang dismissed a direct causal link between AI deployment and tech lay-offs as an explanation that was “too lazy”.

He argued that the implementation timeline of enterprise AI had not matched spikes in unemployment, suggesting that the volatility was driven by a mix of over-hiring and the staggering costs required to develop AI.

That financial strain can be seen among China’s tech titans, where resources are being aggressively diverted to fund the AI arms race.

TikTok owner ByteDance has ramped up investment in AI infrastructure this year, boosting its planned capital expenditure to over 200 billion yuan (US$29.5 billion) – an increase of at least 25 per cent compared with preliminary internal budgets discussed late last year, the SCMP reported last month.

Several current and former employees said ByteDance had been consolidating business lines to free up headcount and computing power for its flagship AI products, including its AI assistant Doubao, its AI coding environment Trae, and the Coze agent platform.

The internal realignment coincided with the rapid expansion of Seed, ByteDance’s foundation-model team. Launched in 2023, the Seed team has swollen to about 2,000 people.

Meituan is playing defence and offence. After weathering a brutal local-services price war with Alibaba that squeezed its profit margins last year, the company has trimmed secondary teams, according to employees.

However, it continues to recruit at the high end. Meituan’s “Beidou” talent programme for top-tier campus technology recruits features openings focused on next-generation frontiers: AI infrastructure, large language models, embodied intelligence, autonomous agents and drones.

Alibaba has also been trimming its headcount and pivoting its sprawling business towards AI. The e-commerce giant shed around 34 per cent of its staff last year, mainly by offloading offline retail operations, according to corporate disclosures.

The macroeconomic impact of AI on employment was expected to be neutral in the long run, GF Securities’ chief economist Guo Lei wrote in a recent report. Still, in the short term, the market might need to navigate a painful “displacement effect” before it could unlock the “reinstatement effect”, he said.

Guo said AI would fundamentally redistribute jobs, reshape the nature of jobs and alter income structures. Workers stuck in less differentiated roles would lose their labour market bargaining power, while those who mastered the use of AI stood to see their productivity soar.

The regulatory balancing act

As the transition accelerates, Chinese tech firms are steering clear of the blunt rhetoric used by some of their Silicon Valley counterparts.

In February, Block founder Jack Dorsey said the US payments firm would reduce its workforce from more than 10,000 to under 6,000, pointing explicitly to the deployment of “intelligence tools” and flatter, leaner organisational structures.

We must do everything possible to protect the livelihoods of hundreds of thousands of employees

Richard Liu Qiangdong, JD.com chairman

In contrast, Chinese tech companies rarely, if ever, admit publicly that human workers are being replaced by algorithms.

Richard Liu Qiangdong, the billionaire founder and chairman of e-commerce powerhouse JD.com – which employed 951,420 people across the company and its affiliates at the end of last year – stressed the company’s responsibility to protect jobs during a speech to staff last month.

“Facing the impact of new technologies … we must do everything possible to protect the livelihoods of hundreds of thousands of employees, including the jobs of our blue-collar brothers,” Liu said, making a reference to the company’s extensive logistics network.

At a recent Apec panel discussion, he said JD.com would retrain its roughly 700,000 delivery and other blue-collar workers in robot maintenance as AI and automation reshape last-mile logistics.

Beijing has stepped up regulatory oversight to ensure the AI transition does not trigger widespread social friction.

The State Council’s “AI Plus” action plan, released in August, called for stronger assessment of employment risks from AI applications, more AI skills training and guiding innovation resources towards areas with greater job creation potential, with the aim of reducing the technology’s impact on employment.

More recently, the State Council unveiled its employment blueprint for the five years ending in 2030. It placed a new mandate at the top of its agenda, saying the country must “strengthen the employment-first orientation of macroeconomic regulation … and adapt to the development of AI to promote employment and entrepreneurship”.

Chinese courts and labour arbitration bodies have also begun drawing limits around AI-related dismissals.

In April, a Hangzhou court ruled that a financial technology firm had unlawfully terminated a quality-control supervisor who had been auditing large language model outputs.

The company fired him after citing the cost advantages of replacing his labour with AI. The worker had rejected an internal transfer that would have slashed his monthly salary from 25,000 yuan to 15,000 yuan.

The court ruled that while adopting AI constituted a voluntary business choice and a standard business risk, it did not automatically qualify as a “major change in objective circumstances” – the legal threshold required under Chinese labour law to declare an employment contract impossible to perform.

The court declared that the fundamental purpose of AI should be to “liberate labour, promote employment and improve people’s livelihoods”.

In an essay prepared for this month’s Lujiazui Forum, an annual financial gathering in Shanghai, Cai, the economist, said that while AI offered a chance to lift China’s labour productivity, its disruptive side effects could not be ignored.

He warned of the risk of a widening of the digital divide between tech-forward and legacy industries, urban and rural areas, and individual workers, with short-term job displacement highly probable, creating a broader macroeconomic risk that would see household consumption lag rapid productivity gains.

The solution, Cai said, was to “invest in people and ensure that intelligence is put towards good”.

But worries persist for those toiling away in the cubicles of China’s tech hubs. Amid corporate denials of sweeping lay-offs, the quiet reality of “optimisation” continues to play out one desk at a time.

Confronted by what he viewed as an uncertain employment future, the Meituan employee contacted by a friend said “some outsourced workers have already been cleared out”, though he did not know the exact proportion.

While lay-offs happened every year, “this round feels quite big,” he said.

Additional reporting by Minxiao Chang

item.title: [SCMP] China challenges Western ‘tribute system’ theory in push to control its narrative power
item.description:
Beijing is stepping up efforts to challenge the Western concept of the “tribute system”, arguing that foreign frameworks distort ancient Chinese diplomacy and misrepresent the country’s contemporary global rise.

China is redoubling efforts to define its own practices, experiences and ideas through original, home-grown social science language rather than through what it says are Western conceptual lenses.

The theory was forged and made popular in the US decades ago as a means to interpret both ancient and contemporary Chinese diplomacy. China’s push for narrative power to win over a broader overseas audience continues to be tested, including among foreign perceptions of Chinese history and practices.
item.content:encoded:
Beijing is stepping up efforts to challenge the Western concept of the “tribute system”, arguing that foreign frameworks distort ancient Chinese diplomacy and misrepresent the country’s contemporary global rise.

China is redoubling efforts to define its own practices, experiences and ideas through original, home-grown social science language rather than through what it says are Western conceptual lenses.

The theory was forged and made popular in the US decades ago as a means to interpret both ancient and contemporary Chinese diplomacy. China’s push for narrative power to win over a broader overseas audience continues to be tested, including among foreign perceptions of Chinese history and practices.

In a recent example, American billionaire investor Ray Dalio wrote in an article published on his Substack on June 19 that “we are in the very early stage of a shift to a tribute system-type order in the Asia region and even beyond”.

He argued in the article “The Tribute System: The New World Order” that while China’s economic and financial powers were growing rapidly, the US handling of Iran’s seizure of the Strait of Hormuz had convinced others that Washington “doesn’t have what it takes to fight to maintain its empire”, prompting a change in thinking by global leaders.

The founder of Bridgewater Associates, one of the world’s biggest hedge funds, said the dynamic was reflected in the many visits by foreign heads of state and their delegations to Beijing since late last year, which Dalio characterised as efforts “to build tribute-type relationships” with Chinese President Xi Jinping.

The “tribute system” is a term coined in the 1940s by John King Fairbank, a Harvard historian credited with founding the academic field of modern Chinese studies in the US, and his collaborator Ssu-yu Teng, for a Sinocentric, hierarchical model of international relations that prevailed before unravelling in the second half of the 19th century.

As China’s global standing has risen, analysts and policymakers in many countries have repeatedly revisited the more than 80-year-old term to assess Beijing’s foreign policy and potential strategic calculations, despite broad objection to the concept within academia.

Even Fairbank had reservations about its use, writing that “tribute” was a “very rough and often misleading” translation borrowed from European vocabulary.

Its use led to views that China could be leveraging its Belt and Road Initiative to build a so-called new tribute system centred around it to extend increasing influence and power across the neighbourhood and beyond, prompting rebuttals from Chinese scholars.

Mention of the notion by Dalio – who has long been seen as a bridge between China and the United States and a frequent visitor to senior Chinese officials – did not appear to strike a chord with officials in Beijing.

“The so-called tribute system is a false image projected by the Western hegemonic logic onto Chinese diplomacy,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Lin Jian said on July 16, responding to a question apparently about Dalio’s argument, even though he was not identified by name.

That was two days after a social media channel named Chaoyang Shaoxia – which is widely believed to be affiliated with the ministry – published a long critique of the concept.

“Using the negatively loaded English word ‘tribute’ to describe the ancient Chinese concept of chao gong is highly misleading to international audiences unfamiliar with Chinese culture,” it said.

According to the tribute system theory, which is called “the Chinese world order”, China’s historical dynasties were considered the centre of civilisation, culturally and morally superior to outsiders, who would naturally come bringing “tributes” – usually produce from their native lands – to pay homage.

In return, Chinese emperors would reward them with fine objects, formally invest their rulers as native kings or chieftains, and grant them access to trade with the Middle Kingdom.

According to Dalio’s post, relations in the tribute system were not between equals but between superiors and subordinates who should treat each other well to preserve harmony.

On the surface, this appears to be a translation issue, but in essence it is a question of who has the power to define

Ding Gang, People’s Daily

If an inferior power treated a stronger one inappropriately, the latter would typically punish it through pressure and deception, although also occasionally by violence, he added.

But Chaoyang Shaoxia noted that the term tribute was “born with the attributes of coercion, violent plunder and one-way exploitation”, as it was derived from a Latin word that originally referred to Roman imperial taxes on provincial populations, and later forced medieval payments from vassals to feudal lords in Europe.

It stated that the formulation did not correspond to chao gong, a term it said was intended to denote “voluntary” acts of reaching out to others based on appreciation and “spontaneous” behaviours of presenting gifts to express goodwill.

The channel said ancient China had followed the principle of hou wang bo lai, or giving generously and taking little. This meant it returned goods to so-called tributary states worth far more than what they had been offered, making the arrangement economically lucrative for them.

It also argued that while modern China had inherited the traditional philosophy of “valuing harmony above all”, it had “completely” abandoned the hierarchical world view of imperial times and firmly upheld that all countries, regardless of their size, wealth or strength, were equal.

The mismatch between “the tribute system” and China’s historical practice “effectively reflects a deeper question of who has the final say and who sets the definitions in the international public opinion sphere”, Chaoyang Shaoxia said.

“For years, China’s ideas and image have faced a problem of being shaped by others rather than by itself. The West has always projected its own historical experience onto China and measured China by its own value standards.

“For cultural concepts unique to China that lack direct English equivalents, or for existing Western translations that carry colonial, exoticising or prejudicial connotations, we can definitely forge a new path.”

The critique comes as Beijing steps up its push to build a “Chinese intellectual system in philosophy and social sciences”, reiterated by Xi in May in a directive urging the development of indigenous, independent theories and knowledge that can explain China’s practices to the outside world without being allegedly monopolised or distorted by Western concepts and narratives.

The effort has extended beyond contemporary Chinese politics, diplomacy and law, to scrutinising foreign origin theories about China’s history, as those interpretations are increasingly seen as relevant to the country’s current domestic governance and foreign policy.

For example, Chinese scholars and officials in recent years have taken aim at the “New Qing History” school of thought that emerged in the US, saying it misreads China’s past and inherently threatens the country’s national unity today by providing historical ammunition for separatism in border regions.

Zheng Yongnian, a Chinese political scientist, cautioned that historical experiences in China were often used as case studies for Western concepts and theories, which would not help the world understand the country accurately.

He said the term “tribute system” was the result of Fairbank imposing Western frameworks on China because he could not find an exact equivalent in the English lexicon.

Zheng said the way ancient Chinese states organised their external relations more closely resembled what would today be described as China’s policy of unilateral opening-up.

Liu Wenming, a history professor at Capital Normal University in Beijing, has also called for re-examining the tribute system as a “foreign concept” to help “eliminate misunderstandings of Chinese history … and to better appreciate the peaceful and friendly nature of the regional order in ancient East and Southeast Asia”.

“Until a more appropriate translation is found, transliteration remains a viable option, namely using chao gong in English,” he wrote in an article published in July last year in Historical Review, a bimonthly journal supervised by the state-run Chinese Academy of Social Sciences.

In its article on July 14, Chaoyang Shaoxia suggested that “the tribute system” could be replaced with “jade-silk covenant” or “treasure ship model”, referring to Ming dynasty admiral Zheng He’s seven voyages into the Indian Ocean in the 15th century. Beijing has long portrayed the historical episode as a symbol of China’s peaceful rise, win-win diplomacy and openness to the world.

However, those alternative translations could also run into headwinds from competing narratives abroad, with many foreign scholars noting that the Chinese mariner’s “treasure ships” were heavily armed. Some also cited records pointing to coercion and conflict when local rulers failed to pay due respect, with others framing Zheng’s expeditions as “power projection” or “proto-maritime colonialism”.

A similar challenge to external messaging has surfaced in discussions surrounding China’s Ethnic Unity and Progress Promotion Law, which took effect last month.

While Chinese officials may use the term “unity” to convey that the legislation emphasises interaction, exchange and blending among ethnic groups in China on an equal footing – premised on the coexistence of differences – overseas media use terms such as “integrate” or “assimilate”.

“On the surface, this appears to be a translation issue, but in essence it is a question of who has the power to define,” Ding Gang, a senior editor with the official People’s Daily, wrote in an article on social media on July 7.

“The public debate surrounding this law is ultimately not just about the legislation itself, but about who has the authority to interpret a particular development path,” added Ding, who is also a senior fellow with the Chongyang Institute for Financial Studies at Renmin University in Beijing.

He said that in the English-speaking world, the word “unity” had never been used to describe how different ethnic groups coexist amid their differences.

Because of differences in knowledge, foreign audiences would “naturally” substitute it with concepts more familiar to them and “automatically” link China’s ethnic policies to their historical memory of Western colonisers’ cultural and racial oppression of indigenous peoples, he argued.

Ding added that the association of “China’s ethnic policy” with “assimilation” had become a common sense-style default perception in Western coverage of China-related issues.

He called for greater attention to the “concepts” that could allow China’s “stories” to properly land with the foreign audience.

“Without conceptual intermediaries that can be recognised within the other side’s cognitive system while accurately corresponding to Chinese practice, even the most compelling stories will remain floating outside their framework of understanding, ultimately to be recompiled and redefined by their own concepts,” he said.

item.title: [SCMP] China, India and Pakistan’s dangerous nuclear triangle just became more complicated
item.description:
The China-India-Pakistan triangle has never been short on danger, but Islamabad’s new defensive alliance has added another variable to an already volatile situation.

Last week, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia signed a pact in Mecca in which they agreed to treat an armed attack on one as an attack on all. The three governments have described it as defensive and not directed at any particular state.

Analysts said its main significance for India lay less in whether it would be invoked, but in how it could alter Pakistan’s strategic position as well as the balance between the three nuclear powers.
item.content:encoded:
The China-India-Pakistan triangle has never been short on danger, but Islamabad’s new defensive alliance has added another variable to an already volatile situation.

Last week, Pakistan, Turkey and Saudi Arabia signed a pact in Mecca in which they agreed to treat an armed attack on one as an attack on all. The three governments have described it as defensive and not directed at any particular state.

Analysts said its main significance for India lay less in whether it would be invoked, but in how it could alter Pakistan’s strategic position as well as the balance between the three nuclear powers.

For several decades their relationship has been marked by intermittent deadly flare-ups, most recently the 2020 Galwan clashes between Indian and Chinese troops and last year’s India-Pakistan conflict.

“The agreement institutionalises a trilateral framework combining Saudi capital, Turkish defence technology and Pakistan’s strategic geography,” according to Brahma Chellaney, a New Delhi-based strategic analyst.

“Regardless of whether such provisions are ever invoked [the pact’s] existence could nonetheless complicate India’s strategic calculus by introducing additional uncertainty into crisis planning and deterrence,” he wrote in a social media post.

That uncertainty is important because India already faces two major security challenges from its long-running border disputes with both Pakistan to its west and China to the north.

It has fought four wars with Pakistan since 1947, in addition to last year’s conflict, and one full-scale war with China in 1962.

There have also been a series of deadly border confrontations with the latter along their Himalayan frontier, most recently the Galwan Valley clash in 2020 that killed 20 Indian and four Chinese troops.

Chellaney linked the Mecca agreement to the fallout from India’s military operation against Pakistan last year.

In the conflict, which started after an attack on tourists in Indian-held Kashmir that New Delhi blamed on its neighbour, Pakistan said it had downed a number of Indian warplanes.

New Delhi’s decision to end hostilities after just 3½ days, Chellaney argued, “helped revive Pakistan’s international image, particularly in the Islamic world”.

He said that perception had raised Islamabad’s strategic importance and helped pave the way for a mutual defence pact with Saudi Arabia last year and then its recent expansion to include Turkey.

With the new deal, Pakistan, China’s closest strategic partner, gains further diplomatic weight and possibly access to more diverse military equipment from Turkey, a Nato member.

Pakistan has gained a formal security framework with two states that possess deep financial resources, technology and diplomatic influence

Saira Bano, Thompson Rivers University

A relatively stronger Pakistan would also keep Indian attention divided between its western and northern fronts, an outcome that has long suited Chinese interests.

The agreement “does embolden Pakistan further”, according to Farwa Aamer from the Asia Society Policy Institute, a think tank in New York.

“Pakistan’s further embedded in the wider regional security architecture ... it’s of interest to Beijing to have Pakistan in a more secure and stable position.

“It serves both its economic investment interests as well as geopolitical interests in the region”, she said.

India now has “to deal with a higher political and security profile of Pakistan in the region where we have major interests”, said Kanwal Sibal, India’s former foreign secretary.

“[Pakistan] will feel more emboldened to pursue its combative diplomacy against India and could take risks on the terrorism front,” he added.

“Pakistan has gained a formal security framework with two states that possess deep financial resources, technology and diplomatic influence,” Saira Bano, from Thompson Rivers University in Canada, wrote in an analysis for the Lowy Institute think tank.

“This sits alongside Pakistan’s deeper strategic and defence relationship with China, transforming what India once viewed mainly as a bilateral rivalry into a wider network of alignments.”

The Mecca agreement does not create an automatic anti-India bloc or give China an unconstrained advantage, she added.

But Bano argued its most “consequential feature” was not the resemblance to Nato, whose members also treat an attack on one as an attack on all, but the way it “collapses the strategic distance between the Gulf, the eastern Mediterranean and South Asia”.

She added: “It is an experiment in regional self-reliance that joins three strategic theatres usually analysed separately.”

Saima Afzal, a researcher specialising in South Asian security, wrote in an analysis for US-based platform Counter Punch that Pakistan’s presence meant a defensive network centred on the Gulf “now reaches into an environment shaped by India-Pakistan rivalry, China’s regional role and nuclear deterrence”.

For India the risks are multilayered and its room for manoeuvre is constrained by the added uncertainty caused by the risk Pakistan’s new allies could join any conflict, the need to protect its Gulf interests and the prospect of closer alignment with Israel.

Its large diaspora in the Gulf is vital to both its economy, in the form of remittances, and energy security strategy.

Any future India-Pakistan crisis might risk deeper involvement from the Gulf states or threaten those interests.

Chellaney observed that all three members of the new pact sit along critical sea lanes, giving India “fresh reason to prioritise naval expansion”.

Bano said: “During a future India-Pakistan crisis, uncertainty over what constitutes an ‘attack’ on Pakistan could complicate India’s calculations even if Riyadh and Ankara have no intention of becoming involved.”

Aamer said India had already been widening its defence partnerships, including those with Israel, Indonesia and the United Arab Emirates, and “will also continue to engage Saudi Arabia for commercial opportunities”.

Countries were increasingly pursuing “wider diversification and hedging strategies” by building broader partnership networks as buffers against future economic and security risks, she added.

The key question is whether the Mecca pact changes the balance of power or simply changes the strategic calculation.

Husain Haqqani of the Hudson Institute described it as “more symbolic than substantive”.

He added: “A shared enemy is the first element of a mutual defence agreement and that is absent here.”

Pakistan and Saudi Arabia have also proved reluctant to get involved in each other’s conflicts, such as those involving Afghanistan, Iran or the Houthis in Yemen.

Bano said India’s priority should be to “preserve [its] influence in Riyadh” and strengthen its defensive partnerships, while Pakistan’s role in the new framework “cannot be separated entirely from Chinese weapons, technology and infrastructure”.

item.title: [SCMP] Why Taiwan is conducting its first-ever mobile network throttling exercise
item.description:
Taiwan is conducting its first-ever mobile network throttling exercise this week to test how the public responds to wartime communications disruptions, a new civil defence measure that has sparked criticism over the government’s preparedness.

The exercise, held in central Taiwan on Monday and planned for northern Taiwan on Thursday, will simulate severe mobile network congestion by reducing 4G and 5G bandwidth for 30 minutes.

About 17 million people, or 73 per cent of the island’s population, are expected to be affected, according to the National Communications Commission (NCC).
item.content:encoded:
Taiwan is conducting its first-ever mobile network throttling exercise this week to test how the public responds to wartime communications disruptions, a new civil defence measure that has sparked criticism over the government’s preparedness.

The exercise, held in central Taiwan on Monday and planned for northern Taiwan on Thursday, will simulate severe mobile network congestion by reducing 4G and 5G bandwidth for 30 minutes.

About 17 million people, or 73 per cent of the island’s population, are expected to be affected, according to the National Communications Commission (NCC).

Rather than a complete internet shutdown, authorities said voice calls, SMS messages and emergency cell broadcasts would continue to function.

Services relying on mobile data, including video streaming, video calls, mobile payments, online banking, e-ticketing, food delivery, QR code verification, cloud synchronisation and app authentication, may become temporarily unavailable.

The first phase of the exercise in central Taiwan on Monday prompted complaints from users who said the throttling had effectively left them without mobile internet access.

Some reported that 4G and 5G connections had slowed to the point where they could not send messages online or even load a browser homepage.

“What throttling? It’s basically a complete shutdown,” one user in Taichung said, while others described having “a signal but no internet speed”, saying the disruption felt more like an internet blackout than reduced speeds.

The drill is part of this year’s expanded Urban Resilience exercises, which replace the long-running Wan An air-raid drills and reflect Taiwan’s growing focus on preparing civilians for network outages caused by war, cyberattacks or natural disasters, according to the defence ministry.

The NCC said northern and central Taiwan were chosen because they had the island’s highest population density and telecommunications traffic, adding that the exercise would eventually be extended island-wide.

Before the tests, Premier Cho Jung-tai stressed that the exercise would be “network throttling, not an internet shutdown”.

He said it drew on the experience of democracies – including Japan, South Korea and the Nordic countries – to test the government’s ability to operate under degraded communications while encouraging people to prepare alternative means of staying connected.

“We hope this exercise will help the public build the ability to cope with communications disruptions through backup measures,” Cho said at a cabinet meeting late last month.

He described communications as a critical pillar of resilience, saying natural disasters, large-scale cyberattacks and other emergencies could all disrupt telecoms networks.

The exercise has nevertheless drawn criticism online and from opposition lawmakers.

Many internet users questioned the practicality of the government’s civil defence handbook, which directs readers to scan QR codes for additional information.

“If the internet is unavailable during wartime, what exactly are we supposed to scan?” one widely shared comment asked.

Others criticised the NCC’s advice to postpone important online activities or switch to fixed broadband during the drill, arguing such recommendations were unrealistic for commuters, street vendors and people working outdoors.

Ko Ju-chun, a legislator from Taiwan’s main opposition Kuomintang (KMT), said reducing mobile bandwidth to about 1 per cent of normal capacity amounted to a large-scale internet shutdown.

Ko disputed the government’s claim that the drill followed international practice, arguing that countries such as Japan and South Korea generally conducted smaller-scale or scenario-based exercises.

“Real communications resilience means backup systems immediately take over when the primary network fails,” he said. “The exercise should test whether backup systems work, not whether the government can cut off people’s internet.”

Fellow KMT legislator Weng Hsiao-ling said the government should compensate the public for any financial losses or damage caused by the exercise.

Ruling Democratic Progressive Party legislator Chen Kuan-ting defended the drill, arguing that a real attack could disrupt communications for an entire day rather than the 30 minutes being simulated.

However, he warned Beijing could exploit the exercise through a false-flag operation by blaming any simultaneous cyberattack or communications disruption on technical failures by Taiwan’s authorities.

Beijing has dismissed the exercise, saying that no matter how many drills the island’s authorities conduct, in the face of the People’s Liberation Army they were “little more than political theatre and an attempt to bolster morale”.

“They cannot alter the doomed fate of ‘Taiwan independence’ or stop the historical trend towards inevitable reunification of Taiwan with the motherland,” Zhang Han, a spokeswoman for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, told a press conference last month.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China and has not ruled out the use of force to achieve reunification. Most countries – including the United States, Taiwan’s main international backer – do not recognise the self-ruled island as an independent state. However, Washington is opposed to any attempt to take it by force.

Analysts also offered mixed assessments of the tests.

Su Tzu-yun, a senior analyst at the government-funded Institute for National Defence and Security Research, said the exercise reflected lessons from recent natural disasters as well as overseas resilience drills that simulate communications congestion.

“It gives people an opportunity during the 30-minute exercise to think about how they would stay in contact with family members if internet access became unavailable,” Su said.

He suggested future exercises could recruit volunteers for closed trials, minimising disruption while allowing authorities to collect more detailed technical data.

Taipei-based military analyst Lu De-yun, a former defence ministry press secretary, said the government had failed to adequately explain the exercise beforehand, unnecessarily alarming the public.

While agreeing that degraded communications were a realistic scenario during war or major disasters, Lu said the authorities “have focused on telling people to prepare their own backup communications without demonstrating what contingency measures the government itself has in place”.

He also questioned why Taiwan was not making greater use of leased low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellite communications services, such as Britain’s OneWeb, as a backup if terrestrial mobile networks are disrupted.

“The government often talks about developing Taiwan’s LEO satellite capabilities but none of that seems to benefit ordinary people. Instead, people are simply told to fend for themselves,” Lu said.

item.title: [SCMP] As US marks 75 years of defence pact with Philippines, can it stay the course?
item.description:
The Philippines and the United States are marking the 75th anniversary of their defence alliance with a renewed pledge to step up joint drills as geopolitical tensions in the region continue to simmer.

While the allies are moving towards more frequent planning for maritime security cooperation and deterrence, there are still questions about Washington’s long-term commitment to the security of the Philippines and the broader region, according to analysts.

At an annual meeting to strengthen security engagement in Manila on Friday, Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of the US Pacific Command, and Armed Forces of the Philippines chief of staff General Antonio Nafarrete reaffirmed their commitment to the mutual defence treaty signed in 1951 and signed a memorandum to map out the next phase of cooperation.
item.content:encoded:
The Philippines and the United States are marking the 75th anniversary of their defence alliance with a renewed pledge to step up joint drills as geopolitical tensions in the region continue to simmer.

While the allies are moving towards more frequent planning for maritime security cooperation and deterrence, there are still questions about Washington’s long-term commitment to the security of the Philippines and the broader region, according to analysts.

At an annual meeting to strengthen security engagement in Manila on Friday, Admiral Samuel Paparo, commander of the US Pacific Command, and Armed Forces of the Philippines chief of staff General Antonio Nafarrete reaffirmed their commitment to the mutual defence treaty signed in 1951 and signed a memorandum to map out the next phase of cooperation.

While Paparo and Nafarrete did not disclose details, US Pacific Command said the plans included expanding large-scale military exercises and specialist exchanges.

In recent years, the US and the Philippines have taken part in joint and multilateral military drills with partners such as Japan, Australia and New Zealand, including in contested waters near the Southeast Asian country.

Expanding ties with other allies

The alliance is stepping up such cooperation as the Philippines sits at the intersection of the South China Sea and the Taiwan Strait – two theatres that could spark a potential conflict between major powers, according to analysts.

Developments near Taiwan would have major implications for Philippine security and US regional planning, said Vina Nadjibulla, co-founder and chief executive of the Centre for Strategic Statecraft, a Canadian foreign policy think tank.

Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-governed island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

“The next phase should be about networked deterrence: stronger Philippine defence capabilities, deeper US-Philippines planning and closer cooperation with Japan, Australia and other partners,” Nadjibulla said.

“The objective should be to make coercion more difficult and give Manila more strategic options, not fewer,” she said.

Nadjibulla noted the increasing sophistication of the joint drills through bilateral planning and real-time information sharing in areas such as air and missile defence, maritime offence, unmanned systems and cyber cooperation.

As such, the treaty between Manila and Washington is becoming “less of a passive insurance policy and more of an active deterrence architecture”.

China’s growing military capabilities and aggressive activities in the South China Sea had accelerated cooperation between the two allies, Nadjibulla said, citing Beijing’s use of water cannons and dangerous manoeuvres during confrontations around Scarborough Shoal and Second Thomas Shoal.

“For Washington, the Philippines now matters not only because of the South China Sea disputes but because its geography is increasingly consequential to preserving deterrence across the first island chain,” she added.

Washington’s island chain strategy dates back to the Cold War. The first island chain stretches from the Kuril Islands through Japan, Taiwan and the Philippines down to Borneo, with the second island chain including the major US base at Guam further east, extending through the Marianas to Palau and New Guinea.

Next stage of alliance

Muhammad Faizal Bin Abdul Rahman, a research fellow at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, said the evolution of the Manila-Washington alliance reflected a shift in the geopolitical landscape.

“While it was important to the US during the Cold War as part of the strategic competition between the Western and communist blocs, it has now become a key strategic and operational frontline in the competition between the US and China,” Faizal said.

Sylwia Monika Gorska, a political analyst at the University of Central Lancashire, said the alliance had moved from the Americans having a large permanent military presence in the Philippines during the Cold War to rotational deployments and counterterrorism cooperation followed by cooperation focused on maritime and territorial defence.

Gorska cited the Enhanced Defence Cooperation Agreement signed by the allies to rotate US troops in the Philippines for longer stays and deploy American equipment on Philippine territory, such as northern Luzon, as central to the shift in defence cooperation.

To further enhance the alliance, Washington and Manila should build resilience in the areas of logistics, communications and command-and-control networks, according to Gorska.

“The next stage of the alliance is therefore not simply geographical expansion of access, but whether distributed forces can remain supplied, connected and operational when the network supporting them is under pressure,” she added.

Chris Gardiner, chief executive of the Institute for Regional Security, said that while the memorandum was another step in strengthening the bilateral partnership, the alliance should be further enhanced by expanding defence cooperation with Japan and Australia.

“The treaty is strong and strengthening because there is a clear strategic confluence of interests,” Gardiner said, adding that the Trump administration viewed closer alignment with the Philippines as more important than its strategy over Taiwan.

However, doubts still linger about Washington’s commitment to the long-term security of the Philippines and the region, according to analysts.

Faizal cited the US aversion towards being drawn into another conflict amid the ongoing war against Iran and signs of Gulf allies reassessing their security ties with Washington.

“This makes it necessary for the Philippines and other US allies to work more closely to ensure that the hub-and-spokes alliance system continues to function by strengthening the spokes [allies] to compensate for the hub [US] becoming less credible,” he explained.

Gorska said while Manila’s other regional allies were stepping up to the plate, they would not be able to replace the US as the anchor of regional security.

“Japan and Australia already give Manila additional sources of surveillance, logistics, equipment, training and operational support, reducing its reliance on Washington for some functions,” Gorska explained.

“What they cannot substitute is the treaty guarantee itself, or the scale of high-end military capability that sits behind it,” she said.

item.title: [SCMP] Why India’s new Himalayan border map threatens a fragile thaw in China ties
item.description:
New Delhi has issued names for 27 locations in Arunachal Pradesh on its official maps, including sensitive sites near the disputed border with China, in a move that an analyst warned could complicate efforts to repair bilateral ties.

The Indian government announced the move on Friday, just a day after officials from the two countries held a working-level consultation in New Delhi to discuss border management and reaffirm the need for peace along the Line of Actual Control.

Beijing has long referred to the northeastern border state as Zangnan, or southern Tibet.
item.content:encoded:
New Delhi has issued names for 27 locations in Arunachal Pradesh on its official maps, including sensitive sites near the disputed border with China, in a move that an analyst warned could complicate efforts to repair bilateral ties.

The Indian government announced the move on Friday, just a day after officials from the two countries held a working-level consultation in New Delhi to discuss border management and reaffirm the need for peace along the Line of Actual Control.

Beijing has long referred to the northeastern border state as Zangnan, or southern Tibet.

In a statement, India’s Ministry of Home Affairs said the Survey of India had issued standard names for the locations to ensure “accurate recognition” and improve public awareness of their geographical and historical significance.

The list includes 21 land areas, four mountain passes, a high-altitude lake and a memorial. The names have been added to official Survey of India maps.

Among them are Longju, a village that was the scene of a 1959 border confrontation, as well as the nearby villages of Maja and Bisa and the high-altitude Thag La, the strategic pass where the 1962 border war between India and China erupted.

The list also includes the Sher-e-Thapa Memorial, which commemorates an Indian soldier who fought in that conflict, and Sambho Sarovar, a high-altitude lake.

Beijing rejected the move as illegitimate, saying on Monday that “Zangnan region is China’s territory”.

“China does not recognise the so-called Arunachal Pradesh illegally set up by India. India’s [attempt] to replace names long used by China with its so-called standard names is illegal, null and void. Still less will it change the fact that Zangnan region belongs to China,” foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said.

Indian media described the step as a response to Beijing’s own mapping campaign since 2017 to assign standardised names to places in Arunachal Pradesh.

According to the state-owned Global Times, China’s Ministry of Civil Affairs has issued six lists of names covering 112 locations, including villages, mountain passes, rivers and peaks.

In essence, India is using maps and place names to construct a narrative of expansion, relying on its own mythology rather than established international norms

Liu Zongyi, Shanghai Institutes for International Studies

New Delhi has consistently rejected China’s renaming exercises, with Indian Ministry of External Affairs spokesman Randhir Jaiswal on Saturday describing them as “vain and preposterous”.

“Arunachal Pradesh was, is, and will always remain an integral and inalienable part of India. Assigning invented names will not alter this reality,” he said.

Beijing rejects Indian sovereignty over Arunachal Pradesh, which borders China’s Tibet autonomous region, and claims the area as historically part of China. Three of the areas included in India’s list of names – Longju, Maja and Bisa – are under Chinese control.

Liu Zongyi, a senior fellow at the Shanghai Institutes for International Studies, said India’s latest move was “primarily aimed at reinforcing its territorial claims” and creating the impression that its sovereignty over Arunachal Pradesh was already settled.

He said the naming exercise was based on what Beijing considered the “illegal McMahon Line” and built on India’s 1987 establishment of the “so-called Arunachal Pradesh”.

According to Liu, the move served both external and domestic purposes.

“By issuing these names, New Delhi seeks both to declare sovereignty externally, including over some sites under China’s actual control, to demonstrate continuity of its claims, and to foster a domestic perception that the territory is beyond dispute,” he said.

He said several of the chosen locations carried “clear military and strategic significance”, such as mountain passes and logistical hubs that could support future Indian deployments and infrastructure projects in the region.

He added that the inclusion of a war memorial reflected an element of “political education and nationalist messaging”.

“In essence, India is using maps and place names to construct a narrative of expansion, relying on its own mythology rather than established international norms,” Liu said.

He contrasted this with China’s approach, which he argued was rooted in sovereignty and historical legitimacy, and in Beijing’s rejection of the British colonial-era McMahon Line, which India regards as the basis of its eastern boundary with China.

“By publishing standardised names, China reaffirms its sovereignty over Zangnan to the international community and underscores its right to exercise lawful authority there in the future,” Liu said.

Pending a comprehensive border settlement, the two countries have fought a war and several deadly clashes over their competing perceptions of the Line of Actual Control.

Liu described the latest naming controversy as evidence that New Delhi’s position on the territorial dispute remained entrenched despite recent efforts to improve relations.

“Rather than seeking resolution through negotiation, it attempts to legitimise its occupation by asserting ‘possession itself equals sovereignty’. This shows that, despite outward gestures of easing relations, India’s stance on fundamental questions remains unchanged,” Liu said.

New Delhi and Beijing have been trying to sustain a cautious improvement in ties after years of tension along the Himalayan frontier.

India is preparing to host next month’s summit for Brics, the bloc of emerging economies that also includes China. Meanwhile, special representatives from the two countries are expected to hold their 25th round of boundary talks in Beijing in the coming months.

There have also been limited signs of practical engagement. Border trade through Nathu La resumed on August 1 after a six-year suspension, while Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and Indian Minister of External Affairs Subrahmanyam Jaishankar pledged at a July 22 meeting in Manila to consolidate positive momentum in bilateral ties.
