On Thursday, senior diplomats co-chaired the 36th meeting of the Working Mechanism for Consultation and Coordination on China-India Border Affairs in New Delhi, joined by representatives from defence, home affairs and immigration agencies.

According to China’s foreign ministry, the two sides discussed border management, cross-border cooperation and official demarcation. They agreed to prepare for the next round of special representative talks and to maintain communication through diplomatic and military channels.

At the New Delhi talks, India also urged China to resume sharing hydrological data amid concerns over Beijing’s construction of a massive dam on the Yarlung Tsangpo (Brahmaputra) River about 50km (31 miles) from the Arunachal Pradesh border, according to Bloomberg.

item.title: [SCMP] Malaysia seeks to deepen trade ties with South Korea in chips, AI, halal sector
item.description:
Malaysia is seeking to elevate its economic partnership with South Korea beyond traditional manufacturing and trade by positioning itself as a long-term strategic partner in high-value industries, ranging from semiconductors and AI to electric vehicles, renewable energy and the fast-growing global halal economy.

Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA) director Redzuan Abd Rahman and Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE) trade commissioner Mohamad Termizi HJ Piee said the two countries’ economic relationship had entered a new phase, with growing opportunities for South Korean companies to leverage Malaysia as both an investment destination and a gateway to the wider Asean market.

“Malaysia and South Korea have built a strong and enduring economic partnership over the past several decades,” Redzuan said. “We believe the greatest opportunities lie in deepening collaboration in industries that are shaping the future of our economies.”
item.content:encoded:
Malaysia is seeking to elevate its economic partnership with South Korea beyond traditional manufacturing and trade by positioning itself as a long-term strategic partner in high-value industries, ranging from semiconductors and AI to electric vehicles, renewable energy and the fast-growing global halal economy.

Malaysian Investment Development Authority (MIDA) director Redzuan Abd Rahman and Malaysia External Trade Development Corporation (MATRADE) trade commissioner Mohamad Termizi HJ Piee said the two countries’ economic relationship had entered a new phase, with growing opportunities for South Korean companies to leverage Malaysia as both an investment destination and a gateway to the wider Asean market.

“Malaysia and South Korea have built a strong and enduring economic partnership over the past several decades,” Redzuan said. “We believe the greatest opportunities lie in deepening collaboration in industries that are shaping the future of our economies.”

According to MIDA, South Korean companies have implemented investments totalling US$11.7 billion across more than 400 projects in Malaysia as of 2025, creating nearly 50,000 jobs. Those investments span chemicals, transport equipment, electrical and electronic products, petroleum products and basic metals.

Redzuan highlighted that the two countries’ respective national development strategies were highly complementary, explaining that while South Korea continued to advance its leadership in semiconductors, artificial intelligence, advanced manufacturing, mobility, batteries and green technologies, Malaysia was implementing the New Industrial Master Plan 2030, the National Semiconductor Strategy and the National Energy Transition Roadmap “to accelerate industrial transformation towards higher-value, innovation-driven and sustainable industries”.

This strong strategic alignment presents significant opportunities for deeper Malaysia-South Korea collaboration in investment, technology and industrial partnerships, reinforcing Malaysia’s position as a strategic destination for South Korean companies seeking regional growth.

Termizi echoed that assessment from the trade perspective, pointing to rapidly expanding bilateral commerce between both countries.

“Malaysia and the Republic of Korea have built a strong and resilient economic partnership, supported by growing trade, complementary industries and close cooperation through Asean and regional trade agreements,” he said.

From January through June this year, bilateral trade increased a whopping 52.3 per cent year on year to US$19 billion, with Malaysia’s exports to South Korea rising 44.2 per cent and imports from South Korea climbing 58.9 per cent.

“From MATRADE’s perspective, the next phase should focus on diversifying trade into emerging sectors such as AI, robotics, medical devices, green technology, digital services and the halal economy, while helping more Malaysian small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) participate in South Korean supply chains,” he said. “Ultimately, our priority is to transform conventional buyer-seller relationships into long-term partnerships involving technology, innovation, joint product development and access to wider regional and global markets.”

‘Gateway to Asean’

As South Korean companies continue diversifying their supply chains across Southeast Asia, both officials highlighted Malaysia’s advantages beyond competitive production costs. Redzuan said Malaysia combined “industrial maturity, strategic location and policy stability” with more than five decades of experience in electrical and electronics manufacturing.

“Malaysia handles roughly 13 per cent of global semiconductor packaging and testing, providing an established supplier ecosystem that significantly lowers market entry risks,” he said.

He also stressed the country’s multilingual, English-proficient workforce, strong intellectual property protection and long-term industrial policy frameworks.

“Unlike markets that compete solely on low labour costs, Malaysia offers South Korean investors an ecosystem capable of supporting capital-intensive, hi-tech and ESG-compliant manufacturing from day 1,” Redzuan said.

Termizi similarly described Malaysia as “a strategic gateway to Asean,” citing its participation in major trade agreements including the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership and the free trade agreement between South Korea and the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, in addition to its multilingual business environment. He added that the coming Malaysia-South Korea FTA was expected to further strengthen bilateral trade and investment, enhance market access and create new opportunities for businesses in both countries.

“These strengths make Malaysia an ideal sourcing partner for South Korean companies seeking to build resilient and diversified supply chains,” Termizi said.

Asked where bilateral cooperation could expand most significantly over the coming years, both officials identified advanced technology industries as priority areas. Redzuan said Malaysia aimed to deepen collaboration with South Korea in advanced electronics, electric vehicles (EV), renewable energy and digital infrastructure, in tandem with the Southeast Asian country’s acceleration of its dual transition towards a hi-tech and low-carbon economy.

“We see South Korean firms not merely as foreign investors, but as long-term strategic partners that co-develop intellectual property, upskill local engineering talent and integrate Malaysian suppliers into global value chains,” Redzuan said.

Termizi likewise pointed to opportunities in semiconductors, AI, robotics, smart manufacturing, medical devices, green technology and digital services.

“Malaysia is already a key player in the global semiconductor ecosystem, while South Korea is recognised for its leadership in advanced technologies and industrial innovation,” he said. “These complementary strengths create opportunities for greater collaboration in supply chains, technology partnerships and regional market expansion.”

Redzuan cited South Korean conglomerates including SK Nexilis, Samsung, POSCO, OCI and Lotte as examples of successful investments in Malaysia, highlighting SK Nexilis’ US$540 million EV copper foil manufacturing facility in Sabah as the company’s largest overseas investment.

He said MIDA supported investors through end-to-end facilitation, including manufacturing licences, tax incentives and expatriate services, while MATRADE connected South Korean companies with Malaysian suppliers through business-matching programmes.

“Together, MIDA Seoul and MATRADE Seoul handhold investors from the initial site selection and regulatory approvals all the way through to commercial operations and supply chain localisation,” he said.

Both officials reaffirmed their commitment to supporting South Korean companies seeking opportunities in Malaysia, noting that MIDA Seoul and MATRADE Seoul were conveniently co-located at the Malaysian Trade and Investment Centre near Jonggak station in central Seoul. That arrangement, they said, gave South Korean businesses a single point of contact for investment- and trade-related inquiries, reflecting Malaysia’s commitment to delivering seamless support throughout every stage of the investment journey.

On sustainability, Redzuan said both countries’ shared commitment to net-zero emissions by 2050 would create significant room for collaboration in renewable energy, hydrogen, carbon capture and storage, solar manufacturing and the circular economy.

Termizi noted that MATRADE launched its Sustainability Action Values for Exporters (SAVE) initiative back in 2019 to help Malaysian exporters strengthen environmental, social and corporate governance practices and remain competitive in global supply chains.

“By combining South Korean technology with Malaysian manufacturing, engineering and market-access capabilities, companies from both countries can jointly develop and commercialise sustainable solutions for Malaysia, Asean and wider global markets,” he said.

Both officials also highlighted the halal economy as an area with particularly strong growth potential.

Redzuan said combining South Korea’s advanced biotechnology and pharmaceutical capabilities with Malaysia’s internationally recognised halal certification system could unlock major opportunities in halal pharmaceuticals, functional foods and cosmetics.

Termizi emphasised that halal had evolved well beyond food: “Another misconception is that halal is only relevant to food,” he said. “In reality, the halal economy now covers cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, healthcare, logistics, tourism and many other sectors, representing one of the world’s fastest-growing consumer markets.”

He encouraged South Korean businesses to leverage Malaysia’s well-established halal ecosystem to expand into Muslim markets across Asean, the Middle East, South Asia and Africa, while also pointing to the MIHAS as a platform for building international partnerships.

This article was first published by The Korea Times

item.title: [SCMP] ‘Surprising’ how quickly China’s military is closing gap with US: analyst Lyle Goldstein
item.description:
Lyle Goldstein is a senior fellow at the Watson Institute for International and Public Affairs at Brown University, and director of Asia engagement at the Washington think tank Defence Priorities.

How do you assess the progress of the People’s Liberation Army’s modernisation drive in the past 10 years and its significance in modern military history? How do you forecast the PLA’s position in 2027, which it set forth as one of three vaguely defined modernisation benchmark years?

My view is that China’s military has made tremendous progress in the process of modernisation over the last 10 years. It’s almost like an aircraft going full throttle or a car that’s going into fourth gear. It really is the pace that has picked up a lot. We had an inkling that this was under way and that major results were going to be forthcoming. But here they are. I have to say, as a military analyst, it’s very impressive. I might even go as far as to say that it could even be unprecedented in its scale and dimensions, and also implications.
item.content:encoded:
Lyle Goldstein is a senior fellow at the Watson Institute for International and Public Affairs at Brown University, and director of Asia engagement at the Washington think tank Defence Priorities.

How do you assess the progress of the People’s Liberation Army’s modernisation drive in the past 10 years and its significance in modern military history? How do you forecast the PLA’s position in 2027, which it set forth as one of three vaguely defined modernisation benchmark years?

My view is that China’s military has made tremendous progress in the process of modernisation over the last 10 years. It’s almost like an aircraft going full throttle or a car that’s going into fourth gear. It really is the pace that has picked up a lot. We had an inkling that this was under way and that major results were going to be forthcoming. But here they are. I have to say, as a military analyst, it’s very impressive. I might even go as far as to say that it could even be unprecedented in its scale and dimensions, and also implications.

If we talk about history, what does it mean in modern military history? This is a very big moment. China has said for a long time it wants to be a world-leading military, a world-class military. Clearly, China is there. The areas where it has achieved that status seem to be increasing every day. In a sense, they have achieved what they’ve set out to do.

I know that a lot of people are very anxious about 2027, what it would mean and so forth. But I don’t think that’s the way to think about it. It goes without saying that, [10 years on] in 2037, China will be much, much stronger. Even so, this is part of a process. There clearly are programmes that are not really mature yet. Most obviously the aircraft carrier programme, but from what I can see, China has indeed a very formidable military.

There are areas where there’s now emerged a big discrepancy between China and other countries, and ultimately that does hurt China because there is fear. You can sense it in the region. There’s quite a palpable anxiety about where the region is going in a world where clearly the United States is playing less of a role and China is playing much more of a role.

If China was more transparent, people would begin to feel less anxious. Although it’s quite reasonable why China has in the past not been so transparent. Chinese military leaders would say, “we’re hiding our weakness” and that transparency is a luxury for the strong. Well, now China is strong, so it pays for China to gradually become more transparent.

Based on its latest modernisation, do you think the PLA is expediting its own pathway for military advancement or is it merely copying the history of other countries’ military development, such as that of the US? What are the major signs that suggest the former or latter?

Unquestionably, there’s been a lot of copying. Obviously, China is very proficient at that, but that is just normal. That’s how militaries improve, by mimicry, by taking the best practices of other militaries. It is an American cultural habit of disdaining the PLA because they say, “they took this, they took that”. And I’ll tell you, a lot of China’s most impressive platforms, the Y-20 military transport aircraft, for example, or the new naval and general utility helicopter Z-20, they look a lot like leading American platforms. No question about it. So, people kind of have a good laugh about that.

But my response is it’s quite plausible that the Chinese platform is actually superior. Just because the exterior looks similar does not mean they’re equivalent. And I do think that they have innovated. And by the way, so many standard Chinese PLA platforms are based off of Russian designs. China doesn’t deny that. They understand that to get ahead, you do whatever you have to do. It has pushed China to the forefront, and it would be foolish to dismiss Chinese development that way.

About five or eight years ago, we started to see some new developments. You could even put it down to the J-20 fifth-generation fighter jets, for example, as a first plunge into a very distinctive Chinese design for a major combat platform. We’re starting to see these things more across the board. It’s pretty clear that China now has the confidence to begin to have distinctive designs, and probably the biggest example is this new set of sixth-generation fighters. They have very different designs, where China begins to be the leader and the other countries are following. That’s a very important historical moment.

When I saw the first headlines about [China’s] September 2025 [military] parade, I remember thinking, “wow, that’s pretty remarkable”. But as I went over the details of what exactly was revealed there – and I thought I’d seen everything in this field – it was a moment of shock, just how many new types of platforms [there were].

I have said for years that it was rather stunning to me that the Chinese navy deploys a supersonic missile aboard its submarines. This was the YJ-18, and it’s pretty shocking. For the last decade, basically, China has had this very impressive anti-ship capability on board its submarines, and the US has no equivalent to that. But now that turns out to be a very dated assessment because now we have this new missile that was unveiled at the parade, the YJ-19, and it has a very distinctive shape, and indeed, Chinese sources confirm it’s a hypersonic missile.

So now China’s submarines are firing hypersonic anti-ship missiles, and the United States is still firing subsonic missiles from its submarines. It suggests that at least in this one realm of undersea warfare, that China is not just ahead but far ahead. That is a new reality. I don’t mean this trend holds for undersea warfare as a whole. Rather, I mean that one narrow domain of submarines firing anti-ship cruise missiles. But that’s an important issue. So, what we’re seeing is something quite momentous.

There has been a lot of talk about the narrowing gap between the US and China in their military capabilities. If the PLA modernisation drive continues, what do you think are the major areas where the PLA may gain an edge over the US?

That is a very tough question, to look into a crystal ball. The good news is the Chinese military has not been tested in combat. The point is that a lot of this is unknown. Now, US weapons have been tested more regularly. But again, that even is not a perfect crystal ball at all because a lot of these wars that the US has been fighting have been against much weaker opponents. So there has been no peer-to-peer engagement, thankfully.

We have seen a very gradual but steady increase in China’s capabilities. I think it started in air defence; we can imagine why Chinese air defence got serious before these other areas. Partly it was the lessons of the Korean war, but it was also that they were able to grasp the Russian technologies pretty quickly and move up several levels.

But what has been surprising now is how quickly they’ve closed the gap. I would even say at this point it’s hard to think of an area where they’re not either closing the gap or pushing ahead. In terms of the navy, sinking ships is pretty important. China seems to take that with utmost seriousness. I’m extremely impressed by this new array of anti-ship cruise missiles that we’ve seen. Basically, China’s done a lot of things in the realm of anti-ship weaponry that suggests that it’s ahead and not just ahead but far ahead.

What do you think are the usual misunderstandings about the PLA in the West? What do you think the US or other regional US allies are overestimating or underestimating about Chinese military capabilities?

I do believe the West engages in a vast tendency towards threat inflation, and I see it literally in almost every media article. You can see that there’s a natural anxiety at a period of major change. This rather pervasive hinting that China has very expansive military goals, whether it’s conquest of the western Pacific or Africa or the Middle East, is not warranted and constitutes analytical malpractice, to my estimate. I hasten to remind people all the time that there’s just no record at all of Chinese military aggression, certainly not in the modern era, and that should give us substantial confidence that we are not confronting some kind of enormous threat.

A lot of people in Washington are fond of saying, “China is much more powerful than the Soviet Union ever was. So we need to not just do what we did in the Cold War, but do two or three times what we did in the Cold War” in terms of gathering up alliances and preparing for war, basically. I think this is very foolish. It is true that China is very powerful and formidable, but I maintain that national security calculations have to take intentions into account, and there is this tendency to try to act like China has very aggressive intentions, which I just don’t see any evidence for.

It’s also interesting and quite dangerous that Westerners tend to underestimate China’s strength, including its military power. One of the things that has to be realised is that China’s industrial strength stands behind its military strength. I tell people, for example, what if the US and Chinese navies go head-to-head and they both experience huge losses, which is quite likely in a naval war, both losing dozens of ships. Tell me which navy can reconstitute faster? The answer is obvious. China has much greater shipbuilding capability, so that could be a huge difference maker.

But overall, people have not come to grips with what it means that China has more than 200 times the shipbuilding capacity of the United States. That is a force multiplier and of great significance. Generally, I would say the US and its allies, in my view, underestimate China’s capabilities and there are many reasons for that. But some of it could be somewhat legitimate in the sense that China’s military in the modern era is untested. We don’t have a single case of China fighting a large-scale naval battle. That is an issue. But I don’t regard that as much of a problem for China’s military.

How successful do you think the civil-military fusion strategy in the Chinese defence industry has been?

China’s military industry is very impressive – it’s both broad and deep. I cannot think of a single area where China has neglected or where we see pockets of weakness at all.

China understands just how crucial this is in conflict. It doesn’t have any illusions about short wars or cost-free wars or wars that don’t impact the homeland. China is well aware that wars are bloody and costly, and the homeland is badly affected and that it often comes down to who is willing to pay the heavier price and who can outproduce the opponent.

As for the civil-military fusion, part of this is just in the DNA of the PLA – the “people’s war” doctrine – looking for that kind of deep integration between society and the military, and that seems to make sense intuitively to many Chinese.

In some respects, however, they’re also reading off the US script, and they’ve studied our military-industrial complex very thoroughly. They know where much of the innovation happens in the US military: it’s places like Caltech and MIT. The Chinese know that very well, and so you can see a real determination to have their leading universities, their leading research centres and their leading companies tied in with the military.

The number of engineers in related fields that are produced, like naval architects, for example, is astounding. If you put China versus the West or China versus the United States, it’s not even close. That’s a very important asymmetry that has served China’s military very well.

The lack of combat experience is a much-talked-about weakness of the PLA. How important is it in your mind?

It does have some importance. Looking on the naval side, it is very striking that in the modern era, China has not fought any major naval battles. It’s not only the practical issues related to that in terms of training, institutional learning and culture, but also there’s a bit of a self-confidence issue, which is natural.

But I do in general think people make too much of this issue. If you want to say that the US military is more combat experienced, well, in what respect? The United States has been fighting wars, say, in Afghanistan or against the Houthis in the Red Sea or in Iraq. I would argue that yes, that is a kind of combat experience, but is it really? Are you learning the right lessons from this combat experience? The Houthis, for example, have almost no air defence. So, what are your pilots actually learning from that experience? All the wrong lessons, it turns out.

Indeed, we’re seeing in the current war with Iran that one reason why US bases have been hit rather severely and US operations have been quite badly disrupted by Iranian missile strikes is that we’re not used to fighting against a country that can deliver some major blows.

I just don’t think the United States has faced a peer military in combat since 1945, and I can’t underline that strongly enough. So, therefore, I don’t think that China is at a major disadvantage due to lacking combat experience.

Unprecedented numbers of top PLA generals have been sacked in the country’s anti-corruption drive over the last few years. How big do you think the impact is on the PLA’s combat readiness in the short term and in the long run?

Here as usual, I’m departing from conventional wisdom. I don’t see any major impact. It may be the opposite. It’s just common sense that you want a military run by younger folks. And having a military run by people in their 40s and 50s is going to be much better for a lot of obvious reasons than by a bunch of elderly gentlemen. Is there corruption in the PLA? Absolutely, but there’s corruption in every military, and therefore, I do not think the PLA is any kind of outlier here.

Every PLA expert has their theory about what is actually going on. My leading candidate theory is that militaries in an authoritarian system like China’s have a big role in succession. So, the most obvious explanation would be that this is related to the succession, and that probably Chinese President Xi Jinping wants to choose the next leader of China and doesn’t want very senior generals “playing in the sandbox”, so to speak.

Another theory I have though – and this is one that keeps me up at night as I hope this is not true – we cannot rule out the idea that there is a real possibility of a Taiwan contingency and that Xi and the people around him are very systematically picking the people that they want – new faces with fresh ideas and fighting spirit, people whose heart is in this and who are ready to command.

I hope that’s not true. I hope I’m wrong here, but we have to consider that as a possibility that the PLA is being radically restructured for war. Unfortunately, that might be true. I hope it’s not.

In the first half of 2026, the number of PLA fighter jet sorties near Taiwan was at its lowest since 2022, when then US House speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taiwan. What do you think this signals about Beijing’s intentions about Taiwan?

Well, if my last answer sounded somewhat pessimistic, I’m generally pretty optimistic about the situation. I think there is a peaceful solution here, and it’s pretty obvious what needs to happen in terms of cross-strait relations and pacifying the situation. It takes goodwill on both sides, which we’re beginning to see.

I’m rather hopeful that both sides will step back from the brink. Both sides will realise that if they accommodate a little bit, there is a solution space here because this war just would be so devastating for everyone. So, I do think common sense will prevail.

The Donald Trump administration has ushered in a more realistic policy in the Asia-Pacific. The summit [with Xi in May], I think, was very good. Both sides are looking for off-ramps. I’m reasonably optimistic that all sides of this equation here – Washington, Beijing and Taipei – all understand this.

China recently conducted a missile test from a nuclear-powered submarine for the first time. What does it say about the readiness of the PLA’s nuclear force and Beijing’s strategic intentions? What is the message of Beijing’s call to speed up building its nuclear arsenal?

That’s a big issue. First of all, the launch that we just saw was quite momentous because it shows China’s rising confidence. The naval part of the triad was previously seen as a much weaker part. So, this demonstrates the filling out of the PLA nuclear triad.

But speaking specifically to China’s submarine-based nuclear missiles, this was a big step because we had seen reports that China likely could now fire these missiles from locations near China. So that’s a very different situation. Five or 10 years ago, Chinese submarines would need to sortie out into the mid-Pacific, or at least into the Philippine Sea and beyond, to get into firing position. But now that doesn’t seem to be the case, and that does change the equation.

The truth is China’s nuclear deterrent is very formidable, and I don’t doubt that in a nuclear exchange China could destroy the United States. Of course, China would also be destroyed. So, I think we are firmly in a condition of mutually assured destruction. While many Americans are wringing their hands about this, I think this is good because both sides will be more cautious. It means that we are coming into a situation of greater balance. That balance implies greater stability in the future.

However, I will say I found the first evidence that I’ve seen of Chinese commentators connecting the nuclear build-up directly to the Taiwan issue, and that is a little bit troubling. Of course, there’s a hypothesis that this could make a Taiwan scenario more likely, and that’s concerning.

Unfortunately, the way I understand nuclear strategy, a lot of it comes down to what we call not just the balance of power but the balance of fervour. In other words, which side cares more? Which side is more willing to take risks and take losses? And unfortunately, in this case, it’s absolutely clear to me that China would win the balance of fervour and would have more credibility to take risks in that scenario. So, it’s just another reason why the United States and China should be extremely cautious and even wary of a Taiwan scenario.

How do you forecast the PLA’s future development after 2027? What role does the PLA have in global geopolitics in the future? Will it have its own sphere of influence?

I’m quite optimistic. I’m very impressed that China has built up its strong military without resorting to the use of major force. It is remarkable that China has not used force on a large scale since 1979. That’s an extremely impressive level of restraint – very admirable. I wish I could say that about my country. Can a great power exercise that kind of restraint? We have a saying in the United States: “If you have a really nice hammer, then everything starts to look like a nail.” So, in other words, if you have very large, robust powerful armed forces, which are almost unmatched, maybe you are tempted to deploy them to solve every problem.

I do think, unfortunately, the United States has fallen into that trap. Arguably, we’ve been in this trap for a very long time. Now I do think China has learned some lessons from that experience and is determined not to become the USSR or the United States. And of course, they say this again and again: “we do not seek hegemony”. China also says they don’t seek a sphere of influence.

I actually think China does have a sphere of influence, but here they are using slightly different terminology. What I think it means for Chinese leaders is that it just simply implies China has a set of core interests logically along its periphery. China will expect that its voice is heard very clearly and will have a veto on what goes on there. But I don’t think China is seeking a sphere of influence to control everything that goes on in Vietnam or Cambodia. That’s not China’s aim. Nevertheless, China will quite reasonably insist that it not be threatened from its peripheral areas.

So that is what we’re seeing in the region, and that is a hard transition to that new era of geopolitics, where China is very strong, and China is going to demand that its core interests are respected. There is a possibility that as a country gets more powerful, its core interests grow and expand. That will be the difficult challenge for Beijing, to resist the temptation or trap, wherein its leaders become that “hammer looking for a nail”.

item.title: [SCMP] The mystery of one man’s fortress in Longgang
item.description:
On the northeastern fringes of Shenzhen, standing among the low-rise tile houses of Longgang district, is a monolith that refuses to explain itself.

Erected during the late 1970s and 80s, the seven-storey building towers over the market town, a monument to something known only to its long-gone creator. Vegetation grows wild on the roof. Iron fencing and rusty cages crown its top. At night, it stands unlit; by day, its bare concrete facade looms over the narrow surrounding streets with the air of a wartime watchtower, attracting young explorers who ride Shenzhen’s Metro Line 3 to Shuanglong station, crossing the city just to see “Longgang’s Weird Building” for themselves.

A glance at the near-windowless exterior provides only hints of the man behind the Weird Building: Wen Yaoguang, a Longgang native who appears to have made his fortune in Hong Kong.
item.content:encoded:
On the northeastern fringes of Shenzhen, standing among the low-rise tile houses of Longgang district, is a monolith that refuses to explain itself.

Erected during the late 1970s and 80s, the seven-storey building towers over the market town, a monument to something known only to its long-gone creator. Vegetation grows wild on the roof. Iron fencing and rusty cages crown its top. At night, it stands unlit; by day, its bare concrete facade looms over the narrow surrounding streets with the air of a wartime watchtower, attracting young explorers who ride Shenzhen’s Metro Line 3 to Shuanglong station, crossing the city just to see “Longgang’s Weird Building” for themselves.

A glance at the near-windowless exterior provides only hints of the man behind the Weird Building: Wen Yaoguang, a Longgang native who appears to have made his fortune in Hong Kong.

What is known of Wen’s life has been pieced together through oral accounts from neighbours, local lore passed between households and recounted to inquisitive visitors. As filmmaker Zhang Shengjia discovered while conducting research for his 2025 documentary, The Haunted Folk Fortress, Wen was, seemingly, an ordinary man driven by an extraordinary vision.

It is thought that Wen was born in Longgang and, sometime before World War II, crossed into Hong Kong, where he found work as a seafarer and later took over some farmland. He lived in Hong Kong through the Japanese occupation (1941-1945). During the city’s economic boom in the 60s, he is said to have received a sizeable land-requisition payout. After 1978, when mainland China began to open up under Deng Xiaoping, Wen returned to Longgang with his fortune and began to build.

Although it has never formally been opened to the public, the curious have found their way inside the Weird Building over the years. Their online accounts and footage – available through a virtual-reality tour – offer further understanding of its interior.

Longgang’s Weird Building is remarkably compact, with a footprint of roughly 36 square metres. Pass through the front entrance grilles and you are met with steep stairways leading both down to a dark, now-flooded basement and up to a small living area and kitchen.

Wen devised alternating-tread stairs as a space-saving solution; left and right feet land on separate, staggered steps, halving the width of each staircase. Throughout the property, staircases are adapted to their particular location; some veer off at unlikely angles, while others do not resemble conventional staircases at all.

Despite the building appearing to have few windows, much of the interior is well-lit and the upper floors offer panoramic views. What looks from the outside like solid concrete is, on one facade, in fact sheets of stainless steel punched with holes measuring roughly 5mm across.

Cast-in-place concrete furnishings are embedded into the structure of the third floor and most of the fourth floor is given over to bathtubs and water tanks, the purpose of which is unknown.

There may be as many as 20 bathtubs and eight toilets in the building, estimates Feng Guochan, executive chief architect at the Shenzhen General Institute of Architectural Design and Research, who had been allowed access by the local government to survey the building. Precise counts are difficult given the non-linear floor plans, says Feng.

The rooftop terrace, with its pavilion, is believed to have once served as a garden.

Rather than bricks or prefabricated blocks, Wen chose to pour everything – walls, floors, curved concrete benches arranged around tables – in situ.

“Choosing this approach is quite a challenge,” says Feng. Cast-in-place concrete requires a lot of formwork and carries the risk of blowouts, where wet material bursts through moulds. “And it’s very slow.”

That may explain why the building took more than a decade to complete but the permanence of concrete is perhaps the point, as the furniture is the building, fused with the structure. “When primitive people lived inside caves, they organised their lives according to the contours of the cave,” says Feng. “Instead of this being imposed by nature, [here] it occurs through one’s own thinking.”

In many ways, Longgang’s Weird Building echoes the qualities of Chinese vernacular defensive architecture, examples of which include the Kaiping diaolou of Guangdong province (fortress-like residences bearing elements of Western architectural traditions built by Chinese who returned from overseas in the 20s and 30s) and the Hakka paolou (fortified watchtowers erected on the peripheries of walled villages in Shenzhen).

Structures built by returnees “often reflect what the owner experienced abroad”, Zhang tells me. “As [this] owner was once a seafarer, the interior of the Weird Building not only reflects this experience at sea – with cabin-like spatial layouts – but continues the functional traditions of diaolou. It has massive water tanks, plots for raising chickens and growing vegetables – all built for self-sufficiency in a crisis.”

While the rest of China was opening up, Wen seemed to want to seal himself off, “like he was preparing for the end of the world”, says Feng.

In Zhang’s documentary, one local resident recalls Wen sitting under a banyan tree on a street corner, contemplating how his building could be modified: “I believe he is much like those of us who enjoy creative work – he is an artist and architect, and he possessed enough passion to persevere with the construction.”

Wen was probably also inspired by feng shui, says Zhang: “It’s rumoured that a feng shui master advised him to keep building to ward off bad luck, and there was definitely some consideration to feng shui principles indoors, too.”

Whatever the inspiration, the idiosyncratic construction has spatial complexity. Floors of differing heights flow into one another and bring to mind Austrian architect Adolf Loos’ Raumplan concept, which conceives of a building as an intertwined three-dimensional puzzle.

Feng describes the structure as resembling a Chinese puzzle lock – each space interlacing with the next, with no continuous floors. It is unlikely that Wen encountered Loos’ work, but the parallels are striking.

“I suspect he never used a floor plan to build this house, because it’s impossible to draw one,” says Feng.

As with Raumplan designs, Wen’s bland facade conceals lavish interiors. The upper floors are adorned with ceramic-tile paintings of Guilin scenery, portraits of women, scenes from traditional Chinese opera and aluminium panelling bearing images copied from the Louvre museum in Paris, France. Wen decorated an entire room with tiles inscribed with moral teachings rendered in calligraphy that were bought in Qingyuan, Guangdong. “In the traditional framework of the diaolou, Wen built a rather hedonistic interior, and you can see that from the design and the structure of the space, centred entirely around his life,” says Gu Ling, a curator who hosted a screening and panel discussion of Zhang’s documentary in February. “There were a lot of these so-called artwork or decorative pieces, and they were all rather valuable.”

Wen had his own way of doing things, adds Feng. “This person is simply someone who’s broken away from the ordinary, who’s always courageously pursuing his own self.”

Feng believes that the Weird Building was possible only because of the times in which it was constructed: after reform and opening up had begun but before a series of regulations introduced between 1982 and the 1990s placed restrictions on urban land ownership and construction.

“It’s a self-built home from a unique era, and the fact that it’s a self-built home within an urban setting makes it such a rare specimen,” he says. “There will never be another Weird Building. You need the right conditions for it to emerge, and currently, those conditions don’t exist.”

The fascination with Longgang’s Weird Building is part of a broader impulse among young Chinese, particularly in the Greater Bay Area, to seek out and document local history before it is swallowed by development and forgotten.

As people who have known eccentrics such as Wen, Zhang Suying, who built a castle out of scavenged material in Longnan city, Gansu province, and Yang San-er, who took 18 years to build a unique timber-framed house in Pingtung, Taiwan, grow elderly, oral histories are becoming increasingly hard to find. The Haunted Folk Fortress is Zhang’s attempt to decrypt Wen’s story before it is lost to time, but his quest has been challenging and his attempts to track down archival footage have proved largely futile: Hong Kong’s ATV filmed the Weird Building but the broadcaster went bankrupt and it’s not clear how its archive can be accessed; TVB also covered it but declined to share the material. Nothing of Wen’s life in the city surfaced in Hong Kong’s public records, either.

It is thought that Wen died around 2000 and, at some point after his death, his family sold the building to a developer that subdivided it into rental units. Online, Zhang found dozens of mentions by people who claim to have lived in the Weird Building or met the owner – but none responded to his requests for an interview.

One key interviewee among the local residents who would talk to Zhang was the father of his cinematographer, who used to haul sand and cement to what was then just a construction site and spoke at length about the man behind the architectural anomaly: “People all said the same thing – that he was strange. Before reform and opening up, there weren’t even buildings taller than three floors. So when he built that big house, everyone thought, ‘Wow, this guy must be really rich to build something like that.’”

Other interviewees speak of construction methods and materials, including green ceramic tiles that were imported from Hong Kong. Their recollections form the backbone of the film, the final version of which remains a work in progress.

It is pure luck that Wen’s structural legacy still stands. In 2013, when local authorities gazetted a nearby Hakka walled village as intangible cultural heritage, the Weird Building happened to fall within its radius of protection.

“Without it, the Weird Building would be gone,” says Gu.

However, “a certain level of conservation is required, since the building has a unique character; the government hopes to develop the entire area, including the Weird Building, and carry out restoration work”. Unfortunately, those plans have been put on hold due to a lack of funds amid a downturn in the mainland property market.

For Feng, who has studied the building for more than a decade, what endures is something more personal than architectural history: “I see a freedom in this old man that I kind of envy. He pursued his own spiritual world, and sensitively expressed his desires.

“People should be able to express themselves through their space.”

item.title: [SCMP] China waits in wings as Mecca pact signals Gulf shift away from US security umbrella
item.description:
The grand security bargain between the United States and Gulf countries is widely perceived to be fraying, creating what analysts see as an opening for Beijing to expand its presence in the region.

For decades, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states relied on Washington’s defensive shield, while it in turn relied on them for access, energy and influence.

Riyadh’s decision to sign a mutual defence agreement with Turkey and Pakistan is the clearest sign yet of that shift.
item.content:encoded:
The grand security bargain between the United States and Gulf countries is widely perceived to be fraying, creating what analysts see as an opening for Beijing to expand its presence in the region.

For decades, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states relied on Washington’s defensive shield, while it in turn relied on them for access, energy and influence.

Riyadh’s decision to sign a mutual defence agreement with Turkey and Pakistan is the clearest sign yet of that shift.

Signed this week in Mecca, the pact declares that an armed attack on one will be treated as an attack on all three, in an echo of Nato’s Article 5.

But the significance of the Mecca pact goes beyond a new regional security arrangement. Three middle powers – a Gulf energy giant, a Nato member and nuclear-armed South Asian state – are taking steps to reduce their reliance on US-dominated security architecture and build their own collective defence framework.

Such independent alliances among middle powers have been rare since the early Cold War, making the pact a potential model for other countries.

It could also complicate matters for countries such as India and prompt them to reassess their own security partnerships.

“For Riyadh, this agreement bolsters the country’s leverage as it both copes with an emboldened Iran and confronts the limits of US deterrence in the region,” Allison Minor from the Atlantic Council think tank wrote in a recent analysis.

She described the pact as “further evidence that Riyadh is abandoning its quest for an Article 5-like security guarantee from Washington.”

Rich Outzen, a former military and civilian adviser at the US State Department who is now with the Atlantic Council, argued that the agreement marked “an inflection point in the emerging multipolar order in the Middle East and South Asia.”

The pact also brings together countries with very different strategic relationships with China.

John Spencer from the Madison Policy Forum, a New York think tank, said Pakistan was “dependent on China with a military heavily equipped by Beijing”.

Highlighting Pakistan’s fragile economy and reliance on international bailouts, he added: “This is the last country a Nato member should be entering into an Article 5-style mutual defence commitment with.”

For China, however, the new arrangement could create an opening.

As Imran Khurshid from the US-based Middle East Forum wrote in an analysis published last month: “China is using Pakistan for weapons promotion as a gateway to enter the region’s defence landscape.

“Moreover, if the potential ‘Islamic Nato’ that many of these countries, including Pakistan and Turkey, discuss takes shape, China might believe it has an augmented market.”

Khurshid added that China had “aggressively advertised its weapon platforms and builds narratives around its defence systems in the region”, including claims about the success of the JF-17 fighter jet and other Chinese weapons during last year’s India-Pakistan conflict.

That military relationship could become more significant as Saudi Arabia deepens its ties with Pakistan.

According to data from the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, more than 80 per cent of Pakistan’s arms imports between 2021 and 2024 came from China.

Under the Saudi-Pakistan mutual defence pact signed last year, Pakistan sent JF-17 fighter jets and other Chinese-made systems to Saudi Arabia, giving them greater visibility and operational experience.

Khurshid said such deals created lasting partnerships because they “typically involve long-term commitments related to maintenance, spare parts, training and logistical support,” embedding Chinese systems more deeply into the recipient’s military structure.

Ali Chishti, from the New Pakistan Foundation, an Islamabad-based think tank, wrote recently that China was “ecstatic” about the Mecca pact and pointed to Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan’s recent visit to Beijing as evidence of Riyadh “deepening ties beyond the West”.

However, Michael Kugelman of the Atlantic Council, pointed out that the three signatories “have gone to great lengths not to cast this as a Nato-style alliance”, adding that it suggested they would want to “avoid the optics of enthusiastically pooling their resources to purchase Chinese arms”.

“Such transactions would therefore be done quietly and also not at great volume ... Turkey may be able to provide to Pakistan and Saudi Arabia what China could, and at a better price,” he said.

The combination of China’s close relationship with Pakistan and its broader strategic ambitions in the Middle East could therefore give Beijing an indirect route into the Gulf’s defence architecture.

The three-way pact also complicates India’s strategic calculus. New Delhi has moved closer to Washington in recent years, but ties have soured sharply during Donald Trump’s second term.

Meanwhile, the US has moved closer to Pakistan, which is trying to help mediate a deal to end the war with Iran.

Any future Indian military conflict with Pakistan could be framed by Islamabad as an attack that triggers the pact’s collective defence clause – a possibility that may push India and Israel closer together.

India’s former foreign secretary Kanwal Sibal described the situation as “on the face of it, a very negative development for Indian interests”.

The country needed to “explore more options with the United Arab Emirates, Israel, Greece and Cyprus. And Afghanistan”, he added. “We should consult Iran. All this is a fallout from the disastrous US aggression against Iran.”

The Mecca pact followed by months of Iranian missile and drone strikes on Gulf energy infrastructure and sustained Houthi attacks.

Despite the extensive US military presence in the region, American forces were unable to intercept every attack.

The US-Israel war against Iran has also led to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a vital route for oil and gas supplies, further reinforcing concerns in Gulf capitals about relying exclusively on Washington for security.

Those concerns have been compounded by reports the war has used up significant stocks of key US weapons.

Around 65 per cent of Patriot air defence interceptors and a substantial share of Terminal High Altitude Area Defence interceptors have reportedly been used up, according to multiple reports citing senior officials, as well as assessments by the Centre for Strategic and International Studies.

Stocks of long-range precision weapons have also been heavily depleted, including virtually all available ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles, while Tomahawk cruise missile inventories have fallen by nearly half.

Restocking will take years, partly because of global supply chain constraints, and the Pentagon has already been forced to delay weapons deliveries to allies and partners.

For Gulf states, the lesson may be less about abandoning the US than about reducing their dependence on it.

Rebeccah Heinrichs of the Hudson Institute pointed to the close ties between Islamabad and Beijing, saying: “It is not in US interests for the Pakistanis to be aligning closer with Saudi and Turkey and our approach towards Iran should keep that in mind.”

But Kugelman said that the new pact, with its “emphasis on burden sharing and implied objective of deterring Iran, should go down well in Trump’s Washington”.

item.title: [SCMP] Can Europe stay united in China trade battle? Ceuta migrant crisis offers a warning
item.description:
The European Union’s traditional August break was supposed to provide officials with some respite ahead of a potentially bruising autumn when it will try to set its fiery trade relationship with China on a new course.

Instead, a border crisis on its southern flank has created turmoil and division among its 27 members, raising questions over how prepared the bloc is for a dust-up with one of the world’s economic superpowers.

“We had a real-time test of what happens when one member state was under coercion,” said Alberto Rizzi, a Rome-based policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, specialising in geoeconomics. “Everybody was very quick to jump on that.”
item.content:encoded:
The European Union’s traditional August break was supposed to provide officials with some respite ahead of a potentially bruising autumn when it will try to set its fiery trade relationship with China on a new course.

Instead, a border crisis on its southern flank has created turmoil and division among its 27 members, raising questions over how prepared the bloc is for a dust-up with one of the world’s economic superpowers.

“We had a real-time test of what happens when one member state was under coercion,” said Alberto Rizzi, a Rome-based policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, specialising in geoeconomics. “Everybody was very quick to jump on that.”

The crisis was sparked on July 30, when an estimated 72,000 mainly Moroccan migrants surged into Ceuta, a Spanish enclave in North Africa, after Moroccan border controls appeared to collapse. At least 75 people died, mostly at sea, with the Spanish authorities estimating more than 100 died.

The surge raised suspicions that the Moroccan authorities had weaponised migrant flows in response to Spanish efforts to improve ties with its neighbour and rival Algeria.

In the immediate aftermath, however, many EU members placed the blame squarely on Madrid, whose openness to welcoming migrants is an outlier in a Europe that is becoming increasingly hawkish on the issue.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni said Spain’s “uncontrolled immigration” policy was a security threat and suspended the Schengen freedom of movement agreement with Madrid, even though Ceuta is not part of the Schengen area.

Finland and Denmark fell in behind Meloni, while Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis called for Spain to be suspended from the Schengen agreement.

A day later, they were among the 22 EU members signing a letter to the European Commission expressing concern over the Ceuta crisis.

While member states later toned down their criticisms of Madrid, the dispute flared up again over the weekend – ensuring the EU’s dirty laundry remained on full public display for a third week – after Spain imposed its own border checks on air and sea travel from Italy.

The episode may seem far removed from the EU’s trade tensions with China, but the question of solidarity will underpin Brussels’ ability to confront Beijing this autumn – particularly once China starts retaliating.

After national leaders discussed how to move forward under the weight of a China shock to European industry in June, Commission President Ursula von der Leyen praised their “clear support for a European response based on unity among member states”.

The Ceuta crisis, however, is a reminder of how easily the capitals can be divided when one comes under attack.

“The reaction was not as united as we would expect from a union of states that aims to become a geoeconomic actor,” Rizzi said. “China doesn’t have to win 27 of them over to weaken the negotiating position.”

A central figure in the Ceuta crisis, Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez is also likely to be a major player in any contest with China.

One of Europe’s few remaining socialist leaders, his open-border policies, embrace of renewable energy, and willingness to stand up to US President Donald Trump have made him a poster boy for the global left.

He also stands out for his embrace of Beijing, making an annual visit to China for the last four years. He is also seeking Chinese investment in Spain’s electric vehicle supply chain and was the sole dissenting voice last October, when national leaders called for a tougher EU policy towards China.

“Sanchez was already the outlier arguing China should be seen as a partner, with repeated visits to Beijing, while France pushes ‘European preference’ and Germany remains the pivotal swing state,” said Sari Arho Havren, a China specialist at the Royal United Services Institute.

This, in turn, made it less likely that Sanchez would quietly fall in behind the Brussels-led push for a tougher China policy, she said.

He already has some history in such matters.

In 2024, the Spanish government flipped its vote in favour of EU tariffs on Chinese-made electric vehicles to an abstention, reportedly after Beijing warned investments could stall and threatened tariffs on the country’s pork exports.

“Madrid has just learned that European solidarity is conditional and retrospective. The rational lesson for a government that expects retaliation from China against its exposed sectors in any trade confrontation is to hedge bilaterally,” Arho Havren said.

The Ceuta episode was, she added, “a stress test” for the expected collision with Beijing, which would “depend on whether member states were ready to absorb costs for each other”.

“The answer we received was certainly discouraging,” she said. “When costs land asymmetrically, the majority’s instinct is to declare the exposed state the author of its own misfortune.”

Commission trade officials are trying to convince nervous capitals not to let the fear of consequences block EU-wide action, and they are already working on a “solidarity mechanism” that would compensate any companies targeted in a tit-for-tat trade war.

China has previously shown its willingness to respond asymmetrically to EU gambits.

When Brussels launched an investigation into EV subsidies in 2023, Beijing went after EU pork, brandy and dairy products, while state media carried copious threats of investigations into the aircraft and automotive sectors.

Frenzied lobbying from threatened industries led Germany to vote against the EV duties, but it failed to convince others to join it.

With the commission preparing new instruments and broader trade investigations to deal with what it sees as unfair trade policies, Beijing has once again vowed to respond in kind.

Matters may come to a head in October, when the two sides’ trade chiefs are due to meet and EU national leaders will meet to thrash out a plan.

Analysts believe the member states are more aligned on the need to act – but the Ceuta crisis has diluted belief that they can follow through.

“Being a geopolitical actor means being able to speak and to present yourself as one, and making it understood from the outside that if you attack any one of us, it’s an attack against all of us. If you coerce one of us, we’re going to respond with an entire EU marketwide response,” said Rizzi.

Cracks have appeared with increasing frequency of late, however, as national interest runs up against abstract notions of pan-European solidarity.

For example, when the EU lined up retaliatory tariffs against Trump’s “Liberation Day” duties last year, France – the most vocal supporter of EU strategic autonomy – quickly lobbied for alcohol to be removed to protect its wine and brandy makers.

Beijing’s promised retaliation will examine again whether Europe is willing to pay the price of unity – but the Ceuta affair provides an uncomfortable preview.

“The lack of solidarity towards a member under hybrid attack does not bode well as the EU stands on the brink of a trade war with Beijing,” said Arho Havren.

item.title: [SCMP] How China’s ‘magic’ rice seeds are transforming the fortunes of Nigerian farmers
item.description:
Just outside the Nigerian capital Abuja, where Green Agriculture West Africa Limited (Gawal) is based, locals do not refer to the company by name, instead as the place where the Chinese supply “magic” rice seeds.

Ahmed Yusuf, 42, credits the seeds with turning around his rice business for good. Before Gawal, Yusuf’s yields averaged just 2 tonnes per hectare, putting him on the verge of forsaking farming after more than a decade of toiling.

“Each year I was making losses, and I couldn’t meet the needs of my family, so I thought, ‘what was the point?’” he recalled.
item.content:encoded:
Just outside the Nigerian capital Abuja, where Green Agriculture West Africa Limited (Gawal) is based, locals do not refer to the company by name, instead as the place where the Chinese supply “magic” rice seeds.

Ahmed Yusuf, 42, credits the seeds with turning around his rice business for good. Before Gawal, Yusuf’s yields averaged just 2 tonnes per hectare, putting him on the verge of forsaking farming after more than a decade of toiling.

“Each year I was making losses, and I couldn’t meet the needs of my family, so I thought, ‘what was the point?’” he recalled.

Yusuf’s fortunes changed after he was introduced to Gawal’s R1 rice strain.

“With this new variety I have been able to stay in business by increasing my yield more than threefold on basically the same effort,” he said.

Yusuf’s success is part of a broader China-backed push to transform African subsistence farming into a highly productive mechanised powerhouse. But this agricultural diplomacy is about more than food security.

Beijing’s hands-off, state-backed approach is directly challenging traditional Western aid models, prompting Washington to counter with its own multimillion-dollar agribusiness interventions to maintain influence on the continent.

Gawal is among a growing number of Chinese companies finding business opportunities in African agriculture, which smallholder farmers dominate.

According to officials, the companies are deploying new techniques, using demonstration farms to accelerate local adoption and help build value chains linking the farms to markets.

Gawal is a joint venture between Yuan Longping High-Tech Agriculture, which is headquartered in Changsha in China’s central Hunan province, and state-owned Beijing-based CGCOC Group.

Founded in 2006, Gawal has spearheaded China’s agricultural diplomacy in Africa, producing new seeds and offering machinery, field expertise and processing capacity.

Its 2,000-hectare (4,900-acre) demonstration farm in Nigeria’s northwestern Kebbi state provides seeds and training to more than 5,000 smallholder rice farmers who also have access to modern technologies under a programme linked to the Nigerian government.

“Seeing is believing,” said Godfrey Ngwoke, an agricultural development programme manager with Nigeria’s agriculture ministry, of the demonstration farm.

“These demonstrations showcase the superiority of new crop varieties and techniques, helping farmers make informed decisions.”

Gawal’s R1 rice variety is among its most popular products. Introduced in 2017 for its resistance to disease and ability to grow on diverse terrain, it yields between 7.5 and 8 tonnes per hectare and became popular with local farmers like Yusuf.

Other varieties, such as Faro 69 and Faro 70, have even greater yield capabilities that range from 11 to 13 tonnes per hectare. Their widespread acceptance has helped boost Nigeria’s rice output by as much as 2 million tonnes a year, according to the company.

Nigeria now consumes an estimated 10.5 million tonnes of rice every year while producing about 7 million tonnes, according to data from the central bank.

Xu Guoxin is part of a team comprising six Chinese and two Nigerians who developed Gawal’s R1.

Holding a bachelor’s degree in agriculture and postgraduate specialisation in crop genetics and breeding, Xu came to Nigeria in 2014, encouraged by the country’s sizeable arable land and large population.

“My professional work focuses on crop variety development, seed systems, agricultural technology promotion and international agricultural cooperation,” Xu said.

“I chose to work in Nigeria because agriculture here has huge development potential and significant opportunities for impact.”

Despite Nigeria’s considerable natural resources and strong workforce, there is still a significant “need for improved technologies, quality seeds and modern farming systems”, Xu added.

This is where Gawal is asserting its presence. Aside from rice, the company supplies improved varieties of maize, millet, peanuts, sorghum and other local staples.

The project falls under a Beijing-backed programme touting “China aid for a shared future” for Africa, emphasising the benefits of shared development.

Xu said Nigeria was chosen for its “leading role in West Africa” and for being “an important hub for regional agricultural cooperation and food security initiatives”.

Beyond Nigeria, CGCOC Group is involved in agricultural cooperation initiatives in Burkina Faso, Ethiopia, Guinea and Zimbabwe.

In addition, China is currently engaged in major agricultural projects in more than a dozen countries across Africa, including what it describes as “friendship farms” in Mozambique and Tanzania.

According to rice farmer Chieke Agu, who gets his seeds from Gawal: “It is packaged as aid, but it is also showing us the Chinese way and encouraging us to use their agricultural technology.”

“We can say that Western aid does the same thing.”

The company’s demonstration farm in Abuja boasts hundreds of newly imported tractor engines for supply to Nigerian farmers and serves as a showroom for Chinese equipment and technology.

Still, Xu cited winning the support and trust of the government and local communities as Gawal’s major achievement.

“Government agencies appreciate the company’s contributions to seed development, agricultural technology transfer and farmer capacity building,” he said.

“Farmers have also responded positively because improved seeds and better cultivation practices have helped increase yields and incomes.”

In support of Chinese efforts, the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), a United Nations agency, started a programme in March to accelerate the mechanisation of African agriculture through the exchange of information in collaboration with the UN Office for South-South Cooperation in China.

The objective was to create a platform to exchange information on best practices in agricultural mechanisation among researchers, entrepreneurs, government officials and farmers from Africa and Asia, as well as other regions.

“Agriculture mechanisation is an essential pillar in the African transformation agenda,” said Meshack Malo, the FAO’s deputy regional director for Africa. “Scalable mechanisation is not an option but urgent.”

To counter China’s perceived influence in Africa’s agribusiness, the US has weighed in with its own interventions.

While Beijing favours big agricultural projects, Washington has focused on private-sector support, mostly aimed at mitigating risk and improving access to finance.

For instance, the US Department of Agriculture provides commercial credit guarantees under its GSM 102 programme to back exports of American agricultural products and the Facility Guarantee Programme for related equipment.

It also provides inputs such as special seeds and fertiliser to support crops such as maize, rice, cowpea and wheat.

China’s agricultural objectives in Africa, as articulated by its Ministry of Foreign Affairs, are to support the African Union’s Agenda 2063.

The main goal is to achieve continental food security by transforming subsistence farming into highly productive mechanised agriculture.

Nigeria appeared to endorse this approach when it announced a US$900 million deal with China in March to establish six giant poultry farms across the country.

Located on farms measuring 7,000 to 10,000 hectares, each will have the capacity to produce a million eggs daily. They will also be supported by feed mills and power stations, as well as feature maize and soybean farms to generate the feed.

Beijing’s decision to implement a zero-tariff regime for African exports means that a significant amount of product surpluses will have the opportunity to be exported to China, given its position as a major destination of African agricultural exports, according to a study led by Zhao Wenjie of China Agricultural University in Beijing.

Published in the peer-reviewed journal Sustainability in March, the study said the contrasting approaches adopted by Western countries and China had influenced project outcomes.

Western aid often comes with exacting conditions involving human rights, good governance and environmental protection.

“While these standards are important, they can sometimes be perceived as intrusive or paternalistic by African nations,” wrote Zhao and his colleagues.

“In contrast, China’s non-conditional approach provides a sense of relief to these countries, allowing for more flexible and pragmatic cooperation agreements.”

item.title: [SCMP] Chinese vloggers are taking to YouTube to ‘set the record straight’
item.description:
At a night market in Shenzhen, Sasa Xu finishes her day with passion fruit tea.

It costs US$2.40, bringing her total spend for the day to US$9.40 – details that close out her video “What low-income life in China really looks like”.

The video has drawn more than 470,000 views since it was posted to YouTube in April. It includes footage of Xu at a traditional wet market and walking through a densely populated “urban village” where many of the city’s low-income workers live.
item.content:encoded:
At a night market in Shenzhen, Sasa Xu finishes her day with passion fruit tea.

It costs US$2.40, bringing her total spend for the day to US$9.40 – details that close out her video “What low-income life in China really looks like”.

The video has drawn more than 470,000 views since it was posted to YouTube in April. It includes footage of Xu at a traditional wet market and walking through a densely populated “urban village” where many of the city’s low-income workers live.

“Through these simple, everyday records, I hope to show overseas audiences the vibrant and multi-dimensional lives of ordinary Chinese people,” Xu said in an interview.

Xu, 30, is an overseas influencer partnerships manager based in the southern tech hub.

She is also one of thousands of ordinary Chinese documenting their lives on YouTube for an overseas audience in a powerful shift in digital storytelling.

From vast cities like Shanghai and Shenzhen to small towns and rural villages, these unfiltered vlogs offer insights not seen in mainstream media.

Xu started her YouTube channel, “Ni hao, It’s Sasa”, in February. She posts about her daily routines and living expenses – content that has already racked up more than 1.7 million views across 28 videos.

She said she launched the channel after observing that online portrayals of the country were often very similar, one-dimensional and simplified.

Viewers have expressed surprise at how comfortable “low-income” life appears to be in China. “US$9.4 for an entire day of meals? It’s hard to buy one meal for that price in America these days, especially in bigger cities,” reads a comment from one US account.

Others have said they appreciated seeing the reality of everyday life in China. “Honest videos like this help people better understand different perspectives,” a commenter in Vietnam wrote.

Xu said her vlogs had even inspired viewers to plan trips to China.

The videos are typically around 15 minutes and document everyday life with an emphasis on authentic perspectives. They have English narration or subtitles, with titles like “What one day’s salary buys in China” or “What life’s really like for a Chinese single man”.

It seems to be working – many of the videos go viral, drawing overseas viewers who are curious about China but want to get what they see as a genuine, non-political portrayal of how an average Chinese person lives.

In the comment sections, overseas viewers praise the safety and tech-driven convenience of Chinese cities and marvel at the peaceful, self-sufficient and frugal lifestyles in rural China.

Some vloggers have said that they moved to global platforms like YouTube to earn extra income because of concerns about job security and the economy – something that resonated with viewers in other countries.

“We’re experiencing the same thing in the West. Job cutbacks, not enough pay, lack of direction and purpose, lack of community,” one viewer in Australia commented under one of the videos.

Chinese vloggers have also embraced artificial intelligence tools to help with English subtitles and voiceovers, meaning they can overcome the language barrier and reach a global audience.

But with YouTube blocked in mainland China – along with many other foreign platforms such as Google and Facebook – vloggers must use virtual private networks, or VPNs, to get around the restrictions.

China’s sprawling, modern cities feature in some videos, but international audiences are equally drawn to stories set in the less populated rural areas.

Gangzi posts about life as a food delivery rider in the city of Xuzhou in Jiangsu province on his YouTube channel, “Chinese man named Gangzi living solo”. In six months he has amassed 30,000 subscribers and more than 3.5 million views.

His vlogs focus on his gruelling work and have drawn empathy, including from overseas delivery riders who exchange stories in the comment sections.

When he returned to his rural hometown, he drew even more viewers keen to see the peaceful atmosphere of the village and close-knit community, as well as traditional parenting dynamics.

These scenes particularly resonated in South Asia. “We Indians and Chinese are so identical culturally,” one viewer wrote in a comment echoed by others.

Some viewers have shown their support with a donation through the platform’s Super Thanks feature to encourage Gangzi to keep posting.

Florian Schneider, a professor in Chinese digital media and political communication at Leiden University in the Netherlands, said the vlogs offered an important corrective to the tropes commonly seen about China in the news.

Schneider gave the examples of hyperbole about rapid technological development and the threat narratives about China’s authoritarianism.

He said the vlogs gave viewers a reality check, that Chinese people were just like anyone else – navigating work frustrations, mundane routines and moments of loneliness.

“All of that creates a much messier picture than what the Chinese state presents in its propaganda, but it may ultimately be more effective at making China relatable, precisely because it is so raw,” he said.

Schneider said the economic downturn in China was a driver for vloggers to monetise their digital content abroad, rather than competing in the overcrowded domestic social media market.

He also noted that many vloggers genuinely wanted to share their version of life in China given that foreign media reporting and Chinese government narratives did not capture their everyday struggles.

“I can imagine showing these lived experiences to people on the other side of the world is both cathartic and, to many, a moral obligation to set the record straight,” he added.

The trend has not gone unnoticed in China, but the English editing and high number of views have raised questions about whether the channels are genuinely the work of individuals or professional agencies.

Beijing has for years invested heavily in boosting its global “soft power” but state-curated or big-budget media campaigns and official cultural initiatives have often failed to win over foreign audiences.

Schneider said mainstream media coverage of China focused on politics and high-level economics, often centring on the party-state.

“As important as that is for understanding the PRC [People’s Republic of China], it leaves out what life is like for average folks,” he said.

“Seeing genuine Chinese people going about their lives on YouTube offers a glimpse of authenticity that sadly often gets buried under political reporting and propaganda, and this is something that clearly intrigues foreign viewers.”

item.title: [SCMP] How Beijing’s hypersonic ‘carrier killers’ could distract US forces in a Taiwan conflict
item.description:
The advancement and diversification of Beijing’s anti-ship missile platforms have bolstered its denial capabilities in the first island chain and could divert US and allied navies from warfare in a Taiwan Strait contingency, according to analysts.

Last week, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV released a video of a Type 052D destroyer firing a YJ-20 hypersonic anti-ship missile from its vertical launch system, showcasing the People’s Liberation Army Navy’s increased ability to target surface combatants.

The YJ-20 is one of China’s first sea-based hypersonic anti-ship missiles to have entered mass production, highlighting Beijing’s advances in its naval defence amid a military modernisation drive to narrow gaps with the US.
item.content:encoded:
The advancement and diversification of Beijing’s anti-ship missile platforms have bolstered its denial capabilities in the first island chain and could divert US and allied navies from warfare in a Taiwan Strait contingency, according to analysts.

Last week, Chinese state broadcaster CCTV released a video of a Type 052D destroyer firing a YJ-20 hypersonic anti-ship missile from its vertical launch system, showcasing the People’s Liberation Army Navy’s increased ability to target surface combatants.

The YJ-20 is one of China’s first sea-based hypersonic anti-ship missiles to have entered mass production, highlighting Beijing’s advances in its naval defence amid a military modernisation drive to narrow gaps with the US.

The hypersonic missile is one of several anti-ship missile varieties that the PLA unveiled during a large-scale military parade in Beijing in September last year. It illustrated the Chinese navy’s strategic focus on establishing robust anti-access/area denial (A2/AD) against adversaries across its coastal waters and the first island chain.

The first island chain is a series of islands and archipelagos in East Asia, running from Japan to Borneo. It includes Taiwan, which Beijing views as part of China to be reunited by force, if necessary.

Most countries, including the United States and its allies, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

According to James Holmes, professor of strategy and holder of the J.C. Wylie Chair of Maritime Strategy at the US Naval War College, Beijing is producing its anti-ship missiles to hold the US Pacific Fleet at a distance, giving the PLA time to “settle matters in the Taiwan Strait, South China Sea or wherever the contingency might be”.
