“If the PLA can keep US-based joint forces from uniting with the Seventh Fleet and other forces forward-deployed to the western Pacific, it can skew the military balance in its favour,” said Holmes, a former US Navy surface warfare officer.

“Even if the PLA remains inferior to the US military on a ship-for-ship, weapon-for-weapon basis, as I believe it does, you can prevail if you manage to concentrate the bulk of your combat power against a fraction of the enemy’s.”

Liselotte Odgaard, a senior fellow at the Hudson Institute in Washington, said China appeared to be pursuing a layered anti-access/area denial strategy designed to complicate US and allied naval operations across the western Pacific.

“Equipping both surface ships and submarines with anti-ship missiles creates multiple attack vectors, increases redundancy and makes Chinese maritime strike capabilities more survivable in wartime,” Odgaard added.

“It also allows the PLA Navy to engage enemy forces at different ranges and in different operational environments. The approach reflects a broader Chinese emphasis on sea denial, distributed lethality and preventing adversaries from operating freely inside the first island chain.”

Last September’s parade also saw the unveiling of the YJ-19, another Chinese hypersonic anti-ship missile. It uses an air-breathing scramjet engine to travel at a speed exceeding Mach 5 and could be launched from submarine torpedo tubes.

In February, the PLA Navy revealed that it had accepted the YJ-19 for service aboard its Type 039B diesel-electric submarine, making it the only non-nuclear submarine in the world with such a weapon.

According to Collin Koh, a senior fellow at the Institute of Defence and Strategic Studies at the S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies in Singapore, China in recent years has made “huge strides” in developing various platforms to launch anti-ship missiles.

Koh called the development of the hypersonic variants of those systems “most shocking”.

“They are trying to achieve what we call overwhelming superiority going forward. [It] isn’t just to match the US symmetrically, but also to give … a certain asymmetry advantage over your adversary.”

The US has yet to put hypersonic anti-ship missiles on its submarines.

The Chinese hypersonic anti-ship missiles are often referred to as “carrier killers”, as the combination of extreme speed and mid-flight manoeuvring to bypass traditional ship defences delivers kinetic and explosive force sufficient to sink or disable aircraft carriers.

The submarine-launched capability of the YJ-19 heightens the threat it poses to US warships. By blending the underwater stealth of the submarine with hypersonic speed, the weapon reduces defensive reaction times to seconds.

While US submarine capabilities remain “very strong”, China’s submarine-launched anti-ship missiles are one of “several threats” to surface ships, according to Bradley Martin, a senior policy researcher at the Rand Corporation.

“China has a wide variety of systems that can threaten US surface ships across a wide area. Submarines are certainly one such capability,” said Martin, a former US Navy surface warfare captain.

“The US does have robust anti-submarine warfare capability, however, that any Chinese submarine would have to face to reach a target.”

Odgaard said submarine-launched anti-ship missiles combined stealth with long-range strike capability, making them “particularly challenging” to counter.

“Aircraft carriers remain extremely powerful, but their survivability increasingly depends on detecting and neutralising threats before launch,” she added.

“Chinese submarine-launched anti-ship missiles could force carrier strike groups to operate farther from contested areas or devote additional resources to anti-submarine warfare.”

“A stealthy submarine armed with long-range missiles can exploit gaps in maritime surveillance and theatre high-value targets,” Odgaard continued.

“Even a limited risk of successful attacks could affect US operational planning because carriers concentrate substantial combat power in a relatively small number of vessels.”

Koh said that coupling anti-ship missiles like the YJ-19 with submarines would be “where the danger is going to be greater” and that would require US and allied navies to “keep pace” with anti-air warfare in defending their surface combatants.

He described the “psychological barriers” created by the deployment of hypersonic missiles on the submarines as pushing the US and allied navies to spend “disproportionately more effort and time in trying to hunt them down”.

“If you have much of your fleet tied down trying to search for these elusive submarines with hypersonic missiles, then essentially you are taking the fleet away from other tasks,” Koh added.

“That could mean the fulfilment of other, more important operational tasks in the Taiwan theatre and elsewhere.”

If the US Navy were devoting so many resources across the Pacific Ocean “trying to hunt down these submarines”, Koh said, “then essentially … the first island chain is very much conceded to the Chinese”.

item.title: [SCMP] How Saudi Arabia-Turkey-Pakistan defence pact acts as ‘insurance’ over US disengagement
item.description:
A defence pact among Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan appears to be aimed at deterring Iran and Israel from tearing up the Middle East with their conflict amid Washington’s inability to guarantee regional security, observers say.

Under the terms of the deal signed on Friday in Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, an armed attack against any one of the three states “shall be regarded as an attack against them all”.

No further details have been made public, but the signatories were quick to clarify that they had not formed a military coalition, and that the agreement served as a deterrent.
item.content:encoded:
A defence pact among Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan appears to be aimed at deterring Iran and Israel from tearing up the Middle East with their conflict amid Washington’s inability to guarantee regional security, observers say.

Under the terms of the deal signed on Friday in Mecca by Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan and Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif, an armed attack against any one of the three states “shall be regarded as an attack against them all”.

No further details have been made public, but the signatories were quick to clarify that they had not formed a military coalition, and that the agreement served as a deterrent.

In a social media post, Saudi Deputy Minister for Public Diplomacy Rayed Krimly said the pact “does not threaten the security of any country in the region and should not be viewed as an escalation of tensions between any two states”.

Erdogan followed suit, saying the agreement “targets no country and is open to the participation of all brotherly countries that aim for the peace, prosperity, and stability of our region”.

Former Qatari prime minister Hamad bin Jassim bin Jaber al-Thani described the tripartite pact as “a step that calls for optimism” and expressed hope that other Gulf Cooperation Council members would “take the initiative to join it”.

Analysts see Qatar as an obvious candidate to join the pact because of its pre-existing defence agreement with Turkey. Kuwait is also a potential signatory following ratification of its expanded defence cooperation agreement with Pakistan in July.

But the United Arab Emirates and Bahrain are unlikely to join the Mecca pact after having normalised relations with Israel in 2020 under the US-led Abraham Accords. The same is likely true of Egypt and Jordan given that their decades-old US-brokered peace deals with Israel require them to intercept threats faced by the Jewish-majority state.

Over time, the Mecca pact may emerge as a third geopolitical “centre of gravity” in the Middle East, analysts say.

But it “will not develop into an Islamic Nato with dozens of countries accepting identical defence obligations”, according to Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of defence studies at King’s College London.

Instead, it will attract “concentric circles of cooperation”, with some states taking part in joint military exercises with the Mecca pact signatories, and others in maritime security, intelligence and defence procurement projects.

Krieg expects Egypt, Jordan and other Muslim-majority states to increasingly coordinate with the grouping “without necessarily becoming formal treaty members”.

But Kristian Coates Ulrichsen, a Middle East fellow at Rice University’s Baker Institute for Public Policy, is sceptical that the Mecca pact can succeed without the active participation of Egypt, the Arab world’s largest military power, or the UAE, the Middle East’s commercial powerhouse.

Regardless, the pact is likely to face an early test by Iran and its “axis of resistance” allies, according to Ulrichsen.

Yemen’s Houthi movement and Iraqi militias, acting in concert with Iran’s Revolutionary Guards, were planning to mount joint missile and drone strikes against the kingdom, a senior Saudi official told reporters on Thursday.

Ulrichsen said the response from Pakistan and Turkey would “provide an indication of whether collective deterrence is workable in practice”.

For Krieg, the Mecca pact “will not transform the battlefield overnight, but it will immediately strengthen Saudi deterrence and make further attacks against the kingdom more consequential”. The biggest immediate effect of the pact is “psychological and strategic”.

Iran would now have to calculate that continuous attacks on Saudi territory could widen the confrontation beyond Riyadh and Washington, Krieg said. “It therefore raises the potential cost of targeting Saudi Arabia.”

Farzan Sabet, an Iran expert at the Geneva Graduate Institute, also saw the agreement as “potentially reinforcing deterrence signalling” against a direct Iranian attack on Saudi Arabia.

There have not been any such attacks since Pakistan, having mediated the first ceasefire of the conflict in early April, deployed some 8,000 troops, air defence systems and fighter jets in Saudi Arabia under the mutual defence pact the two countries signed in September last year.

It is so far unclear if Pakistan’s expeditionary force has been involved in the recent interception of missiles and drones fired at the kingdom by Yemen’s Houthis and Revolutionary Guards-led Iraqi militias.

Sabet does not believe the Mecca pact will pose much of a deterrent to such non-state actors unless Pakistan and Turkey pursue them. Both countries have already stated that their commitment to Saudi Arabia’s defence is purely defensive.

The Iraqi militias agreed to “postpone” further attacks against Riyadh following an appeal by Hadi al-Amiri, the head of another Iran-aligned faction.

On Friday, Amiri urged the groups to “exercise restraint for the sake of Iraq’s highest interests” amid the threat of a second joint Saudi-US air operation against them.

According to Krieg, the practical effect of the three-way arrangement would be greater air and missile defence cooperation, intelligence sharing, protection of critical infrastructure, manpower support and potentially expanded maritime security.

Pakistan and Turkey have already voiced support for a planned Saudi-led international naval coalition to protect shipping in the Red Sea, Bab al-Mandab Strait and Gulf of Aden, launched last month after the Houthis imposed a maritime blockade against Riyadh.

Islamabad could quickly supply Riyadh with personnel, while Istanbul could provide defence systems, technical expertise and defence-industrial support, Krieg said.

The uptick in attacks by the Houthis and their allies on Saudi Arabia has coincided with an agreement between Iran and Oman on a framework for the administration of the Strait of Hormuz. With the accord, Iran could maintain its chokehold on shipping in the strait by curbing oil and gas supplies from its Gulf neighbours.

It is unclear for now whether US President Donald Trump will acquiesce to the arrangement between Iran and Oman, which analysts say would be tantamount to accepting strategic defeat.

Saudi Arabia, Turkey and Pakistan had chosen to join forces because “the regional security order has visibly failed”, Krieg said.

The so-called Third Gulf War has shown that “American military predominance does not automatically translate into protection for US partners”, he added.

Infrastructure in the region remains vulnerable to Iranian missiles and drones, while Washington has also “struggled to restrain Israeli unilateralism”.

Israel has made it clear that it will not withdraw its forces from recently occupied territory in Lebanon and Syria, despite US efforts to find diplomatic solutions that address the Jewish-majority state’s security concerns about Hezbollah and the Islamist government in Damascus.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s hardline coalition government has intensified military operations in Gaza, rejecting a proposed US-brokered agreement announced last week under which Hamas agreed to disarm in return for a staggered Israeli military withdrawal.

“For Riyadh, exclusive dependence on the American umbrella has therefore become a strategic risk,” Krieg said.

Ulrichsen said the Mecca pact brought together three regional powers, all of which had a common need to diversify their defence relationships due to challenges posed by the Iran war and other regional conflicts in recent years.

Krieg noted the three countries’ “unusually complementary needs”, with Saudi Arabia aiming for greater military depth, Turkey seeking to grow its defence industry and Pakistan needing investments and other economic support.

Calling their agreement “an insurance” against an increasingly unpredictable regional system, he added: “It is not anti-American, but it is unmistakably post-dependency. These states no longer believe Washington should have a monopoly over organising their security.”

item.title: [SCMP] Myanmar touts economic potential but is it pie in the sky with it still at war?
item.description:
Rina left Myanmar shortly after the 2021 coup as military violence escalated against pro-democracy protesters like herself and the economy of her country, once a Southeast Asian frontier that had flickered with promise, ground to a virtual halt.

Now in Bangkok, the 21-year-old has found work in a cafe, a regular, albeit low-salaried income, the minimum required by the millions of her age group forced to survive outside a domestic economy in ruins, where civil war has killed an estimated 100,000 people in five years.

But her thoughts on who is to blame for the destruction of her country remain unchanged: Min Aung Hlaing, the junta chief who became civilian president this year after elections in the parts of the country the military controls.
item.content:encoded:
Rina left Myanmar shortly after the 2021 coup as military violence escalated against pro-democracy protesters like herself and the economy of her country, once a Southeast Asian frontier that had flickered with promise, ground to a virtual halt.

Now in Bangkok, the 21-year-old has found work in a cafe, a regular, albeit low-salaried income, the minimum required by the millions of her age group forced to survive outside a domestic economy in ruins, where civil war has killed an estimated 100,000 people in five years.

But her thoughts on who is to blame for the destruction of her country remain unchanged: Min Aung Hlaing, the junta chief who became civilian president this year after elections in the parts of the country the military controls.

He is currently in the Thai capital basking in the welcome of an official visit to Thailand, following trips to China and India that have offered a diplomatic ladder out from isolation since the coup.

In Bangkok, the welcome included a red carpet, honour guard, gala dinner and a chance to offer business leaders a vision of his civil-war-torn nation as a future regional infrastructure and investment hub – rather than the regional basket case his coup created.

“Min Aung Hlaing is the reason we are living here outside our country. The day he is gone – and the military is defeated – we will go back and we will build our country again,” she told This Week in Asia, giving her nickname to avoid any recriminations.

“But we will have to wait. Who knows how long? Maybe it will be three, five or 10 years?”

The realisation that the former army chief – wanted for war crimes at The Hague and sanctioned from the United Kingdom to the United States – is firmly at the helm of an albeit fractured country, has also shaped Thailand’s diplomatic outreach.

Thailand has embarked on what it calls a “calibrated re-engagement’’ with Myanmar, a position it says is inevitable given the long shared border and interests that involve close cooperation, no matter who is in charge in Naypyidaw.

“We have issues every day and need to cooperate … so bilaterally we need to talk, we need to cooperate particularly on issues of border security: the border itself, how to work together to suppress the transnational crimes, scams, drugs,’’ Thai Foreign Minister Sihasak Phuangketkeow told reporters on Thursday evening, adding that air and cross-boundary water pollution were the most pressing issues, referencing toxic run-off that had hit river communities along the Mekong and its tributaries in northwestern Thailand.

While emphasising that Thailand wanted to keep Myanmar pegged to outcomes of a five-point consensus – an Asean bloc peace deal to end violence against civilians and ensure aid gets to the millions of displaced since the coup – Sihasak said there were also economic reasons to extend a hand to Myanmar’s government.

“It’s not just the immediate opportunities,” he told reporters. “Many of the private sector are looking long-term. If Myanmar returns to peace and stability there will be a lot of opportunities, whether in trade and investment.”

While Myanmar’s economy has shown signs of life this year after years of sky-high inflation and negative growth partly caused by a devastating earthquake, experts say it is far from recovering its previous footing which began with political and economic reforms in 2011 – a period of growth abruptly ended by the coup.

“The projects Min Aung Hlaing is pushing with neighbours centre on infrastructure construction, gas development, and energy,” said Htwe Htwe Thein, an associate professor of international business at Curtin University in Australia.

Min Aung Hlaing’s economic plans pivot on highways, railways, dams and power projects, she added, to remodel the war-shattered but strategically important country – pinned between India, China and Thailand – as a manufacturing hub in the heart of Asia’s supply chains.

But “serious obstacles’’ stand in the way of that bright vision, Htwe Htwe Thein added, in a country where the United Nations say 16 million people – nearly a third of the population – need humanitarian relief and foreign investment has collapsed as the war has deepened.

“For one, how do you build infrastructure corridors through active war zones? No serious investor is going to commit capital to projects running through contested territory the government doesn’t fully control,” she said.

“Layer sanctions and the banking restrictions that follow on top of that, and any financing tied to Myanmar comes under heavy scrutiny at every step.”

That leaves economic drivers of jade and gems, tin, copper and rare earths operated by military cronies and shadowy tycoons rather than creating a wider economic base as the likely outcome, she added.

“Real investment has narrowed to resource extraction carried out with little proper due diligence, and also murky financial flows. None of that is capital that builds a manufacturing base or delivers broad-based development.

“It’s extraction and survival financing, not growth.”

While the economic picture uneven at best, Thailand’s renewal of relations has come under scrutiny.

The militaries of Myanmar and Thailand share good relations that have stretched back decades, according to Paul Chambers, an analyst of Thai politics at the University of Oklahoma in the US, adding that Myanmar’s “abominable human rights record’’ has rarely been the deciding factor in their diplomacy.

Myanmar’s diplomatic reintegration in its Asian neighbourhood owed more to military gains of the last 18 months, he said, that were secured in part with Chinese and Russian military aid that had pulled back the patchwork of pro-democracy rebels and ethnic armed groups that at one point threatened to overwhelm the military.

Still, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations is yet to fully readmit Myanmar to its main summits until the five-point consensus is firmly back on track.

Instead, Myanmar’s tip-toe back into the diplomatic fold, represented by this week’s Bangkok trip – after Beijing and New Delhi – reflects the national interests of its neighbouring countries, according to Richard Horsey, Crisis Group’s senior Asia adviser.

“China, India, and Thailand are taking on real reputational risk by doing so, and the rest of the world is watching,” he added.

item.title: [SCMP] Chip off the old bloc: Thailand looks to Siam Silica to propel it to top Asean player
item.description:
Thailand launched its Siam Silica framework last week, a national road map that stamps the Southeast Asian country’s stake in the semiconductor race by building a domestic ecosystem and positioning it as a key hub within an integrated supply chain among Asean member states.

However, analysts say that the country will have much ground to cover as it trails behind neighbours Malaysia and Singapore.

At the unveiling by the Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation (MHESI) on July 27, minister Yodchanan Wongsawat called semiconductor development “a national priority”.
item.content:encoded:
Thailand launched its Siam Silica framework last week, a national road map that stamps the Southeast Asian country’s stake in the semiconductor race by building a domestic ecosystem and positioning it as a key hub within an integrated supply chain among Asean member states.

However, analysts say that the country will have much ground to cover as it trails behind neighbours Malaysia and Singapore.

At the unveiling by the Ministry of Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation (MHESI) on July 27, minister Yodchanan Wongsawat called semiconductor development “a national priority”.

Siam Silica will target five areas: photonics fabrication, advanced packaging, silicon design, quantum photonics and power devices. Thailand aims to establish eight integrated circuit design companies, one semiconductor fabrication plant, and two advanced semiconductor packaging facilities by 2030.

The MHESI also announced it was launching a Higher Education Sandbox degree programme for universities to fast-track deep-tech expertise and develop advanced competencies.

STEMPlus, the ministry’s human resources development and planning platform, will recruit 152 lecturers and scientists, 950 researchers, experts and senior engineers, 553 highly skilled engineers and 1,330 technicians for the programme.

Bangkok’s ambitions also include creating an Asean Talent Observatory to forecast demand in the workforce, incorporating photonics and printed circuit boards into the Asean Semiconductor Roadmap, and growing its Thailand Skill Bridge platform to collaborate on research and development with other countries in the region.

To achieve that, Thailand should push for closer Association of Southeast Asian Nations integration so the bloc could strengthen its resilience and regional bargaining power amid disruptions in the global supply chain, Surin Khomfoi, vice-president of the Office of the National Higher Education, Science, Research and Innovation Policy Council, was quoted as saying by the Bangkok Post.

Thailand could also look into producing power control chips, photonics chips and sensor chips, as there is a high market demand and low number of players in this sector, according to Surin.

Appropriately ambitious

The recently unveiled plans reflect Thailand’s long-standing ambitions to move into higher-value segments of the semiconductor manufacturing chain, such as chip design and wafer fabrication.

In 2024, Thailand established the inter-ministry National Semiconductor Board to promote its semiconductor and advanced electronics industries, and deepen its foothold in global value chains.

However, analysts say the Southeast Asian country faces an uphill battle.

“It’s a tall order, for two reasons. First, Thailand is a latecomer to the semiconductor value chain compared with Singapore and Malaysia. Announcing a road map to build, by 2030, an ecosystem that can rival what those two neighbours have spent decades assembling is very different from actually delivering it,” Pavida Pananond, a professor of international business at Thammasat University’s Thammasat Business School, told This Week in Asia.

“Second, Thailand also lags in the breadth of semiconductor activities it can perform.”

In 2024, Thailand’s semiconductor exports reached 436 billion baht (US$13.8 billion). Malaysia’s total that year was US$95.6 billion, nearly seven times that.

“Thailand exports a much smaller value in semiconductors each year than Malaysia and Singapore. It would have to increase exports by orders of magnitude to catch up, which is unrealistic in the near term,” said Robert Walker, a research fellow at the Lowy Institute’s Indo-Pacific Development Centre.

Thailand’s traditional role in the semiconductor chain has largely been confined to back-end work such as assembly, packaging and testing, according to Pavida.

“Expanding into front-end chip manufacturing and design will take a lot more than financial incentives and a government push to attract investment,” she said. “Both design and front-end manufacturing demand highly specialised technology and skills that simply aren’t as readily available in Thailand today as they are in Singapore and Malaysia.”

While Thailand’s policy appeared to be “well-designed” and “appropriately ambitious and realistic”, it would have to be a “decades-long strategy” – particularly if it wanted to become a leading player in the region, Walker said.

“Siam Silica’s focus on skill pipelines, rationalising government support mechanisms, and trying to leverage regional cooperation all look positive. Thailand is unlikely to overtake leaders like Malaysia and Singapore but can still make itself indispensable to regional supply chains,” he said.

Managing expectations

Thailand would have to be realistic in its expectations, Pavida said.

“Thailand is trying to build this ecosystem in 2026, when Singapore and Malaysia already began that journey some 50 years ago – and neither of them is standing still,” she said.

“So there is a lot of catching up, and even leapfrogging, that Thailand will need to do if it wants to become a central player in an integrated regional supply chain.”

Siam Silica’s success will depend on the effectiveness of its implementation, according to Pradittha Werasakun and Piriya Piriyakrit, senior analysts at BowerGroupAsia.

While Thailand has established its strengths in the downstream semiconductor segment, it needs to solve key issues such as limited wafer manufacturing capability, technology transfer, and high-skilled talent to build the ecosystem required to support its goal as a central hub in the region.

The greater challenge might be political rather than technical, Werasakun and Piriyakrit told This Week in Asia.

“The initiative builds on momentum generated under the previous Pheu Thai-led government, which demonstrated its ability to mobilise investment behind strategic sectors such as data centres. Siam Silica is now being advanced by Deputy Prime Minister and MHESI Minister Yodchanan as a national priority. However, semiconductor ecosystems require sustained policy support over many years,” they said.

“Given Thailand’s changing coalition dynamics, investors will likely pay close attention to whether the initiative remains a consistent cross-government priority or becomes associated with a particular political leadership or ministry.”

The country’s approach to work with Asean could also come up against nationalist ambitions.

“The six Asean countries with a stake in the semiconductor value chain all want to hold on to the highest value-creating segments for themselves. That dynamic may end up making their relationship more competitive than complementary,” Pavida said.

With a bit of patience, though, Thailand could become a leading player in the region, Walker said.

“Thailand has a strong manufacturing ecosystem and pre-existing semiconductor capabilities, with a relatively well-educated workforce. Combined with a competitive wage level, Thailand is well positioned to push a strategy to become a larger semiconductor hub in the region,” he said.

Rather than meeting its competition head on, Thailand could be a helpmeet, Werasakun and Piriyakrit said.

“Thailand’s competitive advantage lies in complementing, rather than replicating, the strengths of other Asean semiconductor hubs,” they said.

Siam Silica was drafted “to attract companies to help Thailand build a semiconductor ecosystem, and not to compete across the entire value chain in this early stage”.

By building on its existing strengths, Thailand could carve out a niche contributing to the broader value chain of the digital economy, Pavida said.

“One bright spot is the country’s dominance in hard disk drives, which are becoming an integral part of the AI ecosystem, as hyperscalers and data centres increasingly need cheap, high-capacity storage at scale,” she said.

“It may not be as glamorous as advanced chipmaking, but it gives Thailand a differentiated path – becoming an essential, if unglamorous, link in the AI supply chain, while building up a more highly skilled ecosystem and workforce over time.”

Ultimately, a more realistic benchmark is whether companies view Thailand’s contributions as indispensable, according to the BowerGroupAsia analysts.

“If Thailand can deepen its strengths in selected segments while continuing to attract strategic investment and develop skilled talent, then it can become an important regional semiconductor node.”

item.title: [SCMP] Climate crisis leaves Malaysia with hot-headed youth
item.description:
Young Malaysians are reporting worsening illnesses, heat-related health problems and disruptions to basic services as climate change intensifies, raising questions over whether the country’s adaptation policies can protect future generations.

Unicef Malaysia’s National Youth Climate Change Survey 2025, released in July, found that climate change was no longer only an environmental challenge but an immediate public health and economic issue.

The survey gathered responses from 1,420 young people aged 15 to 30 across Malaysia between June and October 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Young Malaysians are reporting worsening illnesses, heat-related health problems and disruptions to basic services as climate change intensifies, raising questions over whether the country’s adaptation policies can protect future generations.

Unicef Malaysia’s National Youth Climate Change Survey 2025, released in July, found that climate change was no longer only an environmental challenge but an immediate public health and economic issue.

The survey gathered responses from 1,420 young people aged 15 to 30 across Malaysia between June and October 2025.

Experts warned that policymakers must invest not only in reducing emissions but also in adapting to more frequent heatwaves, floods and other climate-related shocks, or risk deeper disruption to children’s health, education and Malaysia’s future workforce.

Unicef said the survey’s findings showed climate change was affecting young people’s health and well-being, with respondents reporting significant concerns: one in four, or 25.9 per cent, said existing illnesses had worsened, while 19.7 per cent reported skin conditions, 18 per cent cited heat-related illnesses and 14.3 per cent respiratory problems.

More than half said climate-related disasters had affected their access to essential services, including information, education and safe spaces.

Dr Jemilah Mahmood, executive director of the Sunway Centre for Planetary Health, said the Unicef findings showed the issue had evolved from an environmental concern into a public health challenge.

“We are already seeing the classic climate and health picture – direct injury, infectious disease, exacerbation of chronic conditions and psychological burden, all occurring simultaneously in a population aged 15 to 30, at what should be their healthiest years,” she said.

Experts say the findings underscore Malaysia’s need to emphasise adaptation plans, arguing that climate resilience should act as an investment in the country’s future workforce.

“It is no longer an either-or conversation. Malaysia must continue reducing emissions while significantly strengthening adaptation,” said Renard Siew, climate adviser at the Malaysia-based Centre for Governance and Political Studies.

Siew said children and young people were among the most vulnerable to climate change, and the biggest gap remained implementation for adaptation across all sectors.

The cost of inaction would exceed the costs of adaptation, he said, adding that more frequent heat stress, disease outbreaks and climate-related disruptions would affect productivity, increase healthcare expenditure and widen social inequalities.

“Over time, this would weaken our workforce competitiveness and economic resilience,” he said.

Public health experts warn that young children are among the most vulnerable to extreme heat because their bodies regulate temperatures less effectively, leading them to become dehydrated more quickly than adults.

“Their body’s heat-coping mechanism is more easily overwhelmed in these situations, such as getting dehydrated faster and the body’s cooling mechanism being overwhelmed more easily,” Dr Venu Gopalan, a Kuala Lumpur-based private practitioner, told This Week in Asia.

Immediate health risks of extreme heat, he said, included heat cramps, fainting, heat exhaustion and heatstrokes that could even cause death.

Gopalan warned that in the long term, repeated extreme heat exposure could lead to deteriorating kidney function and worsening heart and lung diseases, while increasing the risk of stroke caused by dehydration and electrolyte imbalances.

While Malaysia had big ambitions, climate, health and education often operated independently, Siew said.

“We need climate risk assessments embedded in schools, stronger heat-health action plans, better air quality management, and greater investment in climate-resilient public infrastructure where young people learn and live,” he said.

The Malaysian Meteorological Department has repeatedly issued hot weather alerts this year, as temperatures hit between 35 degrees Celsius (95 degrees Fahrenheit) and 40 degrees between March and May in the northern states and some parts of Sabah.

On Monday, data from the department showed that Kuala Krai in Kelantan registered the country’s highest temperature, at 35.7 degrees, followed by Temerloh in Pahang at 35.3 degrees.

The heat was not without consequences, as the Ministry of Health recorded a total of 73 heat-related illnesses from January to July this year.

According to national news agency Bernama, Public Health Medicine Specialist Dr Hazlina Yahaya said the cases involved 59 reports of heat exhaustion, six exertional heatstrokes, four heatstrokes, two cases of post-partum hyperpyrexia (high fever following childbirth), and two heat cramps.

Four deaths have been reported: two adults and two children aged two and four.

Progress but with gaps

In a statement on July 31, the World Meteorological Organization warned that the extreme heat phenomenon El Nino would continue to intensify steadily, dominating global climate patterns between August and October this year.

The agency said this would increase the likelihood of above-normal temperatures, driving significant shifts in rainfall patterns. “The developing El Nino is expected to shape weather patterns across many parts of the world in the months ahead.”

Gopalan said Malaysia’s current public health measures to address heat-related risks were inadequate, arguing that warnings alone were insufficient, especially for those who could not avoid prolonged exposure, such as outdoor workers, the homeless, and students.

“Early signs of heat stress should be recognised early by the community to enable rapid preventive measures to be taken,” he said. “Simply telling people to stay out of the sun is not practical for large segments of the community.”

Jemilah said while Malaysia had taken important steps – including identifying public health as a priority sector under the National Adaptation Plan, introducing heatwave health action plans and advancing climate legislation – implementation was still far behind.

According to Jemilah, the biggest challenge is ensuring national climate ambitions are translated and coordinated across health, education and local government, particularly as more than half of the young people affected by climate-related disasters reported lacking access to at least one essential service.

“The health aspect is lagging behind the exposure,” Jemilah said.

Siew warned that such gaps reflected a broader weakness in Malaysia’s climate adaptation effort where health, education and environmental policies were still often developed in silos despite their overlapping risks from extreme weather.

Climate adaptation, he added, should not be confined to environmental ministries.

“Even if we achieve our climate targets, the impacts of climate change are already here because children and young people are among the most vulnerable,” he said. “Investing in climate resilience today is ultimately an investment in our future human capital.”

item.title: [SCMP] China hits back at US with barrage of sanctions, drone industry curbs
item.description:
China has hit back against a round of US sanctions with a barrage of counter-sanctions targeting a group of American entities and a tightening of export restrictions on the drone supply chain, the Ministry of Commerce announced on Wednesday.

The export controls will subject any shipments of “drones, their key components and related technologies” to the US to “strict case-by-case scrutiny”, with the measures set to take effect immediately, the ministry said in a statement, citing the need to “safeguard national security and meet China’s international commitments on non-proliferation”.

On the same day, the commerce ministry also added six US entities to its countermeasures list – banning Chinese entities and individuals from cooperating with them – over allegations that they had assisted US sanctions related to China’s western Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, describing their conduct as “egregious”.
item.content:encoded:
China has hit back against a round of US sanctions with a barrage of counter-sanctions targeting a group of American entities and a tightening of export restrictions on the drone supply chain, the Ministry of Commerce announced on Wednesday.

The export controls will subject any shipments of “drones, their key components and related technologies” to the US to “strict case-by-case scrutiny”, with the measures set to take effect immediately, the ministry said in a statement, citing the need to “safeguard national security and meet China’s international commitments on non-proliferation”.

On the same day, the commerce ministry also added six US entities to its countermeasures list – banning Chinese entities and individuals from cooperating with them – over allegations that they had assisted US sanctions related to China’s western Xinjiang Uygur autonomous region, describing their conduct as “egregious”.

A seventh US company, Compliance Testing LLC, was added to the countermeasures list for assisting the US Federal Communications Commission (FCC) in introducing measures that “endanger China’s sovereignty, security and development interests”.

Separately, the commerce ministry launched a national security investigation regarding imported printing and copying office equipment with foreign-made software. US tech firms – such as Microsoft and HP – are seen as major players in the printing software sector.

The inquiry is the first to be launched using the new national security provisions laid out in China’s revised foreign trade law, according to the commerce ministry, adding the investigation would cover the effect of foreign government policies on China’s security interests.

The measures are a response to a string of recent actions by US authorities.

Last week, Washington added 43 Chinese companies to its own entity list under the Uygur Forced Labour Prevention Act, covering sectors ranging from food and cotton to pharmaceuticals, metals and lithium production. Beijing has repeatedly denied allegations of forced labour in Xinjiang.

Meanwhile, the FCC banned the import and sale of new foreign-made robotic devices and power inverters, two sectors where China is a leading global player.

Beijing is extending the rare-earths playbook up the value chain, from raw inputs like germanium to finished-goods components

Alicia Garcia-Herrero, Natixis

“China’s countermeasures have been restrained overall. China values the hard-won stability of China-US economic and trade relations. We hope the US side can work with China in the same direction,” the commerce ministry said in a statement.

But the ministry demanded that Washington immediately rescind its measures, warning that China would retaliate further if the US pressed ahead with new restrictions.

In response, a senior US administration official said Washington was “deeply disappointed” that China “has chosen to announce another round of escalatory measures”.

“While our leaders have a close relationship, expanding the cycle of retaliation will not produce a durable solution,” the person said.

Analysts said Beijing’s response marked a “calibrated escalation” in the US and China’s ongoing trade and technology dispute, which has seen both sides attempt to gain strategic leverage by threatening to cut off access to key resources and technologies.

For some, the drone industry restrictions build on the tactics Beijing used during its trade war with Washington last year, when it tightened export controls over rare earth minerals – a vital industry where it controls most global supplies.

“Beijing is extending the rare-earths playbook up the value chain, from raw inputs like gallium and germanium to finished-goods components in a sector it dominates,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, chief economist for Asia-Pacific and the Middle East at French investment bank Natixis.

Drones were already a point of friction in US-China relations. Chinese companies are the undisputed leaders in the industry, dominating the global supply chain. In December, the FCC banned the import of all new models of foreign-made drones and related components, citing national security risks.

Beijing appears to have taken particular issue with the timing of Washington’s latest actions. The US sanctions were announced on July 31, a day after Chinese Vice-Premier He Lifeng held a video call with US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Trade Representative Jamieson Greer.

During the call, China expressed serious concern over the US’ recent economic and trade moves, Xinhua reported. But Washington had pressed ahead with its measures “in complete disregard” of China’s repeated representations, the commerce ministry said.

The decision “seriously contravenes” the consensus reached by Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump during their recent meetings and seriously harms China’s “legitimate rights and interests”, according to the statement.

The contest is shifting from tariffs towards control over critical technologies, supply chains, and dual-use goods

Matteo Giovannini, Industrial and Commercial Bank of China

For Garcia-Herrero, Beijing was trying to signal it was “keeping its powder dry” as both sides race to “de-risk” their economies – plugging holes in their supply chains before the other side can weaponise the vulnerability.

Xu Tianchen, senior economist at the Economist Intelligence Unit, said Beijing’s move was a reciprocal response rather than an escalation, pointing to Xi’s expected visit to Washington in September.

Xi and Trump last met during the US president’s visit to Beijing in May. At the time, Trump said Xi would visit America “on September 24, or thereabouts”, with subsequent meetings likely to take place on the sidelines of major international summits in November and December.

“Xi’s visit is an important event. Following China’s countermeasures and continued communication between the two sides, tensions are expected to ease,” Xu said, though he added that the possibility of engagement being derailed by further unilateral US actions could not be ruled out.

Matteo Giovannini, a senior finance manager at the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, said the key signal was that “export controls are no longer exceptional policy tools, as they have become a normal feature of strategic competition”.

“The contest is shifting from tariffs towards control over critical technologies, supply chains, and dual-use goods, where both Washington and Beijing believe they possess meaningful leverage.”

item.title: [SCMP] China’s military goal is to stand neck and neck with the US: ex-PLA colonel Zhou Bo
item.description:
Zhou Bo is a retired senior colonel in the People’s Liberation Army, a senior fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, and the author of the book Should the World Fear China? This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is approaching its 2027 centenary, a major benchmark set by Beijing to achieve military modernisation. What is that goal actually about?

China has set two major military goals: one [is for the] centenary of the PLA in 2027 and another [is for the centenary] of the People’s Republic of China in 2049.
item.content:encoded:
Zhou Bo is a retired senior colonel in the People’s Liberation Army, a senior fellow at Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy, and the author of the book Should the World Fear China? This interview first appeared in SCMP Plus. For other interviews in the Open Questions series, click here.

The People’s Liberation Army (PLA) is approaching its 2027 centenary, a major benchmark set by Beijing to achieve military modernisation. What is that goal actually about?

China has set two major military goals: one [is for the] centenary of the PLA in 2027 and another [is for the centenary] of the People’s Republic of China in 2049.

Between those two milestones, China aims to basically achieve the modernisation of its national defence and armed forces by 2035. That means the PLA would not yet be fully modernised by 2027 by China’s own high standard.

The stated highest objective is to build a world-class military by 2049. However, we first need to consider how many countries are considered to have world-class militaries. The Chinese government has not specified this.

If there is only one, then it is obviously the United States. But if there can be more than one, then is China not already the second-strongest military power in the world?

That naturally leads to a comparison with Russia. I do not want to belittle Russia, but it clearly did not perform well at the beginning of the Ukraine war. It lacked effective centralised battlefield command, encrypted communications and adequate logistical support. The conflict has since become a war of attrition.

What about the PLA? Its budget is roughly one quarter that of the United States, but about 1.8 times Russia’s. It has the world’s largest armed forces and the largest number of naval vessels. Its state-of-the-art fighter jets outnumber Russia’s by a big margin. China and the United States are also the two dominant powers in applying advanced military technologies.

So, it depends on how we define a world-class military. If there can be more than one, China is arguably already among them. If there can be only one, then the 2049 objective is clear: to stand neck and neck with the United States.

Would it even be possible for China to surpass the United States? Well, it is difficult to verify whether China will actually overtake the United States. The United States has fought many wars, while China has continued to develop peacefully, and I hope that will continue.

Are there any visible indicators of the PLA’s progress towards its 2027 goal, including developments in areas such as its aircraft carrier fleet and defence budget?

There are two sides to this question.

Some developments are very visible. For example, outside observers can easily determine whether China has commissioned another aircraft carrier or whether a carrier is equipped with the so-called electromagnetic launch system.

However, other factors are much more difficult to assess.

For example, we do not know how effectively soldiers would perform in actual combat. Factors such as combat effectiveness, morale and the ability of personnel to operate under wartime conditions cannot be easily assessed unless a war actually occurs.

What China can do, in my view, is to maintain a clear long-term objective, ever sophisticated training and sustain its investment in defence. By sustained investment, I mean steady investment rather than a drastic or sudden increase.

What is valuable about China’s approach to defence spending is that, from the late 1970s, Deng Xiaoping made it clear that military development had to remain consistent with China’s economic development.

You mentioned that some capabilities cannot be assessed in a peacetime context. Does the PLA face challenges in validating systems such as AI without the combat experience the United States has gained from recent conflicts?

The United States has the advantage of being able to verify its systems in ongoing wars.

China therefore faces a dilemma because it has been at peace and consequently has had no opportunity to verify its weapons in actual warfare.

At the same time, we should not forget that peace itself has been the greatest dividend of China’s peaceful rise. It has provided China with decades of a peaceful environment, allowing the country as a whole to rise to its present level.

Sometimes you want to know how sharp your sword is. If you do not use the sword, how can you know how sharp it is? But you cannot simply cut off someone’s head to find out. This is the dilemma facing China.

Nevertheless, even with this dilemma, people should not draw the mistaken conclusion that the People’s Liberation Army cannot fight.

This is something that is often discussed in the West: the PLA may be unable to fight because China has been at peace. I think this question can be clarified quite easily.

For example, among China’s various missile launches, whether submarine-launched or land-based launches into the South Pacific, has any one of them failed? No, they have not failed. The combat capability of Chinese air power has also been demonstrated by Pakistan in its aerial combat with India using Chinese fighters.

People shouldn’t have doubts about China’s military capabilities. They are supported by a defence industry that is second to none, as well as by ambition, careful planning, and stable and sustained investment. I think the goal is totally achievable.

Do you think the anti-corruption efforts in the PLA will ultimately strengthen or weaken the PLA’s capabilities?

The Chinese government’s approach towards corruption is essentially one of zero tolerance. That is why cases of this kind are exposed from time to time.

We do not live in a vacuum, and the PLA is likewise not immune from the wider environment. It is regrettable that such matters can occur within the military.

However, the exposure of corruption and the decision to bring those responsible to justice can also be understood in another way: they demonstrate that we are trying to cleanse the organisation.

As a result, the PLA could become more effective. Developments have also demonstrated that it has not necessarily been weakened by these cases. As I mentioned earlier, we have seen Chinese missile launches in different locations, as well as the effective use of Chinese weapons systems by the Pakistan Air Force, among other examples.

I therefore believe that these anti-corruption efforts are healthy for the PLA.

Some assessments have linked the PLA’s 2027 centenary goal to Taiwan. How credible is this view, and has the risk of conflict in the Taiwan Strait declined since Chinese leader Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump met in May?

I think the Chinese government still sincerely hopes for peaceful reunification.

This has been demonstrated not only in remarks made by the Chinese leadership, but also, for example, during the visit of the chairwoman of [Taiwan’s main opposition party] the Kuomintang to Beijing. The visit involved not only warm handshakes, but also 10 preferential measures. These measures were, of course, intended for the benefit of the Taiwanese people, and they must have been carefully prepared. This means that they were not simply ideas developed overnight.

People always mention the “stick” element of mainland China without discussing the “carrot” element of its policy towards the Taiwanese people.

The reality is that we want normal cross-strait exchanges. However, the Taiwanese authorities are afraid of such exchanges. It is they who have stopped this kind of cross-strait interaction, including even academic exchanges.

Regarding the discussion of 2027, it is worth noting that, over the past 10 years or so, many American generals and admirals have made conflicting predictions. Has any one of them ultimately been proved correct?

I think this is entirely irresponsible. There is also disagreement at the highest levels of the US government regarding the 2027 claim about Taiwan. For example, the remarks of US Secretary of Defence Pete Hegseth on the situation in the Taiwan Strait are almost the opposite of those of his predecessor Lloyd Austin at the Shangri-La Dialogue.

I believe that China still hopes for peaceful reunification, which is why it has not established a specific timeline. Because China still has hope, it will not provide such a timeline. The absence of a timeline leaves all these people continually guessing, though.

We have not renounced scenarios in which force may have to be used. These circumstances are clearly set out in Chinese law. Nevertheless, I believe that peaceful reunification remains the objective.

Editor’s note: Beijing sees Taiwan as part of China to be reunited by force if necessary. Most countries, including the US, do not recognise Taiwan as an independent state, but Washington is opposed to any attempt to take the self-ruled island by force and is committed to supplying it with weapons.

What is your assessment of US arms sales to Taiwan after the Xi-Trump meeting in May?

I believe that the United States’ arms sales to Taiwan will be more and more difficult in the future, right from now.

If the United States continues to sell arms to Taiwan, China could take three types of action.

First, China could also choose not to honour certain commitments it has made to the United States, including commercial agreements, if it believes that the United States has violated the one-China principle. This could involve products such as Boeing, beef and soybeans. None of these products is indispensable to China.

Second, China could adopt a broader range of countermeasures.

Finally, China could conduct increasingly frequent and sophisticated military exercises around the island to wear down the other side’s nerves.

Eventually, I believe the time will come sooner than the United States expects when it will have to ask itself the ultimate question: what are the actual benefits of selling arms to Taiwan, even if those sales are lucrative, when they create more risks than benefits?

Xi and Trump agreed during their meeting in May to pursue a bilateral relationship of constructive strategic stability. How stable, or fragile, is that relationship?

This concept is significant because this is the first time that China and the United States have agreed upon such a concept. It essentially refers to a form of equilibrium of strength between the United States and China.

I would say that this is more significant for China. Many Chinese people may believe that the United States has bullied China and looked down upon China.

As to whether this stability can be sustained, I believe that the word “constructive” means a great deal. It reflects good wishes for the future, but the question is how the relationship can become constructive rather than destructive.

Given the Taiwan issue, there is no guarantee that this objective can always be maintained. The United States maintains a policy of strategic ambiguity over the Taiwan issue. It is not guaranteed that it would become directly or fully involved in a conflict.

Moreover, the China-US relationship is fundamentally a competitive relationship, although this does not rule out areas of cooperation. The question is which aspect is predominant, and the answer is competition.

There will certainly be many challenges to this form of stability. The Americans may emphasise fairness and equality while China talks about mutual respect. Basically, they are talking about the same thing. But stability most certainly rules out the potential for conflict in the South China Sea and Taiwan.

Regarding Taiwan, do you think the Trump administration – or at least Trump himself – is moving away from the United States’ long-standing policy?

First, he said American soldiers should not fight a war 9,500 miles away. Second, he said that he had not made a decision regarding arms sales to Taiwan.

I think he is inclined to make such a decision, but he may find it very difficult. He didn’t say much on the Taiwan issue in Beijing, but there could be another three opportunities for the two leaders to meet. What would he have to say on the Taiwan issue and the arms sales during those meetings, and how might Beijing react? He has to consider all these matters.

Perhaps this indicates a possible adjustment, although this is only my own speculation. Trump’s proposed arms sale would be the largest in history.

This may mean that the United States intends to sell a larger quantity of weapons on fewer occasions. In terms of frequency, it could make each package larger while reducing the number of individual sales.

If you look at the record, arms sales have become increasingly difficult. Therefore, each time the United States decides to proceed, it may sell a large volume. China would then protest only once, rather than making three separate protests against three different sales.

Militarily speaking, the strength of the Chinese mainland is simply overwhelming in comparison with that of Taiwan. Therefore, it does not really matter what Taiwan buys. Nevertheless, the Taiwanese authorities feel that they have to purchase this insurance no matter how expensive it is.

Does the US effort to rebuild its shipbuilding and defence-industrial base signal a deeper industrial competition with China? How could this affect the long-term military balance and both sides’ ability to sustain a conflict?

From a military perspective, the United States is no longer as capable as it once was of projecting power globally.

Its growing focus on the western hemisphere and the Indo-Pacific reflects the fact that it no longer has sufficient resources to maintain an equally strong presence everywhere.

The US’ shipbuilding industry lags far behind China’s. This impact on its navy is already seen. Some estimates suggest that China’s shipbuilding capacity is over 230 times larger. I understand why Washington wants to rebuild its capacity, including through cooperation with Japan and South Korea, but I doubt this can be achieved quickly.

The picture varies by sector. The United States remains dominant in areas such as AI, but the gap is said to be a matter of months; its broader industrial and manufacturing capacity has clearly weakened.

This raises two questions: has the United States declined, and can it recover?

I describe Donald Trump as “Trump the Declinist”. His promise to “make America great again” implies that America has declined. In his own words, it is “carnage” that helped him to win his first presidency because many voters clearly accepted that argument.

The United States has recovered from periods of perceived decline before, including after the Vietnam war. Some believe it will do so again.

However, I think the situation may be fundamentally different this time. Even during the Vietnam war, the United States still had the world’s strongest industrial base.

Today, that foundation has weakened, suggesting that something more fundamental may have changed.

China conducted a missile test from a nuclear-powered submarine this month and subsequently disclosed information about it. What is your assessment of the test and US reactions?

I think people are somewhat curious about Chinese launches, in part because China actually didn’t have a lot of launches in the past.

A launch of this kind clearly carries strategic implications, although different countries may interpret it differently.

From a military and technical perspective, missile testing is necessary. Even after deployment, periodic tests remain necessary to verify that the system continues to function effectively and that the relevant operational capabilities are being maintained.

However, regarding what US officials reportedly said about China providing only a few hours’ notice before the launch, falling short of the practice of other nuclear powers, I don’t think there is any international standard specifying how far in advance such notifications should be given.

I believe an institutionalised mutual notification mechanism would be desirable, but it is unlikely while the United States continues with the Golden Dome project [a proposed missile defence system integrating land-, sea- and space-based sensors and interceptors].

Golden Dome represents an arms race at the highest level and would [threaten] China-US and Russia-US strategic stability. Although such a concept is broader than military affairs, it is primarily about military stability. During the Cold War, US-Soviet strategic stability was based on an equilibrium between their nuclear arsenals.

However, in my personal view, China-US strategic stability will never be based on numerical nuclear parity. I do not believe China would seek more than 5,000 nuclear warheads to match the American nuclear stockpile.

I have always argued that China should possess enough to ensure that the United States would never consider using nuclear weapons against it first.

If China’s objective is to deter the United States from using nuclear weapons against it, how many warheads would China need?

Even according to the Pentagon’s highest estimate – that China may possess 1,500 [nuclear] warheads by 2035 – the number would still remain far below that of the United States, assuming the estimate is accurate.

My argument is that China should possess enough nuclear weapons to deter any nuclear adventurism by the United States. The required number would depend on two factors: how the US nuclear arsenal develops and how China would need to respond to those developments.

In the worst-case scenario of a conflict across the Taiwan Strait, China would not want to be subjected to nuclear blackmail.

The second concerns the broader global strategic level, where the objective is to maintain strategic stability. This was also mentioned in [China’s] 15th five-year plan. We should preserve global nuclear stability. However, the question is how such stability could be maintained if China possessed only a few hundred nuclear weapons.

People should not be excessively concerned about China’s nuclear weapons because China’s no-first-use policy is one of its longest-standing defence policies.

How will AI capabilities affect the long-term military balance between China and the United States?

American dominance in AI is not a sure thing.

Even where one side may possess an advantage in certain areas, China may be stronger in the large-scale application of AI. This therefore makes the overall situation more complicated.

I think both countries are working very hard on the military application of AI.

The character of warfare has already changed, and military forces must become adaptable. If you observed the military parade last year, you would have seen that the PLA has not merely been watching these developments. It has already taken steps to respond to the emerging challenges.

A challenge is that we are not fully aware of how rapidly artificial intelligence can develop or in which particular fields it will advance most quickly.

During wartime, not only people but also artificial intelligence may learn and develop at the fastest pace. We have seen how rapidly AI has changed the battlefield in Ukraine and in the American war against Iran. This shows us how quickly the entire battlefield is being transformed.

I definitely believe that rules limiting AI’s role, such as in military decision-making, should be established. But sadly, as we saw in many cases, sometimes rules are only made after an incident. During the Cold War, there were quite a few false alarms of nuclear attack. Hopefully we shall never have false alarms triggered by AI.

The US military has continued to strengthen its posture along the first island chain. At the same time, the PLA has increasingly conducted operations beyond the chain. In your view, does the first island chain still carry the same strategic significance that it did during the Cold War?

Regarding the first island chain, I do not believe that it matters as much to the PLA as it once did, because the PLA is much stronger today and the overall US military presence at bases in these countries is not particularly large.

Second, I have serious doubts about whether these US allies could provide effective assistance to the United States in an actual conflict. I think all these countries would seek to hedge against such a possibility.

Japan might be an exception, in the sense that it is legally obliged to provide military bases to the United States. However, whether Japan would go further and fight shoulder to shoulder with the United States is not guaranteed, unless it believed that it faced an existential threat.

That is why, when [Japanese Prime Minister Sanae] Takaichi described such a scenario as an existential threat, she was strongly criticised within Japan itself. There is therefore no guarantee that what she described would actually happen in such a scenario.

There has been stronger military cooperation between Japan and the Philippines recently. How does this development challenge China’s strategic interests?

For military planners, any change in the surrounding security environment is naturally a concern because it adds new factors to their calculations. These are trends that China must watch, but I do not see them as game changers.

In the South China Sea, Japan’s role remains largely symbolic. Despite its assistance to the Philippines, there has not been a Japanese naval presence. I would describe it mainly as a political gesture with limited military implications.

In the Taiwan Strait, we should first remember that even US involvement is not guaranteed. The stronger China becomes, the more reluctant other countries will be to intervene. Japan’s role would therefore be secondary, apart from providing bases under its legal obligations.

Japan would have concerns even about providing bases because it would have to consider its own security. Japan could not simply say, “We are only providing bases and are not involved.”

If US aircraft took off from Japanese bases to take part in combat in the Taiwan Strait, China would regard Japan as involved. Japanese leaders would probably make such a decision only at the last moment.

I believe the Philippines is also aware of the risks. It wants to make use of the United States, but not to the extent that it becomes a target itself. That is why it has imposed conditions on US access to its bases, including limitations on their use for attacks during wartime.

Against the backdrop of strained China-Japan relations, could military encounters between the two increase the risks of a military incident?

Chinese and Japanese naval vessels seldom encounter one another. So, the risk is low. But Chinese and American naval vessels often encounter one another. China, the US and Japan are all members of the Code for Unplanned Encounters at Sea, or Cues, and they also have an air and maritime communication mechanism. These arrangements provide technical rules intended to prevent accidents, although they are not legally binding.

All these rules are technical rules, but politics always exists behind them.

There has therefore long been a tension between safety and security. Technical rules address safety, but security involves broader implications, on which the two sides may never agree.

Returning to this particular case, it would of course be safer if the Chinese and American navies could deconflict at sea. However, even if they maintain a so-called safe distance, the question remains: what constitutes a safe distance?

Unfortunately, there is no regulation or agreement that precisely defines a safe distance.

Safe conduct therefore ultimately relies on three abstract concepts: good airmanship, good seamanship and voluntary judgment – and that judgment is inevitably influenced by politics.

The rules were made because both sides have the bottom line, that is, none of us wants an accident. So, this is contradictory.

item.title: [SCMP] Will new batteries give China’s EVs the jolt they need to charge past their rivals?
item.description:
On a cloudy evening in late April, a tech event hosted at Beijing’s National Convention Centre by Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL) drew nearly 1,000 people eager for a glimpse of next-generation electric vehicle (EV) batteries that could reshape the global automotive landscape.

Gao Huan, chief technology officer for the auto business at CATL, the world’s largest producer of EV batteries, exuded confidence while promoting the new Shenxing product series.

According to the company, its new, third-generation battery can charge from 10 to 98 per cent in under six and a half minutes. BYD’s second-generation Blade battery, by contrast, takes nine minutes to charge from 10 to 97 per cent.
item.content:encoded:
On a cloudy evening in late April, a tech event hosted at Beijing’s National Convention Centre by Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL) drew nearly 1,000 people eager for a glimpse of next-generation electric vehicle (EV) batteries that could reshape the global automotive landscape.

Gao Huan, chief technology officer for the auto business at CATL, the world’s largest producer of EV batteries, exuded confidence while promoting the new Shenxing product series.

According to the company, its new, third-generation battery can charge from 10 to 98 per cent in under six and a half minutes. BYD’s second-generation Blade battery, by contrast, takes nine minutes to charge from 10 to 97 per cent.

With formations of electric current and heating effects projected on a giant screen, Gao sought to reassure his audience about how CATL designs and arranges cells to keep its battery packs safe and efficient.

Though more convenient, fast charging generates heat that can accelerate degradation in lithium-ion batteries, shortening their lifespan.

Gao explained how CATL’s technology isolated individual cells to prevent heat from spreading, saying the Shenxing series used independent sealed exhaust channels, allowing heat and electricity to exit the battery pack through separate paths.

“To accomplish product reliability, we have developed industry-leading testing methods and created a world-leading testing and verification centre,” Gao said. “In manufacturing, we make sure every single battery cell is made under extreme conditions in line with a stringent quality control system, with 7,000 quality checkpoints deployed along [each] product line.”

The battery pack, which accounts for about one-fourth of an electric car’s cost according to industry averages, is among the most important components of an EV and plays a decisive role in the global automotive industry’s shift to electrification, as technological advances are key to easing concerns over production costs, range and vehicle safety.

Higher-performance and lower-priced batteries will further drive electrification of the global automotive industry

Davis Zhang, Suzhou Hazardtex

CATL’s views on the sector carry particular weight.

The company, based in Ningde, in southeastern China’s Fujian province, led the global EV battery market with a 40.2 per cent share in the first five months of 2026, according to South Korea-based SNE Research.

Total global EV battery usage climbed 16.3 per cent from a year earlier to 469.2 gigawatt-hours (GWh), per SNE data. One GWh is enough to power about 20,000 EVs with a range of 500km (311 miles).

The Shenxing batteries’ greatly shortened charging time “materially alleviates consumer range and charging anxiety”, Morgan Stanley said in a research note a week after the CATL tech event. “On the flipside, debates about the safety and durability of ultra-fast charging continue.”

Over the past decade, improvements in manufacturing and rising sales volumes have helped drive down EV battery production costs, bringing some electric cars closer to cost parity with their petrol-powered counterparts.

Attention is now turning to technologies such as solid-state batteries, sodium-ion batteries, faster charging systems, and battery pack designs that enhance thermal management, as more car owners switch from petrol vehicles to electric cars.

In mainland China, the world’s largest automotive and EV market, pure electric and plug-in hybrid cars accounted for 57.4 per cent of the country’s new vehicle deliveries in the first half of 2026, according to the China Passenger Car Association.

The cost of EV batteries was as high as US$1,474 per kilowatt-hour (kWh) in 2010. By 2025, global lithium-ion battery pack prices had fallen to about US$108 per kWh, according to BloombergNEF’s annual price survey.

A price of US$100 per kWh is seen by industry officials and analysts as a threshold for making unsubsidised EVs cost-competitive with their oil-guzzling peers.

China’s manufacturing heft has given its battery makers a cost advantage, with average prices in the country falling 13 per cent year on year to US$84 per kWh in 2025, BloombergNEF added, forecasting an average global battery pack price of US$62 by 2030.

Chinese EV battery makers also continued to dominate the global market as seven companies – including CATL, BYD and Gotion High-Tech – were among the world’s top 10 players, according to SNE Research.

Between January and May, the Chinese companies commanded a 72.6 per cent share of the global EV battery market, SNE data showed.

“Higher-performance and lower-priced batteries will further drive electrification of the global automotive industry,” said Davis Zhang, a senior executive at Suzhou Hazardtex, a supplier of specialised batteries. “Apparently, potential technological breakthroughs in solid-state battery could become a game-changer.”

Compared with existing liquid-based batteries, solid-state variants promise higher energy storage, longer driving ranges and improved safety, with a lower risk of overheating or fire. Beijing has been backing efforts to commercialise all-solid-state batteries, which, unlike conventional lithium-ion batteries, do not rely on flammable liquid electrolytes.

In late June, the Ministry of Industry and Information Technology said China would intensify its research and development into key next-generation battery materials, including solid-state electrolytes, to support the growth of its EV sector.

Several companies have already begun those efforts. Chinese battery maker WeLion’s semi-solid-state batteries, for example, power some of the premium EVs assembled by Shanghai-based Nio.

And in March, the state-owned Chery Automobile, based in central China’s Anhui province, unveiled an all-solid-state battery capable of powering a vehicle for more than 1,500km of driving distance on a single charge.

Chinese battery makers and their supply chain vendors are also striving to extend the lifespan of lithium-ion batteries.

Ganfeng Lithium, the world’s largest producer of lithium metal, aimed to raise the lifetime capacity of its energy-storage battery to 18,000 charges by the end of the year, which would allow it to last as long as solar panels, the company’s president, Wang Xiaoshen, told the South China Morning Post in May.

Gotion High-Tech, the world’s fifth-largest EV battery maker by delivery volume, also launched a new product in May that it said could be fully recharged over 15,000 times.

A solar panel is typically estimated to be able to work 25 years or more, while lithium-ion batteries could last up to 10 years, according to analysts.

In China, there is no industry that is not competitive. That’s why China’s products could evolve so rapidly

Wang Xiaoshen, Ganfeng Lithium

Both Ganfeng and Gotion said they had managed to produce batteries with a capacity of more than 580 ampere-hours (Ah) and were planning to boost it to over 600 Ah.

An Ah is a unit of measurement to reflect the electrical charge a battery can hold and deliver over time.

Such advancements in battery technologies, as well as the reduction of costs, partly resulted from the fierce competition within the sector in China, according to Ganfeng’s Wang.

“In China, there is no industry that is not competitive,” Wang said. “That’s why China’s products could evolve so rapidly.”

Even if battery firms from other countries were able to claim achievements in cutting-edge technologies, China’s prowess in manufacturing and supply chains would support the country in retaining its competitive advantage when it came to mass production, said Yang Jing, director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings.

Chinese battery makers are also moving downstream to enhance profitability and deepen their ties with EV assemblers in fine-tuning thermal designs and battery management.

“If competition boils down to cell chemistry, production scale and price per kWh, margins will inevitably compress,” Gavekal Technologies analyst AJ Cortese wrote in a research report released in May. “But if a supplier’s cell format, pack architecture, thermal design or battery-management logic becomes embedded in a carmaker’s platform, the battery supplier gains more durable leverage.”
